en: The Avadāna of Encouraging Diligence and Energy.
Oṃ, homage to all the glorious Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
He who is glorious, Śrīghana, taught the true Dharma in the world.
May his teachings forever triumph throughout the three worlds.
Then King Aśoka, filled with joy and with palms joined in reverence,
bowed to the ascetic Upagupta and spoke once more as follows:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken teaching; it behoves you to instruct me just as it was taught by your teacher."
Having heard this prayer made by the king, that wise Arhat ascetic Upagupta looked upon the lord of men and spoke thus:
"Listen well, O Great King, to that which was spoken by my teacher; I shall relate it to you exactly as it was told, and having heard it, may you rejoice."
In former times, that Blessed One was the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas, a treasury of compassion, the King of Dharma, the Teacher of the World, the Omniscient One, the Sugata, and the Victor.

The Lord of Sages, who has mastered all branches of knowledge and the arts, possesses the six supernormal knowledges; he is the conqueror of Māra, the knower of the world, the Protector, the Guide, and the Tathāgata.
In Śrāvastī, in the delightful and great Jetavana grove belonging to the high-souled householder known as Anāthapiṇḍada.
It was filled with various trees, adorned with diverse flowers,
bent down by the weight of manifold fruits, and resembling the wish-fulfilling kalpa-trees.
It was resorted to by lotus ponds filled with water endowed with the eight qualities and completely covered with flowers such as lotuses and water-lilies.
It was also frequented by various throngs of living beings bound together by mutual affection,
as well as by flocks of diverse birds with their clamorous songs.
In that divine and enchanting park, beautifully adorned,
a field of merit and an abode of the Jinas, was a monastery decorated with jewels.
Together with the disciples, the monks, and also the hosts of bodhisattvas,
he remained in order to proclaim the Dharma for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Seeing the Perfectly Awakened One, the teacher of Dharma, seated there in this manner, all the worlds gathered together to hear the supreme Dharma.
The gods, the Daityas, the Siddhas, the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras;
the planets, the Vidyādharas, the Nāgas, and even the Garuḍas.
All the world-protectors as well as sages and great seers, brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, ministers, and common people [were present].
Virtuous ministers, Śūdras, caravan leaders, great merchants,
wealthy men, traders, householders, and even the citizens [were there].
Likewise, the people of the countryside, the villagers, and even the pilgrims—
indeed, other beings as well— were seekers of the hearing of the true Dharma.
Taking the five offerings for worship and filled with devotion,
they arrived together, having rejoiced in hearing the true Dharma of the Sugata.
Having all entered there and seen that Sugata, the Jina, they were filled with wonder and joy; having performed worship and bowed down in due order, they remained.
All who were seated there, surrounded and honored, beheld that true guru and stood with concentrated minds to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that all the worlds were composed in concentration,
taught the supreme Dharma, which is virtuous in its beginning, middle, and end.
Thus that Protector, ever seeking the welfare of all sentient beings,
remained in the world illuminating the Dharma like the risen sun.
And at that time, in Śrāvastī, there was a great multitude of people;
[there lived] a wealthy merchant of great fortune and extensive possessions.
Faithful, of noble disposition, and wise, he was dear to all his kinsmen and friends;
yet he was a sectarian disciple, conceited and arrogant because of his wealth.
Then, having taken his beautiful wife who was worthy of his noble lineage, he,
attached to the qualities of sensual pleasure, constantly took delight with her.
Although he enjoyed himself with that wife for a very long time,
neither a son nor a daughter was born to him in any way whatsoever.
Then that sonless householder, longing for the sight of a son, went into solitude and, resting his cheek upon his hand, reflected thus:
"Alas! By fate, I have neither a son nor a daughter even to this day;
therefore, these riches of mine would be in vain, for there exists no one to enjoy them."
"What use have I for these riches and jewels, which are nothing but instruments of suffering, since there is no one to enjoy them? Indeed, I have acquired them in vain."
For one without a son, the world is empty and my existence in saṃsāra is devoid of happiness;
since my dharma does not increase, even that birth is fruitless.
What means shall I employ, since fortune does not exist? For destiny is powerful in this world; what can be done with means, virtues, or strengths?
Where shall I go for refuge here, for I am childless and the ender of my lineage?
Who here would be a true friend to me—one who might rescue me from this calamity?
Surely all my ancestors, seeing that the offering of funeral cakes will be interrupted,
will become hopeless, thinking that after me it will be difficult to obtain [the offerings].
"In every way I am ruined, a destroyer of my family's dharma;
what shall I enjoy in the next world, and who will offer me the funeral oblation?"
Seeing him thus dejected with anxiety, all his kinsmen approached him, greeted him, and asked the cause of his sorrow.
"O virtuous one, why are you so distressed here? And why do you dwell in such sorrowful thought?
If it may be told, you ought to tell us everything in every way."
When he had been asked thus, that householder, letting out a long sigh and looking at all those kinsmen, declared the cause of his sorrow.
"Sirs, let all of you hear the cause of my sorrow:
that even now neither a son nor a daughter exists for me."
"In my home there are riches endowed with every kind of jewel, and abundant in all manner of wealth; yet there is no one to enjoy them."
All that which has been acquired by me through great efforts will perish in vain;
for the king will surely seize the entire estate of one who is childless.
"I am indeed childless and of little merit; death is certain for me.
Once I have become a preta, who else will offer the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa)?"
I have not performed any merit while intent upon the pursuit of wealth;
all that [effort] of mine would thus be in vain—whom can I rely on to deliver me from evil?
Even having enjoyed these pleasures here, what essence remains for me?
For one who is solely attached to wealth, how can there be a good rebirth in the next world?
Thus this thought, dwelling within my heart, torments my mind incessantly;
overcome by such mental anguish, I am as if pierced by a thorn.
Therefore, you must grant me the means to remove that suffering for my own welfare;
otherwise, I shall be ruined and left hopeless both in this world and the next.
Having heard what he had said, all those kinsmen and people,
their hearts overcome with compassion, spoke to him as they sought to awaken his understanding.
"Do not fear, O illustrious one! Abandon your anxiety and listen to my words.
We shall tell you the means for that; perform it with a concentrated mind."
Having performed the propitiation of the deities, make a request for a lineage;
the deities, being thus gratified, will surely grant you a lineage.
(Rm 5) There is a common saying in the world that sons or daughters are born as a result of prayers, through the grace of the gods.
Likewise, there would be no authority in the scriptures regarding the measure of one's actions;
however, through the grace of the gods, one's action is swiftly brought to fulfillment.
That very same action, when opposed by fate, is struck down by obstacles;
therefore, for the sake of securing success through destiny, one should be composed with faith and devotion.
"Having performed the propitiation of the deities, one should accomplish all undertakings.
Thinking thus, you too [should act] for the sake of obtaining a virtuous son.
Together with your wife, perform a prayer to the deity with devotion;
thereafter, when your beloved wife has bathed after her menses, unite with her according to your desire.
Embracing me firmly with passion, plant the seed of the Dharma;
then, through the power of the gods, it will be perfectly realized and established.
"May a son be born from you; let this very truth be your authority.
Having heard these words of theirs, that householder was consoled.
Having promised "So be it," he rejoiced together with his wife [and honored] Śiva,
Brahmā, and the other lords of the gods, as well as Indra and the other sovereigns of the directions.
He saw reservoirs, forests, groves, courtyards, pavilions, and dwellings;
all the planets beginning with the Sun, and the Mothers beginning with Bhairavī.
Having thus propitiated and worshipped according to the prescribed ritual all the gods who are lords of their own families, as well as others residing within the three worlds;
Having prayed for offspring, he thus took delight with his wife;
at that time, a certain great being, having descended from heaven, came to the earth.
He entered the womb of that householder’s wife; thereupon the merchant’s wife quickly became pregnant and heavy with child.
Perceiving that a being had been conceived in her womb, she said to her husband:
"Lord, be gracious; do not be despondent over this matter, but be at ease."
"Indeed, by your good fortune, a being is surely developing within my womb;
for it remains and turns about on the right side of the womb."
"Surely this must be a boy; it is the truth, there is no doubt.
Having heard these words of his wife, that householder was filled with joy.
Having observed the pregnancy of his wife, he concluded that it was indeed true.
Then, having suddenly summoned his kinsmen, friends, and companions,
he joyfully addressed them in their presence as follows:
"Aha! By my good fortune, that which I desired has come to pass;
I am blessed, for by the grace of the deities, I shall not be disgraced."
"Now may I behold the face of my son, long desired;
may he perform his duties for me, and being supported by me, may he in turn support me."
May he obtain his inheritance, may my lineage endure,
may my friends be joyful, and may my enemies be filled with despair.
By whatever gifts and merits have been performed by me,
through the fruit of this merit, may there be constant auspiciousness for both of us.
By the power of this merit, may my mother be free from affliction;
may she give birth to a virtuous son in happiness, and may no evil befall her.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, all his kinsmen, well-wishers, and friends,
saying "So be it," gave their approval and returned to their respective abodes.
Then that beloved woman, pregnant and with her womb gradually increasing in size,
ate food prescribed by physicians and conducted herself as was comfortable for her.
Then, in due time, she gave birth to a lovely and captivating son,
endowed with all auspicious marks, a portion of Bhadra, and possessed of every blessing.
Upon hearing that, the householder was exceedingly pleased and delighted;
seeing that gentle boy, he could not reach satiety.
Then, having summoned his kinsmen and joyfully performed the birth festival,
he spoke again to them in order to bestow a name upon his son.
"Sirs, behold! My long-cherished desire has been accomplished.
Therefore, let a beautiful and appropriate name be bestowed upon him."
Having heard these words of his, all those kinsmen,
filled with joy upon beholding the boy, spoke thus in their delight.
On the very day he was born, all the citizens were filled with joy;
therefore, he became known by the name Nanda.
Then that boy Nanda was properly entrusted by his father to eight nurses, having been fully satisfied with their care for his body.
Then, through the care of those nurses, he grew day by day in due course, like a lotus in a pond.
When he had thus grown to the age of six years,
he became indolent and ceased from all festivities.
Always remaining on his bed or seat, he did not wish to rise;
and while staying on his bed or seat, he never went anywhere after eating.
Although he always remained within his own home, that wise and highly intelligent man,
having studied all the scriptures, became devoted to truth and righteousness.
Then the merchant father, seeing his son thus indolent,
and seeing that he was the repository of all branches of knowledge and virtues, reflected as follows:
This son, whom I somehow obtained through the grace of the deities,
has nonetheless become so indolent due to my own misfortune.
"Though he is the repository of all branches of knowledge and qualities, and proficient in all treatises,
what is the use of this son of mine, who stands like a sick man in a miserable state? For even though his body is healthy, he remains like a beast after having eaten."
What shall I do here, since this son is devoid of effort?
What use is there for such a creature who brings ruin upon the dharma of his lineage?
"Fie on my fate and on all my efforts; they shall all be in vain.
What remedy can I employ? I am utterly shattered in every way."
Thus overcome with such thoughts, that householder reflected:
"Pūraṇa is my teacher; I shall ask him for the means [to achieve this]."
Thinking thus, that householder approached that hermitage; having bowed to Pūraṇa as his teacher, he asked him for the means [to attain liberation].
"O Blessed One, O Lord of Great Supernatural Knowledge, you are my teacher; be gracious toward me.
You ought to grant the instruction regarding that matter which I have asked about."
Having heard this request from him, the heretic, arrogant with pride, said:
"We shall quickly accomplish whatever task you have here; tell us what it is."
Having spoken thus and comforted him, Pūraṇa, who was exceedingly arrogant,
spoke to that householder and enlightened him in every respect as follows.
Having heard what was thus commanded by him, the householder, with joy and palms joined in reverence, bowed to that teacher and spoke.
"O Blessed One, you should know that the son born to me has now grown up,
yet he remains devoid of energy and indolent."
Always remaining on his bed, he eats; having eaten, he sleeps without exertion.
He does not venture anywhere; like a beast, he stays at home.
Having risen from his bed, he has no desire to hear or see;
remaining fixed upon his couch and seat in the house, he dwells forever like a sick man.
"How might I employ a means by which he, having risen from his bed,
may be able to hear, see, go forth, and perform his duties according to his inclination?"
"Thus, O Blessed One, establish my son in the family dharma;
for you alone are my teacher, and it behooves you to act for his welfare."
Having heard this request made by him,
that ascetic Pūraṇa spoke in order to gladden the heart of the householder.
Do not fall into despair; why do you torment yourself with anxiety while we six wise teachers are present?
Therefore, O illustrious one, I shall go with all the heretics by means of my supernatural power and cause the boy to rise up from his fainting fit.
When that boy, having seen all of us,
rose up and paid homage to us, he would be eager to hear the Dharma.
Having heard [the Dharma], one should practice wholesome deeds out of zeal for the Dharma;
endowed with those wholesome deeds, that wise person shall become truly energetic.
Then, being fully prepared, he shall accomplish all his tasks;
virtuous, he will proceed with the duties and practices of his own family tradition.
Having seen that these words of mine are true, accept them correctly;
casting aside despondency, act accordingly.
Having heard what was thus commanded by him, that householder went quickly to his own home with joy and prepared that food.
Then Pūraṇa, having arrived together with other non-Buddhist teachers,
went to the house and sat down upon a couch in front of him.
Then, having approached them as they sat in order upon their seats,
the merchant, filled with joy, suddenly spoke to his son:
"Son, look! The Teachers have arrived at our home.
Therefore, rise up, bow down to these Teachers, and offer them food."
Having been addressed thus by Janaka, the boy did not rise;
he did not even venture to look at him, so how could he have bowed down or offered him hospitality?
Although he was urged many times by his father along with his kinsmen,
the boy did not even wish to look at them as they sat there.
How much less would he, having risen and bowed, offer him food?
Thus he remained, devoid of celebration, even while seated upon his bed or throne.
Then all those heretics, seeing him thus devoid of festivities,
began to try to rouse him by means of various ritual efforts.
Nevertheless, that boy did not rise from his bed at all,
nor did he even wish to see those preachers of his own Dharma.
Seeing him thus remaining unarisen, all those heretics exerted themselves to forcibly raise him up and bring him under their control.
Seeing all those heretics approaching him face-to-face, their voices raised with pride, that boy was terrified and cried out.
Seeing him thus weeping, they all, with their faces cast down out of shame and fear, returned to their respective dwellings, feeling humiliated.
Then the householder, seeing them all thus departed, stood with a broken and despondent soul, bewildered by anxiety.
Then the Blessed One, the Buddha, the all-seeing guide,
seeing [the world], beheld that indolent man in order to deliver sentient beings.
Having observed the succession of that lazy man's modes of livelihood,
[the Buddha] spoke to Āryānanda in order to rescue him from that indolence.
Behold, Ānanda, the son of a householder residing in the city of Śrāvastī, known as Nanda, who is now [living] at Saṃkuśī.
Surely, from the mere sight of me, he will immediately exert his vigor;
rising up at once and bowing, he shall joyfully listen to the Dharma.
Then that wise one shall always practice the Dharma within my teaching;
having gradually fulfilled the conduct of awakening, he shall also attain perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, having gone to his house, in order to shatter the pride of the heretics,
I shall establish them all in the True Dharma and enjoin them to enlightenment.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, Ānanda was filled with joy;
he expressed his approval, saying, "O Blessed One, it shall be done thus."
Then the Blessed One emitted golden rays of light;
having illumined that house with them, he purified it.
When the boy was touched by those rays of the Buddha’s loving-kindness,
he was gladdened and reflected in this way:
"Aha! Whose power is this, by which the world is thus illuminated?
My body is soothed; I do not know from where or how this has come to be."
Having thus adopted this reflection, his mind overcome with curiosity,
he stood in the house looking all around, utterly amazed.
Seeing him thus amazed, the Blessed One, together with the monks,
suddenly went to that house and appeared, illuminating it.
There, that boy saw the Blessed One seated there,
lovely, with a divine radiance exceeding all else, possessing the form of Samantabhadra.
Upon seeing him, he rose up immediately, bowed at his feet with great joy,
personally prepared a seat for him, and spoke as follows:
Welcome, Blessed One, O Protector; be victorious, O Lord of Sages!
Be gracious for the sake of bestowing favor, and sit here upon this auspicious seat.
When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One, together with the monks,
sat upon the seat prepared there and began to teach the Dharma.
Seeing such an outburst of religious zeal arise in the boy,
his parents, kinsmen, and all others were utterly amazed.
There, that boy, his eyes wide with joy and filled with delight,
bowed at the feet of the Sage and drew near to listen to the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the purity of his disposition,
spoke to him in order to teach the Dharma that is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end.
Listen, O noble child; I shall explain to you for the sake of your welfare the cause for accomplishing both sin and merit. Therefore, act accordingly in this matter.
Having obtained this human birth, which is difficult to find and as flickering as a wave of lightning,
one should direct the mind toward the destruction of evil and toward the accomplishment of the goals of merit.
Through evil one goes to a miserable rebirth; through merit one proceeds to a happy state.
By attachment to evil friends, the mind turns toward evil.
Then, devoted to evil, he would commit even dreadful sins;
thereafter, corrupted and most wicked, he would revile the true teachings.
Then, because it is contrary to the Dharma, his power becomes contemptible;
consequently, that contemptible soul is indeed reviled by all sentient beings.
Overcome by despondency, the fool becomes devoid of energy;
when the mind is bereft of enthusiasm, it resorts to indolence.
One who is indolent will accomplish neither any Dharma nor any virtues;
what can one whose soul is detached from both Dharma and action, and who is devoid of virtue, achieve?

A man who is always attached solely to objects of enjoyment is lower even than a beast; what is the use of that man, though he may possess human form, if he is devoid of virtue and eats only for pleasure,
and whose mind never exerts itself toward merit or excellence?
One whose self is ruined by the failure of merit and zeal is struck down by wicked afflictions;
tormented by the hosts of Māra, one is brought under their control and bound.
Under the sway of Māra, he falls into servitude to women;
devoted to that slavery, he dwells in his home like a beast, subsisting on what he has consumed.
One would never have the inclination to hear or even to see the Dharma anywhere;
indeed, without the Dharma, one shall never attain a happy rebirth.
Therefore, increasing one's enthusiasm for merit in order to practice the Dharma,
one should give gifts with the purity of the three spheres for the attainment of virtue.
Through generosity, one accomplishes merit; from merit, the mind becomes purified.
One whose mind is purified should practice ethical discipline; for one who possesses ethical discipline becomes truly wise.
The wise man should cultivate patience; being patient, he is a conqueror of the wicked and is successful.
Being virtuous, he should initiate vigor; being vigorous, he is the best of men.

The Great Being shall attain meditative concentration; as a meditator dwelling in the sublime abodes, being fully mindful, he shall accomplish wisdom, for the wise man is indeed the repository of all virtues.
Recognizing their virtues, one should employ appropriate means to establish sentient beings in the Dharma;
by the power of this merit, one should make a vow for enlightenment.
One should accomplish the ten powers by means of the mind of aspiration for enlightenment;
and by those powers, one shall defeat the most terrible hosts of Māra.
Having conquered all the hosts of Māra, he shall attain the wisdom of perfect enlightenment;
thereafter, he shall set in motion the wheel of Dharma throughout all worlds.
Thus setting forth the Dharma, the Teacher would become the sovereign of the world,
performing the welfare of all the world through the abundance of his great merits.

Always remaining thus in the state of the virtuous, one shall attain the station of a perfectly awakened Buddha; having understood this, my child, you must conduct yourself accordingly in what is auspicious.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Jinas, that boy, with joy,
bowed again with palms joined in reverence and addressed the Blessed One:
"From this day forward, O Teacher, I shall always go for refuge to you;
just as you have commanded, so shall I practice the truth."
Establishing a gaze of compassion, always hold me in your mindfulness;
for you alone are the omniscient one, the guide of the three realms.
Since you have no compassion for me, who am thus devoid of effort,
who else, having approached me in such a state, would lift me up from this laziness?
"By your grace, I consider myself purified;
I am blessed that this most auspicious scripture has been thus revealed."
When he had spoken thus, the omniscient Lord of Sages once again gave him a staff made of fine sandalwood and addressed him.
"Child, taking hold of this staff, strike with a concentrated mind;
then you will surely obtain a great festival of merit."
Having bowed to that [instruction] bestowed by the Teacher, the boy accepted it;
he proceeded to act exactly as commanded by the Lord of Munis.
Having thus instructed him, that Perfectly Awakened One, together with his Saṅgha,
retired to his own monastery and dwelt there teaching the Dharma.
Then that boy, out of joy, took up the staff himself and,
with a concentrated mind, struck it exactly as instructed by the Lord of Sages.
As it was being struck, a sound of merit resounded;
and many treasures of jewels appeared within the house.
Upon hearing that sound, the boy was filled with joy;
seeing the treasures of jewels within his house, he was struck with wonder.
Then, filled with wonder and joy, he thought once more: "Ah! This is truly great valor; therefore, I shall undertake this heroic deed."
Likewise, having gone to Ratnākara and acquired jewels,
he should constantly serve and honor the Sugata together with his Saṅgha.
Having reflected thus and mustered his resolve, that young man set out with merchants to go to Ratnākara.
Then that heroic youth, having made himself the caravan leader throughout that city, caused a proclamation to be made on all sides.
Thus, having heard that proclamation, those merchant-warriors,
with great enthusiasm, desired to go to the great ocean together with him.
Then that heroic man, together with all those merchants,
went to Ratnākara and procured many jewels.
Then the caravan leader, having safely crossed the great ocean together with all his caravans, arrived at his own country.
Then the caravan leader, delighted by the success of his journey there,
addressed all the members of the caravan and, having seen this, spoke as follows:
"Sirs, listen to all of you: that we have arrived safely, know that to be the power of the Lord of Jinas, through his grace."
"Therefore, having respectfully beheld this Lord of Sages,
and having worshipped and prostrated before him, we shall indeed return home afterwards.
Having heard these words of his, all those merchants—
Rejoicing at having seen the Truth, they assented, saying, "So be it.
Having thus conversed,
the caravan leader, accompanied by his entire company, then quickly approached the monastery.
Having seen the Lord of Jinas there, they were all filled with great joy;
bowing at the feet of that Sage, they stood surrounding him.
Then the Blessed One, having seen all the traveling caravans as well,
addressed them and spoke for the sake of increasing their enthusiasm for the Dharma.
"You have arrived; you have come together. Are you not weary or exhausted?
Has the success of your journey been achieved, and are all your affairs well?"
Thus questioned by the Lord of Jinas, they were all filled with joy;
bowing with palms joined in reverence, they spoke with devotion to the Perfectly Awakened One.
O Blessed One, through the grace of such a compassionate gaze of yours,
how could our journey not be successful? Indeed, may all be auspicious for us everywhere.
"O Teacher, that we have arrived here endowed with these auspicious jewels—all this is due to your power; this is truly established as the measure of truth."
Therefore, we have all come together to see you, our excellent teacher;
we desire to honor you, so be gracious, O Teacher of the World!
Having made this request, that caravan leader, together with his merchants,
honored the Saṅgha and presented them with jewels.
Homage to you, O Blessed One, our Protector; we go to you for refuge.
Protect us at all times, for you alone are the Lord of the World.
Having thus praised that Lord of Sages, they were all thoroughly gladdened;
with palms joined in reverence and having bowed down, they desired to go to their own homes.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they were all eager for their own homes,
gave them words of blessing, touched them, and dismissed them with the command, "Go!"
Then all those merchants, having performed three circumambulations and bowed to the Teacher, the Sugata, returned each to his own home.
Then, being further entreated by others as well, that heroic one went once more to the ocean,
the mine of jewels, and procured many precious gems.
Then the householder, the merchant-leader, endowed with great vigor,
having brought the Sugata along with his Saṅgha to his home, began to honor him.
Then, having prepared the provisions for the meal in his residence,
he invited the Buddha together with the Saṅgha and seated them upon auspicious seats.
Then, having worshipped them according to the prescribed rites with offerings for worship,
he gave each of them a robe and satisfied them with food.
Then, at the conclusion of the meal, that caravan leader, with palms joined in reverence, bowed to the Sugata together with his Saṅgha and made this aspiration: Rm_1.195{85} //
Whatever gift has been offered by me within the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One—
by the fruit of this merit, may I become a Perfectly Awakened One, just like this Victor.
Having thus understood that the mind of that householder desired awakening, the Blessed One, the Buddha, smiled and expressed his approval.
Then, five-colored rays of light issued forth from the Blessed One's mouth,
illuminating the three worlds on all sides with their splendor.
Whatever rays have gone downward even into the hells,
they have issued forth as far as Saṃjīva and Kālasūtraka.
Saṃghāta and Raurava, as well as the renowned Mahāraurava;
likewise that called Tapana and thereafter the one named Pratāpana.
Avīci, Arbuda, Nirarbuda, as well as Aṭaṭa,
Hahava, Huhuva, and then Utpala and Padmaka.
These sixteen abodes are indeed known as Mahāpadma;
all those who are in the hot hells have emerged from them.
Having emerged, cooled, and illuminating everywhere,
they illuminated even those cold hells, making them warm.
Among them, those beings who were in the hells, experiencing various sufferings,
felt great bliss when touched by those rays of light.
Then all those beings, endowed with great happiness and filled with wonder, gathered together there and spoke thus to one another:
"Oh, sirs, what a marvel! What indeed could have happened to us,
that we who were always thus oppressed by various sufferings are now all liberated and endowed with happiness?"
"Are we then truly liberated, or have we merely wandered elsewhere?"—
to awaken the minds of all those whose hearts were thus filled with wonder.
The Blessed One manifested a magical creation before them.
There, having seen that emanation, they were all utterly amazed;
looking at one another's faces, they spoke thus:
"O venerable sirs, we have not departed from here to go elsewhere;
rather, this one who has appeared in the form of a Sugata has arrived, never seen before."
"Surely it is through his power that we are thus endowed with happiness."
Having spoken thus, they all, having developed serene confidence toward that manifestation created by the Sugata, bowed down, saying, "Homage to the Buddha!"
Then, having seen that emanation and bowing down with their minds purified,
they were all liberated from every evil and went to a happy rebirth.
And those who went upward, O King, went to the realm of the Four Great Kings;
from there, they went to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, to the Yāma heaven, and to the Tuṣita heaven.
Having illuminated the Nirmāṇarati heaven and the Paranirmitavaśavartin deities,
she went to the worlds of the Brahmakāyika gods and the Brahmapurohita gods.
They went to the abode of Mahābrahmā and likewise to the Parītābha realms;
from there they went to the Apramāṇābha worlds and then to the Ābhāsvara realms.
Then they went to the worlds of Limited Purity, the Immeasurable Purity,
the All-Pervading Purity, the Cloudless, and the Born of Merit.
Then they went likewise to the Bṛhatphala [heaven], and from there to the Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, and finally to the Sudarśana [heavens].
Having thus gone to Akaniṣṭha, they illuminated all these worlds;
and all the beings residing therein were [illuminated] by those rays of light.
Touched by it and having attained happiness, they saw her and spoke thus: "Aha!
How wonderful! Whose meritorious power is this, so auspicious and desirable?"
"By which [rays], when we are touched by them, we obtain great happiness"— thus,
for those whose minds were filled with wonder, he provided a diversion for their thoughts.
Then those rays of light exhorted her with these verses:
"Saṃsāra is indeed impermanent, suffering, empty, and selfless."
Therefore, having abandoned the multitude of afflictions, always venerate the Sugata; go forth, exert yourselves, and apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha.
Shake off the armies of Māra, as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket;
for the wise person who practices with great heedfulness within this discipline of the Dharma.
"Having abandoned the afflictions of existence, he will bring an end to suffering"—
thus did all those rays of light illuminate everywhere.
Having exhorted sentient beings toward what is auspicious, they once again stood before the Sage; then, having performed three circumambulations of that Blessed One, they remained there.
In that manner, all those rays vanished into the *uṣṇīṣa*.
Then Ānanda, having risen with joy and palms joined in reverence, [spoke].
Having bowed to the Blessed One, he asked thus about the cause of his smile:
"Blessed One, an auspicious ray of light has issued forth from you, produced by your smile."
The worlds were illuminated as if by the rising sun;
for the Buddhas, the Victors, never display a smile without cause.
For what reason does the Blessed One now display a smile?
For whatever purpose you have likewise displayed such a smile, [please explain it].
Seeing him, all those virtuous people were struck with wonder and desired to hear [his teaching];
therefore, the Blessed One, the Teacher, [spoke] here to these seekers of the Dharma.
"Having instructed them all, he ought to cut through their doubt. Hearing these words spoken by Ānanda, the Blessed One said to him:
"It is even so, Ānanda, just as you have said;
indeed, the Conqueror never displays a smile anywhere without a cause."
Listen to that purpose for which I smiled;
behold, Ānanda, this householder boy who is indolent.
Thus, through the mere sight of me, they attained such vigor and enthusiasm;
and having thus acquired jewels, the wise man [attained] prosperity.
Thus, one who is faithful and serene in mind, rejoicing in my teaching,

Since this caravan leader Nanda is devoted to my Dharma,
may he attain the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) through the ripening of this merit.
Then, having attained the trainings and fulfilled the ten perfections,
and having gradually conquered the hosts of Māra, he shall attain perfect enlightenment.
Then this Perfectly Awakened One, the Sugata, the Jina, became renowned by the name Arhat, Abhivandya, Atibalavīryaparākrama.
He will become a Tathāgata, the sovereign lord of all phenomena, the Teacher, the source of all knowledge and virtues, the omniscient one, and the sustainer of the three worlds.
Therefore, O Sadānanda, you should always strive to behold the Buddha;
through the merit of beholding the Buddha, may you attain enthusiasm for the Dharma.
Then, having mounted upon vigor, one should joyfully accomplish the true Dharma;
thereafter, having conquered Māra through the powers of the Dharma, one shall attain perfect enlightenment.
Having heard these instructions given by the Lord of Sages, Ānanda, together with the assembly, rejoiced,
saying "So be it," after praising the Guru and bowing down to him.
Thus was it instructed to me by my teacher for the sake of increasing my zeal for the Dharma;
likewise have I related it to you—let this truth be held fast.
Thus, O King, you too, having likewise performed such rejoicing and having offered encouragement for the Dharma, must strive to behold the Buddha.
"Subjects must always be encouraged in their zeal for the practice of the True Dharma"—
having heard this instruction from his preceptor, King Aśoka [acted accordingly].
Having thus promised this truth, he, together with his retinue, rejoiced.
Whoever listens with faith to this *avadāna* of Kauśīdya as told by the Best of Sages;
whoever, having heard it, proclaims it daily and without ceasing, being devoted to the service of the Buddha;
and having abandoned the defilements and conquered all the powers of the Kali age and the factions of Māra—[they shall attain the goal].
Having reached the further shore of the ocean of virtues, he proceeds to the auspicious conduct of Śrīghana.
Thus ends the *Avadāna* on the Encouragement of Vigor against Laziness in the *Ratnamālā*.
II. The Legend of Snāta:
Then that King Aśoka, for whom the observance of the True Dharma was a festival, bowed to his teacher Upagupta and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke: Rm_2.1{1} //
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken teaching;
you should explain it to me just as it was taught to you by your teacher."
Thus entreated by that lord of men, Upagupta, born from a portion of the Jina,
took leave of the king and spoke to him.
"Excellent! Listen well, O Great King, with a concentrated mind to the Dharma;
just as it was taught to me by my teacher, so shall it be explained to you here."
In a time long past, there was the Lion of the Śākyas,
the compassionate one, the King of Dharma, the Teacher of the World, the Omniscient One, the Sugata, the Victor.
The Lord of Sages, the Tathāgata, is the knower of all sciences and arts, possessed of the six superknowledges, the protector who acts for the welfare of all, and the guide.
In Śrāvastī, in the great and delightful Jetavana Grove,
in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada adorned with jewels.
Together with the disciples, the monks, the bodhisattvas, and the lay devotees;
and with the great kings of the gods and asuras, along with the lords of men and their retinues.
And also by the lords of all the worlds dwelling within the three realms,
by the citizens of the four castes, and likewise by others seeking merit.
He was honored, revered, saluted, praised, worshipped, treated with gravity, placed at the forefront, surrounded, and gazed upon.
Proclaiming the Dharma, which is virtuous in its beginning, middle, and end, he dwelt in meditative absorption for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings in the world.
And at that time, those merchant folk who were in Śrāvastī there,
about five hundred in number, assembled at Ratnākara.
Then, having returned, they all entered the wilderness;
there, having lost their way and wandered astray, they roamed about.
Wandering along the wrong path, they arrived at a sandy plain;
having reached it, they all stood there at midday under the scorching heat.
Scorched by the sharp rays of the sun, distressed by the heat of the summer,
their provisions for the journey exhausted, and tormented by hunger and thirst.
Tormented by intense suffering,
they writhed there like fish cast upon dry land, trembling with the fear of death.
Then all those caravans, having gone for refuge with faith,
collectively entreated their respective family lords and personal tutelary deities.
Some remembered the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū), others likewise Nārāyaṇa; some [remembered] Śiva, the Great Terrible One, and others the Lord of the Sun and the planets.
Some [worshipped] Candra, the lord of the stars; some Indra, the sovereign of the gods;
others Agni and Yama, and still others Nairṛtya.
Likewise, they worshipped Vāruṇa, Vāyu, and Kuvera with the Maheśvaras;
and some likewise worshipped Bhairava, the Mātṛkās, Skanda, and Vināyaka.
Likewise, some [worshipped] Mahākāla, others the sages who are lords of ascetics;
some the heroic lords of the Daityas, and others the lords of the Nāgas.
Some [praised] the Four Great Kings, some likewise the lords of the yakṣas;
thus, having recollected all others dwelling within the three realms, they made their entreaties.
When the deities were thus entreated by them, there was not even a single one among them who could then become a protector for the merchants who were sharing in such suffering.
Then all those merchants, trembling with the fear of death,
stood despondent and hopeless, their minds rendered motionless.
There, the one who was a devotee of the Sugata and had seen the truth, being steadfast, saw those caravans whose hopes were ruined; having addressed them, he spoke thus: Rm_2.25{26} //
"Sirs, do not despair; what will be achieved by despair?
Therefore, casting off despondency and relying on fortitude, remain steadfast."
One should cross over suffering and even great hardship amidst calamities through fortitude;
therefore, having established yourself in fortitude, quickly call the Jina to mind.
The Jina alone is the Lord of the World, the protector who has compassion for all;
therefore, having heard our words, remember the Perfectly Awakened One with reverence.
Even in that situation, when such fear arises, who else will be our protector?
Only the Buddha, the kinsman of the world; therefore, go quickly to the Victor.
In every way, may this Lord of Victors, who is compassionate toward all sentient beings,
truly protect us immediately upon seeing us with his eye of compassion.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, all those merchants likewise took refuge in the Fully Awakened One and, recollecting his fearlessness, made their request.
Homage to you, Blessed One, Protector; you are the omniscient Lord of the world. By you alone has the entire world always been protected like a son.
From this day forward, for as long as we live, we all indeed take refuge in you at all times; therefore, O Teacher of the World, protect us!
O Blessed One, Lord, Omniscient One, you alone have always protected the law of the world within saṃsāra; you ought to protect it in every way.
And five hundred merchants all gathered together,
traveling by a wrong path at midday when the heat was blazing.
Having arrived there, they all remained upon that sandy ground;
scorched by the sun’s fierce rays, they were tormented and afflicted by hunger and thirst.
Overcome by intense and extreme suffering, and having encountered the fear of death, they cry out:
"Homage to the Buddha, homage to the Dharma, homage to the Saṅgha—homage, homage!"
Having seen all of us, the five hundred merchants, you alone, O Lord of the World, manifested such power through the majesty of a Buddha out of compassion for us all.
Then that Blessed One, manifesting a great rain from Indra for them, caused cool winds to blow; by that means, they attained a state of coolness.
Having seen that, the caravan leader addressed all the members of the caravan:
"Gentlemen, let all of you listen to what I say for your own benefit."
Therefore, you who are grateful for favors should take this to heart and act accordingly,
since we have arrived as if from the world beyond, having encountered death.
That [reality] is to be known through the grace of the Victorious Lord’s compassionate gaze;
therefore, we all have gone for refuge to that Buddha.
Relying upon the true Dharma, let us indeed always practice;
for saṃsāra is truly impermanent, and life and happiness are impermanent.
The body perishes in an instant, and nothing in existence is eternal;
only the Dharma is of great essence, for by it alone is the world thus protected.
"Therefore, one must go for refuge to the Sage in order to properly uphold the Dharma.
Having heard this spoken by him, all those merchants were filled with joy.
Saying "So be it," and consenting, he then prepared to depart;
and so the caravan leader, having made him his companion, set out together with him.
In order to see the Sugata in the monastery and to obtain the Dharma, he went there with joy;
having arrived there, he entered together with his entire caravan.
Having seen that Sugata and bowed before the Sage, he despaired in the presence of the Muni.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving the purity of their disposition,
taught them the supreme Dharma, consisting of the Noble Truths and the factors of the Noble Path.
Then all those beings, having heard that Dharma with reverence,
were liberated from the view of a self-identity and attained the thought of awakening.
There, some became great devotees who followed the Dharma;
likewise, some were stream-enterers, and others were once-returners.
Likewise, some non-returners, having turned their backs on further existence,
abandoned the masses of the afflictions of saṃsāra with utterly pure intentions.
Having directly encountered the true Dharma, they became practitioners of the Dharma;
some [set their minds] on the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, and others likewise on that of a pratyekabuddha.
Some made the vow for unexcelled perfect enlightenment;
thus all those assemblies were established in refuge in the Perfectly Awakened One.
They became devoted to the practice of the true Dharma and were dedicated to the Saṅgha;
then those monks saw that they were all engaged in the conduct of awakening.
Having bowed down with devotion to the Perfectly Awakened One, they asked him, filled with wonder:
"O Blessed One, how great is this marvel that these merchants have acted in such a manner!"
All those who had fallen into the wilderness were protected by you;
at the mere thought of you, you brought down a rain like that of Indra.
"Cool breezes are blowing; how can you say otherwise?
Thus questioned by those monks, the Blessed One spoke to them:
Listen, O monks, as I describe the karma that was performed by me;
for what other person could indeed experience the fruit of the karma that I have committed?
For he alone who performed a particular action shall eat its fruit;
an action that has not been experienced is never exhausted by any means whatsoever.
It is not burned by fires, nor is it dried up by winds;
nor is it moistened by waters, nor does it sink into the earths.
Moreover, it ripens within the aggregates, the six elements, and the sense-bases;
otherwise, karmas do not yield their fruits.
Just as an action is performed, so too is its fruit considered to be;
virtuous action yields a virtuous result, while indeed, evil action yields an evil one.
Thinking that one should give both mixed together, one should act for what is auspicious;
for actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Having obtained the necessary conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit;
that which was performed by me in the past, its fruit is now being experienced.
That ancient event is now being told; listen well and with respect.
Once upon a time, there was a Buddha named Candana, a king of Dharma.
The omniscient one, the Arhat, the Lord of the world, the Teacher, the Sovereign of the lords of the world, perfected in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the world, the Victor.
The Tathāgata, the Greatly Wise One, became a perfectly awakened Buddha, a leader;
at that time, on that occasion, he was the Lord of Sages named Candana.
Proclaiming the True Dharma together with the monks,
he traveled throughout the various regions for the benefit of all sentient beings.
He took refuge in a certain delightful city, a royal capital,
there to illuminate the conduct of awakening for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings.
He dwelt in the Victor’s hermitage together with his disciples, the monks;
then the king, the lord of that land, heard that the Buddha had arrived.
Accompanied by his ministers, the people, and the citizens, he went out to meet him with joy;
having approached there suddenly and beheld that Sugata, the Sage, he [prostrated].
Having bowed with palms joined in reverence, he stood joyfully to one side.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that the king had approached, [spoke].
He taught the supreme Dharma, auspicious in its beginning, middle, and end:
"Listen, O King, to the essence of existence—the Dharma that is eternal and free from sloth."
The world is born through Dharma; by means of Dharma one ascends to heaven.
Therefore, always placing Dharma foremost, he should protect his subjects.
The wise know that the duty of protecting the subjects is the root of kingship;
having abandoned the vow of protecting the subjects, what is the use of many other vows?
Therefore, O King, you must protect your subjects in accordance with the Dharma for their welfare;
thus, you should always restrain them from the ten unwholesome actions.
Subjects should be engaged in the Dharma; through that merit, you will be liberated.
At the outset, subjects should be joined to generosity, which is the cause for the state of perfect awakening.
By those merits, O auspicious one, the subjects will flourish and prosper;
in a world devoted to virtuous deeds, the king himself prospers through those merits.
Therefore, having personally given gifts, you should establish your subjects in moral conduct;
through moral conduct the body is purified, and one whose body is purified becomes wise.
Having conquered all enemies through patience, the wise one shines resplendent;
thereafter, by means of the power of his vigor, he shall establish all sentient beings in happiness.
Then, having conquered the afflictions and meditated, one should accomplish awakening;
through the mind of the vow for awakening, the adept should accomplish wisdom.
Then, through skillful means, the wise one should lead the world toward awakening;
thereafter, having utterly conquered the Māras, he shall attain the knowledge of perfect enlightenment.
Having attained there the mastery of flavors, one becomes a lord of the ten stages;
then, having brought all those dwelling within the three realms under one's control, [one proceeds].
Having established [others] in the Dharma of the Sugata, one should personally practice for nirvāṇa.
Knowing this, O Great King, as the means for attaining the state of Nirvana— if you have a desire for liberation, then practice these [virtues].
Then, may you always attain auspiciousness and the happiness of worldly existence;
and by gradually fulfilling the perfections, may you fully attain nirvana.
Nirvāṇa is the supreme knowledge; nirvāṇa is the supreme happiness;
nirvāṇa is the supreme merit; nirvāṇa is the supreme goal.
Thus, having understood that all well-performed deeds are the cause of nirvāṇa,
one should establish oneself in the Dharma and likewise encourage all living beings.
Thus, having awakened that king and established him on the path to enlightenment, the Buddha Candana then paused for a moment.
Then that king, the ruler of men, having heard that Dharma with reverence, was filled with joy; rising up, he arranged his upper robe over one shoulder.
Standing on the ground with his knees, bowing with palms joined in reverence,
and with a very serene face, he prostrated at the feet of that sage and made this request.
Homage to you, O Blessed One, Protector; I go to you for refuge.
Teaching the True Dharma here, may you be victorious together with your retinue.
When the lord of men had thus entreated him, that sovereign of sages,
having promised "So be it," took up residence there for the three-month rainy season retreat.
Then the king, together with his harem, joyfully gratified that lord of sages and his assembly with offerings of food and various forms of respectful worship.
And at that time, the rain-gods dwelling there, provoked by the conduct of the people, did not release a shower of rain upon the earth.
Then, during that drought, the reservoirs and other water-holding places lost their water day by day and were dried up until only mud remained.
The trees were without flowers or fruit, their branches and leaves shattered and fallen away.
They were like lifeless posts, devoid of enjoyment, shunned even by birds; they were ruined by the lords of the earth and parched by the seeds of the Kula dynasty.
Then, devoid of grass and reduced to desolation, the land became like a desert;
due to the lack of food and drink, countless living beings died.
Some, struck by hunger and thirst, sat down as if dead;
others, with dejected faces in their homes, were despondent, tormented by the fear of death.
Looking at one another’s faces, they sat sighing;
some, seeing a cloud in the sky, offered prayers day and night.
"Alas, we are undone!"—having uttered these words, some stood there despondent;
thus they lamented in various ways, overcome with exhaustion.
All the citizens there also trembled with fear of death;
and seeing this, the king too was moved by compassion for those terrified of death.
Having summoned all his ministers and counselors, he spoke thus:
"Alas, what a tragedy! How is it that such a famine prevails right here now? What shall I do? I know no remedy; tell me the means to counteract it."
We shall employ that means by which this great calamity of famine will be swiftly pacified; therefore, act according to the prescribed method.
Having heard this command of the king, those ministers, the country-folk, and the citizens,
having worshipped the deities according to the prescribed rites, entreated them for his pacification.
O deities, be gracious; we bow down before you. Whatever offense we have committed against you, that must be forgiven by all means.
Quickly pacify this famine and drought that has arrived;
by causing a timely rain here, ensure that there is certainly an abundance of food.
Thus, some [worship] Vidhātṛ, some Viṣṇu Janārdana,
some Śiva Maheśāna, and some Indra, the lord of the gods.
Some [worshipped] the lord of the planets, some the world-protectors of great supernatural power,
and some the goddess Mātṛkā, Skanda, Vighneśa, and Bhairava.
Some, having beheld the hosts of Mahākāla, others the nāgas and lords of the waters, and others the clouds, bowed down and entreated them for rain.
In this manner, all the people, having worshipped their respective chosen family deities according to the prescribed rites and offered prayers, entreated them for abundant rain.
Thus, even though they were all entreated by them, those deities,
being thwarted, were simply unable to release rain there.
Then all those people, seeing that [city] destroyed by the rain,
cried out in lamentation and fled, devoid of hope.
Then the king, seeing them with their hopes shattered by the famine and observing the planets likewise, became dejected in countenance and reflected:
"Alas! A great calamity will befall my kingdom;
how shall a remedy be applied here for its pacification?"

"What is the use of my being a king who destroys fame and dharma, since I am unable to protect my subjects when they are afflicted by calamities? Fie on me, who have become the lowest of kings! What sin have I committed?"

If a king does not protect his subjects residing within his own realm, how can he be considered a powerful king? He is regarded as nothing more than Death himself.

If a king who is consecrated for the very purpose of benefiting those [subjects] should not act for their benefit, how can he be a king? He is one who destroys his own fulfilled purpose.
Cursed be he who, having destroyed his own reputation, virtue, happiness, and wealth,
perishes himself and, having ruined others, will certainly go to the hells.
Moreover, I am also a human being, equal [to others] in my sense faculties;
therefore, I am constantly served by all of them with focused attention.
If I do not provide protection for these beings even in times of calamity, when— freed from such [faults]— shall I go to a happy rebirth?
Bound by these debts at all times and obstructed in every way,
driven by my past actions, I shall certainly go to the hells.
Then, when I am confronted by the messengers of Yama, what shall I do?
Seeing that terrifying [realm] and those cruel ones, I shall fall down, utterly bewildered.
At that time, there will be no compassionate protector found there;
only Dharma shall protect, and one should practice that auspicious Dharma.
The lords of sages have declared that dharmas are manifold; among them, they proclaim the supreme Dharma of the Sugata, which is auspicious in the beginning, middle, and end.
By means of that very [merit], having established purity throughout all worlds,
all sentient beings are protected both in this body and in the hereafter.
Likewise, here too, in order to perform what is auspicious and to fully attain the True Dharma, one should go for refuge to the Perfectly Awakened One and attend upon the Saṅgha.
Therefore, having quickly constructed a beautiful lotus pond there,
he bathed the Perfectly Awakened Sugata together with the Saṅgha.
Having gratified him with great honors, worship, and meals,
he then bowed to that Sugata for the sake of pacifying that famine.
When the world is suffering from a lack of rain, I shall pray with devotion;
then that Blessed One will surely cause a good rain to fall here.
Having established auspiciousness everywhere, one should always ensure an abundance of food;
consequently, there shall never again be famine here at any time.
"Surely there will be abundance and prosperity everywhere on all sides.
Having thus reflected and resolved with his mind, that lord of men—
Having suddenly summoned all his ministers, he spoke to them thus:
"Listen, O ministers, to that which has been reflected upon by my mind."
Having rejoiced in that, you should perform it with concentrated minds,
for today a drought has arisen and famine is approaching.
Therefore, surely, for the sake of abandoning that evil of ours,
we shall take refuge in the Perfectly Awakened One in order to fully attain the True Dharma.
May you always desire to serve the Blessed One together with his Saṅgha; may that very Lord, the Protector, always bring about auspiciousness here.
And having brought about good rain, he will surely cause an abundance of food;
then, even now, there would be auspiciousness for us here on all sides.
Always upholding the true Dharma, may we enjoy happiness and partake of it;
through the Dharma there is constant purity, and through the Dharma one overcomes adversity.
Everything is protected by Dharma; through Dharma one goes to a good rebirth.
All the lords of sages declare that the auspicious Dharma is that of the Sugata.
Worship that Perfectly Awakened One with reverence in order to fully attain the True Dharma;
for the Buddha alone is the kinsman of the world and the benefactor of all sentient beings.
The Buddha alone is the friend of the world, bestowing happiness upon all sentient beings;

The Buddha alone is the sustainer of the world, the bestower of the wealth of Dharma and happiness;

the Buddha alone is the lord of the world, the fulfiller of the accumulations for enlightenment.
The Buddha alone is the Lord of the world, the teacher of the path to perfect enlightenment;

The Buddha alone is the Great Being, the possessor of the six superknowledges, and the Lord of the world;

That very Blessed Buddha is to be served by those who seek what is auspicious,

By him, this perfected Dharma-king, the Jina, shines and triumphs as he illuminates the practices of awakening throughout the three worlds. (Rm 30)
Just as he always practices benevolence, so too will he act here.
Just as he establishes the beings dwelling in the three realms in the True Dharma,
so indeed should he awaken us and cause us to enter therein.
Then, having all of us upheld the true Dharma, which is auspicious, pure, and blissful,

Thinking thus, we should always joyfully serve this Lord of Jinas, Candana, with great honors and worship.
Having spoken thus, and being assented to with "So be it" by all those ministers,

Having arrived there and entered, and having seen that sage Candana, he bowed with palms joined in reverence and made this request: * *Rm_2.152{24}* (Ratnāvalī 2.152)
Homage to you, O Blessed Teacher; we have come to you for refuge.
Therefore, be gracious toward us and forgive our transgression.

Then, having thoroughly cleared the city and its streets on all sides,
they had the surface of the earth sprinkled with fragrant water.
Then, having had flowers strewn everywhere,

Then, having had an excellent lake constructed in the center of that city,
he had it filled with fragrant water and made most beautiful.

Then, having prepared and arranged the articles for worship and the utensils for food, together with musical accompaniments.
