Having arrived there suddenly and seeing that sage Candana,
he bowed with palms joined in reverence and requested permission to depart.
O Omniscient Blessed One, the time has now come to depart;
everything has been accomplished and perfected, so you should please come quickly.
When the king had thus made his request, the Perfectly Awakened One, together with the Saṅgha,
took up his bowl and robes and went toward that city.
When that Blessed One, the Buddha, displaying his miraculous power,
illuminated the worlds with his radiance and proceeded toward the city gate, he arrived there.
Then the ocean, along with its waters, trembled, and a most auspicious wind blew;
and all those who were afflicted by hunger and thirst became completely satiated.
Those beings who had impaired faculties became possessed of complete faculties;
those who were destitute became wealthy, and those who were diseased became free from illness.
Those held in bondage became liberated; the suffering became happy;
the insane regained their right mindfulness; and the naked were clothed in fine garments.
All those women who were pregnant gave birth with ease; even those bound by long-standing enmity conducted themselves with friendliness.
And those beings who were devoted to evil, practicing the ten unwholesome paths of action—
they all became completely satisfied and proceeded forth, desiring merit.
Thus, all other evil portents that were there likewise came to an end; they were all marked by auspicious signs.
Thus, having destroyed all inauspiciousness in every way and having brought about prosperity everywhere, he entered that city together with the Saṃgha.
Having thus proceeded in a clockwise circumambulation in this manner with great festivities, one by one.
Thus he was being honored by all of them— the gods, asuras, and humans alike.
Placing that king at their head, they proceeded along the royal highway;
having reached that lake, they saw it and took refuge upon its shore.
Then that Blessed One, the Buddha, stood upon the seat as it had been prepared,
wearing only a single robe, in order to bathe there in that lake.
Then the king and all the people bathed that sage Candana,
together with his community, in succession with water from golden jars.
Having bathed elsewhere, the Blessed One then stood upon a seat prepared as was fitting, together with the Saṅgha, manifesting his own supernatural power.
Then the king, having caused that Buddha, who was seated together with his Saṅgha and clad in his robes, to be honored, worshipped him with all the articles of worship.
And then he fully satisfied and gratified him with pure and exquisite foods, as well as with various side dishes, the five nectars, and drinks.
Then, at the conclusion of the meal, having cleansed his mouth and other parts,
the king sat upon a low seat with his palms joined in reverence.
With his lotus-like face beaming with great serenity, that minister, together with the citizens, bowed down and asked for forgiveness from him and his Saṅgha, making this request: Rm_2.186{88} //
O All-Knowing One, Blessed Lord, Protector, forgive our transgressions;
be gracious and protect us in every way, having seen us as evildoers.
Therefore, quickly bring about good rain for the destruction of that famine,
and for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, proclaim the True Dharma.
When the king, who sought the welfare of the world, had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, spoke these words of blessing: *Rm_2.189{91}*
May you have health, O King, and may there be auspiciousness for you everywhere;
may there always be abundance here, and may you attain awakening without obstacle.
Having thus bestowed his own words of blessing, the Fully Awakened One, together with the Saṅgha and accompanied by the king and his people, then returned to his own hermitage.
In this manner, that king of men performed continuous service for three months toward this Lord of Munis with honors and worship.
Then Śakra, the great Indra, having seen that worship of the Sugata,
sent down a timely rain for the sake of pacifying that famine.
Then, the reservoirs filled with water and surrounded on all sides,
shone forth as they were covered with lotuses, blue lilies, and other flowers.
With its grasses sprouting new shoots and its lawns fully grown,
the earth shone as if covered and draped in garments of green cloth.
And the trees, covered with green leaves and graced by blossoming flowers, shone brightly with their excellent fruits.
And thus, having gradually sprouted and grown, the crops, fully ripened and perfected, flourished on all sides; thereafter,
all the people experienced such a state of abundant harvests.
Having seen him and uttered "Ānanda," they rejoiced, filled with great delight.
Then the king, seeing them all filled with great joy and delight, addressed them once more and spoke to awaken their understanding.
Sirs, behold the majestic power of this Perfectly Awakened One,
by the majesty of whose merit there is abundance for all beings from the very moment of their birth.
Therefore, one should always and constantly offer worship with great honors and veneration to this perfectly awakened Lord of the World, who remains eternally as he is.
Thus, if they should always honor this Perfectly Awakened One, the Lord of the World, with offerings, there shall always be auspiciousness here.
Therefore, this perfumed stūpa, adorned with the nails and hair of this Lord of Munis, should be established and constantly served with offerings.

Having spoken thus, and being granted permission by them with the words "So be it," the king went together with them to the Buddhist hermitage, and having bowed to him, he made his request to the sage.
Homage to you, O Blessed One, our Teacher; we abide in refuge unto you.
We shall always act in this manner, remaining devoted to your service.
Therefore, be gracious; always wandering among worthy recipients and teaching the Dharma, be victorious, and do not go elsewhere—out of compassion for us.
When the king had thus petitioned him, the Blessed One and Candana,
seeing that monarch together with his people, spoke as follows with a serene countenance:
O King, I have not accomplished awakening for the sake of a single person;
rather, out of compassion, I have done so for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Therefore, I shall never remain here together with my community;
rather, I shall wander everywhere to proclaim the true Dharma.
If you desire to serve me constantly with faith,
then establish a stūpa for my hair and serve it always with offerings.
Consequently, in this kingdom there shall always be abundance and auspiciousness;
and famine shall never at any time assail it anywhere.
Thinking thus, you yourself should go and take refuge in the Three Jewels,
and you should diligently urge all sentient beings toward the True Dharma.
Having spoken thus, that lord of sages, having likewise clipped his own nails and shaved off his hair, gave them himself to the king.
Then the king, having bowed to that Buddha and taken those hairs and nails, returned to his own abode with great joy.
Having arrived there in the middle of the city, near the edge of a lotus pond,
he had his hair and nails cut off and erected a fragrant stūpa.
Once that [image] was completed, he established it according to the ritual with great festivals;
then, with a serene mind, he performed constant service through acts of honor and worship.
By the power of this merit, may I become a Sugata in this blind world that lacks a guide, in order to bring benefit to the world of living beings.
Having thus made this vow in his mind,
that lord of men bathed the stūpa with fragrant waters and worshipped it constantly.
Having established me as well and having gone for refuge with joy,
he honored me with great enthusiasm, prostrating with the eight limbs.
Likewise, all people also took refuge in him with faith;
and all those who had gone there for refuge attained final liberation.
I alone remained among them as that lord of men;
having maintained the vow for perfect enlightenment, he did not pass into nirvāṇa in this manner.
And by the power of this merit, a bountiful rain was brought forth;
there, at all times, there was an abundance of food and freedom from calamity.
And through the power of this Dharma, I now everywhere receive worship,
honor, respect, fame, righteousness, and happiness.
"Wherever I go, in every direction,
I am thus honored with hospitality and worship along with the Saṅgha."
Having propitiated that Teacher, those who desire fame, dharma,
and happiness should always and constantly practice with diligence in virtuous deeds.
Through virtue, there shall always be happiness everywhere in the world;
through evil, there is likewise suffering, and through a mixture [of both], there is a mixture [of both].
Therefore, having desisted from evil and having abandoned such mixed actions,
those who desire happiness should strive with diligence to practice only what is wholesome.
Having heard these and other instructions given by the Lord of Munis, all those members of the Saṅgha believed with certainty in the reality of karma within the abode of existence.
Always abstaining from evil deeds, even those that are mixed with good,
and ever devoted to virtuous actions, they all proceeded on, composed in mind.
Thus, O King, you should always desist from evil and even from that which is mixed with it, and practice dharma in every way for the attainment of happiness.
Having completely restrained the subjects from all evil conduct and having caused them to hear the true Dharma, they should always be established in what is wholesome.
Likewise, may there always and eternally be good rain everywhere, even regarding all objects of sense; thus may there be auspiciousness free from affliction.
Having heard this instruction given by the teacher Upagupta, King Aśoka, together with his retinue, rejoiced, saying, "So be it."
Those who, having heard this *Snātāvadāna*, cause it to be heard by others so as to awaken them,
will surely go to the abodes of the Sugatas with bodies purified and freed from sin.
Thus ends the Story of Snāta from the Garland of Precious Avadānas.
(Rm 36) III. The Cakrāvadāna.
Then King Aśoka, having bowed once more with palms joined in reverence,
spoke to his teacher Upagupta, wishing to hear another well-spoken teaching.
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear yet another well-spoken word;
you should tell it to me just as it was related to you by your teacher."
When the king had thus entreated him, that ascetic monk Upagupta, born from a portion of the Victor, spoke again to the monarch in this manner:
"I shall speak to you that well-spoken word as it was instructed to me by my teacher;
listen attentively, O King, having properly composed your mind."
He who was formerly the Great Buddha, the omniscient Śrīghana, the Jina, the Tathāgata, the King of Dharma, and the master of all sciences and arts.
The Teacher, the Arhat, the Sugata, the Protector, the Guide of the three realms—
he, the Lord of the Śākyas, exists in the world for the benefit of all beings everywhere.
Having taught the true Dharma and illuminated the path to enlightenment,
he was surrounded by a community of monks and disciples, as well as by the assembly of bodhisattvas.
And likewise, together with the assemblies of female lay disciples and the assemblies of male lay disciples,
they resorted to Rājagṛha, at the Jina’s hermitage in the Bamboo Grove.
Residing in the great grove called Kalandakanivāpa,
he taught the supreme Dharma, which is auspicious in its beginning, middle, and end.
Therefore, gods, asuras, and humans, yakṣas, kinnaras, gandharvas, siddhas, vidyādharas, and others [came] to hear that teaching of the Dharma.
The Garuḍas and the Naga kings were filled with great joy,
as were the Brahmins, the Kṣatriyas, the kings, and the princes.
And the Vaiśyas, the guild-leaders, the Śūdras, the ministers, the maternal kinsmen, the caravan leaders, the citizens, the wealthy men, and the merchants;
In this way, all the other worlds as well were filled with joy by means of great honors, worship, and likewise all kinds of requisites.
Having worshipped and saluted the Fully Awakened One, the Sugata, the Sage,
and having circumambulated him while keeping him to his right, he stood; all the others likewise stood.
All those who desired the true Dharma gathered there to listen.
And at that time, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a certain merchant named Subhaga,
a caravan leader who was very wealthy, wise, and of noble character.
Therefore, for the sake of maintaining his lineage according to the family tradition, he married Subhadrāṅgī, who was equal to him in her birth-status.
Then that couple, full of passion and bound by affection, rejoiced with delight,
enjoying themselves as they pleased according to their desire.
Then, for that householder who was solely devoted to sensual enjoyments and,
through negligence, indifferent toward the duties and conduct of his own family, [the consequences followed].
For one who is indifferent toward worldly affairs, devoid of exertion,
slow in the means of acquisition, and spends only what he has, [wealth perishes].
Day after day, as he constantly incurred excessive expenditures without any income,
his riches reached exhaustion like lakes in the summer season.
Then the wife of that householder, who was devoted to the family tradition,
seeing the depletion of their wealth, reflected thus within her home:
"This man, my husband, is a wealthy caravan leader and merchant;
having enjoyed his fortune at home, he dwells there without any exertion."
Where there is excessive expenditure and no such income, how long could that wealth endure? It would gradually go to exhaustion.
Therefore, how can this person remain at ease when deprived of the accumulation of enjoyments by which the worlds are sustained?
He would surely become old, and likewise he would become poor;
having lived thus in vain, how could he remain at home happy?
How can that man be happy whose wealth is not present in his home? He would not even be able to eat for himself, let alone practice generosity.
Without giving, what essential happiness can be attained in saṃsāra?
For it is through giving alone that fame, merit, and happiness are obtained.
Through generosity the mind is purified; one whose mind is purified becomes wise.
Through wisdom ethical discipline is accomplished; one possessing ethical discipline becomes a doer of good.
Having performed virtuous deeds and practiced the true Dharma, he shall go to a happy rebirth;
therefore, I [take] this protector, my husband, this man, my lord.
I would urge them toward the acquisition of wealth for the sake of attaining the happiness of the true Dharma;
for in this world, a man possessing wealth is capable of accomplishing all his purposes.
The wise declare that wealth is the root of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
for it is indeed the means by which a man fulfills the duties of the three aims of life.
The wise declare that a virtuous wife who follows her husband is his companion;
for I am the virtuous wife of this husband, devoted to the accomplishment of dharma and artha.
Having encouraged my mind, I shall exert myself toward the acquisition of wealth.
Having thus resolved, that virtuous woman looked upon her husband with respect and spoke in order to encourage him toward the accomplishment of dharma and worldly prosperity.
"You are my master, my sustainer, and my lord; indeed, you alone are my deity.
Therefore, I shall speak the truth for your sake, so that there may be happiness for you both here and in the hereafter."
Listen to this truth as it is; do not think otherwise.
Since you are a man who was once wealthy, a caravan leader, a merchant, and a master,
it does not look well for you to remain here after having always enjoyed such pleasures.
Therefore, having abandoned negligence, for the sake of attaining fame, virtue, and happiness,
acquire wealth by following the true Dharma.
One should acquire enjoyments through wealth; one should protect the body through enjoyments;
one should accomplish Dharma through the body; and through Dharma, one shall obtain true happiness.
Furthermore, in whatever house the master is inactive in his affairs,
all the people there will likewise remain despondent.
Furthermore, in whatever house the master is engaged in business,
all the people there should likewise apply themselves with diligence.
And that house in which the great enthusiasm for giving is not found— would that house not be as unpleasant as a deserted forest or a cremation ground?
In whatever house there is always and constantly a great festival of the merit of giving,
that very residence will appear as delightful as heaven itself.
Moreover, what is the use of that householder who, lacking enthusiasm for the merit of giving,
dwells like a beast, merely consuming [food] himself?
Blessed are those heroic men, endowed with fame, virtue, and happiness, who,
having exerted themselves in the practice of giving, dwell in comfort after having enjoyed their pleasures.
Indeed, for those very people who, having performed meritorious acts of giving, enjoy happiness themselves, life in saṃsāra is truly well-endowed with essence.
For it is by means of giving alone that people are enticed toward fame, virtue, and happiness;
otherwise, they would never obtain them, and thus the perfection of giving would be rendered purposeless.
And for how long could those who remain established in pleasure after having enjoyed it live?
Having inevitably abandoned everything in every way, once dead, they would go to the abode of Yama.
There, having seen those companions of his karma and having judged that karma, Yama, the Lord of Dharma, shall impel him toward the experience of the fruits of his actions.
May he impel those who are evil-doers and wicked toward an evil rebirth,
and may he impel those who perform meritorious deeds and are auspicious toward a happy rebirth.
In this regard, all living beings everywhere, both in this world and in the next, experience the fruits of their actions, whether they be painful or pleasant.
Through virtue one may go to a good rebirth, endowed with fame, righteousness, and happiness;
through evil one may go to a miserable rebirth, beset by reproach and suffering.
Thinking thus, O Lord, O Master, for the sake of attaining fame, dharma, and happiness,
apply yourself to your family’s traditional occupation and exert yourself in the acquisition of wealth.
Always exerting great enthusiasm for giving in order to attain a good rebirth,
and enjoying happiness according to your desire, protect the people forever.
Then may you always have auspiciousness here and in the hereafter;
your human birth shall surely be fruitful, and you shall attain a happy destiny.
Having heard these words of his wife, that wise householder merchant looked at his beloved and dear wife and spoke to her thus:
"O dear one, you are my beloved wife Subhadrā;
whatever you have spoken is the truth, and I shall certainly do it in every way."
"But you are my dear wife, beloved and exceedingly charming;
so how could I abandon you, my beloved, and go elsewhere for the sake of wealth?"
For I am indeed a caravan leader; how then could I acquire jewels through base occupations? Therefore, I shall go to the ocean, the mine of jewels.
Therefore, my dear, since Subhadrā is virtuous and follows the path of dharma,
remain here, attending to the affairs of the household, and dwell as you please after having eaten.
"Maintain your fortitude until I have reached home;
I shall return very soon. Remember me and do not grieve."
Having heard what her husband had said, that wife, filled with remorse and with tears streaming down her face, bowed to her lord and spoke to him.
"O Lord, O beloved Master, how can you depart, leaving me behind?
How could I remain at home without you, just as I do in the forest?"
Whether in seeing or hearing [the image], or in the anointing with fragrant oils, in touching, eating, drinking, or in being adorned with fine garments; Rm_3.65{63} //
Furthermore, regarding fragrance, the limbs, speech, or even walking at times,
as well as in the enjoyment of sleep, I have no desire whatsoever.
Remembering only you and sighing again and again,
scorched by the fire of separation, I shall surely go to my death.
When I am dead, who indeed will protect your wealth in your home?
Having heard of my death, you will surely burn with the fires of separation.
Then, what will you do with these prosperities and jewels?
For the King will surely seize the entire estate of one who has no son.
Having thus exhausted yourself by identifying with that [worldly state], do not go far away into the vastness;
remaining at home together with me, enjoy happiness and apply yourself to spiritual effort.
"Here too there are many guilds of merchants and great folk;
spread out your wares and together with them, easily acquire wealth."
And for how long shall we live when no offspring exists?
Therefore, what is the use of many jewels to us? Do not go to the ocean of jewels.
Having enjoyed happiness for as long as you live, and having given gifts to those who seek them,
acquire wealth through conventional means and take delight while remaining in your own home.
Do not run away anywhere, my dear; for what could one find even in the ocean of jewels that a living being cannot obtain at home, namely the wealth produced by one's own karma?
One's own performed karma will produce a fruit corresponding to that creation;
everywhere, both the great and the small surely receive it.
Likewise, those virtuous people in the world who possess wealth and are the refuge of excellent qualities—
even they, in an instant, become destitute and take recourse to mendicancy.
Furthermore, even those who are wicked in the world, as well as those who are poor and devoid of virtue,
receive honor worthy of respect and are served by virtuous people.
Likewise, those wise merchants and caravan leaders who had gone to the ocean for the sake of jewels— some of them returned in safety.
Some there, having had their ship wrecked upon the ocean along with their wealth, fell into the water, were submerged, died, and went to destruction.
Some, having exerted themselves and crossed over by the power of vigor alone,
return home with empty hands and in poverty, having fallen away from their goals;
in this same way, all sentient beings are fashioned by their own performed karma.
Having thus experienced the fruit [of their actions], they indeed wander through the cycle of existence within the six realms of rebirth.
Thus, knowing that prosperity and adversity are determined by the measure of one's karma, do not distress yourself; having practiced the Dharma, dwell in happiness.
Thus, may there indeed be constant auspiciousness for us both everywhere;
and having enjoyed happiness throughout our lives, may we go to a good rebirth.
Having heard what was thus spoken by his wife, and seeing that beloved, charming wife, the son of the caravan leader addressed her in this way:
"O noble lady, it is true that you have said that one's own karma is the measure;
thinking thus, I wish indeed to go even to the ocean of jewels."
"What was not to be will not be; and what is destined to be cannot be otherwise.
This must surely hold true in every case; therefore, he strives to go across the ocean."
If such good fortune is mine, may there indeed be well-being on my journey;
having obtained many jewels, may I return successfully accomplished.
"Surely it is not my good fortune, but rather a misfortune there, that I am submerged in this great holy ford; having died, I shall go to the abode of the gods."
Just as great warriors, for the sake of attaining fame, merit, and happiness, enter the field of battle with great enthusiasm to conquer their enemy; so too [do the Bodhisattvas].
In that regard, some heroes who have been slain, though endowed with fame and virtue,
go immediately upon death to experience the bliss of heaven.
"I too am a merchant's son, indeed the offspring of a caravan leader; therefore,
I shall go to that very ocean of jewels, and nowhere else."
If I reach home in safety, endowed with fame, jewels, and happiness;
or else, having died and become purified, may I attain bliss in heaven.
Thinking thus, my dear and auspicious lady, do not despair; dwell in happiness until I have returned home, during which time you should worship your chosen deity.
"In every way I shall go for the sake of attaining glory for my own family;
for I am irreversible in this task, so do not restrain me."
Having heard these words of her husband regarding his insistence on departure,
that virtuous woman bowed to her husband and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
"O Lord, if you wish to go by any means to the great ocean,
proceed with a concentrated mind, maintaining fortitude and observing the path."
May there be well-being for you as you travel on the road, everywhere, by day and by night;
may there likewise be well-being upon your return—may there always be constant auspiciousness.
Endowed with the great success of your journey, prosperity, fame, virtue, and happiness, may you return safely and swiftly; may there always be auspiciousness for you.
Having heard what his wife had said, the caravan leader agreed, saying "So be it," and after summoning all the members of the caravan, he spoke to them.
"Gentlemen, for the sake of attaining the happiness of the Dharma,
I desire to set out upon the ocean, the mine of jewels, having established the livelihood of my own family."
If you desire to go there together with me, then take that merchandise and come quickly; let us travel.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, all those merchants joyfully and immediately took their merchandise and set out to go there.
Then the caravan leader, together with those five hundred,
performed the rites for a safe journey and set out, filled with joy.
Then, having gradually passed through villages and districts,
and having traversed wilderness regions, they reached the shore of the great ocean.
Then, having boarded the ship together with those five hundred [attendants] and hoisted a bright banner, they gradually entered the ocean.
Thus, having embarked upon their ship and being carried by a favorable wind,
they surely crossed various islands in succession and arrived at the Ocean of Jewels (Ratnākara).
Having reached Ratnākara, those deities were filled with great joy;
yet, having quarreled among themselves, they were unable to return.
Because they had been at odds for so long, they did not obtain the jewels;
and repeatedly remembering their kinsmen, they all remained there, delayed.
In the meantime, that virtuous woman, the beloved of the caravan leader,
considered her home to be empty and joyless without her husband.
From the day her husband, the caravan leader, set out from the city,
that woman began counting each passing day.
Constantly remembering her husband, distressed by the pain of separation,
sighing repeatedly, and thus lacking self-control, she was consumed by grief.
Her limbs were emaciated, her complexion pale, and her hair coarse and disheveled;
she had no desire for adornment and was clothed in soiled garments.
In seeing and hearing, in bringing forth fragrances, in eating and drinking, in touching and even in walking; Rm_3.112{10} //
Whether in a curiosity-house, or elsewhere in a delightful and wonderful place,
I do not take pleasure in any such objects as much as I am distressed by them.
Afflicted by the pain of separation from her husband, despondent like a sick woman,
and overwhelmed by unbearable passion, she was devoid of any thought for the means of maintaining her fortitude.
Relying on her husband’s return and summoning a moment of fortitude,
she sat right there in the house, remembering only her husband.
He did not seek sleep upon his bed, nor did he turn his mind toward any other thought;
having thus meditated upon the Lord, he remained as one who knows yoga, absorbed in contemplation.
Then, seeing that devoted wife Yauvanī thus distressed, a certain auspicious friend spoke to her in private:
"O blessed lady, why do you appear so dejected as if you were afflicted?
Do not despair; tell me, my dear, what it is that you desire."
O noble lady, follower of your own family dharma, why do you not take delight in festivals,
in wonders, and in all objects of the senses?
You no longer desire to see or hear regarding food or ornaments; what is the use of despondency? That which has been accomplished for you, enjoy it as you please.
When his friend had spoken thus, the caravan leader’s beloved also looked upon that beautiful woman, her friend, and spoke as follows: (Rm 44) Rm_3.121{19} //
"O noble lady, I do not seek wealth, nor am I excessively attached to sensual pleasures; rather, I am devoted to the Dharma. Therefore, how could I [live] without my husband?"
Therefore, having abandoned sense objects and remembering that very husband of mine,
I remain in my own home, free from desire even for enjoyments.
"When will my beloved husband return home?"—
fixing my mind on this thought, I remain like a yoginī.
"As long as that beloved husband does not return to his own home,
for that long I shall not eat, even if the foods are delicious."
Even regarding all sense-objects, I have no desire except for my beloved;
there is no other thought in my mind, and therefore I remain thus at all times.
"As long as my lord has not been seen by me, I shall remain thus;
even if my life must depart, I shall not go outside the house."
For women, the husband is indeed their deity, and even dharma is attained through service to the husband;
therefore, remembering my husband, I, a devoted wife, offer this oblation.
"Where shall I practice the Dharma, since there is no man in my home?
Therefore, meditating upon my husband with my mind alone, I shall worship him day and night."
"Fie on my birth, which would be in vain for one who has no husband in her youth; what shall I do in old age, lacking both a master and wealth?"
Today death itself is better for me than a long life lived in falsehood;
for even after staying for a long time, that very same suffering of death must inevitably come.
If he, depending upon whom alone I live, should not return,
what is the use even of this life, which consists of nothing but suffering?
Blessed indeed are those auspicious women who, accompanying their own husbands,
dwell having always practiced the Dharma at home and enjoyed happiness.
May no woman like me ever become unfortunate or a partaker of suffering; for what is the use of perfect enjoyments to her whose husband is not present in her youth?
"Nevertheless, what shall I do? For I am a noble woman devoted to my husband;
therefore, remembering that very husband, I shall remain steadfast for all time."
Having heard what she had said, that well-wishing friend spoke to her and to the other friend in order to perform what was beneficial through that means.
"O blessed lady, you have spoken the truth; for to women, the husband is indeed a deity.
Nevertheless, O blessed one, I shall speak out of affection for you; listen to that."
As long as her husband dwells in the home, delighting in the essence of sensual pleasure, so long should the woman constantly serve him, following the dharma by his permission.
When the husband is not at home, having gone to a distant land,
the wife should worship the deity until he returns to the house.
He is your deity and ours; Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa Hari.
Therefore, remembering Him daily by the name of the Lord, worship and revere Him.
He alone is the god who grants desires, the sovereign lord of the realm of desire;
established in the nature of worldly existence, he bestows the pleasure of delightful enjoyments.
Indeed, impelled by his very power,
your husband, accompanied by his wealth of jewels, departed swiftly for his own welfare.
Therefore, your birth in this world has become fruitful; having given gifts together with the Lord and enjoyed happiness, dwell in comfort for as long as you live.
Having heard what her friend had said, that devoted wife agreed, saying "So be it," and then spoke again to her friend: *Ramayana* 3.144 (verse 42)
"It is true, noble lady, that you have spoken for my benefit;
therefore, remembering the name of the Lord Hari, I shall practice accordingly."
When my lord has returned in safety, bearing an abundance of jewels,
then indeed I shall give a single golden wheel to Viṣṇu.
Having thus made this vow, she meditated upon Viṣṇu in this manner.
Homage to you, O Blessed One Viṣṇu, Hare, Nārāyaṇa, Lord!
Be gracious; look upon me, this woman, and quickly restore my husband to me.
"When my husband, my lord, returns safely to his home,
then, O Hari, I shall offer this golden disc to you."
