"O Blessed One, this great arising of merit and happiness for us was brought about neither by our mother, nor by our father, nor by our kinsmen."
Neither by kinsmen, nor by friends, nor by companions and well-wishers, nor even by blood relations, nor by those in the world of the ancestors, nor by others [can one be saved].
Neither by the king, nor by ministers, nor by counselors, nor by the citizens;
neither by teachers, nor by Brahmins, nor by ascetics, nor by forest-dwellers.
Neither by the gods, nor by the Daityas, nor even by the lords of the worlds,
nor indeed by any others has that which has been done by you ever been accomplished.
Since the ocean of our blood and tears has been dried up,
and since the great mountain of our bones has been crossed by us.
Through your power, the most terrible path to the lower realms, fraught with many evils, has been closed;
the highly meritorious path to heaven has been opened, and the path to Nirvana has been found by me.
Through your grace, I have today obtained the perfectly pure eye, free from all defects;
I have attained the peaceful state beloved by the noble ones, and I have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of suffering.
O Sage, worshipped by the lord of men, by gods, and by asuras; you who are free from birth, old age, death, and the like;
whose appearance is so difficult to obtain even in thousands of lifetimes—today your sight has become fruitful.
Then, having bowed at the lotus-feet of the sage and performed three circumambulations,
she, filled with joy, remembered the Sugata, the Lord of Jinas, and once again ascended to heaven.
Thus, having arrived in heaven, that celestial maiden rejoiced,
just as a merchant who has gained profit or a sick man who has been freed from disease.
Just as a laborer in agriculture who has obtained a crop fully ripened, or like a merchant caravan leader who has gained his wealth through a successful journey; Rm_5.86{86} //
Then all those monks, having seen such a radiance,
were filled with doubt and wonder, and they questioned that Lord of Sages in this way:
"Blessed One, who has come into your presence tonight?
Is it Brahmā, or the king of the gods, or even the hosts of world-protectors?"
"We do not know this person who has come here tonight; therefore,
you ought to enlighten us all, for we are filled with wonder."
Thus questioned by those monks, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages,
addressed all those assemblies of monks and spoke as follows.
For that Brahmā, O monks, is not he; nor is that lord of the gods;
nor indeed are the guardians of the world who have come here tonight.
Moreover, did you see on the road the young girl who went along with me,
by whom I was honored and strewn all over with *sāla* flowers?
Having scattered flowers over me, she went again to the forest for the sake of her household;
while climbing a tree to gather blossoms, she fell from it.
Then, agitated by that fall and with her mind overcome by pain,
she merely recollected the Three Jewels and, casting off her body, went to heaven.
Having reached that heaven and having remembered me, the Sugata,
she has come here once again to see me and to hear my Dharma.
I taught her that supreme Dharma of perfect enlightenment;
having heard it and rejoiced accordingly, she departed for heaven, filled with joy.
Thus, monks, those who desire what is auspicious should always keep this in mind, and having gone for refuge, they should constantly serve the Three Jewels.
Those who honor the Three Jewels, having recollected them and gone for refuge, do not go to an evil destiny; they always proceed to a happy destiny.
Those who, out of negligence, revile the Three Jewels and reject them, do not attain a happy rebirth; they dwell forever in hell.
Therefore, having recollected the eternal Three Jewels and gone for refuge,
cultivate them with reverence and devote yourselves to them with the aspiration for awakening.
In this way, may auspiciousness be yours always, everywhere, and at all times;
and having fulfilled the conduct of awakening in due order, you shall also attain perfect enlightenment.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, those monks joyfully assented,
saying "So be it," and they constantly venerated the Three Jewels.
Thus has that which was instructed by my Guru been declared to you by me;
having heard this and having caused others to hear it, always venerate the Three Jewels.
Then, by practicing the conduct of awakening (bodhicaryā) step by step,
you shall be completely liberated from all evil and proceed to the Land of Bliss (Sukhāvatī).
Having heard this which was thus instructed by the venerable monk Upagupta,
the king, together with his retinue, approved, saying, "So be it."

Those who, with joyful minds and through faith, having heard this *Śālapuṣpa-avadāna*— which was spoken by the Best of Sages and is the power of the Perfectly Awakened One— proclaim it to others, desiring enlightenment,
shall be liberated from all afflictions, possessors of every virtue, and devoted to the conduct of awakening.
Having acted for the benefit of the world, they enter the abode of the supreme Victors with great joy.
Thus ends the Śālapuṣpāvadāna.
VI. The Sūkaryavadāna.
Once again, this Lord of Ascetics, Upagupta, born from a portion of the Victor,
spoke to the king in order to proclaim the merit arising from the recollection of the Three Jewels.
I shall explain to you that state of possessing great merit, which arises from the recollection of the Three Jewels; listen, O King, with a concentrated mind.
Indeed, it is the natural law for gods destined to fall from heaven that five portents appear within themselves.
For at the time of his passing, even unstained garments would become soiled,
and unfading garlands would suddenly wither.
A foul odor would issue from his body, sweat would break out from his armpits,
and when the time for his fall arrived, he would find no stability upon his own seat.
These five signs shall appear for all those subject to falling from heaven at the moment their descent is imminent.
Thus, for a certain son of the gods who was subject to the law of falling away,
these five omens appeared prior to his descent.
Then that son of the gods, subject to the law of decay, being despondent and realizing that his fall from heaven was inevitable, cried out in distress.
Having whirled about while staying in his own celestial chariot, and having fainted after turning around,
he regained consciousness once more and lamented, wailing in distress.
"Alas, Mandākinī, you who are filled with golden lotuses and carry holy waters!
Having bathed in you, how shall I fall away and go to a miserable rebirth?"
Alas! Having abandoned Caitraratha, where shall I sport as I desire?
Alas! Having left the lovely Nandana grove, where shall I find delight?
Alas! Having abandoned the divine Miśrikā grove, where shall I now delight in the lovely Kuhā?
Alas! Having abandoned the Pāruṣya grove, where shall I sport with the throngs of apsarases?
Where shall I find happiness without the pale woolen rug?
Alas! Having abandoned the assembly of the gods, where shall I hear well-spoken words?
Alas, alas! Having fallen from the beautiful city of Sudarśana to Vraja, when shall I behold again the Vaijayanta palace?
Alas! When I was formerly gladdened together with the gods headed by Śakra, where now is that happiness of mine, such that I shall not even be able to hear of it?
"Alas, O Queen! Having abandoned the nectar of immortality, what shall I now consume?
Having enjoyed divine sensual pleasures, I shall once again resort to a miserable rebirth."
"How much suffering must I endure while dwelling in the hells?
Having fallen from this divine and great enthusiasm, I have gone to hell."
Tormented by great suffering, how shall I endure it then?
Alas, I am ruined by my own sin; what evil deed have I committed?
Since I have fallen from this heaven, why should I go again to the hells? I shall employ a means by which I might not go to an evil rebirth.
Who could be my teacher here who might establish me in the Dharma?
For by the Dharma even a living being is protected, even when situated in hell.
Without Dharma, even a god here falls again from heaven;
what shall I do, where shall I go? I perceive no remedy in this matter.
In every way, having passed away from here, I shall surely go to an evil rebirth;
and having passed away from here, where in the world will I obtain a birth?
Having thus steadied his mind with fortitude, he perceived by means of his own intellect that after passing away from this life, he was to obtain birth as a pig on the seventh day.
Having thus seen his own state of sleep, he fell down unconscious;
then Mahendra saw him fallen upon the ground, deprived of his senses.
Having seen him, he approached suddenly and sprinkled him with showers of nectar;
then, having regained consciousness, he slowly rose up toward his lord.
Having seen him, he embraced his feet, bowed down, and while weeping made this petition:
"Alas, alas! O Lord, you are Mahendra, the sovereign and master of all the worlds."
Seeing me fallen here below, you ought not to disregard me;
for you are the king of the worlds, the master, the sustainer, the lord, and the sovereign.
O Lord and instructor of the Dharma, you ought to protect me;
for indeed, apart from you, no other protector exists for me here.
Therefore, O Lord, look upon me with compassion and lift me up;
for if even you, O Protector, are unable to save me, [what else can be done]?
"Alas! Who else but you could have rescued me so that, having bathed with you in the Maṇḍākinī, I am now purified in soul and shall not go to hell as a wretched man?"
And how could I go to hell and dwell there practicing impurity,
after having constantly moved about with hosts of apsarases in the Nandana grove?
Delighted, I used to enjoy myself with divine songs and instrumental music; today, however, I have fallen here upon the earth, in the outskirts of Rājagṛha.
"Indeed, on the seventh day, I shall take birth as a pig;
there, I shall with great difficulty consume even impurities such as urine and excrement."
Having obtained [food] and having eaten it, I shall wander, harassed by packs of hunters,
having thus become the offspring of a pig for many thousands of years.
Having thus enjoyed divine nectar and delighted with you, I shall dwell perpetually, moving about while turning back, within the mire of impurity.
For how could I go to the hells and wander about consuming impurities,
having abandoned this wish-fulfilling tree that grants whatever fruit one desires?
"Taking refuge under a tree in the wilderness, what shall I eat then?
In every way I have fallen from this state, for I am driven by my own karma."
And I shall go to hell to experience various sufferings;
therefore, O compassionate one, you must provide me with the means [to escape them].
By which I may quickly be freed from an evil rebirth and attain a heavenly state;
protect me in every way, O Lord, if you have compassion for me.
Seeing me fallen, you ought not to remain indifferent;
for you alone are the Teacher of the world, the sovereign, and the Lord of all beings.
Therefore, it behoves you to exert yourself quickly to rescue me;
O Lord, this vision of yours shall indeed be my very last.
"Indeed, a reunion would be difficult to attain even in hundreds of thousands of births"—
thus lamenting, that son of the gods addressed the Lord of the Gods.
Having bowed at his feet and gazed upon him, he stood with tears streaming from his face;
then Śakra, the lord of the gods, seeing him thus lamenting, [spoke].
With a heart overcome by compassion, he spoke to comfort him:
"Do not weep, O noble one; take heart and be steadfast."
Why are efforts made at all, since death is certain in every way?
For Death is indeed possessed of great power, the bringer of an end to all sentient beings.
All are carried away by death; by what is death itself slain?
For it is unextinguishable everywhere, even throughout all the three realms.
For all living beings, death is certain and inevitable;
therefore, do not fear death, for what can be accomplished through despondency?
Therefore, maintaining fortitude, take refuge in the Triple Gem;
having gone for refuge, remember them constantly with a concentrated mind.
Then, having escaped from an evil rebirth, you shall attain a happy state;
for this alone is the great means for attaining auspiciousness within saṃsāra.
For there exists nothing else that is constant amidst the universal certainty of death;
therefore, setting aside all other concerns, one should keep the Three Jewels in mind.
Recite "Homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha" and take refuge;
those who die while maintaining mindfulness of the Three Jewels partake in merit.
Having gradually attained the conduct of enlightenment, they went at the end to the Land of Bliss;
and you too, possessing great merit, having died while recollecting the Three Jewels, [shall go there].
"Having gradually attained the conduct of awakening, you shall go to Sukhāvatī.
Having heard this command from Indra, that son of the gods then—
Having expressed his assent with the words "So be it," and having bowed once more, he spoke thus:
"From this day forward, O Great Indra, I shall always keep the Three Jewels in mind."
"Having gone for refuge to them, one should indeed become a lay follower (upāsaka).
Having said this, he stood before Mahendra with palms joined in reverence.
Having recollected the Three Jewels, he uttered this salutation:
"Homage to the Auspicious Buddha; homage to the Protector Dharma."
Homage to the Saṅgha, the Protector; I always bow and worship it.
From this day forth, I shall always go for refuge to the Three Jewels.
"May I always be a lay devotee; I bow to you and shall constantly remember you.
Having spoken thus, that son of the gods, having met with the law of time, passed away.
By virtue of his great merit, he was reborn in the Tuṣita heaven;
for it is the natural law of the gods that those gods who have passed away from heaven [are born here].
They would indeed go to the lower worlds and not to the higher realms;
then Śakra, that lord of men, saw him fallen from heaven.
He looked downward to see where he had taken birth,
and whether or not he had been conceived in the womb of a sow.
He looked for him everywhere but could not see him anywhere;
then Śakra was struck with wonder and looked again with his divine eye.
He observed thus: "Where does this one take birth?
Alas, he has been born among the animals and is being reborn among the hungry ghosts.
Then he looked all around to see if he had been born in the hells; yet, among those three states of woe, he did not see him anywhere.
Then he saw whether he had been born in the worlds of men;
yet even there, the Lord of the Gods did not perceive him anywhere.
Then he was reborn in the realms of the Four Great Kings;
yet, looking everywhere throughout them, he did not see him.
Then Śakra, filled with wonder, looked about among the thirty-three gods;
yet even there he did not see him anywhere at all, nor in any direction. Thus he searched throughout all the worlds for the source of that being's appearance.
Not seeing him, Śakra was struck with wonder and thought again:
"Oh, what a great marvel this is, that even I cannot see it!"
Where indeed is he born? I do not believe that its mode of occurrence can be known;
who else but a Buddha could possibly know his way of being?
The Buddha alone is the seer of the world, possessing the six superknowledges and knowing the three times;
therefore, having gone from here, I shall attend upon the Perfectly Awakened One.
"Having thus informed him, I ought now to ask about his conduct.
Having reflected thus in his mind, that Lord of the Devas was filled with wonder.
He suddenly descended upon the Victor’s hermitage in Jetavana forest;
there, beholding the Sugata, he was filled with joy and wonder.
Having prostrated and stood before him with palms joined in reverence, he said:
"O Blessed One, may you understand that for which I have come here."
Nevertheless, I wish to ask this; you should deign to instruct me:
one son of the gods has passed away, fallen from heaven and departed.
"He is not seen by me anywhere throughout the six worlds;
O Teacher, where is he born? He is not seen by me anywhere."
"In what place does his birth occur? You ought to instruct us on that.
Having heard these words of Indra, the Fully Awakened One, the Lord of Sages, [replied].
They pointed out the abode of that meritorious being to Indra:
"O Kauśika, there is a world-system renowned by the name Tuṣita."
"Having gone there, that deity rejoices after passing away from the Three Refuges"—
having heard this and other such words instructed by the Lord of Sages, the ruler of the thirty-three gods [acted accordingly].
Filled with wonder and a deeply serene mind, he bowed down and uttered this praise:
"O, the Buddha! O, the Dharma! O, the Sangha, the bringer of auspiciousness!"
Those beings who go for refuge to the Buddha do not go to an evil rebirth, even if they go merely for the sake of seeking protection. They go to an abode of merit.
Having abandoned all transgressions, those who go for refuge to the Dharma attend upon the divine world; they do not go to an evil rebirth,
but having cast off human bodies, they attend upon divine bodies.
Those who go for refuge to the Saṅgha do not go to an evil rebirth;
having abandoned all sufferings, they enjoy divine happiness.
Blessed are those auspicious persons who, recollecting the Three Jewels, proceed with certainty toward death as they advance toward the state of perfect enlightenment.

Then the Blessed One, having heard this well-spoken speech by Śakra, spoke to Kauśika, the lord of the gods, describing it accordingly: *athāsau bhagavāñ chrutvā śakreṇaivaṃ subhāṣitaṃ / tathānuvarṇayan prāha kauśikaṃ taṃ surādhipam //* Rm_6.83{83} //
It is even so, O Lord of Gods, just as you have spoken;
blessed and auspicious are those men who take refuge in the Three Jewels.
Those who go for refuge to the Buddha do not go to an evil rebirth;
having utterly conquered the enemy of the afflictions, they shall attain perfect enlightenment.
Those who go for refuge to the Dharma do not go to an evil rebirth;
liberated from the dharmas of Māra, they shall attain the dharmas of awakening.
Those who go for refuge to the Saṅgha do not go to an evil rebirth.
Completely liberated from their transgressions, they proceed to Sukhāvatī.
Those who do not take refuge in the Lord of Sages wander in the ocean of existence;
fallen from the path to perfect enlightenment, ruined, they go to an evil rebirth.
Those who do not hear the true Dharma are scorched by the afflictions;
being wicked and delighting in the teachings of Māra, they are ruined and go to an evil destiny.
Those who do not honor the Saṅgha do not know the true path.
Constantly tormented by suffering, they fall and go to an evil destiny;
those who revile the Three Jewels are wicked partisans of Māra. They do not walk upon the true path; being ruined, they go to an evil destiny.
Therefore, those virtuous men who always desire a fortunate rebirth should,
with joy, call to mind the Three Jewels and take refuge in them.
Those who remember the Three Jewels do not go to an evil destiny;
having abandoned all transgressions, they quickly go to Sukhāvatī.
Having heard the Dharma of the Lord of Jinas in Sukhāvatī and rejoiced in it,
they attain the thought of awakening and practice the conduct of awakening.
Then, having gradually fulfilled those [perfections] and reached the further shore of conventional practice,
and having attained the conduct of ultimate reality, they shall fully obtain nirvāṇa.
O Kauśika, having understood that this is indeed the seed of the paths to enlightenment,
those who desire awakening should constantly practice the recollection of the Three Jewels.
One should never at any time abandon the constant recollection of the Three Jewels;
having gone for refuge to those Three Jewels, practice accordingly.
Having heard this command from that Lord of Sages, Kauśika, having thus given his assent, rejoiced with a serene mind.
Then, having bowed to the Blessed One with palms joined in reverence,
and having circumambulated him three times, he bowed once more and departed for heaven.
Then, having gone to the city of the gods and staying in the Sudharmā assembly hall,
he addressed the inhabitants of the celestial realms and related what had occurred.
O all you hosts of gods, listen with concentrated minds to that which is called the wonderful, highly meritorious cause of perfect enlightenment.
It is indeed the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the gods that whichever gods fall from the celestial realm (*nāka*), they all go downwards; none of them go upwards.
But now, those gods who have fallen from the heavenly realm should go to the higher realms by taking refuge in the Three Jewels, and not to the lower realms.
"Behold, such-and-such a son of the gods has gone for refuge to the Triple Gem;
having fallen from heaven, he has been reborn here in Tuṣita and rejoices."
And you too, having seen that, being composed in mind toward the Three Jewels,
go for refuge and always honor them with devotion, keeping them in mind.
Then you shall never go to the miserable realms;
having always enjoyed divine bliss, you will proceed to Sukhāvatī.
Those who go for refuge to the Buddha do not go to an evil rebirth;
having completely conquered the enmity of the afflictions, they shall attain the state of perfect enlightenment.
Those who go for refuge to the Dharma do not go to an evil rebirth;
liberated from the teachings of Māra, they shall attain the qualities of a Buddha.
Those who have gone for refuge to the Saṅgha do not go to an evil destiny;
liberated from all misdeeds, they shall go to Sukhāvatī.
Those who do not venerate the Three Jewels wander in the ocean of existence;
revilers of the True Dharma, fallen and ruined, they go to an evil destiny.
Wandering through the miserable realms and experiencing various sufferings, those wicked ones continue their course; they do not go to a happy rebirth at all.
Those who always desire to abandon suffering and attain happiness should constantly remember the Three Jewels and, having gone for refuge, worship them.
Then may you always have auspiciousness, may you never go to an evil destiny,
may you go only to a happy rebirth, and may you also attain perfect enlightenment.
Thus commanded by that Lord of the Gods who sought their welfare,
all the gods then went for refuge to the Three Jewels.
And always recollecting [him], they entered [the path] with such reverence.
In this way, those gods who at that time had gone for refuge to the Three Jewels did not fall into a lower state even after passing away from heaven.
Then, ascending upwards, they went to the Tuṣita abode;
having gone for refuge to the Triple Gem, they took shelter with Maitreya.
Likewise, Śakra, seeing them all taking refuge in Maitreya, rejoiced along with the gods, expressing his approval.
Thus it was declared to me by my teacher, and so shall it be told to you by me;
considering this, O Great King, go for refuge to the Triple Gem.
Then, may auspiciousness be yours eternally and certainly everywhere;
having attained the stages of the conduct of awakening in due order, may you reach the state of perfect enlightenment.
And having diligently awakened the subjects, O Great King,
you have established them in the refuge of the Three Jewels for the increase of the Dharma.
Having heard these well-spoken words thus instructed by Upagupta, the king, together with his retinue, rejoiced, saying, "So be it."
Those who desire to attain merit, who with joyful minds constantly hear or cause others to hear this *Sūkarikā-avadāna*, do not go to an evil rebirth;
having conquered the hosts of afflictions, they act for the benefit of the three realms and remain devoted to the conduct of awakening.
The inhabitants of the Tuṣita heaven enjoy the company of the Bodhisattva Maitreya to their heart's content.
Thus ends the Sūkaryyavadāna in the Ratnāvadānamālā.
VII. The Vapuṣmatkumārāvadāna.
Then King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence and filled with joy,
bowed down to his teacher Upagupta and spoke once more as follows:
"Venerable One, I wish to hear yet another well-spoken teaching;
for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, you should please grant it."
When King Aśoka, the ruler of the earth, had thus made his request,
the ascetic Upagupta, seeing the king, spoke to him.
"Excellent, O King! Composing yourself, listen for the increase of merit;
I shall relate to you exactly as it was told to me by my teacher."
In former times there was the Blessed Buddha, Śrīghana, the Lion of the Śākyas,
the teacher of all branches of knowledge and virtues, the guide of the three realms.
The Sugata, the Arhat, the one of great supernormal knowledge, the King of Dharma, the Tathāgata, the Victor,
the portion of Samantabhadra, who possesses the four sublime abodes.
At one time, he dwelt there in that most excellent city named Kapila,
in a delightful grove of banyan trees, together with his disciples.
And at that time, the gods, asuras, great kings, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras had assembled there to hear the Dharma.
Garuḍas, serpent-kings, perfected ones, knowledge-holders, planetary spirits,
yogins, ascetics, sages, and celibate students;
Kings and kṣatriyas as well, vaiśya ministers and counselors,
guild-leaders and caravan-traders, and even the citizens and country-folk.
In this way, other beings as well, who desired the qualities of the true Dharma,
all approached and paid homage to that Lord of Sages.
Having honored him, placed him at their head, and surrounded him on all sides,
they stood waiting with palms joined in reverence to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they were all seekers of the Dharma,
taught the supreme Dharma, which is virtuous in its beginning, middle, and end.
Having drunk that nectar of the Dharma, they were all thoroughly gladdened;
honoring it with constant faith, they attended upon him and served him.
And the Blessed One, likewise always for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings,
remained together with the community of monks after having performed the teaching of the True Dharma.
And at that time, in that city of Kapilavastu,
there was a Śākya who was a great saint, possessing vast enjoyments and immense wealth.
He brought home a wife from a family equal to his own, and together with that beloved, he took his pleasure, providing her with every enjoyment.
While he was thus enjoying himself, his wife became pregnant;
then, in due time, she gave birth to a son who was divinely beautiful.
With a complexion surpassing that of mortals, adorned with divine ornaments,
possessing a subtle skin, beautiful limbs, a fair hue, and a captivating appearance.
He was of great majesty, pleasing, handsome, and inspiring;
he was beautiful, with well-nourished limbs, adorned with all the auspicious marks.
There, having seen that boy Subhadrika, his father was suddenly filled with joy; he summoned his kinsmen and spoke to them thus.
"Sirs, behold this son of mine, who is divinely beautiful;
having performed the birth ceremony for him, let his name be proclaimed."
Having heard this spoken by him, his kinsmen, being of one mind,
beheld that divine child, of excellent complexion and exceedingly beautiful.
Having closed their eyes and reached a consensus, and having observed the marks on his body,
they spoke together to establish his name after performing the birth festival:
"Since this boy possesses a divine form and is exceedingly beautiful..."
"Therefore, let him be known by the name Vapusmān.
Having spoken thus, all those members of his kinly group [departed].
Having gone before that Śākya, they spoke thus:
"This son of yours possesses a divine form and is endowed with virtues."
"Therefore, let this son of yours be known by the name Vapuṣmān.
Having assented with "So be it," the father [spoke] to that son, his own offspring.
He was entrusted for protection to eight nurses;
then that boy was attended by those foster-mothers with their various ministrations.
Protected, nurtured, and nourished like a lotus in a pond,
as he gradually grew up, he eventually became a prince.
Then he proceeded to sport together with his friends and companions;
wherever that handsome youth wandered as he moved about upon the earth, [he was followed].
In every direction there, the regions of the earth became pure;
such was he, whose intention was auspicious and who was renowned for great merit and majesty.
Compassionate, possessed of great faith, bearing the welfare of both himself and others,
desiring the Dharma, of auspicious nature, worthy of worship and honor, and having conquered his senses.
The handsome prince was worthy of salutation;
then, impelled by the ripening of his past karma, the young boy [proceeded].
Accompanied by his circle of friends, that handsome prince went out from the city;
then, seeing the Jetavana forest from afar, he was filled with joy.
He suddenly approached that great garden to enjoy himself;
then, having sat down and beheld the garden, he was filled with joy.
Seeing the ascetics of peaceful form in the monastery, he entered full of joy;
there he beheld the Blessed One seated amidst the assembly.
Adorned with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor characteristics,
embellished by a fathom-wide radiance, desirable, and possessing a splendor exceeding a hundred suns.
Seeing that form of Samantabhadra, like a jewel-limbed being come to life, he, with a deeply serene mind, approached and stood before him.
Having bowed at the feet of that sage, he sat down to listen to the Dharma;
then the Blessed One, seeing that his mind was purified, [taught him].
He taught the Noble Truths and the Path that accomplishes enlightenment;
having heard what was spoken by the Sugata, Vapuṣmān was filled with great joy.
Distressed by his pursuit of worldly existence, he desired the quality of the True Dharma;
having shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity with the vajra of wisdom, he [attained it].
Having attained the fruit of stream-entry, the wise one became a seer of the truth;
considering cyclic existence to be unstable, he was entirely free from desire for the enjoyments of worldly life.
He desired to practice the religious life in the well-proclaimed dispensation of the Sugata;
then, having gone before the Lord of Munis with palms joined in reverence, he spoke.
Bowing at his feet with a serene countenance, he requested the going forth into homelessness.
Homage to you, O Blessed One, Teacher; may you be my refuge in this world.
Grant me that vow of renunciation, so that I may lead the life of a celibate student.
Seeing that he had thus made his request, and perceiving that the young man was truly devoted to the practice of the religious life, the Blessed One spoke to him as follows:
"O Prince, if you indeed have a desire to practice the life of renunciation, then first obtain the permission of your parents; having done so, come back, and I shall grant it to you."
Having heard this instruction of the Lord of Sages, he said, "So be it," and bowing at his feet with a joyful heart, he quickly returned to his own home.
Then, having arrived at home and stood before his parents,
he bowed with palms joined in reverence and related the events that had occurred.
"O Mother, O Father, today the Fully Awakened One is seen, never before beheld;
he is complete with all the marks of perfection, divinely radiant and most beautiful."
Seated in the midst of the assemblies, he speaks the supreme Dharma;
his well-spoken words, an ambrosia never heard before, are being heard.
Having drunk that nectar of your well-spoken words, my mind is not yet satiated;
I now desire to take a vow to drink that ambrosia once again.
Many other monks who were practitioners of the holy life also saw it.
Those of peaceful conduct, pure in nature, and whose minds are filled with compassion and pity—
now indeed I desire to practice the vow that is concordant with them.
"If you have compassion for me, grant me your permission.
Such were the words of his own son, which were as firm as a thunderbolt.
Hearing this, the two parents fainted and fell to the ground;
then, through their son's efforts, they regained consciousness once more.
Embracing her own son, she lamented for him thus:
"Alas, my son! How can you be so ignorant? Alas, my child! You are our beloved."
"Alas, my son, by whom are you being deceived? Alas, my father, what indeed do you desire?
Alas, Jīva, how can you go away somewhere, having abandoned us here in solitude?"
"You are delightful and very dear; by what sorrow will you depart?
Has some suffering ever been inflicted upon you by us at any time?"
"From what does what suffering arise? Tell me that, if you wish," thus did that father lament to his son with his mind.
Restraining him with persistence in order to awaken him, he spoke thus:
"O prince, you are still in the bloom of youth; you are very delicate and have been raised in comfort."

"O son, you are unable to endure cold and heat, you are accustomed to whatever you desire for enjoyment, and you are unacquainted with even the slightest suffering; how then could you renounce the world?"
Having renounced the household life and gone forth, you should always dwell in foreign lands;
clad in robes, you should personally sustain yourself by begging for alms.
How would you dwell in the forest and wilderness where many creatures roam?
How would you travel through the impenetrable jungle, crowded with many bandits?
And how could you remain alone at the foot of a tree in a desolate place?
Standing in a cemetery, beholding the corpses, how would you not tremble?
And how could you sleep in an empty house inhabited by spirits?
How can you wish to practice such an extremely difficult course of conduct?
"Therefore, do not set your mind on the vow of renunciation; turn back!
Having heard these words of mine, remain at home and enjoy happiness."
For those who constantly wander forth, there is suffering; what is accomplished by this practice of hardship?
If you have a desire for the Dharma, my son, remain at home and observe the vows.
Listening to the treatises on Dharma and causing many people to hear them,
and having practiced giving, you, with a purified soul, should constantly venerate the Triple Gem.
"For one who has nothing at all in his house, and no kinsman or friend,
nor even the support of a companion, the life of renunciation is appropriate.
But what will be achieved for you, my son, by this mendicancy that ends in a beggar's bowl?"
"Abandon that desire in every way; practice the Dharma at home and live happily.
Having heard what his father said, Vapuṣmān was filled with apprehension.
Bowing once more at the feet of his parents, he replied, awakening them:
"It is true, father, that there is happiness in the home; it is the highest among all duties."

Even if you possess abundant wealth, great pleasures of sensual enjoyment, dependents in your home who must be supported, and the riches required for those ends— you should still strive for it [the Dharma].
For there is great hardship in acquiring wealth, and even in its preservation, one must exert effort;
there are many ways for prosperity to perish, such as kings, fire, water, and thieves.
In an instant they might snatch it away; how then could one endure that suffering?
At the end of prosperity there will be misfortune; whose prosperity is ever stable?
In adversity, fortitude fails; from a lack of fortitude, one becomes afflicted;
being afflicted, one falls into fault; how then can there be a mind set upon merit?
When Lakṣmī is angry with one who lacks merit, she will not resort to his dwelling at all;
and in a home devoid of Lakṣmī, how can there be any sphere for Dharma?
But in prosperity, one gains pride; for from pride, intoxication is born.
From intoxication, one becomes negligent regarding the Dharma; how then can there be Dharma in the home at such a time?
But that which is to be enjoyed through desire obtained by unrighteousness is a means solely for evil;
for the sake of desire the worlds are tormented, and for the sake of desire they partake in suffering.
They are frustrated for the sake of sensual desires; therefore, how can there be happiness in desire?
For thus, my dear, do various fears exist everywhere.
For those dwelling in existence within the three realms, who is there whose fear does not exist?
By fate, sufferings and pleasures arise everywhere.
Wherever the afflicted self goes in pursuit of happiness, there arise sufferings and fears born of the mind and its defilements.
In whatever place he may go, even there he is struck by sufferings and fears arising from karma; yet wherever he goes with a mind fixed on the Dharma and a desire for the welfare of others,
in all those places he moves about happily and without fear.
The ascetic finds delight precisely in that which is a source of fear for the world:
in solitude, in uninhabited wildernesses, at the roots of trees, and in mountain caves.
A renunciant may dwell happily meditating even in an empty house or a cremation ground;
for the yogi who guards his own duty and has a self-controlled mind, from what source could there be fear?
What is the use of much speaking? My mind seeks Nirvana;
therefore, being indifferent even toward my own body, I shall go forth as a wanderer to attain that Nirvana.
Therefore, grant me permission to accomplish the vow of renunciation;
if permission is not granted, I shall die, of this there is no doubt.

Having heard these words of insistence from his son, the father, afflicted by the pain of separation, spoke again to that son: (Rm 92) Thus, having heard such persistent speech from his own son, the father, pained by the sorrow of parting, spoke once more to that son. (Rm_7.85{85})
"O son, do not act so rashly with a mind longing for death;
even if you are entirely irreversible and must certainly go, [do not hasten it]."
Since you desire to undertake a vow with a mind seeking the true Dharma,
go forth, my son, out of faith in the well-proclaimed teaching of the Buddha.
Having heard what was thus spoken by her husband, his mother fell down in a swoon;
after a long time she regained consciousness and, weeping, spoke to her son.
"Alas, my son! How can you go away somewhere in solitude, leaving me behind?
Alas, you are my very life; why do you see [this] and yet desire to renounce the world?"
"Mother, never at any time have I caused you even the slightest suffering;
by what sorrow, then, does your mind desire to go forth into the religious life?"
"Renunciation is fitting, my son, when one is old or impoverished;
but since you are still young, how could you possibly practice renunciation?"
"As long as I have life, my son, do not go anywhere;
as long as there is prosperity in the house, dwell there happily after enjoying it."
"When I have met my death, when I have fallen into misfortune at home, and when I am abandoned by kinsmen and friends— then you may go as you desire."
Even when his parents had spoken thus, Vapuṣmat, fearing obstacles,
bowed at their feet and suddenly departed from the house.
Then, having gone to the Bamboo Grove and bowed with reverence to the Sage,
he joined his palms in supplication and requested ordination.
"O Lord, having received permission from my father, I have now come;
therefore, grant me the going-forth, the vows, and the five precepts."
Having received full ordination and the training rules for virtuous conduct,
I shall practice the holy life, firm in my resolve for perfect enlightenment.
From this day forward, O Great Buddha, I go for refuge to you,
along with the Dharma and the Saṅgha, with devotion of body, speech, and mind.
When this was said, the Blessed One, having looked and touched that head with his hand, took hold of him while addressing him: "Come, monk; you are a youth."
When the Sugata said, "Come," he stood there with shaven head, holding an alms-bowl, possessing a radiant body and wearing saffron robes;
his senses were instantly pacified, and through his devotion to the Buddha, he shone with a golden luster.
Having attained self-possession through the grace of the Sage, he applied himself and dwelt in meditative concentration;
indeed, exerting himself on the path to awakening, he strove thus in the Dharma of the Fully Awakened One.

Having realized that all of saṃsāra is struck by impermanence and that the course of the three realms is destructive, he abandoned all afflictions; thus, self-restrained, he became a preeminent Arhat in the presence of others, a member of the Saṅgha.
Completely free from passion, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, his mind like space, dwelling in the fragrance of virtue,
he shattered the shell of ignorance as if it were an egg, and attained the superknowledges and the analytical insights.

Because he was utterly indifferent to gain and honor, he became worthy of worship, respect, and salutation by the gods, asuras, and humans of Śakra’s realm; for he was one who dwelt in the divine abodes (brahmavihāra).
Then all those monks, filled with wonder upon seeing him,
bowed down to the Blessed One and asked about his past deeds.
"By what karma, O Protector, has he become so handsome and exceedingly beautiful; and having gone forth, how did he attain Arhatship and become a knower of the self?"
When they had thus questioned him, the Blessed Lord, the Protector, spoke to them:
"O monks, listen; I shall tell you what karma was performed by him."
By this it is shown: "What action has been performed by one, how could it be experienced by another?
For whatever action has been performed by someone, that very person indeed experiences its result."
In the ninety-first eon, there arose in the world one named Vipaśyin, the omniscient Arhat, the King of Dharma, the Tathāgata.
Endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the doer of good, the Victor;
the omniscient, unsurpassed Protector, the charioteer of men to be tamed.
The Teacher, the guide of those dwelling in the three realms, the mine of virtues,
the giver of the jewel of the True Dharma— that Blessed One is a sun of merit.
He took refuge in the capital city of King Vaṃdhuma,
together with hosts of monks, disciples, and also groups of bodhisattvas.
For the benefit of all sentient beings, he taught the supreme Dharma,
which is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end, and follows the conduct of awakening.
Then, having performed all the deeds of a Buddha without exception,
he entered into nirvāṇa, as calm as a fire when its fuel is exhausted.
Then King Bandhumat had his body cremated with fire;
having enshrined his relics, he erected a great and lofty stūpa.
There, having established a stūpa made of jewels with its sixfold parts,
he caused a great festival to be performed with constant offerings and worship.
Having generated great enthusiasm through songs, instrumental music, and dances that spread immense joy, they established a truly magnificent festival.
One day,
a certain impoverished man arrived at the courtyard of that [house] on another such great festival day.
Having entered there into the courtyard of the stūpa, he beheld flowers scattered all around that had become withered.
Seeing those withered and impure flowers scattered all around, he reflected thus:
"This is the shrine of the Lord of Munis, Vipaśyin, that ocean of virtues."
A stupa made of precious jewels is worshipped by all the worlds;
yet this [stupa] is honored even by these withered flowers from the offering, stirred by the wind.
For it becomes crowded, soiled, and indeed disfigured by impurity;
therefore, these flowers are everywhere considered as *nirmālya* (worn-out offerings).
Having removed [the impurities], I shall quickly cleanse this for the sake of purification.
Having reflected thus, that poor man indeed removed the withered flower offerings.
Having swept the courtyard of the stūpa on all sides until it was level,
he saw that the entire courtyard of the stūpa was now free of dust and thoroughly purified; with a joyful heart, he bowed and made this aspiration:
"Whatever merit I have acquired here by removing the withered offerings from this stupa of the Jina, by sweeping it clean, and by making it beautiful—
by this merit, may I always be liberated from the miserable realms."
May I become a knower of self, attaining such qualities and knowledge;
and may I likewise [attain] such a Teacher, the Perfectly Awakened One, the sun of wisdom.
Relying upon [this practice], may I attain a fortunate rebirth;
thus maintaining my vow and constantly taking refuge in this way.
Having gone for refuge to that stūpa, may I always worship the Three Jewels.
O monks, what do you think? As for that man who was poor—
This very person endowed with such a body must indeed be known as him and not otherwise,
because he has purified the courtyard of the stupa through his contemplation of the qualities of the Perfectly Awakened One.
Having thoroughly swept and completely purified [the ground] on all sides at that time,
by the ripening of that merit, he was now born into a wealthy family.
Because a prayer was made by that pure-minded one after bowing before the stupa, he has become handsome, lovely, and possessed of a divine body.
Therefore, even today within my teaching, he has become one who has gone forth and attained arhatship;
thus has he pleased the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Sugata, the Jina.
"By this monk who has attained awakening and lives the holy life—
know that such is the nature of action, whether well-done or ill-done."
By whomsoever an action was performed, by that very person its fruit is experienced;
for actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Having obtained the necessary conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit;
for karma that has not been experienced is never exhausted by any means whatsoever.
Karma is not burned by fires, nor is it dried up by winds;
it is neither moistened by waters, nor does it decay within the earth.
Otherwise, the course of actions would not exist at all until the end of existence;
white deeds would always result only in purity, and black deeds would always result in miserable rebirths.
Indeed, mixed [karmas] are experienced by all beings together with those that are unmixed;
therefore, having cast aside black karmas as well as those that are mixed, [one should cultivate white ones].
"Those who desire happiness should practice only auspicious deeds"—
thus did all those monks and the people gathered in the assembly respond.
Having drunk the nectar of the Buddha’s speech, those who desire merit rejoiced;
"It is even so, O Great King," thus did I hear it spoken by my teacher.
Having heard this, you too should likewise perform meritorious deeds alone;
for merit alone is the savior, the friend, the ally, and the benefactor.
No one else whatsoever exists here or in the hereafter for those wandering in existence;
therefore, having heard this for oneself, merit should always be performed with reverence.
"And having thus caused the people to hear [the Dharma], always establish them in merit"—
this was the instruction given by the preceptor, the monk Upagupta.
Having heard this, the king, together with the people, rejoiced, saying, "So be it.
Those who hear this celebrated life-story of the embodied one here, and those who cause others to hear it—
With minds purified and liberated from afflictions, they surely proceed to the abodes of the Sugatas.
Thus ends the *Vapuṣmat-avadāna* in the *Ratnāvadānamālā*.
VIII. The *Praśnottara-avadāna*.
Then King Aśoka, longing for the virtues of the Perfectly Awakened One,
bowed to his teacher Upagupta and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke thus:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken word;
you should relate it to me exactly as it was instructed to you by your teacher."
When the king had thus questioned him, Upagupta, the ascetic born from a portion of the Jina, spoke again to that lord of men.
Listen, O King, I shall speak just as it was told to me by my teacher;
having heard it, you too must likewise perform this means for accomplishing Dharma.
And once upon a time, that Lion of the Śākyas— the compassionate one, the omniscient Sugata, the Protector, the Teacher, and the Lord of the three realms— [appeared].
The Buddha is the lord of all sciences, the possessor of the six superknowledges, the sovereign of sages;
he is the conqueror of Māra, the subduer, the Arhat, the King of Dharma, and the Tathāgata.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, he dwelt together with his disciples at the Jetavana monastery, located in an hermitage outside Śrāvastī.
And also by hosts of bodhisattvas, by lay followers and mendicants,
by hosts of gods and asuras, and by humans of the four castes and so forth.
And by the four great kings together with their armies and retinues,
and by all the citizens who desired the qualities of the True Dharma.
Having been honored and worshipped, and having circumambulated him while being placed at the head of the assembly, that Blessed One shone as he sat upon the lion-throne in the midst of the hall.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that assembly gathered together,
taught the supreme Dharma, which is virtuous in its beginning, middle, and end.
Having drunk that nectar of the Dharma, all those people were filled with joy;
bowing once more to the Blessed One, they returned to their respective abodes.
Then, at night, that Blessed One entered the meditation chamber;
having assumed the cross-legged posture, he remained there, absorbed in meditative concentration.
Then, on that night, a certain deity descended from heaven and,
illuminating the Jeta Grove with her own radiance, sat down there.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that goddess who had approached him,
gazed upon her, addressed her, and enlightened her in this way.
"Welcome, O deity! Is it well with you? Come, sir; tell me for what purpose you have come, and I shall fulfill it."
When the Lord of Munis had thus instructed him, that deity,
having found the opportunity to inquire, approached him joyfully and with great delight.
There, having gone before him, bowed at his feet with palms joined in reverence,
and performed three circumambulations, he stood to one side of the Sage.
Then, through the power of that deity, the entire Jeta Grove shone forth,
clearly illuminated by a magnificent radiance.
Seeing him thus illuminated, all those members of the monastic community were struck with wonder; rising suddenly, they approached and stood before him.
Then that deity, having risen with palms joined in reverence, went before him and,
bowing down to the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, asked this:
O All-Knowing Blessed One, Teacher, for the purpose of that for which I have come to you,
please instruct me and awaken my mind.
Which men go to a happy rebirth? Which men are destined for heaven? And for whom does merit constantly increase, day and night?
Some go to an evil destiny, and some men fall into the depths;
for others, moreover, sin constantly increases by day and by night.
What must one give to be powerful, and what must one give to be adorned?
What must one give so that the world is happy, and what must one give to possess vision?
What indeed is a sharpened weapon? Or what is the hālāhala poison? What is a blazing fire? And what is a great, dreadful darkness?
What indeed has been grasped by a mortal? What has been completely cast off here?
What is the impenetrable armor? And what is the sharp weapon here?
Who indeed is called a thief? What is considered wealth by the virtuous?
And who, within the world of the three realms, is said to have been robbed?
Who here in this world is truly happy, or who is the supreme lord?
Who is eternally adorned, and who here is truly wise?
Who indeed is a compassionate kinsman, and who is an enemy of evil intent?
What is great and terrible suffering, and what is the greatest supreme happiness?
Furthermore: What in the world is both dear and beneficial? Or what is harmful yet not unpleasant?
What indeed is a disease that causes suffering? And who truly is the best of physicians?
By what is this world shrouded? By what is the world brought under control?
Why does one abandon friends? And why does one not go to heaven?
By what means are friends increased, and by what are enemies pacified?
By what does one attain heaven, and by what does one go to liberation?
By what is this world bound, and by what is the world liberated?
Through the abandonment of what here is it said that one attains nirvāṇa?
Why is it that neither kings nor thieves, even when rushing forward with weapons raised, are able to carry off the women or the men?
Does the seven-flamed fire not burn? Does the wind not shatter? Or do the waters not moisten? And does the earth not wear away?
You ought to sever this doubt of mine even now:
who has gone from this world to the next world, utterly deceived?
What indeed must one slay to sleep in peace? And what must one slay so that one does not grieve? Of which single dharma do you speak when you mention its "slaying," O Gautama?
O Blessed One, since you have been asked this by me and are all-knowing and wise,
you ought to sever my doubt and instruct me correctly.
Being thus questioned by her, the Blessed One, the Jina who is omniscient,
looked upon that goddess and spoke this answer to her question.
Listen well, O goddess, having made your mind concentrated;
I shall now utter the reply to this question of yours.
Those here who plant groves, those who build bridges, and those who provide water-stations, vehicles, and shelter; Rm_8.42{42} //
Those men who are free from envy through faith, virtue, truthfulness, and patience—they go to a happy destination; those men are destined for heaven.
For indeed, for those very mortals, streams of merit flow forth continuously and increase perpetually, day and night, without interruption.
Those who commit the ten unwholesome deeds and thereby revile the True Dharma— those people of evil conduct go to an evil rebirth and wander [in saṃsāra].
And those mortals who are aggressors, having lost the dharma of their own lineage—
those men, fallen from grace, go to hell as partakers of suffering.
For those most wicked beings, streams of evil flow constantly and without interruption, day and night, forever indeed. (Rm 8.47)
The giver of food becomes strong and enjoys pleasures; the giver of clothing becomes resplendent;
the giver of drink becomes happy and satisfied; and the giver of a lamp becomes possessed of keen vision.
Malicious speech is a sharpened weapon; passion is the hālāhala poison;
hatred is a blazing fire; and ignorance is a dreadful darkness.
That which was taken up and that which was given by oneself— whatever was left behind here in the house—
is the impenetrable armor of patience and the sharp, great weapon of wisdom.
Unwholesome discursive thought is a thief, and virtue is considered the wealth of the noble;
those by whom virtue has been cast down are truly plundered in this world.
One who has few desires is happy in this world, contented, and supreme;
one who possesses virtuous conduct is eternally adorned, while one whose virtue is lost is truly wretched.
A compassionate person is a kinsman; merit is a friend; one of evil intent is an enemy;
the suffering of hell is terrible; and the cessation of the aggregates is the supreme bliss.
For sensual desires are pleasant yet unwholesome, while liberation is wholesome and dear to the virtuous;
hatred is a disease that causes affliction, and the Buddha alone is the supreme physician.
The world is shrouded by ignorance and brought under the power of delusion;
through greed one abandons friends, and through attachment one does not go to heaven.
Through renunciation friends increase; through loving-kindness enemies are pacified.
Through virtuous conduct one attains heaven; through wisdom one goes well to liberation.
The world is bound by craving and is liberated by its absence;
through the total abandonment of thirst, it is called "nirvāṇa."
Neither kings nor thieves, even when rushing forward with weapons raised, are able to seize away the merit of either a woman or a man.
Fire does not burn merit, nor does the wind shatter it;
water does not moisten merit, nor do the earths cause it to decay.
He who has not accumulated merit while enjoyments were available has gone from this world to the next utterly deceived.
Having slain anger, one sleeps in peace; having slain anger, one does not grieve.
I always strive for the destruction of this single quality, anger.
Having heard this exchange of questions and answers, that deity was filled with joy;
bowing again to the Blessed One and praising him, she spoke as follows:
Blessed are you, O Blessed Buddha, who provides the answer to every question;
the omniscient teacher of the worlds, the Lord of Sages endowed with the six superknowledges.
And I do not see the state of a brahmin or final nirvana for a hero;
for a true hero has transcended all fear and possesses the power to protect the world.
Having spoken thus, the deity again performed three circumambulations,
bowed at the feet of the Lord of Sages, and departed from that very spot for heaven.
Then all those monks, having heard what was taught by the Teacher and having thoroughly understood this truth, practiced their duties correctly.
"Thus it is, O Great King, as it was proclaimed to me by my Guru;
having heard this and understood it, be devoted to the True Dharma."
Through righteousness one shall go to a happy rebirth; through evil one shall go to a miserable state.
Therefore, placing righteousness at the forefront, protect your subjects properly.
Abandoning the ten unwholesome actions, practice the conventional discipline;
one who desires heaven must give all necessary requisites as a gift.
Having abandoned association with the wicked, having repeatedly destroyed the poison of passion,
and having extinguished the fire of hatred, ignorance itself must be utterly destroyed.
Having abandoned thoughts of sensual desire, with a mind dedicated to the vow for enlightenment,
and having purified the three bodies, let the wealth of ethical discipline be acquired.
Having fully understood the non-existence of the aggregates and having recognized the enemy as one of malicious intent,
and maintaining the armor of patience, may you conquer the wicked hosts.
Having completely conquered the qualities of Māra, one should always exert oneself with steadfastness, vigor, and great enthusiasm in the accomplishment of the qualities of perfect enlightenment.
Having conquered the afflictions, pride, and intoxication, and having made the mind concentrated,
one should meditate upon the means for achieving enlightenment for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having seen the world arisen as an illusion, shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, let it be impelled upon the path of the Sugata by the lamp of wisdom.
Thus, O King, having understood this, you should avoid the company of the wicked;
remain constantly devoted to the company of the virtuous and serve the Triple Gem.
O King, having thus diligently awakened all subjects, you must always urge them toward the practice of virtuous conduct.
Thinking thus, may you, O King, attaining the essence of cyclic existence,
gradually fulfill the conduct of awakening and reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard this which was thus instructed by the venerable monk Upagupta,
the king, together with his assembly, acclaimed it, saying, "So be it."
Those who joyfully listen to the sūtra known as the *Devatāparipṛcchā* and cause it to be heard by others, having enjoyed happiness, go to Sukhāvatī.
Thus ends the *Devatāparipṛcchāsūtra*.

Then King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence and full of joy,

"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken word;

When the king had thus questioned him, Upagupta, born from a portion of the Jina,

Listen, O King, I shall tell you what was spoken to me by my teacher;

O King, in a former time, the Lion of the Śākyas— an ocean of compassion,

For the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, the Blessed One was in the city of Kapilavastu,

Together with the community of śrāvaka monks and the assembly of bodhisattvas,

It was attended by lay followers and monastics who had come to hear that Dharma,

By people of the four castes, including those from the cities and the countryside,

Thus honored, worshipped, surrounded, and placed at the forefront,

There, having seen that assembly gathered together, the Blessed One taught the supreme Dharma, which is virtuous in its beginning, middle, and end.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, all sentient beings were filled with joy;

And at that time, in that city of Kapilavastu,

Possessing great wealth, being deeply devoted to the ancestral rites, and having very extensive possessions, he was a generous and virtuous man; steadfast and endowed with happiness, he dwelt there.
At that time, that Śākya took as his wife Subhadrāṅgī from a family similar to his own, who followed the religious customs of her own lineage.
Then that Śākya Rohiṇa, out of passion for great pleasures, took delight in sporting with that very beloved woman.
Although he took such delight and sported with passion in this way,

Then Rohiṇa, eager to obtain a son for his daughter and intent on the thought of a son, remained in his chamber and reflected thus: Rm_9.19{19}
"I possess such wealth in my house, yet I have neither son nor daughter;

"Who will perform my funeral rites? And who will offer the funeral cake?

Thus, dejected by his thoughts, he remained in the chamber of sorrow.
Holding his cheek in his hand, he stood indifferent to enjoyments;

Seeing him, all his well-wishers, friends, and kinsmen tried to awaken him, saying:
"Why do you remain thus, dear friend? What sorrow has arisen?"
"If there is something to be said, you ought to tell us everything," they all—

Standing before them, Rohiṇa spoke all this:
"Sirs, listen all; the nature of suffering is being described by me."
"I possess great wealth in my house, yet there is no one to enjoy it;

"If you have any affection for me, then tell me a remedy.
Having heard this request of his, they were all bound by their affection.
Teaching him the means for the continuation of his lineage, he said:
"O noble one, do not give way to grief; indeed, there exists a remedy for this."
Having performed the propitiation of the deities, ask for a son from yourself;

"Whether it be a son or even a daughter, there will be one; of this there is no doubt.

O King, if it were indeed the case that offspring is produced solely through the grace of a deity,
then each individual would certainly possess such offspring.
Just as a universal monarch might have a thousand sons, yet,
O Lord of Men, [he is truly so called] only through the manifestation of three specific conditions.
Indeed, sons and daughters are born to living beings when these conditions are met:
the parents are filled with passion, the mother is healthy and in her fertile season, and a gandharva is present at the right time; then the embryo comes into being.
Then, at that time, the wife of Rohiṇa, who was full of passion for him, having bathed and become pure, began the act of love.
Then a certain deity, having fallen from heaven to experience the results of her karma,
entered the womb of that Śākya’s wife.
Then, realizing that she had conceived a child, she stood before her husband in private and, filled with joy, announced it thus: *“I have conceived a child.”* (Rm 9.43)
"O Lord, I am pregnant; from us two a lineage shall arise.
Therefore, may you, with your approval, carry out all the necessary rites."
Having heard what his wife had said, Rohiṇa was delighted;
seeing that his wife was pregnant, he smiled and replied to her.
"O blessed lady, consider my words as truth and remain composed."
Do not be negligent in this matter if you have affection for me;
thus it will be well for you, O blessed lady, if you shall give birth to a son.
"Then I shall cast you out if you give birth to a daughter"—
hearing these words from her husband, that woman’s pregnancy longings intensified.
Afflicted by the fear of separation from her husband, she became deeply distressed.
Then, at the proper time, she gave birth to a daughter, Divyasundarī,
whose limbs were clothed in white garments yet stained with the impurities of the womb.
Then, having heard that a daughter had been born, Rohiṇa, out of anger,
entered the maternity chamber himself to reject his wife.
Led before her husband by that daughter of Prajāpati,
the auspicious-limbed and divinely beautiful girl stood there, her body draped in white garments.
Then Rohiṇa, seeing his daughter,
a divinely beautiful woman whose limbs were draped in white garments, was struck with supreme wonder.
"Oh, by my good fortune, I have obtained this daughter of auspicious form,
since she is born already clothed in white garments that were with her at birth!"
Therefore, this woman has surely been brought down by a celestial maiden in person;
she will be a virtuous practitioner of the true Dharma, of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, that Śākya father, gazing upon the girl after a long time,
stood as if transfixed, his eyes unblinking and unsated, like one who has fainted.
Then, having summoned his kinsmen and joyfully performed the birth festival,
he spoke again to them regarding her naming ceremony.
"Sirs, for this daughter of mine, Bhadrāṅgī, let a beautiful and renowned name be given that is appropriate to her; let it be made auspicious."
When he had thus entreated her, all those kinsmen of hers, upon seeing her naturally clad in white garments, spoke as follows: Rm_9.58{57}
Since this girl was born gentle, with auspicious limbs, as divine and beautiful,
and clothed in white garments, let her therefore be known as Śuklā.
Having thus conversed, all those kinsmen took leave of Rohiṇa and spoke to him in this manner.
"O noble one, since this daughter of yours has been born with auspicious limbs, divine beauty,
and clad in white garments, let her be called Śuklā."
Having granted her consent by saying "So be it," the father, being pleased,
entrusted his daughter Śuklā to eight nurses.
Then, through the attentive care of those nurses,
she whose limbs were most beautiful grew like a lotus situated in a lake.
And just as that Śuklā gradually grew up,
so too did that garment grow and become stainless.
And yet his body was no longer that wretched thing smeared with filth;
rather, it shone stainless and pure, emitting a fragrant scent.
When that girl Śuklā had gradually grown up,
she became a maiden who captivated the minds and eyes of all the world.
Then, having approached her teachers to learn the sciences,
that wise woman quickly reached the further shore of knowledge after training in them step by step.
Then, whosoever beheld that divine and beautiful Śuklā,
they all, gazing upon her, were struck with wonder and fell into a state of infatuation.
Then those brahmins and others, their minds drawn by his virtues,
repeatedly entreated Rohiṇī through their respective messengers.
"O Brahmin, I am indeed the best by birth; therefore, you ought to give me the white one," thus did the sons of the brahmins entreat Rohiṇī.
"I am a prince, O hero; therefore, let my daughter be given to me.
Thus did the princes persuade Rohiṇa.
"I am a Vaiśya, a sustainer of subjects; therefore, you ought to give her to me.
Thus did the sons of the Vaiśyas repeatedly entreat Rohiṇī.
"I am the son of a minister; therefore, let Śuklā be given to me.
Thus did all the sons of ministers entreat Rohiṇa.
"I am indeed the son of the chief minister; therefore, grant her to me.
Thus did the minister's sons request Rohiṇī.
In this way, other inhabitants of the world as well, who were conceited regarding their own material forms,
requested that white cow Rohiṇī through their respective messengers.
Thus, being entreated by all those great people who were ever-present,
Rohiṇa, with a dejected soul, remained there and reflected as follows:
"Alas! My sorrows have arisen; how can there be a remedy for this?
Now, on account of my daughter, I shall be utterly destroyed."
If I give this beautiful daughter to one,
then indeed all the others will become my enemies.
"Surely this daughter of mine, my enemy, will kill me;
what use have I for such a daughter who brings only suffering? (Rm 9.79)
Thus dejected by his thoughts, his mind agitated by that anxiety,
he stood in the treasury chamber without celebration, resting his cheek upon his hand.
Seeing her father thus dejected, his face clouded by such thoughts, his daughter Śuklā bowed down and spoke to him as follows:
"Why do you stand thus, dear father? What suffering has arisen for you? Tell me that, O father, if you have affection for me."
Having heard these words of his daughter, her father, his heart filled with rage and devoid of affection, looked at his daughter Śuklā and spoke thus: Rm_9.83{81}
"O wicked daughter, because of you great suffering arises for me;
what is the use of speaking this before you, since there is no remedy at all?"
"Surely you, my daughter, are an enemy who will destroy me in every way;
what use have I for you, a daughter who brings such suffering?"
Having heard what was spoken by her father, Śuklā, her heart deeply pained, suddenly bowed to her father and, weeping, spoke thus:
"Father, for what reason does this sorrow arise in you? How is it so?"
"If you are my daughter's husband, this must be told by all means;
I shall employ such a means that your suffering will be destroyed."
"Therefore, my dear, you ought to tell me all of this in its entirety.
When his daughter had spoken thus, her father Rohiṇa replied once more:
Therefore, my daughter, why do you speak thus when there is no remedy?
Many suitors for your hand, such as princes and others, are seeking you.
The princes, the brahmins, the vaiśyas, and the śūdras—
the sons of ministers, the sons of counselors, and the sons of caravan leaders and others— [all followed him].
In the same way, there were others as well— those who prided themselves on their virtues or possessions,
as well as city-dwellers and villagers who took pride in their lineage and physical appearance.
I am constantly sealed by all these seekers of you;
how shall I act in this matter? I have no conscious intent.
For you alone are my daughter, yet those who beg for you are many;
if I give you to one, all the others would become my enemies.
"Therefore, having cut you into pieces, I shall indeed offer you to all [the gods];
for when this is done, my merit will be secured."
"Otherwise, my merit would never indeed be wholesome," her father said; hearing this, Śuklā became fearful of death.
Having bowed at his father's feet like a daughter, she spoke thus:
"Be gracious, O Father; do not feel distress on my account."
"I shall act for you in such a way, dear father, that no fault shall be found; I am not one who seeks pleasure, so grant me your permission."
"Having gone forth, I shall practice the vow in the teaching of the Blessed One"—
hearing these words spoken by his daughter, her father Rohiṇa [responded].
Fearing the separation from his daughter, he spoke to her once more:
"O daughter, do not by any means set your mind on the practice of the religious life."
"You are a young woman, my daughter; you would not be able to practice the life of renunciation.
The vow of renunciation is arduous and difficult to perform even for men."
But you, my daughter, are young, with limbs as beautiful as Subhadrā’s, delicate and divinely lovely; how will you endure to perform a vow in such a place of hardship?
Therefore, O young girl, do not act thus; abandon the thought of renunciation.
If you are not a seeker of sensual pleasures, you will certainly not be given away to anyone.
Therefore, daughter, stay in your own home, observe your vows, and live happily;
for if you, daughter, are desirous of love, [then remain here] while they are desirous of you.
If you perform the ritual of a self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*) and choose him yourself,
then there will be no fault on my part, nor indeed any fault on yours.
For this very procedure prevails everywhere in all the worlds;
therefore, O auspicious one, choose for yourselves a husband from among those princes.
Having observed the vow together with that very husband, live happily;
then, having produced offspring and enjoyed your pleasures as you wish, [you shall attain liberation].
"Having practiced the conduct of worldly life, you may likewise attain heaven at the end;
therefore, daughter, do not set your mind upon the practice of renunciation."
"What would be accomplished for you by this renunciation, or by such great and difficult ascetic practices?"—
when his father had spoken thus, she, pure and averse to sensual desires, [replied].
Desiring to practice the true Dharma, she spoke thus to her father:
"I am not a seeker of sensual pleasures, my dear; I long for the state of perfect enlightenment."
Therefore, having renounced even those things that are objects of enjoyment, I desire to practice the noble vow;
for sensual desires are fraught with fear, provide no refuge, are accompanied by afflictions, and are like poison.
Therefore, I have no desire for sensual pleasure; my mind is set on Nirvana alone.
Among all beings—whether gods, asuras, or humans—who are possessed by passion for sense-desires, [I am free].
All those afflicted and blind ones wander even into sinful states;
having committed such sins, they likewise go to the miserable destinies.
And those dwelling in hell endure various sufferings,
as do even the wise Brahmins who are Vedic students of sacred knowledge.
Even they— ascetics possessing great supernormal powers, pure in soul, and masters of their senses— go to an evil rebirth when fallen through attachment to sensual desires;

Ascetics, yogins, and even the Nirgranthas and the sky-clad Digambaras;
Even they, having fallen through passion for sensual pleasures, go to an evil rebirth;
so too do kings and kṣatriyas, having fought one another.
Even in battle they meet their end for the sake of fulfilling his desires;
likewise, ministers and counselors also cause those who seek their own interests to be slain.
Through those sins they go to an evil rebirth, even because of their desire for it—
even the great heroes who, as warriors, have fought one another in battle.
Even for the sake of fulfilling their desires, merchants and caravan leaders go to their deaths in battle, being excessively greedy for jewels and wealth.
Some fell into the ocean and died; some perished in the wilderness;
some died in the great forest, and others were harassed by bandits.
Some, afflicted by hunger and thirst and beset by disease, died on the road; others, overcome by cold, wind, and heat, perished, exhausted by fatigue.
Some died right there in their homes, some were afflicted by disease,
some died while carrying heavy burdens, and others perished overcome by fear.
Some were devoured by creatures— all this being caused by desire—
and farmers remained engaged in their labors throughout the day, intent upon the duties of the warrior class.
Having returned home at the end of the day, they lie down as if dead;
so too do other people, such as artisans, servants, and the like.
And the male and female servants were likewise constantly and without rest engaged in their respective tasks for the sake of providing for the family and its wealth.
Afflicted by weariness, they endure all that suffering for the sake of sensual desire;
likewise, there are those who are wicked, such as thieves and others, who seize the property of others.
They even commit sins for the sake of desire;
some steal the property of others and cause it to be stolen as well.
Some, with cruel minds, even kill and carry off everything;
for the sake of wealth, what will the wicked, greedy, and merciless not do?
Some strike their parents; they even kill their teachers.

Some kill their wives, sons, and daughters, as well as their brothers and sisters, and even their companions, male and female servants.
For the sake of their own desires, they [subjected] all— children, the elderly, and women—

(Rm 151) Thus, not even one of these things exists for me in any way whatsoever.

"In every way I am ruined; homage to fate and to karma!

Some die in the home; some die even while being born;

In this way, the worlds beginning with the gods, subject to pleasure and pain,

Some, having experienced happiness in childhood, become partakers of suffering in youth;

Some, who were suffering in childhood, become partakers of happiness in youth;

All desire happiness; no one desires suffering.
Likewise, they exert effort in manifold ways to attain happiness.

And likewise, even with the treatments of physicians, the diseases of the sick increase and do not subside at all; that too is due to the power of destiny.

Some, having engaged in a great battle and being slain by one another, abandoned their bodies and went to heaven; that too was due to the power of destiny.
Thus, merchants who had gone to the ocean to obtain jewels,

Even Rāma, though the conqueror of demons, was slain in battle by his own son;
