"O father, what indeed must be done here by you and by me as well?
For the course of destiny is the authority for all living beings."
Thinking thus, do not harbor despondency in your heart;
abandon it, take refuge in the Fully Awakened One, and worship him while constantly recollecting him.
The Buddha alone is the teacher of the world, the protector, the benefactor of the world,
the savior from miserable rebirths, the lord, the sustainer, and the guide to the happy realms.
Thus, having recollected the Sugata and taken refuge in the True Dharma,
and having rendered service to the Saṅghas, accumulate merit with a concentrated mind.
The merit accomplished through the Three Jewels can never be exhausted;
even if by chance misfortune should occur, one still gains excellent merit.
The world is protected by merit; through merit one goes to a happy rebirth.
Therefore, relying on fortitude, gather merit, which is a great jewel.
Since death is inevitable in this world, what can be accomplished by despondency?
Thinking thus, remember that Buddha and worship him with a concentrated mind.
Likewise, by taking refuge here in that very same Fully Awakened One,
and by recollecting him and honoring him, I would surely meet my death.
If that Lord of Jinas has compassion for me, a sinner,
then by the grace of his compassionate glance, may I live again free from disease.
If, by the power of destiny, I should die, then through the merit of remembering him,
may I entirely abandon an evil rebirth and once again attain a happy state.
Knowing this, my dear, you should not give way to despondency;
for in this cycle of existence, death is inevitable for all who are born.
Having spoken thus, although afflicted by pain, Vaḍika took recourse in fortitude;
having taken refuge in the Perfectly Awakened One and recollected him, he remained composed.
Thus, having heard these words spoken by his son, that preeminent householder merchant recognized this as the truth; recollecting the Buddha, he spoke accordingly.
Homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; may I always remember them.
From this day forth, I shall forever and eternally go for refuge to you.
If you have compassion for the world, protect us who are deeply suffering;
having beheld us with a compassionate gaze, you ought to rescue us swiftly in every way.
Just as you have protected other beings in the three worlds,
so too, beholding us with compassion, you ought to protect us in every way.
"O Blessed One, Protector, protect me! May I bring my son back to life;
out of compassion, having granted me your favor, bestow this jewel of a son upon me."
If this son should live through the grace of your glance,
let him dwell in your refuge and observe his vows with devotion.
Having thus recollected this and taking refuge in the Perfectly Awakened One,
that merchant, upon seeing his son, stood there with his delusion dispelled.
At that very moment, the Blessed One, the Sage, beholding the worlds with a compassionate gaze in order to protect them, saw those who were full of suffering.
Seeing them thus suffering, the Blessed One, that Lord of Conquerors,
suddenly emitted a Buddha-ray in order to protect them.
Then, by those rays of the Perfectly Awakened One, which were golden in color,
that house was illuminated from all sides after they had completely overspread it.
Then, rays of loving-kindness were again emitted by that Blessed One and, being serene, they touched his body.
Then, as soon as his body was touched by them on all sides,
it became refreshed, attained happiness, and reached a state of well-being.
Then that Vaḍika, having regained his health and with a purified mind, looked at his father in amazement and, addressing him, spoke thus: Rm_13.174{174} //
Oh, the majesty of the Buddha! Oh, the power of the Dharma!
Oh, the radiance of the Saṅgha! Behold, dear father, the splendor of the Sage!
By the mere recollection of whom compassion is extended toward the world— may this blessed Buddha, who thus abides forever, be victorious! (Rm 178) 13.176(176)
"By the power of whose compassion we live free from disease and in happiness, and by whom I have been liberated from sins"—thus he truly acknowledges [the truth]. (Rm 13.177)
Therefore, go for refuge to that very Teacher, the Perfectly Awakened One;
remembering him throughout existence, may I honor him with full devotion.
Having thus recollected the qualities of the Buddha, Vaḍika was filled with joy;
with palms joined in reverence and remembering him once more, he bowed down and made this request: Rm_13.179{179} //
Homage to you, O Blessed One, Protector; I go for refuge to you.
As long as existence lasts, may I always be a servant of the Three Jewels.
Thus, having recollected the Sugata, Vaḍika was awakened;
remembering again and again and bowing down, he stood there, having attained a state of well-being.
Then the Blessed One, the Buddha, seeing that his mind was pure,
approached the gate in order to teach him the True Dharma.
Upon seeing that lord of sages, who possessed the radiance of the sun, standing at the gateway,
the gatekeeper was struck with wonder and immediately entered the house.
There, having seen the householder Vaḍika, he approached him respectfully and, standing before him, made this request with great urgency: *Rm_13.184{184}*184*
"Householder, the Lord of Sages has arrived here at the door of your house;
therefore, go there at once, address him, and bring him in."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, Vaḍika was filled with serene faith;
rising up suddenly, he approached and joyfully bowed before that Lord of Sages.
Having bowed to that Sugata, having joyfully prepared a seat in his house,
and having invited him with a formal request, they ushered him in, making their entreaty.
Welcome, Blessed One! O Sage, we desire you as our refuge.
May the Lord of the World enter; may you be victorious upon this auspicious seat.
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha, the Blessed One,
sat down upon his own seat and addressed Vaḍika in this manner.
"Vaḍika, what is this suffering of yours, and how does it oppress you?
Speak! Thus questioned by the Blessed One, Vaḍika spoke as follows.
O Sage, physical and mental suffering has arisen within me;
may you, out of compassion, pacify that affliction with your gaze.
Having heard this request, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages,
taught the Dharma of loving-kindness for the sake of pacifying her mental suffering.
Always practice a mind of loving-kindness toward all beings here in this world;
by this, indeed, the burning of your mind will always be pacified.
Having thus instructed him, the Lord of Sages thought once more:
"Let him bring the great medicinal herb named Vatsendrakṣīrikā."
Having understood this thought of the Teacher, the lord of the gods took the great medicinal herb named Kṣīrikā and presented it to him.
There, that king of the gods, having bowed down to the Blessed One and presented that great medicinal herb right before him, spoke thus:
"O Blessed One, may you accept this divine medicine;
by means of it, may you accomplish what is necessary here for the attainment of happiness."
When Śakra had spoken thus, the Blessed One, the Sage, seeing her, took her by the hand and, having given her [the gift], instructed her in this manner.
"Vadika, take this [ointment] which alleviates physical suffering;
let your body be treated with these medicinal applications."
When the Lord of Sages had thus instructed him, Vaḍika, having expressed his approval,
accepted her and attended to her exactly as directed.
Then his body, freed from diseases and fully nourished,
gradually attained a tranquil beauty and shone resplendently.
Then, just as instructed by the Teacher, Vaḍika cultivated loving-kindness in his heart toward the world, just as he would toward his own beloved son.
Then his great mental suffering subsided,
like fire in a heart drenched with great loving-kindness being quenched by waters.
Then that Vaḍika, restored to health, with his senses purified and his mind clear, bowed down to the Blessed One and made this request with great reverence: Rm_13.204{104} //
I salute your feet; I go to you for refuge at all times. And likewise, O Lord, you ought to protect me always through your compassion.
If, as you say, your Teacher possesses no compassionate gaze, then I am dead; even now I would have gone to hell and experienced its sufferings.
Since you remain thus established in yourself through the state of the waters of compassion,
it behoves you always and at all times to continue to bestow such grace upon me.
Having thus made this prayer, Vaḍika, filled with joy,
again bowed with palms joined in reverence and stood gazing at the Lord of Sages.
Likewise, his father, the merchant, together with his wife, being filled with joy,
took refuge in the Three Jewels and paid homage to that Perfectly Awakened One.

Then that householder, the merchant chief, seeing the Sugata with joy, bowed with palms joined in reverence and requested thus with devotion: (Rm 180) *tataḥ sa gṛhabhṛc chreṣṭhī dṛṣṭvā taṃ sugataṃ mudā / kṛtāñjalipuṭo natvā prārthayad evam ādarāt //* Rm_13.210{210} //
I worship your feet, O Teacher; I always go to you for refuge.
Thus, out of compassion, you ought to always show us favor.
Then the Blessed Buddha commanded, "So be it," and having leaped into the sky by means of his supernatural power, he returned to his own hermitage.
There, the Blessed One arrived and took his seat in the midst of the assembly;
having announced this rain, he remained there, teaching the Dharma.
Then that Vaḍika, recollecting once more the qualities of the Buddha,
desired to honor the Saṅgha and the Sugata with food offerings.
Then, having bowed down to King Prasenajit, O Lord of Men,
he reported all these events and spoke as follows.
"O King, I am gravely ill; I go for refuge to the Three Jewels.
By the compassionate gaze of those Three Jewels, may I live, liberated from my diseases."
Therefore, I now desire to invite that Lord of Sages, together with the entire community, to my home and honor him with offerings of food.
Therefore, having shown me favor for the sake of increasing the merit of the worlds,
and having granted your consent to that, please give your permission, O Lord.
Having heard this request made by him, the king gave his approval;
looking at Vaḍika and praising him, he issued his command.
O Vaḍika, you are truly a great benefactor, for you have gone for refuge to the Buddha;
thus, with constant faith, always honor the Three Jewels.
Having heard that the king had granted his permission, Vaḍika, filled with joy,
bowed to the monarch and departed for his own home.
Having arrived at that house and obtained his father's consent,
he proceeded to the monastery to extend an invitation to the Teacher.
Having sat down there, he joyfully beheld Śrīghana;
bowing with palms joined in reverence, he made this request with great devotion: Rm_13.223{223} //
"O Blessed One, may you understand the purpose for which I have approached you;
nevertheless, I pray before you here: please grant me your favor."
That I have been freed from disease and have, as it were, obtained a new birth,
I consider this to be due to the grace of your compassionate gaze.
Therefore, I desire to honor all of you, the entire Saṅgha, with meals at my home; may you deign to favor me by doing so.
Having heard this prayer thus offered by him, the Blessed One, the Sage,
expressed his approval by saying "So be it," and remained there in silence.
Then Vaḍika, perceiving that the Blessed One had consented,
bowed at the feet of that Sage with joy and quickly departed for his own home.
There, in his house, he quickly prepared all the necessary provisions together with his kinsmen and friends for the purpose of honoring the Sangha with a meal worthy of them.
Then, having prepared all the necessary materials and arranged the seats,
he sprinkled pure water all around upon the ground.
Then, together with his kinsmen, he went quickly to the monastery to invite the Buddha Śrīghana and his community of monks.
Having sat down there and joyfully beheld Śrīghana together with his community, he bowed with palms joined and made this request with great reverence: Rm_13.232{232} //
"O Blessed One, that which is to be accomplished is being achieved; the time has now come.
Therefore, you ought to go forth to victory together with the community of monks."
Having heard what he requested, that Lord of Sages replied, "So be it," and taking up his bowl and robes, he set out together with the entire Saṅgha.
Manifesting that miracle everywhere on the roads and throughout the city, he entered that house.
Having arrived at that house and accepted the water for washing his feet and the respectful offering (argha),
he sat down upon a comfortable seat and remained there in due order together with his retinue of monks.
Then, seeing that Buddha seated upon his own throne together with the Saṅgha, Vaḍika honored him with all the requisites for worship and every kind of flower.
Then, with all kinds of divine foods— well-prepared, highly palatable, and endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor— he completely satisfied her.
Then, at the conclusion of the meal, having removed the bowl and other utensils and having cleansed his mouth and so forth, he offered betel nut and medicinal herbs.
Then, having bowed with joined palms before the Sugata and his Saṅgha with joy, he stood before them and, recollecting, made this mental aspiration: Rm_13.240{270} //
By this merit, may I become a knower of the self in this blind world that lacks a guide, just as this Blessed One, the Buddha, is.
Just as this Lord of Sages has protected the world,
so shall I protect all people on every side.
I shall cause those who have not crossed over to cross; I shall liberate those who are unliberated;
having comforted those who are not at ease, I shall establish them in nirvāṇa.
Thus, with joy, he made this aspiration in his mind;
perceiving this, the Blessed One, the Buddha, out of delight, manifested a smile.
Then, five divine rays issued forth from the mouth of that lord of sages and spread through the three worlds, illuminating them.
Whatever rays extended into the lower world into the hells became cool in the hot hells, and likewise warm in the cold ones.
Then, touched by them, all the inhabitants of hell attained great happiness and, filled with wonder, spoke thus: Rm_13.247{277} //
"Aha! What happiness! How indeed could it be thus elsewhere? To what have we gone?
By whose power of merit does this happiness arise for us?"
When they were thus consumed by anxiety, the Blessed One, in order to awaken their minds,
dispatched an emanated Buddha and showed him to them.
There, having seen that emanated Buddha, they were all filled with joy and wonder; closing their eyes for a moment, they spoke again as follows: Rm_13.250{280} //
"Aha! This man Samantabhadra is now seen;
surely it is by his power that happiness has truly arisen for us."
Having spoken thus, they were all inspired with faith toward that Buddha and cried out: "Homage to the Buddha, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha!"
Then, by virtue of the merit arising from mindfulness of the Three Jewels, all those beings were liberated from the miserable realms and attained a happy rebirth.
Thus, having illuminated everything on all sides, those rays returned once more to the Sage, having uplifted all sentient beings.
Likewise, whatever rays were extended upward,
they illuminated all the worlds of the gods on every side.
Illuminating everything up to the very peak of existence,
they spread forth and likewise moved about, uttering a great roar.
Indeed, cyclic existence is impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self;
therefore, having abandoned the higher realms within that existence, devote yourself with reverence to the true Dharma.
Go forth and exert yourselves; apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of death as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket.
Whoever always practices with heedfulness within this discipline of the Dharma will,
having abandoned the cycle of births, bring an end to suffering.
Having heard that great sound in this way, all those gods,
expressing their approval by saying "So be it," went for refuge to the Three Jewels.
Thus, having illuminated everything on all sides, those rays returned once more and came into the presence of that sage.
Then all those rays, having gathered together and come to rest,
circled him three times to the right and vanished into the crown of the Sage's head.
Then Ānanda, having beheld him, was struck with wonder; rising suddenly and bowing with palms joined in reverence, he questioned the lord of sages in this manner.
O Blessed One, five-colored divine rays have issued forth from your mouth and proclaim [your teaching] everywhere in all directions.
The Victors, the Buddhas, never display a smile without a cause;
beholding your smile, all become filled with wonder.
All those gathered here in this assembly desire to hear its cause;
therefore, in order to sever their doubt, please explain that cause.
Having heard what he thus requested, and having looked upon that entire assembly as well as Ānanda, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, spoke to him.
Behold, Ānanda, how this Vaḍika, rejoicing with faith and devotion toward the Saṅghas, has performed worship by honoring them.
Through the ripening of this merit, may this wise and accomplished Vaḍika,
having gradually fulfilled the practices of awakening, become a sovereign of the ten stages.
Having conquered all the hosts of Māra, he will attain perfect enlightenment and become a Buddha,
a Tathāgata named Ślakṣṇavāṇī.
Because he has made this aspiration with serene confidence in the Three Jewels, he will certainly become a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Thinking thus, Ānanda, go for refuge to the Three Jewels;
having honored and relied upon them, worship them constantly with a concentrated mind.
Those beings who, having remembered with faith, have gone for refuge to the Three Jewels, do not go to an evil rebirth; they become partakers of awakening.
Thinking thus, those who desire awakening should honor the Three Jewels with faith and joy, and having recollected them and gone for refuge, they should remain devoted to them.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, Ānanda was delighted;
together with the world and the Saṅgha, he joyfully assented, saying, "So be it."
Then that Blessed One, having bestowed words of blessing upon his nephew Vaḍika, took leave of him once more and spoke to him.
O illustrious Vaḍika, you have gone for refuge to the Triple Gem;
by constantly practicing the conduct of awakening, may you fully attain perfect enlightenment.
Having thus fully understood this truth, and bearing in mind the welfare of all sentient beings,
remember the Three Jewels in that manner and worship them constantly with a concentrated mind.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Sages rose up together with the community;
having taken leave of Vaḍika, he likewise departed for his own monastery.
Thus, that Vaḍika constantly took refuge in the Three Jewels;
always performing what is beneficial for the world, he practiced the conduct of awakening.
This was instructed to me by my teacher, O lord of men, and it has been heard by me;
thus it is told to you, O King—having heard it, indeed, proclaim it.
Likewise, O Indra among kings, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings, you too,
having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, must practice the conduct of awakening.
Thus, may there always, eternally, and everywhere be auspiciousness for you;
and having fulfilled the conduct of awakening in due order, may you attain perfect enlightenment as well.
Thinking thus, O Great King, you ought to protect all beings in every way, awakening them as well and firmly establishing them in the true Dharma.
Having heard what was thus instructed by Upagupta,
the king, along with his retinue, replied, "So be it," and rejoiced.
Those people who, having heard this avadāna of the virtuous Vaḍika, rejoice in it,
all become devoted to the welfare of the world and indeed attainers of the qualities of enlightenment.
Thus ends the Vaḍikā-avadāna in the Ratnāvadānatatva.
XIV. The Gāndharvikā-avadāna.
Then King Aśoka, desiring to hear another well-spoken verse,
bowed to the ascetic Upagupta and requested thus with great reverence:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken teaching;
it would be fitting for you to instruct me just as it was explained by my teacher."
Having heard this request made by that lord of men, and having looked upon the king, the Son of the Conqueror again instructed him in this way.
Listen, O King, to what has been told by me, just as it was spoken by my teacher;
having heard it and approved of it, you ought to act accordingly for the sake of auspiciousness.
Long ago, that Blessed Buddha was staying in the monastery adorned with jewels in the great park of the Jeta Grove, in a hermitage outside Śrāvastī.
Together with the monks who were disciples, as well as those clad in rags and observers of vows,
along with the nuns and other beings of great resolve, the lay devotees.
Having dwelt there, established in the assembly of all sentient beings,
he began to teach the Dharma for the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
Then, all sentient beings approached to drink that nectar of the True Dharma issuing forth from the lotus-like mouth of that Lord of Sages.
The lords of the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Śakra, as well as all the sovereigns of the world,
the lords of the Daityas with their hosts, the Yakṣas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas—
The hosts of Vidyādharas, the lords of the Nāgas, the Mahoragas, the Garuḍas, the lords of the Kinnaras, and others as well, all assembled there.
Brahmins, seers, ascetics, celibate students, renunciants, yogins, the learned, as well as other adherents of various sects— Rm_14.11{11} //
Kings and kṣatriyas as well, heroic princes, ministers and counselors, and even vaiśyas who were lords of the people; Rm_14.12{12} //
There were also guild-leaders, merchants, caravan leaders, and great crowds of people;
citizens, country-folk, villagers, and even wandering pilgrims.
In this way, all other beings and the entire world gathered together and sat down in that monastery to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
There, having seen that Śrīghana, having honored him, bowed down to him, treated him with hospitality, and taken their stand around him on all sides; Rm_14.15{15} //
Beholding that Lord of Munis, they stood before him with palms joined, their faces radiant with clarity, composed in mind, desiring to hear his teaching of the Dharma.
Seeing them thus seated in attendance, the Blessed One, the Victor,
began by means of the Noble Truths and fully taught the True Dharma.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, all sentient beings were filled with joy;
having paid homage to the Triple Gem, they became practitioners of the path to enlightenment.
Even then, about five hundred musicians born in the city of Śrāvastī wandered about together in a state of intoxication.
Then, seeing her intoxicated with passion, the son of the lord of the Gandharvas,
named Supriya, rose up out of envy to destroy that intoxication.
Then Supriya, who was highly skilled in all the arts of the Gandharvas,
took up his divine lute and approached that very place.
Proclaiming the seven notes on a single string and the twenty-one melodic modulations, he proceeded, displaying his own intellectual mastery.
Thus proclaiming throughout the six great cities and the surrounding towns, he arrived at Śrāvastī.
Seeing him seated there and hearing that wondrous sound, all the citizens approached him in amazement.
And those five hundred musicians,
having heard and seen all this, were filled with wonder.
Then, having seen all those things, even those five hundred abandoned their respective pride and arrogance and were filled with remorse.
Then all of them, filled with fear due to their dispute with him,
went into the presence of the king and reported what had occurred.
O Lord, may you understand why we have come here; therefore, it behoves you in every way to protect us who are terrified by fear.
"Surely this one named Supriya, the son of the lord of the Gandharvas,
has arrived here to conquer us and utterly destroy our pride."
"Listen to our request: since that [destruction] would also be an act of pride on his part, let a true counter-measure be taken against him immediately. Rm_14.30{30}

Having heard this petition made by them all, that lord of men addressed them all together and commanded them thus right there in the city: *iti vijñāpitaṃ sarvais taiḥ śrutvā sa narādhipaḥ / sarvāns tān samupāmaṃtrya pura evaṃ samādiśat //* Rm_14.31{31} //
"Be free from anxiety in this matter; do not despair.
We shall know the right time for this; let him proceed according to his wish."
Having heard what was thus commanded by the king, they gave their assent;
abandoning that terror born of the fear of dispute, they all became serene.
Then Supriya, seeing those conceited men there, reflected thus in his mind for the purpose of destroying their pride: Rm_14.34{34} //
"Even this king might be conceited regarding his knowledge of the Gandharva arts;
therefore, I shall engage him in debate here in the presence of the assembly."
Having thus formed this resolution, that arrogant Supriya went to the assembly hall in order to reproach the king.
There, having seen that Supriya had arrived, the king prepared a seat, invited him, bowed down, and spoke thus:
"Welcome to you, sir; please sit upon this seat and be gracious to me.
For what purpose have you come here? You ought indeed to instruct me."

Having heard what was thus spoken by him, Supriya, standing in the assembly and looking toward the king, spoke these words before him: (Rm 14.3
Listen, O King, to that great fame of yours which has been heard by me as I have related it;
I have come here specifically to behold your virtues.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, show me your own Gandharva qualities;
who is your teacher or preceptor? Show him to me as well.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, that eloquent king looked at Supriya and said, "So be it."
"Excellent! Look, O illustrious one; I shall show you that teacher who is my instructor, possessed of great supernormal knowledge, and the sovereign of all the qualities of vidyā."
"He is my teacher right here and now for the sake of the welfare of all beings;
he dwells in the great grove of Jetavana, teaching the Dharma."
"Excellent! Behold, O fortunate one, that teacher of mine who bestows the aim of my welfare.
Therefore come, we shall go together; I will show him, the Teacher, to you."
Having heard this which was related by that lord of men, Supriya, rejoicing and saying "So be it," spoke of his departure.
"Excellent, O King! I desire a teacher; show me one.
Let me engage in debates with him; lead me there quickly."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, the king said, "So be it," and desiring to go to the monastery, he took that dear friend with him.
Then that king traveled together with his beloved and proud [son],
as well as with those five hundred other musicians.
At that moment, the Blessed Buddha, the Lord of Sages,
out of compassion beheld the world in order to deliver its sentient beings.
Then, seeing Supriya approaching in this manner together with that lord of men, he reflected thus within his mind:
"Oh, would that the wise one named Pañcaśikha, the delight of the Lord of the Gandharvas, might come here taking his lute!"
Having perceived that this was what the Lord of Sages had contemplated in his mind,
Pañcaśikha also desired to go there accordingly.
Then, accompanied by seven thousand gandharvas,
he suddenly set out, taking up his lute with its lapis lazuli staff.
Thus, moving through that monastery, he sat down;
seeing Śrīghana, he bowed to him and brought forth his lute.
Then, having worshipped the Sugata with devotion, his mind serene,
he sat down in that assembly to drink the nectar of that sublime Dharma.
Then Supriya, too, seeing him and filled with pride and arrogance,
began to play that lute before him so that it might be heard.
From its sounding forth, the seven notes and twenty-one melodic scales arose,
utterly bewildering the minds of all people.
Then all those people, having heard that sound with joy,
including the king at their head, were filled with supreme wonder.
Then the Blessed One, in order to humble his pride,
began to play that lute with its lapis lazuli stem.
For on each individual string,
various *mūrchanās* were likewise produced, distinguished by many different notes.
Then, from that sound, verses were uttered as an exhortation, as follows:
"In this very existence, everything is suffering, empty, and indeed without self."
Knowing this body to be like a lute, the sense-faculties to be like its notes, and the thoughts to be like the melodic modulations, apply yourself to awakening.
Having heard this verse, all the people, including the king and others,
realized that it was true and conceived the spirit of enlightenment.
Then Supriya, having heard this and reflected upon it with approval,
abandoned his pride and arrogance regarding his mastery of the Gandharva arts.
Then, having returned the lute to the fragrant chamber and become dispassionate,
he desired to go forth into homelessness there within the teaching of the Blessed One.
Then, having bowed to that Śrīghana and being filled with joy,
Supriya stood before him with palms joined in reverence and requested ordination.
"I revere your feet, O Teacher; I go to you for refuge.
Therefore, having shown me favor in this matter, you ought to grant me the going forth."
Having heard what was thus requested by him, and having perceived that the Gandharva’s intention was pure, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, spoke to him accordingly.
"Gandharva, if you wish to go forth into the Dharma of the Sugata, obtain the permission of your parents; then depart, and I shall grant you the vows."
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, Supriya, filled with joy,
said "So be it," bowed to that Sage, and went home by means of his miraculous power.
Having arrived there suddenly, he joyfully bowed to his two parents; standing before them with palms joined in reverence, he made this request with great respect: Rm_14.72{72}
"Listen to my wish, dear father, if you have compassion for me;
having bestowed your favor upon me, enjoin me to the true Dharma."
For having seen the Dharma of the Sugata, I desire that vow;
having attained the going-forth, I wish to reach nirvāṇa.
Indeed, saṃsāra is impermanent; therefore, I have no delight even in this.
For death will inevitably come to all living beings as well.
Having seen this thus in this saṃsāra, I have no desire for objects of enjoyment; being free from longing, I wish to attain perfect nirvāṇa by taking up the vow of renunciation.
Moreover, that Lord of Sages does not remain here forever;
for once he has completed his work as a Buddha, he will in every way proceed to final nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, in this world, a Lord of Sages will not always arise in such a way;
only rarely does one so arisen teach enlightenment to the world.
Likewise, birth in a favorable state is difficult to obtain, as is the moment of leisure;
if such a moment is not attained here, how will one ever acquire the Dharma?
Without Dharma, what essence is there here in this saṃsāra even for those who are happy?
For the body and life are both momentary and perishable, like a drop of water on a blade of grass.

Through the Dharma one may go to a happy rebirth and even attain perfect awakening; therefore, having embraced the practice of renunciation, one should desire to attain nirvana in this very life. (Rm 189) Rm_14.81{81}
Therefore, my dear father, if you have compassion for me, your own son,
then show me favor in every way and grant me your permission.
Having heard this request made by him, that wise lord of the Gandharvas looked at his son for a very long time out of affection and spoke thus: Rm_14.83{83} //
"It is true, as you have declared; nevertheless, listen to my words:
the practice of the wandering life is difficult to perform, so how would you be able to carry it out?"
For you are young and heedless, your mind overcome by passion;
being deeply attached to the pleasures of sensual enjoyment, how could you observe that vow?
Having gone forth, with a dispassionate mind and free from desire for the enjoyments of saṃsāra,
one should abandon all possessions and dwell forever alone in the forest.
Whether from a noble family or even a lowly one, having begged for food according to the Buddha’s teaching, you should eat it;
for how can you hope to attain meditative concentration after eating in such a manner?
Knowing thus that this is difficult to accomplish in the fulfillment of the vows of renunciation, do not let your mind act impulsively; restrain yourself with composure.
If you so greatly desire, my son, to take up the life of a renunciant,
then wait until old age and practice that vow while taking refuge in the Three Jewels.
Therefore, while you are still young, enjoy the pleasures of the home as you desire;
then, in old age, having undertaken that vow, always take refuge in the Three Jewels.
If your birth in this wandering through existence were thus fruitful,
you might enjoy happiness by maintaining your vows, or else attain final liberation.
Having heard these words of mine and having reflected upon them, you have been awakened;
therefore, enjoy happiness at home for now, while remaining mindful of the Three Jewels.

Having heard what was thus spoken by his father, Supriya became apprehensive; seeing his father once more, he spoke as follows to awaken him: *iti pitroditaṃ śrutvā supriyaḥ so 'bhiśaṅkitaḥ / punas taṃ pitaraṃ dṛṣṭvā bodhayann evam abravīt //* Rm_14.93{93} //
"O dear one, it may indeed be so; nevertheless, I shall speak.
Having heard this and understood it, you must awaken."
Birth in a noble family is difficult to obtain; even there, the opportune moment is difficult to find.
The appearance of a Sugata is difficult to encounter, and to practice his vow in this world is likewise difficult.
Thinking thus in this saṃsāra, which is agitated by afflictions, pride, and arrogance,
and seeing that death is inevitable, one should desire to attain nirvāṇa here.
Therefore, out of compassion, you ought to grant me permission in this matter;
for by means of those Dharma-preachers, you too shall attain a happy rebirth.
For this reason, O Father, do not delay there for long;
having granted your favor immediately, give me your permission.
Having heard what he had thus requested, that lord of the gandharvas, after a long time,
scorched by the fire of the pain of affection and with his face bathed in falling tears, spoke.
O dear son, out of affection I have restrained you;
if you desire to attain ultimate peace, then practice accordingly.
Having taken refuge in the Perfectly Awakened One and gone forth, maintaining the vows and honoring the Three Jewels, practice always with a concentrated mind.
Having heard what his parents had said, Supriya was delighted;
bowing at the feet of his parents, he immediately departed from the house.
Then, having gone there quickly, he approached the monastery;
having arrived there and seen the Lord of Sages, he sat down before him.

Having approached that Śrīghana there with palms joined in reverence, he stood before him and, his lotus-like face beaming with great serenity, made this request with earnest devotion: Rm_14.104{4} //
O All-Knowing Blessed One, Teacher, just as it was commanded by you,
I have now come here after having obtained my father's permission.
Therefore, I have come here for refuge to you, my Teacher;
I shall practice the holy life (brahmacarya), so please grant me the going forth (pravrajyā).
Having heard what he had thus requested, the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World,
perceiving his pure intention, instructed him once again.
"Come, O monk Supriya, practice here the auspicious holy life;
having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, rely upon meditative concentration."
Then, having seen that saṃsāra is agitated by a multitude of afflictions, and that the body consists of five festering wounds while life is as transient as a bubble on the water; Rm_14.109{9} //
Having maintained the restraint of meditative concentration and being intent on accomplishing perfect awakening,
he conquered the enemy of all afflictions and directly attained the state of an Arhat.
Then the monk Supriya, having attained the higher knowledges, accomplished and wise,
shattered every limb of ignorance and became a yogi free from conceptual construction.
Regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with the three spheres completely purified,
he was like unto the axe and the sandalwood, his mind equanimous like space.
Averse to the enjoyments, honors, respect, and gains of cyclic existence,
free from afflictions, with a completely purified self, he is a celibate practitioner, untainted.
He shone forth, becoming one to be venerated, worshipped, acclaimed, and honored by all the inhabitants of every world, including the realms of gods and asuras.
Then, beholding the Arhat Supriya, who was thus endowed with auspicious faculties,
everyone present in that assembly was struck with wonder and became serene.
Then all those worlds— the gods, the Daityas, the Kinnaras,
the Yakṣas, the Siddhas, the Gandharvas, the Nāgas, and even the Rākṣasas— [were filled with wonder].
The Garuḍas, as well as other Vidyādharas together with the Apsarases,
and all the lords of the worlds, have likewise gone for refuge to the Three Jewels.
There, within the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One, they were diligent in providing protection, shelter, and defense for the members of the Saṅgha on all sides.
Having seen that, those five hundred musicians also, rejoicing with serene minds, closed their eyes and spoke thus: Rm_14.119{19} //
All of us here are engaged in lowly work;
unacquainted with happiness, we are afflicted by suffering, distressed, and live in hardship.
Because we did not previously accomplish even the slightest merit,
we have all become miserable and of low conduct here on account of that.
Therefore, we must honor this Teacher, the Lord of Sages, together with his Saṅgha, by providing him with food and worshiping him according to the prescribed rites.
Surely, through the ripening of this [merit], may we become fortunate;
then, in accordance with our merit, may we proceed upon the path to awakening.
Then, having gradually attained the auspicious practice of the conduct of awakening,
and while practicing it, may we obtain nirvana through its maturation.
Thinking thus, we all, having made our request to the king,
desire to honor the Sugata together with his Saṅgha by offering them meals.
Having agreed, saying "So be it," and all having expressed their approval,
they immediately proceeded to make their petition to the king.
Having approached him there and seen that king with joy, they bowed with palms joined in reverence and requested thus with great respect:
Victory to you, O God, Great King! Protect the worlds with righteousness.
We have come to make a certain request.
You should indeed understand this; nevertheless, we make our request.
Having heard us, may you, out of compassion, show favor and be gracious toward us.
"O King, since we are all here engaged in lowly occupations,
we desire to honor the Sage together with his community by offering them choice foods."
Therefore, having granted us your permission, you ought out of compassion to deliver us;
we offer this petition, so be gracious, O lord of kings!
Having heard this request made by them, the king was delighted;
he addressed them all and commanded them once again as follows.
May it be well for all of you; let your noble desire be fulfilled.
Therefore, let that be done with faith and reverence toward the honoring of the Buddha.
The karma performed toward a perfectly awakened Buddha will certainly not exhaust its fruit;
rather, by gradually fulfilling the conduct of awakening, one shall attain final liberation.
Therefore, in every way, you should with devotion and great respect honor the Sage Śrīghana together with his Saṅgha by offering him food as is appropriate.
Having heard this command from Indra, they all, with joy,
responded "So be it," and after bowing to the king, they then departed.
Then, having reached a consensus, they went quickly to the monastery; seeing Śrīghana, they bowed and entreated him with great reverence as follows:
"O Blessed One, may you understand the purpose for which we have come;
nevertheless, it would be fitting for you to grant us this favor."
Since we desire to worship and honor you all, the members of the entire Saṅgha, according to the prescribed rites, even with offerings of food; Rm_14.139{39} //
Therefore, having looked upon this with compassion and having bestowed your favor upon us,
it behooves you to come to the city tomorrow along with the Saṅgha to achieve victory.
When they had all thus entreated him, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
remained silent and dwelt there for the sake of increasing their merit.
Then, all of them, perceiving that the Blessed One had consented,
bowed once more to that Śrīghana and departed swiftly for their own city.
There, having all together purified the ground on every side and prepared their own seats, they thus brought about the necessary assembly.
Then, having prepared offerings for worship, various foods, flavorful delicacies,
and well-prepared drinks, they were filled with joy.
There, they went to invite the Sugata and the entire Saṅgha;
having approached the monastery, they paid homage to Śrīghana.
With palms joined in reverence, they all stood together and bowed,
earnestly entreating the Saṅgha headed by the Perfectly Awakened One.
"O Omniscient Blessed One, Teacher, the time has now come;
therefore, you ought to go forth to conquer together with the Saṅgha."
When they had thus entreated him, the Blessed One, seeing them, took up his bowl and robe together with the Saṅgha and set out, radiating great light.
Displaying miracles throughout all those paths and bringing auspiciousness to everyone, he entered that city.
Thus moving in a clockwise direction all around that place,
illuminating it and bringing about auspiciousness, he proceeded through that region.
There, having taken water for the feet and the guest-offering in due order along with the community of monks,
he sat down upon his own seat and remained there, radiant like the sun.
Then, seeing that Śrīghana and the entire community seated upon their thrones,
they all began to offer worship out of joy.
Having thus worshipped that assembly headed by the Buddha in due order,
he satisfied and gladdened them all with appropriate foods.
Then, at the conclusion of the meal, they removed those bowls,
washed their hands and so forth, and thoroughly cleansed that ground.
Then, having offered betel nuts and other gifts, they all once again joyfully stood before him with palms joined in reverence after bowing down.
And all those musicians went for refuge to the Three Jewels;
having formed the aspiration for awakening, they departed with concentrated minds.
With the playing of musical instruments and songs, including flutes, lutes, and drums,
he approached Śrīghana together with his Saṅgha and fully gratified him.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that their hearts were purified by devotion, released a smile from his mouth for them all, O Uddhava.
Then, auspicious rays of five colors, arising simultaneously with that smile,
went everywhere throughout the world and spread like rays of nectar.
Some of them, having gone down into the hells on all sides,
illuminated and touched them, bestowing happiness everywhere.
Then those denizens of hell, touched by that radiance, were filled with happiness;
wondering "What is this?", they closed their eyes and spoke thus: Rm_14.161{61} //
"Aha! How is it that such happiness has now arisen for us?
Alas! To what place have we gone today, and by whose power of merit?"
Thus, in order to awaken the minds of those whose hearts were filled with doubt,
the Blessed One dispatched an emanated Buddha in every direction.
There, having seen that follower of the Sugata, all those dwelling in hell were struck with wonder; approaching him with serene minds, they paid him homage.
"Homage to the Buddha, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha; homage always!
Having spoken thus and having bowed down, they went for refuge to them.
By the power of this merit, they all rose from hell and suddenly attained rebirth in heaven, practicing the true Dharma.
Having thus rescued all those sentient beings from every side,
they all once again approached the presence of the Perfectly Awakened One like rays of light.
Some ascended upwards as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven, illuminating it on all sides; having proclaimed [the news] there, they exhorted them in this way:
"Indeed, saṃsāra is impermanent, empty, and devoid of self"—
having thoroughly understood this truth, one should venerate the Three Jewels with reverence.
Depart and go forth; apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the armies of Māra, as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket.
Whoever always practices with heedfulness in this Dharma of the Sugata will,
having abandoned birth in cyclic existence, bring an end to suffering.
Thus exhorting all those gods from every side,
all those rays of light went into the presence of the Sugata.
Then all those rays, having come together and united, O Sage,
performed three circumambulations of him and entered into his ūrṇā-hair.
Seeing that, the people in the assembly, their minds agitated with wonder,
stood there filled with curiosity, reflecting, "What is this?"
Then Ānanda, beholding them all filled with wonder and joy,
rose, bowed with palms joined, and addressed that Teacher.
O Blessed One, the five-colored radiance issuing from your mouth has illuminated all directions and now enters back into the circle of hair between your eyebrows.
Seeing this, all these members of the assembly are filled with wonder and desire to hear the cause of it; therefore, you ought to explain it.
For Buddhas never display a smile without a cause;
please explain that for which you, the Teacher, have smiled.
Having been thus entreated by his disciple, that lord of sages,
looking upon him, the assembly, and the hall with joy, commanded as follows:
Behold, Ānanda, how all these musicians have joyfully performed such hospitality for me and my entire retinue.
Through the ripening of this merit, all these beings as well, in another existence,
will gradually attain the conduct of awakening, free from afflictions and pure in intention.
Free from the conduct of Māra, completely pure in the three spheres,
all those Pratyekabuddhas, the Victors, are designated by their colors, voices, and names.
Seated on remote beds and seats, compassionate toward the lowly and the wretched,
those great beings who perform auspicious deeds will become worthy recipients of offerings.
Having observed this thus, if you so desire,
then always worship the Triple Gem here with devotion and respect.
Those who always worship the Three Jewels with devotion and due honor shall forever leave behind the miserable realms and attain the excellent state.
(194) Thinking thus, those who have a desire for the auspicious happiness in this saṃsāra should honor the Three Jewels and worship them constantly with faith. Rm_14.186{86}
Having heard what was thus commanded by the Lord of Sages, all those people made this very truth their vow and worshipped the Three Jewels at all times.
Seeing that, all the monks, their minds uplifted with wonder,
bowed with palms joined in reverence and questioned that Lord of Sages.
Since such great honor has thus been rendered to you, O Blessed One,
by what supreme merit is it right for you to grant [this] instruction?
When all those monks had thus entreated him, that Lord of Jinas,
having gazed upon all those śrāvaka monks, gave this instruction:
Listen, O monks, to the merit that was performed by me in the past;
having heard it as it is told here, rejoice with faith.
In former times there was the Blessed Buddha, the Victor named Prabodhana—
the omniscient one, the Sugata, the Teacher, the King of Dharma, and the Lord of Sages.
The Lord is the master of all vidyās, the Tathāgata, the Guide; he has conquered Māra, is the Knower of the World, the Sustainer, the Subhadra, the Arhat, and the benefactor.
Then that Blessed One, the Buddha, while wandering on a tour through the countryside, arrived at another royal capital together with his community of monks.
There, beneath a tree in the pleasure garden of that lord of men,
he entered and sat upon his seat, remaining as radiant as a blazing fire.
Then, on one day, the king sat down there, deeply attached to music performed by those who sing of beloved women, in order to enjoy himself.
Having seen the Sugata seated there, resplendent with brilliant light, he immediately approached him, bowed down, and performed a circumambulation.
Beholding him established in meditative concentration, he remained for a long time in attendance,
desiring to obtain the nectar of the true Dharma issuing from the lotus of his face.
With those excellent musical instruments being played, the king awakened the Sage;
thereupon that Sugata, the Buddha, quickly arose from his meditative absorption.
Then he beheld that lord of men arrived with his inner apartments;
having seen the king, the perfectly awakened one, the enlightener, [approached him].
Having thus invited him to fully teach the True Dharma, he spoke:
"Come, O King of great arms; welcome to you, O lord of the earth!"
Relying fully upon the True Dharma, practice the conduct of awakening;
always bestowing gifts here, maintain ethical discipline with a concentrated mind.
Purify the worlds through patience; accomplish the vigor of the Dharma;
having concentrated the mind upon awakening, acquire the jewel of wisdom.
By the power of that jewel, may you attain the path to perfect enlightenment;
through that, may there be constant auspiciousness for you always, both in this world and the next.
"Bringing benefit to all sentient beings, may you attain only the happy destinies";
thinking thus, O Great King, take refuge in the True Dharma.
Having taken refuge in the Triple Gem, always honor and worship them with devotion;
for the merit performed toward the Triple Gem is never exhausted.
"Always producing only good fruits and bestowing awakening"—
thinking thus, O Great King, he went for refuge to the Triple Gem. (Rm 195) Rm_14.207{7}
Having taken up the vow of the conduct of awakening, practice it always with a concentrated mind;
in this way, may auspiciousness surely be yours at all times and in every place.
"Having attained enlightenment by degrees, may you reach the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha"—
thus was the king instructed by that Arhat and Lord of Sages.
Having heard this and replied, "So be it," the awakened king rejoiced;
then, filled with joy, he [honored] that Lord of Sages together with his assembly.
Having honored him according to the prescribed rites, he satisfied him with various foods.
Then, at the conclusion of the meal, the king, with palms joined in reverence and full of joy, bowed down to that lord of sages and made this aspiration from his heart: Rm_14.211{11} //
By this merit, may I, having attained perfect enlightenment in this blind world that lacks a guide, become a Sugata, a Conqueror.
Having understood that this aspiration had been joyfully made by that lord of men,
the Sugata bestowed upon him a corresponding word of blessing.
May victory be yours always, O King; protect your subjects with righteousness.
May your aspiration for awakening be fulfilled with certainty, just as you have resolved.
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Lord of Sages, the king,
joyful and with palms joined in reverence, bowed to that Lord of Sages and spoke to him.
From this day forth, O Teacher, having always gone for refuge to the Triple Gem and having taken up the vow of complete enlightenment, I shall practice with concentrated mind.
Therefore, you ought always to look upon me with a compassionate eye;
I am forever established in your very refuge.
Having thus made this earnest supplication, the king, together with his retinue, bowed joyfully to that Blessed One and returned to his own city full of delight.
Then that Blessed One, the Teacher, having risen together with his community of monks, and having performed auspicious rites everywhere, returned to his own hermitage.
"Monks, let it be known that he who was that king, the servant of the Perfectly Awakened One, was none other than myself; he should be regarded as such."
With great enthusiasm, I performed worship for that Protector, Prabodhana, with faith by playing musical instruments and singing songs.
By the ripening of that merit, it is now that I am being thus honored here by these very musicians with great festivities.
Realizing thus that the great merit arising from devotion to the Perfectly Awakened One is so vast,
those who seek what is auspicious should take refuge in the Three Jewels and practice devotion.
And you too, always and eternally relying upon the Teacher, the true Guru, the Jina,
the Perfectly Awakened One, dwell in meditative composure.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, all those monks joyfully replied,
"So be it," and constantly venerated the Three Jewels.
"Thus was it instructed by my teacher, and thus have I heard it, O lord of men;
so now has it been related to you for the increase of your merit."
Thus, O King, you too have gone for refuge to the Three Jewels;
upholding the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One, practice the Dharma with a concentrated mind.
And likewise, O King, having diligently awakened your subjects,
you should respectfully engage them in the Dharma that accomplishes perfect enlightenment.
If you act thus, prosperity will surely be yours at all times in every respect;
having gradually attained awakening, you shall reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard this instruction from the Teacher, King Aśoka,
along with his retinue, replied "So be it" and rejoiced greatly.
Those people who, having heard this *avadāna* of the Gandharva women, rejoice with joy—
having their minds completely liberated from all evil, they shall experience every happiness and attain awakening.
Thus ends the *Gāndharvikā-avadāna* within the *Ratnāvadānatattva*.
(Rm 197) XV. The Avadāna of Sūkṣmatvacas.
Then King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence, joyfully [spoke].
Having bowed to his teacher Upagupta, he spoke again in this manner:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear yet another well-spoken word;
it behoves you to teach it to me just as it was explained by my teacher."
When the king had thus made his request, that ascetic, a son of the Sugata, beholding King Aśoka, instructed him once more in this way: Rm_15.3{3} //

so may you, O Teacher, deign out of compassion to act for us.
Having heard this prayer made by them all, the wise Maudgalyāyana agreed, saying "So be it," and remained there in silence.
Then, having surveyed all those hungry ghosts and comforted them, the ascetic Maudgalyāyana spoke this once more:
Therefore, all of you, when tomorrow the communal feast has commenced,
come with due respect to behold the Blessed One together with his Saṅgha.
Having heard this instruction from the Arhat, those hungry ghosts also replied,
"So be it," and having bowed to him, they departed for the forest.
Then that Buddhist monk, Maudgalya, a self-knowing ascetic,
went to Rājagṛha and attended upon those kinsmen.
Having gone there to all those dwellings of their kinsmen, he reported the entire account of what had occurred to them in this manner.
Then, having respectfully summoned all those kinsmen there, he spoke to them in this way for the sake of their liberation from the state of the departed spirits: Rm_16.47.47.
Listen, O highly fortunate ones, all of you with concentrated minds;
I shall proclaim the cause of liberation for you and your kinsmen.
For those of your own lineage are stingy and evil-intentioned;
they cling to material possessions and practice the ten unwholesome paths of action.
Nor did they ever give even the slightest gift to anyone, anywhere;
nor, upon hearing of or seeing gifts given by others, did they speak disparagingly of them.
Arhats or monks, as well as beggars who had come to their homes,
were reviled and threatened by them, and were forcibly driven out of the houses.
"Like hungry ghosts (pretas), these people always eat only after begging for alms";
thus, upon merely seeing the Arhats and ascetics, they reviled them.
Due to the ripening of these very actions, you have now become pretas in this forest;
constantly struck by hunger and thirst, you wander about in extreme misery.
Therefore, in order to liberate them from that great evil,
I now truly desire to perform an act of giving here within the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One.
"Let these southern regions be made known by his name;
then, freed from that sin, they shall all surely go to heaven."
Therefore, in this matter, you who have been requested by me according to my ability should all, out of faith,
provide the necessary provisions for the communal meal.
When the communal meal for the Saṅgha has commenced here, all those female spirits (pretikās) will also come together to see it; you too ought to go.
When the compassionate Maudgalyāyana had spoken thus and made his request,
all those born into that [animal] species heard it and were filled with wonder.
Then they were all amazed, and for the sake of that deceased one’s liberation from the state of a preta,
they desired to offer the provisions for a feast with faith.
Some presented him with gold, some with jewels, and others with silver and other minerals, as well as various kinds of wealth.
Some gave rice, some gave various grains;
some gave peas, and others even gave wheat and barley.
Others gave kulmāṣa, lentils, mung beans, chickpeas, mustard seeds, mung beans, and likewise all other kinds of grains.
Sesame, priyaṅgu, and white mustard seeds; hemp and black mustard as well;
roots, stalks, kadamba trees, and leaves, flowers, and sprouts.
Others joyfully presented various fruits that were well-ripened with ginger, fragrant and highly wholesome.
They joyfully gave various tastes, such as bitter, sour, and salty, as well as ginger, long pepper, and black pepper.
Some offered asafoetida and cumin seeds, others offered viḍa salt, rock salt, and so forth;
others, with faith and joy, gave ghee and oils.
With joy they gave parched grain, flour cakes, and other sweetmeats,
as well as curds, milk, honey, and molasses.
Likewise, others gave sugar-candies as well with faith and joy;
others gave medicinal herbs that are wholesome and digestive.
They provided betel nuts, betel leaves, areca nuts, cloves, and other such items;
they also provided all kinds of drinks and various foods.
All those kinsmen provided these for the community to eat.
Having thus given all their possessions, they were all filled with joy;
bowing with palms joined in reverence, they spoke to that ascetic Maudgalyāyana.
"May the Venerable One, having shown favor and having honored the entire Saṅgha headed by the Perfectly Awakened One, provide them with a meal, bringing them complete satisfaction."
"We too shall come when the communal meal has begun,
in order to see all those hungry ghosts who have arrived together with their kinsmen."
Having heard their request, he agreed, saying "So be it," and taking all those goods, he went to his own hermitage while instructing them.
Then that venerable monk, moving about in the monastery, saw Śrīghana; having bowed to him with palms joined in reverence, he took refuge at his side.
There, the Blessed One, seeing Maudgalyāyana standing before him, smiled with a most serene countenance and, addressing him, spoke these words:
"Is all well with you, my child? From where have you come here?
O high-minded one, tell me what news has occurred in the worlds."
When the Lord of Sages had thus instructed him, the wise Maudgalyāyana bowed to the Blessed One with palms joined and spoke as follows.
O Blessed One, Teacher, through your compassion, may I possess skill in all matters as I go about begging for alms in the city of Rājagṛha.
There, at the edge of a forest on the road, five hundred hungry ghosts (preta) saw me; approaching and bowing down to me, they spoke as follows:
"Venerable sir, please understand this: we who are these female spirits were all born in Rājagṛha; indeed, we were formerly householders and citizens."
At that time, we ourselves were ruined, practicing the ten unwholesome actions; through the power of our own destiny, we have become hungry ghosts and wander about. (Rm 210) Rm_16.81{80} //
Therefore, out of compassion for us, please explain the web of karma for the sake of liberating our deceased kin from the state of hungry ghosts, as well as for all our other relatives.
"Even though we have made this request for alms, he ought to honor the Blessed One on our behalf, together with the Saṅgha, and provide him with a meal. Rm_16.83{82} //
"Please bow down on our behalf to the Fully Awakened One together with his Saṅgha;
and you should likewise grant us the dedication of the offerings in our names."
Then, surely, we shall all be liberated from the realm of hungry ghosts;
freed from our misdeeds and purified, may we attain the abode of the gods.
Having thus made this prayer of ours, may you, lifting us up through your compassion and establishing us on the path to awakening, deign to protect us at all times.
Having heard these words of theirs, he likewise went to Rājagṛha and,
having related the news in the presence of those kinsmen, he spoke.
Having requested alms from them, I shall conduct myself here;
thus do I desire to honor the Blessed One together with his Saṅgha.
Having thus made this prayer to you, the Teacher and Master of the World,
please grant your consent and, out of compassion, deliver them.
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
having promised "So be it," remained silent and dwelt there.
Then, perceiving that the Blessed One had given his consent, Maudgalya quickly prepared the full array of food together with the citizens.
Then, on the following day when dawn had broken and all his goals were accomplished,
he joined his palms in reverence, bowed to that Lord of Sages, and spoke as follows:
"O Blessed One, having fully accomplished all the necessary preparations, it will be successfully achieved;
therefore, you ought to come at once together with the entire Saṅgha."
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages,
summoned a monk and said, "Let the gaṇḍī be struck."
Having heard what was commanded by the Lord of Sages, that monk replied, "So be it," and having assented,
he immediately took up the gong and struck it.
Hearing that sound of the gong, all those members of the Saṅgha also came suddenly to the monastery and paid homage to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One sat down there upon his own seat,
and all those members of the Saṅgha also took their respective seats in due order.
Then all their kinsmen and other citizens also came there,
full of curiosity, and stood waiting to see those departed spirits.
Then all those hungry ghosts were cast away by the winds of karma;
having gone far into many other worlds, they remained there, utterly bewildered.
Then that ascetic, having observed all the members of the community assembled there,
as well as his own circle of kinsmen and relatives who had become pretas, proceeded to look upon them.
Not seeing the pretas there, Maudgalyāyana, his mind filled with wonder,
looked all around, thinking, "Why have they not come here?"
Looking everywhere, he did not see her on any side;
filled with doubt, he looked there once more with keen vision.
Not seeing those hungry ghosts anywhere, he was filled with wonder;
yet, being composed and possessing right vision, he saw them everywhere throughout Magadha.
And even there, he did not see anyone at all;
then, being greatly astonished, he looked elsewhere with his divine vision.
In Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Kaliṅga, as well as in Saurāṣṭra and Magadha—
and even there, not seeing them, he looked all around in the hells with his divine eye, yet he did not see them there either.
Then, surveying all around the realms of the Four Great Kings with his divine eye, he did not perceive him there either.
Even there, not seeing them, Maudgalya, filled with wonder,
searched in all the temples in succession.
There too, Maudgalyāyana, being greatly amazed at seeing her on all sides and utterly perplexed by not seeing those [other Buddhas], moved about in the presence of the Blessed One.
There, having gone before that Teacher, the Lord of Sages,
he bowed with palms joined in reverence and asked about the circumstances of this event.
O Blessed One, though I survey all the worlds with my divine eye, I do not see any of those hungry ghosts; where have they gone now?
This has been prepared to perform worship for you by means of their names;
as for those who have not arrived here, where have those hungry ghosts gone?
"They are not seen by me anywhere; though I look everywhere, not even one has come here. Where indeed have they gone now?"
Having seen that my mind is thus perplexed, O Teacher of excellent vision,
you ought to explain their destiny and awaken me to it.
When Maudgalya had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the omniscient one, looked at Maudgalya and said this to him:
"O Maudgalya, do not exert yourself; you will only meet with weariness.
All those hungry ghosts have now gone to a realm that is very far away."
All of them have entered the invisible realm, driven by the winds of karma, even by ascetics, divine seers, and Pratyekabuddhas.
If you, having taken refuge here, desire to see them all, I shall show them all to you; behold the majesty of the Buddha’s power!
Therefore, having taken up the gong here, strike it quickly:
*Oṃ namo bhagavate aparimitāyurjñānasuviniścitatejorājāya tathāgatāyārhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya*. It is as follows:
Oṃ, merit, merit, great merit, immeasurable merit, you who have accumulated an immeasurable store of merit and wisdom!

Oṃ, you who are purified of all conditioned phenomena, O nature of reality, risen like the sky, pure by nature, surrounded by the Great Vehicle—svāhā! By means of this hundred-and-eight-syllable mantra, those who have not attained conscious awareness [are purified]. (Rm 16.118)
"They shall all come here, summoned by the sound of the gong"—
having heard this command given by the Teacher, he was awakened.
Suddenly, he struck the gong in the midst of that assembly;
and hearing the sound of that gong, all those hungry ghosts as well—
With pure intentions, they approached the monastery in order to see him.
There, all those hungry ghosts, having seen Śrīghana with joy,
circumambulated him three times and bowed down with palms joined in reverence.
Having bowed down in succession to her and to the entire assembly, they were filled with joy; then, all of them, having retired to a secluded spot, stood gazing [upon him].
There, all their kinsmen, the citizens, and others as well,
stood filled with curiosity upon seeing those departed spirits gathered together.
In this way, all those pretas, upon seeing their own kinsmen who had approached them— brothers and other groups of relatives— stood before them in such a manner.
Then that arhat Maudgalyāyana, possessing great supernormal knowledge, beheld all those hungry ghosts who had approached him; having bowed, he spoke thus to the Lord of Sages:
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, all those hungry ghosts have arrived;
therefore, it behooves the Blessed One, the Teacher, to show them favor.
Having thus offered [the food], that son of Maudgalya, having honored the entire Saṅgha headed by the Perfectly Awakened One in due order, fed them and satisfied them completely.
Then, seeing that entire assembly satisfied and joyful,
he quickly removed the bowls from their hands and thoroughly cleansed their hands and other limbs.
Then, having given him an elixir consisting of *khapura*, *sūkṣmailā*, betel, and other ingredients,
and having offered a request for forgiveness, he entreated the lord of sages.
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, you who are the Teacher together with the Saṅgha,
it behooves you to perform the dedication of merit for these hungry ghosts.
Having heard this prayer, all those female spirits joyfully bowed to the Sage together with his community and waited upon him with reverence.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all approached him together with the Saṅgha,
bestowed upon them all an auspicious instruction regarding their offerings.
Whatever merit indeed arises from this gift, may it follow after the hungry ghosts;
rising up, may all these hungry ghosts proceed to the abode of the gods.
Having thus instructed [them], the Blessed One, that lord of sages, then began there once more with the Noble Truths concerning the Immeasurable Life.
He fully taught the true Dharma, which consists of the greatness of the qualities of the *dhāraṇī*.
For those wandering in existence, birth as a human in saṃsāra is difficult to obtain;
even when human birth is attained, the perfection of the opportune moment is exceedingly rare.
For when human birth is not attained, how can there be happiness for living beings? Since suffering alone is constant in existence, how could one direct the mind toward merit?
Without a virtuous mind, how could a living being practice the true Dharma?
Without the presence of the true Dharma, how could one attain a happy rebirth?
Constantly and eternally among the hungry ghosts, tormented by hunger and thirst,
and likewise wandering among animals and in the hells, he shall experience sufferings.
Therefore, those humans who have attained birth here in this world should always listen with joy, reverence, and faith to the True Dharma, having made a diligent effort.
By merely hearing the True Dharma, one shall obtain great merit;
through the ripening of this merit, one shall always serve a true guru.

(Rm 213) By means of the instruction of a true guru, one should always practice only in accordance with the true dharmas; through the ripening of this merit, one shall always proceed toward a happy rebirth. Rm_16.142{30}
Having enjoyed pleasures there, one should always proceed toward what is auspicious.
By the power of this merit, one shall attain great prosperity;
and amidst the abundance of such great prosperity, one should practice generosity toward those in need.

Through generosity, prosperity increases; and a man possessed of prosperity shines, endowed with right understanding, a repository of virtuous qualities, and possessed of fame, good fortune, and happiness.
Then, having heard the teachings of the Sugata and being constantly awakened by them,
one should take refuge in the Three Jewels and always worship them with devotion and respect.
By the power of this merit, may one attain the thought of awakening;
for once the thought of awakening is obtained, one becomes a virtuous Bodhisattva.
Then, having gradually fulfilled the ten perfections through the thought of awakening, that great being shall attain the threefold awakening.
Then, having conquered the hosts of Māra, being pure in the three spheres,
and having directly attained the state of an Arhat, he shall reach the state of Nirvāṇa.
Having understood this, a mortal should give to one who asks;
through giving one may go to a good rebirth, while the non-giver shall go to a miserable state.
Having always experienced various sufferings in the miserable realms, he,
perpetually afflicted by suffering, would continue to take delight only in evil deeds.
As a result of the ripening of this evil, he will indeed proceed with negligence, taking no heed even as he indulges in the ten unwholesome actions.
Then that most wicked one, a reviler of the true Dharma, evil-minded,
himself ruined, is an atheist and a rogue who ruins others as well.
Then, thoroughly defiled by extreme evil and having even reviled the Victors,
he will go to the very terrible hells and dwell there, wandering for all time.
Even as he thus wanders eternally through the hells in suffering,
no one at all would be able to rescue him except for a follower of the Sugata.
As long as one does not remember the Buddha, for that long one shall dwell in hell;
but the very moment one remembers the Buddha, one’s intention becomes purified.
Then the Buddha, having beheld him with his enlightened eye out of compassion,
touched him with his merit-making hand and swiftly delivered him from that [distress].
Then, having purified that sinner with the waters of the Dharma, the Buddhists should gradually establish him on the paths to enlightenment, awakening him.
Then, with his mind purified and devoted to the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One,
he took refuge in the Three Jewels and practiced only the true Dharma.
Then, for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, he, being fully intent upon the conduct of awakening,
should strive to gradually fulfill all the perfections.
Then, having fulfilled all the perfections while remaining in meditative concentration,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva shall indeed become a son of the Buddha.
Then, having conquered the hosts of afflictions and purified the three spheres,
one attains the threefold awakening and reaches the state of nirvāṇa.
Thinking thus, always and eternally having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels,
and relying upon the True Dharma, O humans, practice with joy!
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, all those people, including the brahmins, fully understood it; having realized the Truth, they acted accordingly.
Thus, having heard that teaching of the Dharma, all those pretas bowed with joy to Śrīghana; then, with purified souls, they departed.
Then, having seen and heard that, all his kinsmen were filled with wonder;
they bowed to the Sage together with his assembly and returned to their respective homes with joy.
Then that Blessed Buddha, having arisen together with his community of monks,
took recourse in the abode of meditation and remained absorbed in meditative concentration.
And Maudgalyāyana, having accomplished his purpose and being filled with joy,
bowed down to the Teacher and returned to his own hermitage.
Then all those hungry ghosts, having gained serene faith in the Perfectly Awakened One and having recollected the Three Jewels, passed away from there and went to heaven.
For all those who had been born there were endowed with great happiness;
their bodies being perfectly pure and beautiful, they were filled with wonder and spoke as follows:
"Aha! What great happiness is ours! What is happening now?
From where have we passed away, and where are we being born? By what karma are we [thus]?"
Then, through the power of the Buddha, all those sons of gods who had previously been hungry ghosts, having recollected [their past lives], were awakened and spoke thus:
Sirs, that we have all become ghosts is due to the power of the Buddha and through the compassionate vision and effort of the Arhat monk Maudgalyāyana.
Having attained the vision of the Perfectly Awakened One, they have gone for refuge to the Three Jewels;
touched by this merit, they possess the complete purity of the three bodies.
Then, having passed away from the realm of the hungry ghosts and arrived in the heavenly world,
we now enjoy such great divine pleasures here.
Having fully understood this truth regarding that Teacher, the Guru of the World,
let us all go once more, pay him honor, and share [the merit] together.
Having thus conversed, all those sons of gods, preceded by the deceased, bathed in auspicious waters and were clothed in divine garments.
With their limbs anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with celestial ornaments,
they took up divine articles for worship and, amidst great festivities,
illuminated the entire Bamboo Grove on all sides with their radiance.
Having approached the monastery and joyfully beheld that Śrīghana,
they bowed, circumambulated him, and, filled with great delight, attended upon him.
There, having honored that Lord of Sages with all those divine offerings and articles of worship, they all attended upon him with devotion, treating him with due respect.
And there, having taken their places in a secluded spot, all of them, eager to hear the true Dharma, stood with palms joined in reverence and composed minds.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all assembled,
began with the Noble Truths and fully taught the True Dharma.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, all those who were formerly hungry ghosts and the sons of gods attained excellence in the qualities of the Dharma.
Then they all, joyful and desiring the state of perfect enlightenment, bowed again to that Teacher, gazed upon him, and spoke as follows: Rm_16.184{72}
"O Blessed One, since we have all been liberated from the bonds of karma,
we have now fallen away from the world of hungry ghosts and have gone to heaven."
Having enjoyed divine pleasures together with the gods and rejoiced,
we now always practice, having heard the qualities of the true Dharma.
Therefore, O Compassionate One, we believe that this was surely due to the grace of the compassionate gaze of that great-minded Maudgalyāyana.
Having obtained the sight of you and having drunk the nectars of the Dharma,
we joyfully honor the Three Jewels with faith and devotion.
With our bodies encompassed by this merit and with purified intentions,
we joyfully come once again to behold you.
And thus, having drunk the nectar of the noble Dharma through the grace of the compassionate gaze of your Teacher, we do not attain contentment.
Therefore, having thus always gone for refuge to you,
we wish to serve you again with devotion, having approached you with due honor.
Therefore, may you, having bestowed upon us the favor of becoming our refuge through compassion,
deign to teach the true Dharma so as to protect us at all times.
Through your grace, we have crossed the ocean of suffering,
and the mountain of the view of a self-identity has been shattered by the vajra of wisdom.
The eye of wisdom has been attained, and existence has been seen as consisting of illusion;
the Noble Path has been reached, and the report of Nirvana has been obtained.
Blessed are we all that we have gone for refuge to you;
having drunk the nectar of the noble Dharma, we obtain great joy.
Blessed are all those people who have gone for refuge to the Buddha;
having always drunk the nectar of the Dharma, they perform acts of service within the Teaching.
Thus may you, the Teacher of the World, out of compassion for all sentient beings,
remain forever in happiness after having fully taught the True Dharma.
Thus, all those sons of the gods named Prabhā, filled with joy,
bowed down to that Lord of Munis and, being well-pleased, departed for heaven.
There, all those gods went for refuge to the Three Jewels;
desiring the state of perfect enlightenment, they always took delight in recollecting it.
Then, having risen at dawn, the Blessed One, being delighted,
addressed his disciple Maudgalyāyana and spoke thus:
