Excellent, Maudgalya! It has been accomplished; it is fruitful for you, O compassionate one, that you have performed service with such a well-adorned body.
Those for whose sake you made offerings to the Buddha by means of begging have all been reborn and established in the worlds of the gods.
All of them have come into my presence tonight;
having perceived their noble disposition, I have taught them the True Dharma.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, they were all filled with joy;
having realized the Truth, they departed and went to the abode of the Thirty-three gods.
There, even in heaven, they all took refuge in the Three Jewels;
desiring the qualities of perfect enlightenment, they always and constantly devoted themselves to them.
Whatever deed is performed under whatever name, its fruit is enjoyed by that very person.
Thus, to bring benefit to the world, one must perform the means for acquiring merit.
Thus, those who perform virtuous deeds after having benefited the world are great beings, Bodhisattvas, sons of the Victors.
Having understood this, one who is intent on bringing about the welfare of the world should practice with a concentrated mind solely in the means for accomplishing the true Dharma.
Having heard what was thus instructed by the Teacher, that noble-minded Arhat,
being enlightened, acknowledged it as true and rejoiced.
Then that Arhat, possessing great supernormal powers, went before his kinsmen and respectfully reported all of this, exactly as it had been taught in the scriptures.
And all those kinsmen, having heard what was announced by that Arhat and knowing it to be true, attained great joy.
Then all those kinsmen took refuge in the Three Jewels;
with constant faith and respect, they devoted themselves to them with great care.
Thus was it instructed to me by my teacher, O lord of men, and heard by me;
it is now being related to you out of affection and for the sake of enlightening the world.
Having understood this, O Indra among kings, you ought to cause the worlds to perform the worship of the Three Jewels, which is the means for the welfare of the hungry ghosts.
In that way, may auspiciousness truly be yours always and on all sides;
for the great merit arising from the welfare of all beings is indeed a fruit of true excellence.
Thinking thus, O Great King, awakening all the worlds and establishing them in the auspicious Dharma, protect them with a concentrated mind.
Having heard what was thus commanded by the Teacher, King Aśoka,
together with his retinue, replied "So be it" and rejoiced.
Those humans who hear this *Pretāvadāna* and those who even listen to it,
all of them, having thus acquired merit, shall enjoy happiness and move about in the world.
Thus ends the Pretikā-avadāna within the Ratnāvadāna-tatva.
XVII. The Kacaṅgalā-avadāna.
Then the great king Aśoka, filled with joy,
bowed down to the ascetic Upagupta and spoke once more as follows:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear yet another well-spoken word; it behoves you to instruct me just as you have been instructed by your teacher."
Having heard this request made by the king, that wise Arhat ascetic Upagupta looked upon the lord of men and spoke thus:
"Listen well, O Great King, to that which was spoken by my teacher; I shall declare it to you just as it was told, and having heard it, may you rejoice."
In a time long past, there was the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas,
the Lord of Sages, the Omniscient One, the Sugata, the Teacher, the King of Dharma, and the Guide.
In the vicinity of Śrāvastī, in the forest hermitage of Jeta, the auspicious abode, he dwelt in a monastery together with his disciples— the monks as well as the novices.
By the nuns of virtuous conduct, by the assemblies of laywomen,
as well as by the laymen and others who have gone for refuge to the Three Jewels.
Accompanied by hosts of bodhisattvas who were intent on uplifting sentient beings,
he wandered through the world, illuminating it with the rays of the Dharma.
All the worlds have assembled to drink that nectar of the True Dharma:
Śakra and the other gods, Brahmā and the world-protectors.
The Daityas, Nāgas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Kinnaras,
Rākṣasas, Garuḍas, and Vidyādharas— all of them set forth together.
Then all of them, placing him at their head, surrounded him on all sides along with his assembly and stood before him with concentrated minds.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all assembled,
taught the supreme Dharma, which is auspicious in the beginning, middle, and end.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, they were all thoroughly gladdened;
having understood the excellence of the Dharma, those of pure intention rejoiced.
At that moment, a woman named Kacaṅgalā, seeking old mangoes, was walking near the well carrying a water-jar.
There, having seen her and recognized her as one born from a previous life, the Blessed One addressed Ānanda and spoke thus in their presence:
"Go, Ānanda, and request nectar from this old woman, saying:
'O Mother, the Blessed One is thirsty; let that water be given to him.'"
Having heard this command from the Blessed One, Ānanda said, "So be it," and immediately approaching that old woman, he spoke to her thus: Rm_17.17{17}
"O Mother, the Blessed One, my Teacher, is thirsty right now;
therefore, by giving me this water, may you attain the Great Dharma."

Having heard this prayer thus offered by him, that venerable nun, looking at Ānanda with a joyful heart, spoke as follows: (Rm 218) Having heard what he had thus prayed for, that virtuous elder nun, looking toward Ānanda, spoke thus with joy.
"Venerable sir, it is well; I myself shall bring a jar filled with the nectar of immortality there and give it to you. Please proceed."
Having heard what was thus spoken by her, Ānanda was awakened;
he approached, related this very matter, and took his place before the Teacher.
Then, having quickly filled a jar with pure water,
she herself took it up and went directly toward him there.
Having approached that place, she beheld the Lord of Sages,
adorned with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor characteristics.
Resplendent with a fathom-wide aura, possessing a radiance exceeding that of a hundred suns,
he was like a moving jewel, gentle and auspicious in every way.
Upon seeing him there, streams of milk flowed incessantly from her breasts, arising from the affection she felt for her son.
Then, through the power of the Dharma, having remembered his son from a previous birth, he cried out, "O son! O son! and approached to embrace him.
Then all those monks, upon seeing her thus afflicted, suddenly rose up and began to support her.
Having seen that, the Blessed One, the Teacher, suddenly summoned all those members of the Saṅgha and instructed them once again as follows:
"Monks, do not support this old woman; release her here!
For in the past, she has been my mother for five hundred births."
This woman, who was my mother in a previous birth, driven by the power of maternal affection for her son,
runs toward my body desiring to embrace me.
If these two are not restrained here, even from my own phlegm,
her warm blood will surely flow from her throat this very instant.
Recalling my gratitude and seeing this longing for her son,
I grant her an embrace of my body out of compassion and pity for her here.
Having heard this instruction from the Teacher, all those members of the Saṅgha,
perceiving her to be the Teacher’s former mother, stood there filled with wonder.
At that very moment, raising her arms, she beheld that lord of sages;
having run toward him suddenly, she embraced him and bowed for a long time.
Then, after a long time, that old woman rose up and, with palms joined in reverence and full of joy,
gazed upon Śrīghana and stood before him with a composed mind.
Then the Blessed One, seeing her standing before him,
began to teach the True Dharma, starting from the Noble Truths.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, even though she was old, Kacaṅgalā became pure in intention, auspicious, and awakened to the conduct of enlightenment.
Having shattered with the vajra of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity— which has twenty peaks rising above its base— they were awakened by the realization of the Truths.
Having directly realized the fruit of stream-entry and having exerted herself with diligence, she bowed with palms joined to that Sage and spoke these verses: Rm_17.39{39} //
(Rm 219) That which ought to be done by a son who performs difficult deeds for his mother has been accomplished by you here; my mind is now intent upon liberation. Rm_17.40(40)
Having been rescued from the miserable states of existence, I have now been established with great effort in heaven and in liberation, for the sake of attaining supreme awakening.
Therefore, having bestowed your favor upon me, you ought now to grant me the vows of renunciation, which are the means for attaining the state of perfect enlightenment.
Taking refuge in you, I shall be intent upon honoring the Three Jewels;
having undertaken the vows of renunciation, I will practice the holy life.
Having heard what she had requested, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
perceiving the purity of her mind, instructed her in this way.
"If you have faith, O mother, in the means for attaining renunciation,
then having obtained your husband's permission, come here first and practice self-restraint."
Having heard what was thus commanded by the Lord of Sages, she was filled with joy;
having promised "So be it" and bowed to the Sage, she then departed.
Thereupon, having gone quickly to the house, she joyfully bowed with palms joined in reverence to her husband, and standing before him, spoke thus: Rm_17.47{46} //
"O Lord, listen; I shall tell you a wonder: today, seeking water, I took a jar and went outside to the vicinity of a well."
There, seeing me approaching, the great ascetic Ānanda suddenly came forward and asked the Blessed One for water.
Then, having suddenly filled a jar with pure water and holding it myself, I approached the assembly to offer it.
There, upon seeing that Śrīghana, my heart was deluded by affection,
and a continuous stream of salt water flowed from both my breasts.
There, blinded by affection and passion, I ran toward that sage with upraised arms to embrace him as if he were my own son, even though we were in different existences.
Seeing me thus rushing toward them, all those members of the Saṅgha also rose up and ran forward, desiring to strike me down.
Then the Blessed One, seeing them all thus arisen,
suddenly addressed them and commanded them as follows:
"You ought not to prevent me in any way from this,
which is indeed my merit produced over a hundred lifetimes."
Therefore, seeing me here, she— filled with the passion of maternal love for her own child and desiring to embrace me— is running toward me with her face upturned.
If she were held here before me while in such a state of fainting,
she would undoubtedly die, shedding warm blood.
Having heard this instruction from the Teacher, those members of the Saṅgha were thus awakened; they bowed down to me and each took their place upon their own seat.
Having heard all that was thus related by that Lord of Munis, I, becoming fully awakened, indeed remember my former existence.
Then, my heart overcome with wonder and greatly rejoicing,
I stood respectfully before him to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
There, having seen me standing before him in this manner, the Blessed One,
beginning with the Noble Truths, taught the excellent Dharma.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, my mind is exceedingly delighted;
yet, thirsting for its flavor once more, it desires to drink it again.
All of them there were members of the Saṅgha, satiated by the nectar of the True Dharma;
they were pure in soul, possessed of auspicious limbs, and completely purified in the three spheres.
Pure in virtue and of auspicious conduct, they were filled with compassion and pity;
they established the welfare of all sentient beings and were free from longing for the gains of cyclic existence.
Exerting themselves in concentration, dhāraṇīs, and vidyās, they remained composed;
having directly attained the state of an Arhat, they were free from conceptual construction and stainless.
"O Lord, having taken refuge in the Perfectly Awakened One and being intent on accomplishing perfect awakening,
they are seen by me seated together in the monastery."
"I desire to undertake the vow of renunciation in order to attain a conduct similar to his;
therefore, O Lord, out of compassion, grant me your permission in this matter."
Having heard this account concerning his wife, he, being extremely impoverished,
stood motionless, gazing at her alone, struck with wonder and paralyzed.
Then, gazing at his wife for a very long time in this manner, he,
terrified by the fear of separation, spoke slowly as follows:
"O woman, have you lost your senses that you speak thus?
How can such a thing be told by you; who here will believe the truth?"
That Blessed One, the Buddha, was the son of a universal monarch (cakravartin),
the sovereign lord of the entire triple world, the King of Dharma, and the Guide.

The Teacher of the world, the Lord of the world, the Omniscient One, the Sugata, the Victor, the Indra of Sages, the Conqueror of Māra, the Arhat, the one possessed of the six superknowledges, the Tathāgata.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, whose form is Samantabhadra,
possesses the ten powers, is of great renown, practices the holy life, and has conquered his senses.
He indeed becomes the refuge, the one worthy of honor, the one to be saluted, and the one to be worshipped by all embodied beings, including the worlds of the Subrahmans, gods, and Daityas.
"You alone are such an unfortunate woman, pained by extreme poverty—
a slave dependent on others, a servant, wretched, and ill-favored in form."
How was it that, though born from the womb of one such as you, he became so great,
and having attained the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), practiced the conduct of awakening?
Since, through the ripening of merit, he has fulfilled the perfections in succession,
he has now attained awakening and has indeed become a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
By the distribution of this merit, how is it that you have such a fate?
For even now, in such a state, not even a trace of happiness is found.
Therefore, do not speak thus; having spoken in such a manner, you will not shine at all.
Who, upon hearing these words of yours, would accept them with confidence?
"Alas! Your limbs scorched by the fire of slander and tormented by great suffering, you will surely meet death after vomiting forth warm blood."
For one may indeed go to hell due to the intention of speaking falsely;
how then could you possibly not likewise go to hell?
In the hells, you will certainly remain for a very long time, overwhelmed by intense sensations as you experience various sufferings constantly and eternally.
Having heard these words spoken by her husband, the old woman Kacaṅgalā stood there with a broken heart, despondent and bewildered.
Then, having regained consciousness after a very long time,
she saw her husband once more and spoke in order to awaken him.
"O Lord, be gracious to me in this matter and speak thus in every way:
'What I have spoken is the truth; do not consider it to be false.'"
If my word should prove false, by that I shall go to hell;
but if my word is true, may I here attain a good rebirth.
Therefore, in this case, separation from us shall surely come about in both ways;
for death must inevitably occur for all living beings.
What is the use of such a life, which is nothing but a portion of suffering?
For where there is no Dharma, how can there even be happiness?
In this cycle of existence, the purpose of birth and the means for attaining a body is solely for the sake of Dharma;
without Dharma, what use are these to us, since they lead only to the acquisition of suffering?
Thinking thus, even those who are great, illustrious, and wise,
having abandoned all possessions, go forth into the hermitage of the Jina.
Thus, having fully understood this, O Lord, I have gone for refuge to the Perfectly Awakened One; now I desire to practice the means for attaining the True Dharma.
Therefore, you ought to grant me permission for the vow of renunciation;
by means of this share of merit, may you also attain a happy rebirth.
If permission is not granted for the accomplishment of the vow of renunciation,
then how shall I prevent [myself] when suddenly seized by death?
"How much longer shall I live, I who am old and my senses decayed?"—
thinking thus, you ought not to restrain me in this way.
Moreover, I am an old woman, aged; what affection do you have for me? O you with frail limbs, what purpose could there possibly be in an old woman like me?
And you too are overcome by old age; you are aged and your faculties are weakened.
So why now, for one who is old, do you harbor such affectionate attachment toward me?
Even now, what hope for happiness can there be for us two, whose bodies are overcome by old age?
Death will inevitably seize us here and swallow us both.
Then what shall I do, and what will you do?
I shall sit here in grief alone, and you likewise shall sit there in grief.
In this saṃsāra, that which is destined to happen must inevitably come to pass;
for no one here ever experiences otherwise than what is destined.
In this world, all living beings, having taken hold of their own performed karma,
have gone, are going, and will go to the abode of Yama after casting off the body.
There, by the command of Yama, all who partake in the fruits of their own actions— those who were righteous went to a good rebirth, while the sinful went to an evil rebirth.
Thus all these beings, experiencing the fruits of their own destiny,
wander perpetually, enjoying both pleasures and pains.
Thus, O Lord, having understood this, those who always desire happiness should always strive with diligence to practice the Dharma alone within this cycle of existence.
"The Dharma that is most excellent and supreme, arising from the vows of the Sugata—has this not been proclaimed by the Buddhas, and have you not heard it as well? (Rm 17.104)
Therefore, I have gone for refuge to the teaching of the Lord of Sages;
O Lord, I now desire to receive the vows of renunciation.
By the ripening of this merit, may my three spheres be completely purified;
having directly attained the state of an Arhat, may I reach the state of Nirvana.
"By means of this classification of the Dharma, may you also go to a happy rebirth.
Thinking thus, O Lord, please grant me that permission.
Remaining here in your own home, having gone for refuge to the Triple Gem,
enjoy happiness for as long as you live, and always practice virtue with diligence.
Through the ripening of this merit, you too shall become thus wise;
thereafter, a longing for the Dharma of the Sugata will arise in your mind.
Then, having gone with faith to the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One yourself,
and having obtained the restraint of the going-forth, you shall personally attain the state of an Arhat.
Thinking thus, O Lord, if you desire the true Dharma,
then you ought to grant me permission for the vow of renunciation.
Having heard what she said, that poor man was awakened;
after gazing at his wife for a very long time, he spoke thus slowly.
"Alas, beloved! How can you wish to abandon me?
What shall I say in this matter, when you speak to me thus?"
If you possess the resolve and steadfastness, take refuge endowed with faith;
go forth, having taken up the vows, and live concentrated in truth.
Having heard what was spoken by her husband, that old Kacaṅgalā, though aged,
bowed to her husband and then proceeded, filled with joy.
Then, having gone there in haste, she arrived at that hermitage;
beholding Śrīghana before her, she approached him.
Having gone before him there, with palms joined in reverence and filled with joy,
she bowed down to that Lord of Munis and thus requested ordination.
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, I go for refuge to you;
therefore, out of compassion, you ought to grant me the going forth.
Having heard this request made by her, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
touched the head of that aged woman with his right hand.
"Come, mother, practice the holy life with a concentrated mind.
Having said this and taken hold of her, she spoke again in the midst of the Saṅgha:
Go, mother; go for refuge to Gautamī, the daughter of Prajāpati.
She, the mother of the nun Arahatī, will grant you the going forth.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, she was delighted;
having assented to the Teacher with "So be it," she bowed to him and then departed.
Having approached there and seen Gautamī with joy, she went up to her,
bowed with palms joined, and requested ordination.
O Mother, I come here joyfully for refuge to you;
therefore, may you, the Mother of the World, grant me the going forth into the religious life.
Having heard this request, Gautamī, with approval,
touched her head with her hand and accepted it as belonging to the Saṅgha.
There, she immediately went forth into the order of the Prajāpatis according to the prescribed rule;
her head was shaven, she held a begging bowl in her hand, and she wore a garment of kāśāya cloth.
Gentle in her senses and beautiful in form, though aged, that Kacaṅgalā shone with exceeding beauty, possessing a tranquil mien as she stood in the midst of the community of nuns.
Then, through the grace of the Teacher and of Gautamī, that bhikṣuṇī applied herself with great effort to the study of meditative concentration, dhāraṇīs, and vidyās.

Having abandoned the mass of ignorance and attained mastery in knowledge and supernormal powers, she shone with a perfectly pure form, endowed with the qualities of the analytical knowledges and other virtues.
Then, having discerned that the wheel of existence is unstable and fluctuating,
and having understood that the courses of conditioned phenomena are destructive, she [proceeded].
Having conquered the entire host of afflictions and being purified in the three spheres,
she directly attained the state of an Arhat and became a practitioner of celibacy.
Then she, having conquered the afflictions, free from conceptual construction and stainless,
possessed a fragrance like sandalwood and regarded a clod of earth as equal to gold.
Free from desire for the enjoyments and honors of cyclic existence, like space itself,
she brings about the welfare of all sentient beings and has reached the further shore of all the sūtras.
That eloquent woman became one who was to be saluted, honored, and revered by the worlds of gods and asuras dwelling within the three realms.
When that Blessed One, the Teacher, having briefly instructed the bhikṣuṇīs with well-spoken words, retired to his meditation chamber.
Then that eloquent nun Kacaṅgalā taught the sūtra in the midst of the assembly of nuns.
Having heard that which was taught by her there in the form of a sūtra, the Blessed One addressed all those monks belonging to the Saṅgha and commanded them thus:
"O monks, this is the foremost among the nuns in my hermitage,
namely this Kacaṅgalā, who composes portions of the sūtras."
Having heard this and other such instructions from the Lord of Munis, all the members of the Saṅgha,
filled with wonder, questioned that Lord of Munis regarding his past deeds.
"Blessed One, what deed was performed by her in the past?
It would be well to awaken all those seated here in this assembly."
By this means, she has now become an elder nun within the teaching of the Buddha;
having directly attained the state of an Arhat, she lives as one who practices the holy life.
What former karma was performed by these [beings], where, when, and in what manner,
such that they even become foremost among those who compose portions of the sūtras?
Furthermore, what was the nature of the past karma, and when and how did it occur,
by which you were not held here in this final dwelling in a womb?
Having fully understood this past deed of hers, may the Blessed One deign to awaken all those seated here in this assembly.
(Rm 224) When all those monks had thus petitioned him, that Lord of Sages, seeing them all belonging to the Saṅgha, addressed them and gave this instruction: Rm_17.145{46} //
Listen, all you monks, to everything that was done by her in the past;
I shall relate it all for the awakening of your minds.
In the past, while I was a bodhisattva practicing the conduct of awakening,
this woman was my mother without interruption for five hundred births.
At that time, she created an obstacle for me while I was giving gifts;
because of that, even today she remains poor and unfortunate.
At that time, she was entreated by me in many ways for the sake of going forth;
yet she did not grant me permission, but instead stubbornly created obstacles.
As the ripening of this karma, though old and suffering,
she has obtained the restraint of renunciation and practices within my teaching.
If she were not [my mother], then she would have created obstacles for my giving;
yet she is never at all poor here now.
If they had not created this obstacle to my going forth, I would have practiced the vow in my youth; I am certainly not an old man now.
"Because she then created such an obstacle for me regarding this gift and vow,
she has now become an old woman and remains poor, even as she practices her religious observances."
Because no merit whatsoever was previously performed by her in the past,
I have not been held now in this final womb.
Since that great goddess Māyā is the accomplisher of the goal of great merit,
I have been held here by her within this final womb.
Furthermore, O sons of the twice-born, in the past in that city of Vārāṇasī,
she was poor and wretched, her limbs scorched by the fire of suffering.
Then, having gone for refuge to the teaching of Kāśyapa, the Lord of Munis and Teacher of the World, she went forth and practiced the religious vow.
There, she, who was highly skilled and proficient in the meaning of all treatises,
taught the true Dharma of all the sūtras to the bhikṣuṇīs.
Then that nun, provoked by some business matter there,
addressed all those nuns with the term "slave."
As the ripening of this karma, she is now extremely miserable;
serving others as a maidservant, she possesses an unfortunate appearance.
And because she joyfully practiced that spell there at that time,
by its power this celibate woman suddenly becomes an Arhatī.
And because she then taught that discourse there,
she is now the foremost among those who speak the sūtras.
"Thus, O monks, you should all consider that for all embodied beings wandering in saṃsāra, both happiness and suffering arise from karma."
By whomsoever an action was performed, by that very person is its fruit experienced;
an action that has not been experienced never perishes anywhere at any time.
Karma is not burned by fires, nor is it moistened even by waters;
it is not dried up by winds, nor does it perish within the earth.
Furthermore, even if there were no fruit of action in its ripening,
that very seed which is sown in the earth would produce its own fruit.
Otherwise, an action performed would never bear fruit anywhere;
in the ripening of a virtuous action, there would always be only virtue.
The blackness of the black remains [black], and that of the mixed remains mixed;
having understood this, one should abandon both the black and the mixed.
Those who desire what is auspicious should always practice only the auspicious here;
through the auspicious one shall go to a good rebirth, and through the dark, always to a miserable state.

Thinking thus: "By a mixture of these two, one will certainly go to the [other] destinies," those who always desire what is auspicious in this saṃsāra should always practice virtue after having taken refuge in the Three Jewels.
Those who always revere the Buddha do not go to an evil destiny;
always in a good destiny, having performed what is auspicious, they go to the abode of the Victors.
Those who always listen to the Dharma do not go to an evil rebirth;
having enjoyed auspicious happiness at all times, they go to Sukhāvatī.
Those who give gifts to the Saṅgha do not go to an evil rebirth;
having always enjoyed auspicious happiness, they go to the refuge of the Victors.
Thinking thus, having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels in this saṃsāra,
you should always serve them with devotion and attend upon them with due honor.
Action performed toward the Three Jewels yields a great fruit as its maturation;
it is immeasurable, incalculable, and the means for accomplishing the state of perfect awakening.
By the power of this merit, may Bodhisattvas always exist in the world and,
having accomplished the welfare of all sentient beings, move about according to their will.
Assuming various forms, all are intent on accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings;
having fully taught the true Dharma, they protect the three worlds.
Having gradually fulfilled all the perfections and being endowed with merit,
they have conquered the entire host of afflictions and are completely pure in the three spheres.
Having conquered the hosts of Māra and attained supreme perfect enlightenment,
and having established the Dharma everywhere, they subsequently entered into nirvāṇa.
Those Victors who have passed away also attained enlightenment in due course and reached the state of final liberation through their diligent devotion to the Three Jewels.
Even those Victors of the present, having attained awakening through the merits arising from honoring the Three Jewels, shall likewise proceed to final liberation.
Those future Victors as well, having attained enlightenment through the very merits arising from the veneration of the Three Jewels, will likewise proceed to final nirvana in due course.
And I too, surely striving thus in the service of the Three Jewels,
shall now attain enlightenment through the power of this merit.
In the same way, I too, having made the entire world consist of Dharma and having established all beings in enlightenment, shall thus certainly attain final liberation.
Thus, all those who here take refuge in the Three Jewels and devote themselves to them, having attained perfect enlightenment, have reached final liberation.
Thinking thus, those who desire the state of liberation in this saṃsāra should always practice virtue by taking refuge in the Three Jewels.
Having acted thus, and having enjoyed the true Dharma as well as true happiness here,
you shall gradually attain awakening and reach final liberation.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, all those people, including the members of the Saṅgha, said, "So be it," and being thus enlightened, they rejoiced.
Then all the people there took refuge in the Triple Gem;
with reverence and faith, they constantly applied themselves with joyful approval.
By the power of this merit, at that time and on all sides,
there was always an abundance of auspiciousness and energy, free from all calamities.
Thus it was told to me by my teacher, and thus have I heard it and related it;
having heard this, O King, you too should always take refuge in the Three Jewels.
Likewise, having caused the subjects to hear the Dharma and awakening them,
you ought always to cause them to practice devotion to the Three Jewels.
In this way, may auspiciousness be ever certain for you everywhere;
and by gradually fulfilling the perfections, you shall attain enlightenment as well.
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, King Aśoka,
together with his retinue, replied, "So be it," and rejoiced.
Those who hear this *avadāna* of Kacaṅgalā, and whoever here causes it to be heard,
having abandoned evil, they all indeed enjoy happiness and go to a happy rebirth.
Thus ends the *Kacaṅgalā-avadāna* within the *Avadānatattva* of the *Ratnamālā*.
(Rm 227) XVIII. The *Dhanikā-avadāna*.
Then King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence and filled with joy,
bowed down to his teacher Upagupta and spoke once more as follows:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear yet another well-spoken word;
just as it was taught by my teacher, so may you deign to teach it to me."
Having heard this prayer made by the king, that wise Arhat,
the ascetic Upagupta, looked upon the lord of men and spoke thus:
Listen with a concentrated mind, O King; I shall relate to you exactly as it was told by my teacher, for the sake of increasing your merit.
Long ago, at one time, that glorious Śākyasiṃha,
the Lord of Sages, the Omniscient One, the Sugata, the Teacher, the King of Dharma, and the Guide, [dwelt there].
Together with the monks who were disciples, as well as the novice nuns,
and with the laymen of great faith and the assemblies of laywomen.
And also by hosts of Bodhisattvas, great beings seeking virtue,
who illuminate the conduct of awakening for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
In the city of Vaiśālī among the Vṛjis, near the lake called Markaṭahrada,
he dwelt in a gabled-roofed cave-abode, illuminating it with his radiance.
To drink that nectar of the True Dharma, all have gathered there:
Brahmā, Śakra, and the other lords of gods, as well as the world-protectors stationed in their respective directions.
The planets, the hosts of Siddhas, the Sādhyas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras;
the Garuḍas, the Nāga kings, the Vidyādharas, and the Dānavas.
The Rākṣasas along with their hosts, the sages practicing celibacy,
the Brāhmaṇas, the Kṣatriyas, the lords of the earth, and even the kings who rule over men.
Likewise, there were princes, Vaiśyas, and ministers;
householders, merchants, citizens, caravan leaders, and great men.
Merchants and artisans, as well as others seeking auspicious results,
both villagers and countryfolk, and even wandering pilgrims [all gathered there].
In this way, other people as well, desiring the nectar of the true Dharma,
all arrived there together and beheld that Lord.
Beholding that Śrīghana seated in the midst of the assembly, honored by the entire community, they all took refuge in him.
Having bowed, circumambulated, and honored them in due order,
they again bowed with palms joined and, having turned all around,
stood with concentrated minds to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all assembled,
taught the practice of awakening (bodhicaryā), which is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end.
Then, having heard that noble Dharma, all the people were filled with joy; perceiving the excellence of that Dharma, they rejoiced in return. (Rm 18.18)
At that time, in that great city of Vaiśālī, there was a wealthy householder named Dhanika, who was noble, possessed of all virtues, and wise.
Faithful, of noble intent, a giver, pure in conduct, and discerning,
he was the supreme among virtuous men because of his dedication to the welfare of all sentient beings.
His wife was named Śīlavatī, a companion in dharma;
his son was called Vandānya, and his daughter-in-law was named Satyavatī.
Then all those twice-born ones there, being devoted to the Teacher of the World,
reached a consensus and made an agreement regarding the invitation for his worship.
Sirs, since this Lord of Sages has arrived here with his Saṅgha, desiring our welfare, in order to fully teach the True Dharma;
Therefore, this Lord of Sages must be honored by us with great respect;
consequently, he should be invited here by all of us acting together, and not otherwise.
If one person, out of intoxication with wealth, issues an invitation [to a monk],
he should be expelled by all, because he creates an obstacle to the Dharma for others.
Then that wealthy man, unaware that they had acted thus in accordance with the occasion,
himself desired to honor that Lord of Sages.
Then that illustrious and wealthy merchant, possessing an abundance of divine riches,
went in person to invite the Sage together with his community.
Having approached there and joyfully bowed to that Śrīghana together with his Saṅgha, he stood before him with palms joined in reverence and made this request: *Rm_18.28{28}*
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, I desire to worship the Blessed One together with his Saṅgha; seeing this, please show me your favor.
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
promised him "So be it," and having become silent, remained there in meditation.
Then all those brahmins, having gathered together and approached,
bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and extended an invitation for a meal.
Having heard that and seeing them with their minds full of devotion, the Blessed One said:
"I have already been invited today, together with the Saṅgha, by this man."
Having heard this, all those brahmins, their minds divided,
waited for the next [instruction] and slowly went to their respective homes.
Then that wealthy man, realizing that the Lord of Munis had taken up residence there, was filled with joy; having bowed to the Sage, he quickly departed for his own home.
Thereupon, having gone to his own home, he quickly prepared the requisite provisions for a meal worthy of him, together with his kinsmen and circle of attendants.
Then, having cleansed the area all around the place where the food was to be served,
he adorned it with jeweled banners, canopies, and flags.
Then, having spread out seats made of divine jewels there in due order, he perfumed them with fragrant incense.
Then, having risen in the morning, bathed, and dressed in clean garments,
he joyfully prepared the requisites for worship, including water for the feet and the guest-offering.
Accompanied by his kinsmen and loved ones, he entered that gabled hall;
having bowed with palms joined to the sage, he made this request with great reverence.
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, the time has now come;
it behoves you, together with the Saṅgha, to grant me victory in my abode.
When he had thus entreated him, the Blessed One, together with his Saṅgha,
took up his alms-bowl and set out, covered by his robe.
There, having ensured safety along the path in every direction, the Blessed One,
illuminating [the way], gradually arrived and sat down at Vaiśālī.
Seeing the Lord of Sages, Śrīghana, thus arrived together with the community of monks, all the people of Vaiśālī paid him full honor.
Thus being honored, saluted, and greeted,
illuminating his noble character and acting with kindness, he moved about together with the Saṅgha.
Having gone there to his house with his community, that Lord of Sages accepted the water for washing the feet offered by him and sat down upon his own seat.
Then all those members of the Saṅgha there, having received that water for the feet in due order, took their respective seats.
Then that wealthy man, seeing the Lord of Sages together with his community seated upon their respective seats, honored them with the various articles of worship.
Then, with divine offerings and most excellent foods endowed with exquisite flavors, he fully satisfied the Blessed One together with his community of monks.
Having eaten that delicious food, the Blessed One, together with his community,
attained satisfaction and was filled with joy, as if satiated by nectars.
Seeing that the sage was satisfied without the company [of others], that wealthy man joyfully removed the bowls and other items from his hands and washed them.
Then, filled with joy, he himself gave to the community headed by the Buddha a rejuvenating elixir consisting of pure medicinal herbs, betel nuts, betel leaves, and other such ingredients.
Then, filled with joy, he bowed to that lord of sages together with his assembly; standing before him with palms joined in reverence, he made this request with great earnestness.
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, I have gone for refuge to you;
I worship you with devotion alone, so please forgive my transgression.
Always beholding me thus with a compassionate gaze, may you, together with your community of monks,
bestow your favor upon me and protect me in every way.
Then the Blessed One, the Teacher, together with his Saṅgha, having expressed his approval and looking toward Dhanika, spoke thus in a manner that brought him joy: Rm_18.55{55} //
O householder, may you always and eternally possess certain health;
may there be the fulfillment of your vow for awakening, and may all be auspicious at all times.
Then his beloved wife Śīlavatī, having given her consent,
joined her palms in reverence and made obeisance, entreating that Lord of Sages.
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, tomorrow I wish to perform an offering here to you; therefore, you should deign to favor me.
When she had thus petitioned him, the Blessed One, seeing her intention and perceiving it to be imbued with faith, gave his promise and remained there in silence.

Then the Blessed One, the Teacher, having arisen together with his community of monks, illuminating the auspiciousness [of the place] and performing acts of kindness, took up residence in his own hermitage.
Then, on the following morning, having bathed and dressed in pure garments,
she prepared all the necessary materials and dispatched a messenger to the sage.
That messenger, having gone quickly to the monastery, bowed with palms joined to the Lord of Sages and his Saṅgha, and addressed him once more in this way:
"O Blessed One, O Protector, O Omniscient One, the time has now arrived;
therefore, it is fitting for you to come there immediately, together with the Saṅgha."
Then the Blessed One, having thus performed this auspicious act together with his community of monks,
went to the house of Dhanika, accepted water for washing his feet, and sat down upon a seat.
Then, seeing the Lord of Sages seated upon that throne together with his community, Śīlavatī honored him according to the prescribed rites.
Then, filled with joy, she fully satisfied the entire Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, with foods provided with divine offerings.
Then, seeing that he had been fully gratified and having purified her hands and other limbs, she gave him betel, areca nut, and so forth, and after bowing down, she took her seat beside him.
Then the Blessed One, having bestowed his blessing upon him along with the community of monks, rose up and retired to his own dwelling.
Likewise, on the following day, every other wise son of the creditor also went to that monastery,
paid his respects, and invited him.
The Blessed One, having likewise perceived his mind to be thus endowed with faith,
expressed his approval by saying "So be it," and remained there in silence.
Then, having bowed to that sage, he returned quickly to his own home;
filled with joy, he prepared all the necessary provisions together with his kinsmen.
Then, having risen at dawn and bathed, surrounded by pure water, he approached the monastery and, having bowed, spoke thus to the Sage: Rm_18.72{72} //
O Blessed One, O Protector, O Omniscient One, the time has now arrived;
therefore, it is fitting for you, the Sangha, to come to my home.
Then the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha, rose up; that Tathāgata, having accepted the water for washing the feet in that house, took his seat upon the throne there.
Then, filled with joy, he honored the entire Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and satisfied them equally with divine foods.
Then, having removed the bowls and washed his hands and so forth,
and having offered betel nuts and other items, he bowed and took his seat before him.
Again, having bowed with palms joined and offered a request for forgiveness,
he beheld that Lord of Munis together with his Saṅgha and took refuge in him in this manner.
Then his daughter-in-law Satyavatī, also filled with joy, bowed down to the Blessed One and his community and invited them in this way: Rm_18.78{78} //
The Blessed One, having perceived her mind endowed with faith,
expressed his approval by saying "So be it," and remained silent, bestowing his grace upon her.
Then the Blessed One, having bestowed his blessing upon him along with the community of monks,
and having thus performed a virtuous deed for the world, departed and took up residence in the hermitage.
Then she too, having bathed in that same manner at dawn and clothed in clean garments,
urged that lord of sages, together with his assembly, through her messenger.
Likewise, that Blessed One, having arisen together with his Saṅgha and having manifested auspiciousness as he proceeded, entered her house.
There, having received water for his feet and the guest-offering, the Blessed One, together with the community of monks,
sat upon a beautiful seat and remained there, illuminating the surroundings.
Seeing the Lord of Munis seated in that manner, she was filled with joy;
having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, she gratified him with various foods.
Having observed that the Sugata, together with his Saṅgha, was satisfied,
she removed the bowls from their hands and thoroughly washed their hands and other limbs.
Then, having offered betel nuts and other gifts, and likewise having requested forgiveness,
she bowed to that Sage together with his Saṅgha and stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
Thus the Blessed One, having bestowed his blessing upon her together with the Saṅgha,
departed through the air and took refuge in his own hermitage.

Then that wealthy man, out of devotion, again invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha with an abundance of divine and marvelous supernatural powers, saying: Rm_18.88{89/} // [Note: The provided text fragment ends here; the verse number 88 corresponds to the first part of the verse.]
On the third day he was thus invited by his son, and on the fourth day by his daughter-in-law;
in this manner, the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha, was entertained with divine enjoyments.
Having heard that, all those twice-born men and the subjects of Vaiśālī,
finding no opportunity for worship of the Teacher, cried out in protest.
Then all those brahmins, together with the citizens, having reached a consensus and being enraged at Dhanika, made an effort to expel him from the city.
Having thus understood that equality, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, summoned that wealthy man and instructed him in this way before him: Rm_18.92{93} //
"O virtuous householder, all these twice-born men of Vaiśālī are angry because they were not granted an opportunity for a communal meal here at my hands."
Therefore, having shown patience in this matter, you should awaken all the twice-born;
having established discipline here in the Dharma, you ought to inspire them with faith.
Having heard what was thus commanded by the Lord of Sages, that wealthy man,
having assented in this manner, approached all the twice-born and spoke as follows.
"Gentlemen, I did not know the cause of your anger; therefore, tell me here clearly for what purpose you are now angry."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, all those brahmins,
their faces consumed by the fire of anger, reviled that creditor.
Thereupon, a certain virtuous and compassionate brahmin, who understood the purpose of meritorious deeds,
addressed that creditor and spoke to awaken him.
"O virtuous householder, I shall explain to you exactly how we have reached a consensus in this matter; having heard it, may you awaken to its meaning."
Sirs, this Lord of Sages has arrived here together with his Saṅgha, desiring our welfare, in order to fully teach the True Dharma.
Therefore, this Lord of Sages should be honored by us with great respect;
for this reason, he must be invited here by all of us acting together, and not otherwise.
If one person, out of pride in his wealth, extends an invitation [to a monk],
he should be expelled by all, since he creates an obstacle to the Dharma for others.
"O virtuous one, we have established this agreement, approved by all;
yet you alone, having transgressed it, have always performed worship of the Teacher."
For this reason, all these brahmins are thus enraged;
they wish to expel you, who obstructs their other dharma.
Furthermore, although the Blessed One will certainly not remain here forever,
everyone now desires to perform worship of the Blessed One.
And this Blessed One, the Teacher, the King of Dharma, the Lord of Sages,
has now arisen here for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Likewise, practicing here in order to bring benefit to all sentient beings,
he moves everywhere after having fully taught the true Dharma.
Likewise, he has come here to bring us benefit;
having fully taught the true Dharma, he triumphs together with his Saṅgha.
Therefore, in this matter, you ought to grant a festival for the veneration of the Three Jewels to all people in the world,
so that the merit of everyone may increase.
"You alone are one; do not, however, always practice devotion in this way.
All together, you must always perform devotion to the Teacher."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, that creditor was awakened;
looking at the brahmin and bowing down, he spoke as follows: Rm_18.111{12} //
Indeed, I was not aware that such an agreement had been made by you;
therefore, you ought to forgive my transgression in this matter in every respect.
If you possess faith in the worship of the Three Jewels always,
then indeed perform the worship of the Perfectly Awakened One here at all times.
When no worship is being performed for this Perfectly Awakened One together with his Saṅgha,
at that very time I shall indeed perform the veneration of the Perfectly Awakened One.
Having heard what was thus related by him, all those twice-born ones,
recognizing it as true, became propitiated toward him.
Then all those brahmins, having gathered together with the citizens,
approached to invite the Blessed One along with his Saṅgha.
There, all those brahmins, having gathered together with the citizens, bowed to that Lord of Sages with palms joined in reverence and joyfully made this request: Rm_18.117{18} //
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, we always desire to pay honor to you for three months; please grant us your permission.
When they had all thus entreated him, the Blessed One, the Sage, seeing the purity of their intention, remained silent and consented to that.
(Rm 233) Then all those brahmins, perceiving that the Blessed One had consented, together with the citizens, bowed to the Sage and returned to their own city.
There, those brahmins of the city, having cleansed it on all sides,
adorned the sacrificial ground with lofty banners and canopies.
There, having prepared the seats and performed the preparation of all necessary requisites,
all those people exerted themselves with great enthusiasm.
Then those brahmins, having bathed in the morning and clad in clean garments,
gathered together at that hermitage and, having bowed, made this request to the sage:
"O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, the time has now come;
it is fitting that you, together with the Saṅgha, should come to that city."
Then the Blessed Buddha, together with his Saṅgha, covered in robes and taking up his alms-bowl, set forth, radiating light.
There, on all the roads, the Blessed One, together with his Saṅgha,
illuminating and manifesting auspiciousness, proceeded and entered that city.
There, in that well-cleansed field, the Blessed One, together with his community of monks,
accepted the water for washing the feet that had been offered and took his seat upon his own throne.
He fully satisfied the entire Saṅgha, headed by the Perfectly Awakened One;
then, seeing that the Sugata and the Saṅgha were satiated, he looked upon them.
Having brought those vessels, he cleansed his hands and so forth;
then he offered betel, areca nut, and the juice of great medicinal herbs.
Having given [the gift] and made their request for forgiveness, they bowed down to him and his Saṅgha.
Then all those brahmins and the citizens, filled with joy,
stood with composed minds to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
There, having seen that they had all assembled before him, the Blessed One,
beginning with the Noble Truths, fully taught the True Dharma.
Then, having bestowed his auspicious blessings, the Blessed One, together with the members of the Saṅgha,
illuminating and bringing about auspiciousness, went and took refuge in his own hermitage.
In this way, the people of Vaiśālī continuously provided the Teacher and his Saṅgha with appropriate food throughout the entire three-month rainy season retreat.
Then, at the end, the creditor, along with his wife, son, and daughter-in-law,
honored the Saṅgha headed by the Fully Awakened One with divine enjoyments.
The Blessed One, having likewise bestowed auspicious blessings upon them,
then rose up together with the Saṅgha and, proceeding on, took his rest at the hermitage.
Then that creditor, together with his wife, son, and daughter-in-law,
having perceived the truth, became forever devoted to service toward the Three Jewels.
By the power of this merit, he became once again exceedingly prosperous with glory;
having brought benefit to all the world, he always proceeded in auspiciousness.
Seeing that, all the assembled monks were filled with wonder;
bowing down to the Blessed One, they asked him about his former deeds.
"Blessed One, what was done by this wealthy man in the past?
Where, how, and when did it happen? You ought to tell us all of this."
When the monks had questioned him thus, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages, beholding all those members of the Saṅgha, then instructed them in this way:
(Rm 234) Thus, when questioned by those monks, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages,
having looked upon all those members of the Saṅgha, then gave this instruction.
"Listen, all you monks, to what was done by this bull, and what was done by his wife, his son, and his daughter-in-law; that shall now be told."
Formerly, in Vārāṇasī, there was a florist named Kamala who,
during a time ravaged by famine, fell into extreme poverty.
His esteemed wife was named Patnavikā, his son was called Kuvalaya,
and his daughter-in-law was known as Pāṭalā.
Then one day, having arrived in the evening at a garden near his house that was in full bloom, a pratyekabuddha took up residence there.
All of them, indeed wearing only a single garment, took turns in the king’s palace;
having offered flowers, they departed and sat down in their own dwellings.
Then those householders, seeing a blazing radiance there in Udāna, were struck with wonder, asking, "What is this great flame in the garden?"
Suddenly rising up, they went everywhere throughout that garden to look about; searching, they beheld him illuminating [the place].
There, having approached him and seen him established in meditation,
they bowed with palms joined in reverence and, filled with joy, returned to their own homes.
There, seated in their own homes in the morning, eager to worship him,
those who were poor experienced distress like birds whose wings have been clipped.
Then that gardener, eager to perform worship for him,
thoroughly searched his own house and looked for that object.
Having searched everywhere throughout that house in every direction, and finding not even the slightest bit of wealth, he reflected thus:
"Alas! What evil deed must I have committed in the past, that now I am destitute and poor? What is the use of life for me in this state?"
"Since there is not even the slightest substance in my house,
with what shall I perform worship for this Great-Souled One?"
"Having come here of his own accord, this Pratyekabuddha, my son, has taken refuge in my garden; having meditated, he remains there, illuminating [the surroundings]."
Therefore, I must now pay due honor to this Sugata;
when might he come again of his own accord to this delightful city?
Therefore, tomorrow morning, let one who knows my self depart from here with an empty bowl;
thus, for me, even this birth shall be as empty and fruitless as nothingness.
Since he who is worthy of honor and worship is not worshipped in any way at all, what auspiciousness arises there? Or how, and from where, could there be merit for him?
Without merit, what essence is there in this saṃsāra? Birth is fruitless; for even after enjoying pleasures here for a very long life, is there not indeed nothing of value?
If life and birth, which exist for the sake of merit, are destroyed here,
what is the use of that life or birth which accomplishes only evil?
Therefore, death is better for me here than a long life lived in vain;
for in this saṃsāra, death is certain and inevitable everywhere.
"What is the use of nourishing this body by always experiencing suffering?
Therefore, by some kind of gift, I shall honor this Jina."
By merit may I always go to a happy rebirth, and by sin, to an evil rebirth;
therefore, I shall indeed strive to abandon that sin and to attain merit. (Rm 18.162)
If he is not worshipped here, when and where will he ever be seen again?
O blessed lady, apart from the worship of the Buddha, from what else could one obtain merit?
As long as merit is not attained, one wanders through the miserable realms;
therefore, for the sake of attaining happiness, merit should be performed with diligent effort.
Therefore, here, with even a mere fraction of my own possessions,
I shall attend upon this one of great supernormal knowledge, serving him with devotion.
Having thus meditated and reached a firm decision, the florist was filled with joy;
he addressed his wife, son, and daughter-in-law, and spoke to them as follows:
"O dear daughter-in-law, O son, listen to my words;
regarding that which I wish to do here, you must grant me your favor."
Since this one of great supernormal knowledge has come here of his own accord,
there is not even the slightest bit of wealth to be found in our house.
Therefore, by what means shall we here perform worship for this Great-Souled One?
If we do not honor this Sugata, this sage and ascetic,
then where, when, and how shall we ever obtain merit?
In this saṃsāra, without merit, birth and life are fruitless;
therefore, we must strive by every means to attain that merit.
Through merit one always attains a happy rebirth, and through evil a miserable one;
therefore, let us certainly perform meritorious deeds in order to attain the happiness of a happy rebirth.
"We possess one single garment as our entire property;
having covered him with even this, let us now depart."
"We shall not go naked before the king's court; what will become of us?
Having heard these words of mine, you ought to give your approval."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, his wife, son, and daughter-in-law all gave their approval and said, "Let it be done so."
Having made this agreement, they all, filled with faith,
went there and, covering him with that single garment, paid him honor.
Then they were all filled with joy; with palms joined in reverence, they bowed at the feet of that sage and made this aspiration: Rm_18.177{78} //
By this gift of clothing, may we all possess virtuous intentions,
attain a happy rebirth, and never be deprived of divine prosperity.
Having always propitiated the Teacher, the Sugata, the Buddha,
and having performed worship of the Three Jewels, may we become practitioners of the path to enlightenment.
When he perceived that all of them, being joyful, had made such a vow,
that one of great wisdom commanded, "So be it."
Then, having brought joy to their minds, that Sugata, the Sage,
flew up like a bird and went to his own hermitage, illuminating it with his radiance.
Having seen that, they were all delighted and, praising the benefits of the Buddha’s Dharma,
they recollected the Three Jewels and always experienced happiness.
By virtue of that merit and his aspiration,
this florist Dhanika was reborn with divine radiance and supernatural power, accompanied by his wife, son, and daughter-in-law.
Through the practice of purifying the mind and through even the most modest acts of giving,
those endowed with spiritual strength attain abundant riches by means of their resolute intentions.
Whatever action— whether well-done or ill-done— is performed in the Buddha-fields,
having attained a state of greater magnitude, it always bears fruit within existence.
Thinking thus, one should always perform virtuous deeds in this saṃsāra;
through the merit well-accumulated in the Buddha's teaching, they obtain the perfection of awakening.
Having heard this instruction from the Teacher, all those belonging to the Saṅgha recognized that the glory which is the fruit of giving has its root in the purity of the mind.
Having heard that, those brahmins too, amazed by his merit,
joyfully remembered the Blessed One at all times and departed with approval.
Likewise, all those brahmins and the citizens as well became purified by that merit and were intent upon virtue.
Wealth of jewels offered playfully is like the tip of a blade of grass, while even a blade of grass offered with faith is priceless;
for the mind experiences manifold splendors, and the mind is the cause of the arising of all that is auspicious.
"Thus was it instructed by my teacher, and so have I heard;
having heard this, O Great King, you should always perform virtuous deeds."
And having diligently awakened the people as well, O Great King,
you shall gradually attain enlightenment and reach the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having heard this which was declared by that Arhat, King Aśoka,
together with his retinue, acknowledged it, saying "So be it," and rejoiced.
Those people who hear this *Dhanika-avadāna* and those who even listen to it,
having enjoyed happiness in that auspicious realm, shall all find peace and go to the abode of the Victors.
Thus ends the *Dhanika-avadāna* within the *Ratnāvadānatattva*.
(Rm 237) XIX. The Legend of Raivata. Then King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence, joyfully—
Having bowed to his teacher Upagupta, he spoke once more as follows:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken word;
it would be fitting for you to instruct me just as it was explained by my teacher."
Having heard this request made by the king,
that noble-minded Arhat Upagupta looked upon the lord of men and spoke as follows:
"Listen well, O Great King, to that which was spoken by my teacher; I shall declare it to you exactly so. Having heard this, let it be understood."
Through their cruelty, those with double tongues cast forth the treacherous poison of false slander upon those adorned in pure garb;
afflicted by a succession of misfortunes, curses, and torments, they enter the cavern of the darkness of intense malice.
For example, formerly there was a Buddhist monk named Raivataka in a hermitage in Kaśmīra, who took compassion for all living beings as his refuge.
Once, in a secluded spot within a mountain range rich in wealth,
he dyed his robes with an infusion of tree bark.
At that moment, the cow and calf belonging to a brahmin named Piśuna, having strayed from their herd, were lost in the forest.
Then that brahmin, having seen him and suspecting him of being wicked,
searched everywhere and went there as well to investigate.
There, seeing smoke rising from the fire in that vat for boiling the robe-cloth, that twice-born man thought it was a calf being cooked.
Then that brahmin, together with his kinsmen who held weapons in their hands,
climbed the mountain to see it and suddenly arrived in its vicinity.
There, having seen that monk Raivata, the twice-born man approached with reverence and beheld the water-jar struck by Cūḍika’s arrow.
Seeing that, he became apprehensive and, approaching with humility, asked him: "What is this being done by the monk?"
When he had been asked thus by the brahmin, the mendicant Raivata respectfully said to that brahmin, "This is my attachment to the saffron robe."
At that moment, due to the ripening of her past karma,
she became afflicted with a disease characterized by the consumption of beef and the drinking of blood.
Happiness takes on the nature of suffering, even that which is pure turns to blackness;
when fate has turned adverse, even dharma becomes unrighteousness.
The manifestation of false sins, the anger of one's father, and the loss of one's position—
this is the perceptible sign of the ripening of demerits.
Faults manifest, vices come into the light, undertakings meet with failure, and the intellect falls apart.
When the time for the ripening of past misdeeds arrives, what great calamities indeed do not fall upon men?
Then that brahmin, too, wondering what was in the jar,
decided, "I shall see," and approached to look.
Apprehensive because of the scent of forbidden meat and blood,
that twice-born man did not see a lump of meat in the pot, though it was well-cooked with various spices.
Perceiving this manifest fault, the twice-born man, enraged with fury and trembling violently with intense indignation, rebuked him and spoke.
"Oh, how wonderful! This man of virtuous conduct remains here in this lonely forest;
such deeds as these are not seen in anyone else here."
The body is adorned with the robes of renunciation, yet its actions are those befitting barbarians;
who can know the peace of one under a false vow whose sins remain concealed?
When he had spoken thus with reproach, Raivata also reflected:
"Since this fault is directly observable, what can I say, left without an answer?"
When it is said, "This blow was sent by fate," who would agree?
A person who denies what is evident before his eyes becomes an object of ridicule.
Having adopted a state of total silence, I endure all that has come upon me;
this is my unrequited ordeal, like fire rising from the water.
One quickly perceives an excellence of virtue in a fault, and even a fault in a virtue; one sees poison in nectar, and nectar in poison.
This woman, a sorceress by destiny, constantly displays a truly wondrous form at the proper time.
Having thus meditated in his mind, the high-minded Raivata,
having called to mind his own deity, remained absorbed in yoga.
Seeing the sage Raivata standing there, having fully taken recourse in meditation,
he became exceedingly enraged and, having reviled him, spoke as follows:
"O evil-minded monk, why do you sit here in this desolate forest, having committed such a cruel and wicked deed?"
"O most wicked one, speak! For whose sake did you kill the children and the bull here, so that this meat may be cooked for yourself or for another?"
Even upon seeing another struck down, you are defiled by those sins;
how then, having yourself slain the bull, are you not consumed by those sins?
"Shame, shame on you, O mendicant Rebhi, for while upholding the vows of renunciation within the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One, you have taken refuge in this desolate forest!"
"Having performed such deeds that cause great suffering, why do you now practice asceticism? O, O! Have you not heard what was spoken by the Fully Awakened One?"
Now, even having heard this, you truly have no faith therein;
why indeed, having committed such a sin, do you practice the vows of renunciation?
Having accomplished only evil deeds, you remain here,
though you are one who has gone forth, whose soul is dispassionate, and whose three spheres are completely purified.
One should always practice with a mind composed, maintaining a view of compassion toward all sentient beings.
One should never, under any circumstances, take the property of another that has not been given;
with a soul endowed with compassion and mercy, one should not cause suffering to living beings.
One should never enjoy sensual pleasures through unrighteous means,
nor should one ever speak a falsehood here in any way whatsoever.
One should never, under any circumstances, utter harsh speech,
nor should one speak words of slander in the presence of anyone.
One should not utter frivolous speech toward anyone,
nor should one ever cultivate ill will toward anyone in any way whatsoever.
And likewise, one should never entertain covetousness toward anyone at all.
One should never, under any circumstances, cultivate wrong view at any time;
one should abandon these ten roots of evil in every way.
Those who, through negligence, touch these and proceed [with their ritual],
they all, tormented by the afflictions, wander in existence as miserable beings.
Then, scorched by the fire of the afflictions and intent solely upon evil deeds,
they wander through the hells, constantly experiencing nothing but suffering.
Thinking thus, having abandoned all these ten things in this saṃsāra,
the virtuous, being composed, always proceed only toward what is auspicious.
"By virtue they go to a happy rebirth, and by sin they always go to a miserable one;
this has been declared by all the Victors—why is this not heard by you?"
"How can you, having renounced the world while disregarding this, act in such a way? Shame on your mind that desires to eat my calf! (Rm 19.49)
For one who has gone forth, pure in soul and purified in the three spheres,
possessing a mind of compassion for all sentient beings, should always conduct himself in meditative concentration.
Having acted for the benefit of all sentient beings, remaining concentrated in celibacy,
sustained by mere alms-food, and entirely free from longing, one should proceed toward what is auspicious.
The yogi, devoted to meditative concentration, upholding the ultimate reality of the *dhāraṇīs*,
has completely conquered all afflictions as well as all the hosts of Māras.
Having abandoned all possessions, free from conceptual construction and stainless,
having directly attained the state of an Arhat, one should practice the holy life (brahmacarya).
Thus, a monk who has gone forth and constantly dwells maintaining excellent virtue,
having attained auspicious awakening, shall reach the state of final liberation.
But you, though having gone forth as a renunciant, have committed such a great and terrible sin; having indulged in this desolate place, you now wander with the conduct of a barbarian.
"Alas! You are truly ruined here, since, possessed as you are by this sin, you shall suddenly go to hell and experience sufferings for a long time."
What evil deed did you commit previously in another life, that even though you have attained the Dharma here in the teaching of the Sugata, you remain so ill-intentioned?
Therefore, compose yourself and once again observe the vow of expiation;
this is for the complete purification of this sin and for the successful completion of the vow.
In this way, there shall be purification of your body and, in due course, auspiciousness;
with your three bodies completely purified, practice the restraint of the renunciant life.
Then, having completely conquered the afflictions as well as the hosts of Māra,
you will directly attain the state of an Arhat and become a practitioner of the holy life.
Then, with your self completely purified, free from conceptual construction and stainless,
you shall attain auspicious awakening and reach the state of final liberation.

Indeed, due to his own karmic fault, his robe has turned into flesh;

"What then can I say in this matter? For destiny performs all actions.

"Sometimes my intellect falters and my speech forgets what has been said;

Having thus reflected and reached this conclusion, that brahmin, overcome with despondency,

My companions have been forgotten, and no one has recognized them;
punishment falls upon the innocent while it reaches the sinful king.

"O King, this is not your fault; it is the fruit born of my own karma.

There I remained, observing silence and reflecting upon destiny;

That all calamities embrace the neck with longing, and that all prosperities—though delightful through the forceful enjoyment of every limb—cause only affliction;
that wandering which is the abode of the happiness of free will is itself a long-term bondage: such is the fruit of the vine of saṃsāra for men, variegated by the ripening of their own karma.
Having heard this which was proclaimed by that Arhat, King Nanda was struck with wonder, and out of curiosity, having gazed upon that ascetic, he spoke thus:
O wise one, for whom was this the fruit of an evil deed? What action was performed in the past? You ought to explain that.

Formerly, in Vārāṇasī, there was a man named Kutha of cruel conduct;

he took that calf's meat and departed from there in haste.
There, the cowherds, having searched everywhere for their lost calf,

Thereupon, seeing them all pursued, Kutha himself was suddenly set upon by the pursuers and fled into the interior of the forest.
There, having placed that meat before a Pratyekabuddha who was absorbed in meditation, he hid himself in a secluded spot.
All those cowherds, having pursued him along with his followers,
beheld that Pratyekabuddha there and approached him.
Thereupon, Kutha approached those cowherds,
showed them beef, and pointed him out as the thief.
There, all those cow-herders, upon merely seeing that beef before the sage, suddenly struck that sage out of anger.

Then Kutha, hearing that the ascetic had been held in captivity, was scorched by the fire of remorse and thought thus: "Alas! (Rm 19.137).
"Alas! Even by me, a sinner, such sins are being committed;

Because this Pratyekabuddha, who meditates in solitude and knows himself,

Thus, having remembered the Fully Awakened One with reverence,

Then, having regained consciousness through the power of the Fully Awakened One,
he suddenly rose up and approached his presence.
Having approached them there, he bowed before those cowherds with palms joined in reverence, and having begged for their protection from fear, he spoke.
"O sirs, whatever evil I have committed here shall now be confessed;
therefore, having heard it, you ought by all means to grant me forgiveness."
Indeed, no fault exists in this Pratyekabuddha;
yet, being exceedingly wicked, I pointed him out to you, saying, "This is a thief."
Therefore, let this Pratyekabuddha sage be released here;
for he is always to be honored with food after having been treated with hospitality and worshipped.
"Let this sin not ripen upon my head alone;
therefore, I myself am the one to be slain here, so let this ascetic be released."
Having heard what he said, all those cowherds became enraged; they suddenly bound him, reviled him, and beat him severely.

Having encountered such a gathering, you ought by all means to perform the yoga;

"This bondage has been incurred by me alone through the turn of fate;
therefore, since he too is not at fault here, let him be released."
Having heard this instruction given by that Pratyekabuddha, they realized it was so; then, they released their anger.
Then all those cowherds, having heard the words of that sage,
suddenly bowed down and released him from his bonds.
Then all those cowherds, having joyfully clothed that solitary sage in a robe and honored him, satisfied him completely.
There, having approached him with palms joined in reverence and bowed down, they, tormented by their offense, made this request with great earnestness: Rm_19.159{58} //
"O Blessed One, it is known by us that there was no fault on your part;
therefore, you too ought to grant us forgiveness in this matter."
Having heard this request made by them, that Pratyekabuddha,
seeing all those cowherds, comforted them and spoke as follows:
"Sirs, do not despair; there is no fault here.
I understand this mode of livelihood, for the followers of the Sugata truly know the purpose of existence."
Having spoken thus, that omniscient Pratyekabuddha rose up;
then, leaping into the sky, he departed for his own hermitage, taking flight.
Seeing that, all those people and cowherds were struck with wonder;
remembering that very Sugata, they always practiced in accordance with the True Dharma.
I was that very wicked cow-slayer named Kutha;
through those sins, I have thus experienced sufferings in the hells for a long time.
Even in this life, he has incurred twelve years of suffering due to his transgressions;
this is his own fault here, not mine, owing to the turn of fate.
Thus, O Great King, since good and evil depend upon one's own destiny within this saṃsāra, those who desire true happiness should always perform meritorious deeds.
In this saṃsāra, merit alone is that which grants the accomplishment of all essential goals;
without merit, performed deeds do not succeed in any way whatsoever.
Through merit one is born in heaven; through merit one goes to a good rebirth;
through merit there is always well-being; and having performed [meritorious deeds], one goes to the abode of the Victors.
One deserving of execution is released by means of a staff through the power of merit alone;
likewise, one deserving of a blow is spared from that blow due to the influence of anger.
O King, by the mere bristling of his hair, he who is worthy of anger is released from his merit;
so too are all those who possess happiness and are endowed with every prosperity.
O lord of men, all of them should be known as doers of merit;
by merit the mind is purified, and the wise man becomes one of pure intention.
One of sound intellect should always and constantly engage only in auspicious deeds;
being of virtuous conduct, with purified limbs, truthful in speech, and having conquered the senses.
One whose intention is completely pure and who is steadfast should be dedicated to the welfare of sentient beings;
likewise, one whose self is endowed with merit should be a knower of the meaning of all branches of knowledge.
He shall become a knower of the Dharma and its purpose, endowed with excellent virtues and glory;
thereafter, having attained the prosperity of Maheśvara, he will be intent on the welfare of the world.
Having given gifts, one should always enjoy happiness and constantly practice what is auspicious;
through the ripening of this merit, one becomes completely purified in the three spheres.
Pure in conduct and purified in soul, one should always observe the noble vow;
by the power of this merit, one accomplishes the goals of patience, the Dharma, and worldly purpose.
One should act with an equal regard for oneself and others, endowed with the happiness of loving-kindness;
through the ripening of this merit, one will be possessed of the qualities of zeal for the Dharma.

Knowing this, O Great King, if you desire to attain the state of nirvāṇa,

Merit alone is a great jewel that follows one everywhere;

Having understood this, O Indra among kings, one should abandon attachment to evil and always perform meritorious deeds alone within this cycle of existence.
Thus, through evil, they are always joined with the very states of woe;

Thinking thus, O Great King, if you desire constant well-being,

Neither auspicious nor inauspicious karma ever perishes without being experienced;

Karma is not burned by fires; indeed, it is only the body that is burned. Karma is not moistened by waters; rather, it is only the physical frame that is moistened.

In the ripening of a black deed, there shall always be nothing but suffering;

Thinking thus, O Great King, one should always abandon here what is dark and what is mixed, and conduct oneself only among those things that are beautiful.

Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, King Aśoka,

Merit alone is the essence of existence, for it bestows true happiness everywhere.
