the Blessed One taught the Dharma of perfect enlightenment for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
All the worlds have assembled to hear his teaching of the Dharma:
the gods beginning with Brahmā and Śakra, the world-protectors, and the dānavas.
The planets, Vidyādharas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas,
Kinnaras, Garuḍas, Nāga kings, and Rākṣasas— those seeking auspiciousness— [were present].
Sages and brahmins as well, kings and princes, vaiśyas, ministers, counselors, householders, and great men— Rm_20.53{43}—
Merchants and caravan leaders, artisans and city-dwellers, as well as villagers, country folk, followers of other sects, and pilgrims.
In this way, other worlds as well, possessing the qualities of the true Dharma, were cut off;
they all approached and entered that hermitage.
There, having seen that Śrīghana preceded by the community of monks,
they bowed down, circumambulated him, and honored him in due order.
Then, having prostrated and circumambulated him on all sides,
they stood with concentrated minds to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all assembled,
taught the true Dharma, which is auspicious in its beginning, middle, and end.
Having drunk that nectar of the true Dharma, they were all fully awakened;
having understood the excellence of the Dharma, they always venerated the Three Jewels.
There, that buffalo, recollecting the events of his previous birth, thought thus in his mind regarding the casting off of that body: Rm_20.60{50} //
"Alas! A terrible sin was previously accumulated by me through my wickedness;
therefore, as has been declared, I have become this wicked buffalo here."
Therefore, what should I do here, O beast, to purify that sin?
Having recollected the Triple Gem, I shall observe the Upoṣadha fast.
Having now given this body here to sentient beings with faith,
and having meditated upon the Sugata in my mind, I shall remain ready to die at this very moment.
Therefore, having cut this body apart— its skin, flesh, blood, and so forth,
as well as all its bones, marrow, and the rest— let all living beings enjoy it with joy!
Whatever beings joyfully consume this body as a delicious food,
may they all, having practiced the Dharma, go forever to the realm of the gods.
Thus, through the ripening of this merit, may I leave behind this sinful refuge,
attain birth in a happy state, and always serve the Sugata.
Having thus meditated and reached a firm decision, that buffalo, with a serene mind,
abandoned food and, like one performing asceticism, practiced penance while recollecting the Buddha.
Thus, that buffalo, having meditated and recollected the Three Jewels,
cast off his body and, with a purified soul, went to the abode of the gods.
Having been born there in heaven, endowed with great bliss,
his mind filled with wonder and serene faith, he then reflected thus:
"Aha! Having passed away from where and wandering where has this happiness arisen?
By whose ripening of merit does such auspiciousness as this arise for me?"
As he, who had formerly been a buffalo king, was reflecting in this way,
his mind overcome with wonder, there arose in him this thought:
"Aha! Having passed away from the animal realm, I have now become a god here in the world of the gods through the merit of mindfulness of the Perfectly Awakened One."
Therefore, I shall go now to see that Lord of Sages;
having taken refuge with faith, I shall listen once more to the True Dharma.
Thus, that son of the gods, preceded by Mahiṣa, being filled with joy,
desired to go there to behold that Lord of Sages.
Then, filled with joy, he bathed, clothed himself in pure celestial garments, anointed his limbs with divine perfumes, and adorned himself with celestial ornaments.
Taking divine offerings for worship, he went with the hosts of gods that night to the hermitage, illuminating it for the Lord of Sages.
There, having seen that Śrīghana, he approached him with joy;
having bowed and circumambulated him, he honored him according to the prescribed rite.
Then, having bowed with palms joined to that lord of sages,
he took his place before him to hear the teaching of the true Dharma.
Thus, having been inspired with faith, he and his divine sons, his companions,
approached the Blessed One with palms joined in reverence.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all assembled,
began with the Noble Truths and thoroughly taught the True Dharma.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, the god who had previously been Mahiṣa rejoiced together with the gods and attained a distinction of the Dharma.
Having shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rises with twenty peaks,
by means of the vajra of wisdom, he attained the stage of stream-entry.
(Rm 252) Having seen the truth, that father, having bowed with palms joined in reverence to the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, uttered this inspired exclamation three times: *Rm_20.83{73}*
O Blessed One, this was done for us by you; indeed, it was not by our father, nor by our mother, nor by the king, nor by anyone else at all.
By that very purification of our committed sins performed by you,
the entire surrounding region has been dried up, its flow of blood and tears completely parched.
The mountains of bones have been leaped over, the path of evil has been closed,
the paths to heaven have been opened, and the path to liberation has been shown.
I have attained the stainless eye and likewise the peaceful state of the Noble Ones;
I have crossed over the ocean of suffering, and the path to awakening is now seen.
Therefore, by the grace of your compassionate gaze,
my birth in this cycle of existence has now become fruitful, for I am now a son of the Buddha.
From this day forth, having always and eternally gone for refuge to you,
I shall fix my mind upon awakening and practice the auspicious conduct.
Therefore, having bestowed your favor here, may you, the Teacher and Master of the World,
out of compassion, ever looking upon me, deign to protect me thus.

Having heard this prayer made by that god, and having perceived his pure intention, the Teacher gave him this instruction: iti saṃprārthitaṃ tena suparvaṇā niśamya saḥ / śāstā tasyāśayaṃ śuddhaṃ samalokyaivam ādiśat // Rm_20.91{81} //
O good man, listen; I shall speak what is beneficial if you desire constant well-being:
having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels, worship them always with great reverence.
Those who, having taken refuge in the Buddha, always worship him with faith,
even if they are intent upon the conduct of Māra, go to the abode of the Victors.
Those who constantly listen to the Dharma of the Sugata with faith and joy,
being liberated from all evils, go to Sukhāvatī.
And those who perform acts of honor toward the Saṅgha with faith and reverence—
all of them, having escaped from an evil destiny, proceed to the abode of the gods.
Those who, having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, always honor them with devotion, do not go to an evil rebirth; they always go to a fortunate rebirth.
Always remaining in a good rebirth and having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels,
they bring benefit to the world, enjoy happiness, and always delight.
Then, having fulfilled all the perfections in due order and attained the threefold awakening, they shall fully reach nirvana.
Thus, if you desire to attain the true bliss of nirvāṇa,
take refuge in the Three Jewels and worship them constantly with a concentrated mind.
By the power of this merit, with the three spheres completely purified,
may you gradually attain awakening and reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard what was thus instructed by the Lord of Sages, he was fully enlightened;
and having assented with "So be it," he spoke again as follows:
Today my desire has been fulfilled and made fruitful;
having attained the jewel of awakening, I am now truly a son of the Buddha.
Always remaining in your very refuge,
I shall practice the vow of awakening while honoring the Three Jewels.
Having thus made this prayer, that son of the gods was filled with joy;
having bowed once more to Śrīghana along with his companions, he departed for heaven.
Having arrived there in heaven, he dwelt together with the gods;
recollecting the Three Jewels, he lived on, enjoying happiness.
On that night, seeing a great splendor and radiance,
all those cowherds were filled with wonder and became apprehensive in their hearts.
Then, having risen at dawn, they all, filled with curiosity,
gathered together and quickly went to that hermitage of Buddha.
There, having seen that Śrīghana, they all were filled with joy;
bowing with palms joined in reverence, they stood before him with great respect.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all assembled,
taught the supreme Dharma, which is virtuous in its beginning, middle, and end.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, they were all awakened;
bowing once more to the Blessed One, they asked thus with great reverence:
"O Blessed One, who was it that came here to this hermitage tonight, illuminating it? You ought to explain that."
Thus questioned by those keepers of the buffalo herd, the Blessed One, the All-Knowing, looked at them and taught the events of the past.
That wicked buffalo here, seeing us and being pursued,
became terrified upon perceiving danger on all sides and has come to me for refuge.
Then, having heard my Dharma and recollecting his former birth,
he will develop serene confidence in me, renounce food, and cast off his body.
Then, through the merit of our remembrance, he was freed from evil; with purified intellect, he has now been reborn as a god in the heavenly world.
This very son of a god, illuminating this place tonight,
has come here with the hosts of gods to see me at Alakā.
Having heard my true Dharma, he perceived the Truth and was filled with joy;
thus, together with the hosts of gods, he departed for his own abode in heaven.
Having heard these words thus commanded by the Lord of Sages, all those buffalo-herders, overcome with extreme amazement, spoke thus among themselves: *Rm_20.118{8}*
Oh, how wonderful indeed it is that even one who had fallen into the animal realm,
having encountered the Buddha as his true guru and heard the Dharma, became wise.
Having developed serene faith in the True Guru and the Sugata, and having abstained from food,
he performed the recollection of the Three Jewels three times and, casting off his life-breath, went to heaven.
Then, having returned here from that place as well, he went for refuge to the Perfectly Awakened One;
having honored him and heard the Dharma, he realized the Truths and departed for heaven.
Even in heaven, having gone for refuge to that same true guru,
he practiced with faith and devotion, remaining concentrated and performing virtuous deeds.
Blessed is this Sugata, the Teacher, who brings auspiciousness to all sentient beings;
for even a beast, by merely clarifying its mind toward him, has gone to heaven.
But how could we humans, having approached this lord of sages, this true guru, not worship him with faith? (Rm 20.124)
(Rm 254) Likewise, having heard the true Dharma through the grace of this excellent teacher,
how could we not always achieve what is auspicious? Rm_20.125(15)
Having understood the specific qualities of the Dharma, having seen the truth, and being composed in meditation,
we shall surely attain a happy rebirth by paying homage to the Three Jewels.
Therefore, let us all now worship and honor with faith and great respect this true guru, the lord of sages.
Having heard that true Dharma with faith, may we attend upon the Three Jewels and always practice what is virtuous.
Therefore, first of all, let us now honor this Sugata together with his Saṅgha here with food as is fitting, for their full nourishment.
Having thus conversed, they were all filled with joy;
agreeing that it should be so, they went to that hermitage of the Buddha.
There, having seen that Śrīghana together with his saṅgha, they were filled with joy; bowing with their palms joined in reverence, they made this request with great devotion: Rm_20.131{20} //
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, we desire to worship the Blessed One together with his Saṅgha; therefore, please grant us your favor in this matter.
Having heard this request made by them, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
remained silent and stayed there for the sake of increasing their merit.
Perceiving that he had thus taken up residence, they were all filled with great joy;
having bowed at the feet of that lord of sages, they departed for their own homes.
There, all of them, filled with joy, quickly prepared a complete array of suitable foods, such as curd, milk, and rice.
Then, having gone there at the appointed time to that Buddha-hermitage with joy, they bowed down to the Lord of Sages together with his Saṅgha and addressed him thus:
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, the time for the assembly has now arrived; therefore, may the Blessed One deign to accept this offering from the Saṅgha.
When they had thus entreated him, the Blessed One, together with his Saṅgha,
arose and proceeded toward the place of the meal, illuminating the surroundings with his splendor.
There, having received water for the feet, all those members of the Saṅgha, headed by the Perfectly Awakened One, took their respective seats in order.
Seeing all those members of the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, seated upon their respective seats, they were all filled with joy and honored them in due order.
Then they fully satisfied the Blessed One and his community with excellent divine foods, including milk-rice accompanied by various side dishes.
Then, seeing that the Sugata and his Saṅgha were satisfied,
they quickly removed those bowls from their hands and thoroughly cleansed them.
Then, with joy, they presented to the Saṅgha, headed by the Fully Awakened One, a medicinal elixir consisting of various groups of water-born and land-growing herbs.
Then those herdsmen, with palms joined in reverence,
joyfully bowed to the Blessed One, the embodiment of splendor, together with his community of monks, and stood before him.
Seeing them all thus seated together, he, the omniscient one,
having instructed them in the noble Dharma, established them on the path to enlightenment.
Having drunk that nectar of the true Dharma, they all rejoiced and resolved to go forth into homelessness within the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One.
Then all those buffalo-herders, having reached a unanimous agreement,
bowed with palms joined in reverence and entreated that Lord of Sages.
"O Blessed One, O Lord, O Omniscient One! We desire to go forth into homelessness under your teaching; it behooves you to grant us that."
Having heard this request made by them, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
looked upon all those of pure intention and commanded them thus:
"I do not grant the going forth without the permission of one's mother and father;
therefore, O preta, once you have obtained their permission, I shall then grant it to you."
When the Lord of Sages had thus instructed them, they all rejoiced;
having quickly bowed to that Lord of Sages, they went to their respective homes with joy.
Having gone there quickly and having diligently awakened your parents and kinsmen to the truth, perform [the rite] after obtaining their permission.
Having gone there in haste, they approached the Blessed One; bowing with palms joined at his feet, they made this request with great reverence: Rm_20.153{42} //
O Blessed One, All-Knowing One, our fathers have arrived having received permission;
having bestowed their favor upon them there, it behooves you to grant them the going forth.
When they had thus entreated him, the Blessed One, the Teacher, having touched their heads with his right hand and gazed upon them, gave this instruction:
"Come together, all you monks, endowed with faith;
having undertaken the vow of renunciation, lead the life of a celibate practitioner."
When the Lord of Sages had thus instructed them, they all appeared with shaven heads,
carrying khikkhirī bowls and clad in garments of kāśika cloth.
Then, through the grace of the Teacher, they all became pure in intention;
having attained the thought of awakening, they were pure in conduct and had mastered their senses.
Having completely shattered the qualities of ignorance, they have attained mastery in true knowledge;
having fully acquired the analytical insights, they are endowed with the path of truth.
Striving in concentration, dhāraṇīs, and vidyās, remaining composed,
endowed with patience, and pure in nature, they became monks who were practitioners of yoga.
Then, considering all of saṃsāra to be impermanent and unstable,
and seeing that the courses of all conditioned phenomena are as destructive as snakes, [they attained liberation].
Having abandoned the entire multitude of afflictions and having also conquered the hosts of Māra,
those practitioners of the holy life attained the state of Arhatship in person and proceeded onward.
Then all those monks had the three spheres completely purified;
they were free from attachment, possessed of great supernormal powers, non-conceptual, and stainless.
Regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, free from desire for honor and gain, with limbs whose minds are like space, they turn their backs on worldly profit.
Those who practice for awakening became worthy of worship, honor, and veneration by the worlds of gods, asuras, and others dwelling within the three realms.
(Rm 256) Having seen that, all the monks, their minds uplifted with wonder,
bowed to the Blessed One, the Sage, and asked about his former deeds.
"Blessed One, what deeds were performed by that son of the gods who was formerly a buffalo, by which he became a buffalo?"
And what deed was performed by these keepers of the buffalo herd in the past, by which,
having attained arhatship, they have become practitioners of celibacy?
Having instructed us in all this, O Teacher, you ought now likewise to awaken our minds.
When he had been questioned thus by those monks, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages,
looked toward all those monks belonging to the Saṅgha and commanded them as follows:
Listen, all you monks! I shall now relate those deeds performed in the past by him who was formerly a buffalo.
And I shall now likewise relate all those deeds which were performed in the past by these keepers of the buffalo herd.
Just as in the past the Buddha Kāśyapa was an Arhat, a Tathāgata,
the All-Knowing One, a Sugata, a Teacher, a King of Dharma, and a Guide.
At that time, the Blessed One, having taken up residence in the Deer Park hermitage in the city of Vārāṇasī, dwelt there together with his community of monks.
At that time, under the teaching of that lord of sages, there was a single monk, a mendicant well-versed in the Tripitaka, possessed of great wisdom, and skilled in discerning the definitive meaning.
Then, at one time, surrounded by five hundred monks and seated in the assembly hall, he taught the true Dharma.
Those monks, possessing the trainings and endowed with the qualities of those in training,
repeatedly questioned that teacher in order to fully understand the meaning of the Tripitaka.
When the monks had questioned him in this manner,
the teacher became enraged and reviled all those disciples and trainees who were his śrāvakas.
Then all those disciples, seeing their teacher enraged, bowed down, showed him due respect, and spoke again as follows:
"Sirs, do not be angry; be gracious, O treasure-house of compassion!
That which was correctly explained by you is not understood by us."
Therefore, you ought to instruct us once again on this matter in full detail and with perfect clarity,
for the sake of awakening our minds.
When they had thus entreated him repeatedly, the Tripiṭaka, being exceedingly enraged,
rebuked all those disciples in this manner and spoke as follows:
O buffaloes, you are indeed such; do you understand my words?
What more shall I say, which even upon hearing it, you do not comprehend?
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, they all became incensed and likewise replied to that teacher, the ascetic Arhat.
Since we are all buffalo, may you, as the lord of the buffalo, be our protector;
may you act toward us exactly as our teacher has instructed.
Thus, by all those disciples— both those in training and those beyond training— who had been provoked to anger,
something wicked was spoken out of wrath in the presence of the true guru.
Afflicted by the fear of this sin and tormented by remorse,
they bowed down to that Arhat, their teacher, and spoke once more as follows:
"Alas! We are all fools, since out of anger we have rejected even our true guru and offered him such a reply."
How can we endure this terrible sin?
Therefore, you ought by all means to forgive us out of compassion.
Likewise, even in another birth, having encountered you alone as our true guru and spiritual friend, may we attain perfect self-restraint.
Having thus made this prayer, all those monks,
relying upon that teacher and hearing the Dharma, always devoted themselves to it.
Then, at that time, all those disciples, including the Tripitaka master, passed away;
they were reborn once more in the miserable states of existence.
Due to the ripening of his harsh speech and actions, even for five hundred births,
this teacher who was once a master of the Tripitaka became a buffalo in the assembly hall.
Just as all those śrāvakas [suffered] due to the fault of their verbal actions,
so too did these buffalo-keepers always become such in existence.
In this case as well, that wicked buffalo becomes Tripiṭa;
and these buffalo-herders also become monks.
And as for this buffalo here, because of the merit performed by Kāśyapa, his mind became exceedingly serene upon seeing me; having bowed, he went to me for refuge.
Through the ripening of this merit, this wise man, having attained the Noble Truths, becomes a son of the gods, one who has seen the truth.
These buffalo-herders as well, through the ripening of the merit of Kāśyapa,
have attained the state of an Arhat after going forth and have become practitioners of the holy life.
Thus, indeed, by means of the ripening of their karma, all living beings wander in the prison of existence,
experiencing pleasures and pains within cyclic existence.
Karma is not burned by fires, nor is it dried up by winds;
it is not moistened even by waters, nor is it exhausted within the earths.
Karma is never exhausted anywhere by any means without being experienced;
for nowhere else could there be any other course for karma.
In the ripening of wholesome karma, there shall always be only wholesomeness;
likewise, in the ripening of black [karma], there shall always be only suffering.
Just as when mixed things are cooked, the results are likewise mixed;
realizing this, one should always conduct oneself only in what is auspicious throughout existence.
By whomsoever an action was performed, by that very person is its fruit experienced;
the fruit of action in saṃsāra must necessarily be undergone.
For actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the necessary conditions and the right time, they surely bear fruit for living beings.
Thinking thus, having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels in this saṃsāra,
you should always worship them with devotion and respect in every way.
Those who always and constantly revere the Three Jewels and have gone for refuge do not go to an evil destiny; they always proceed to a happy destiny.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, those members of the Saṅgha were filled with joy;
and all the people, having paid honor, constantly took refuge in the Three Jewels.
This was told to me by my teacher, and thus it is now spoken by me;
you too, O Great King, should always conduct yourself in this way for the sake of what is auspicious.
And always, having caused the subjects to hear the Dharma and awakening them,
establish them on the path to enlightenment and protect them with a concentrated mind.
In that way, may auspiciousness be yours forever and certainly everywhere;
having attained enlightenment in due course, may you reach the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, King Aśoka,
together with his retinue, consented, saying "So be it," and rejoiced.
Those people who hear this account of the buffalo and those who even behold it, having indeed enjoyed all manner of happiness here, will surely go to the abode of the Sugata.
Thus ends the Mahiṣāvadāna within the Avadānatatva.
XXI. The Nāvikāvadāna.
Then Aśoka, the lord of the earth, having bowed with palms joined in reverence to his teacher, the ascetic Upagupta, spoke once more as follows:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken teaching;
it would be fitting for you to instruct me just as it was explained by my teacher."
When the king had made his request, the wise Arhat Upagupta, having heard him,
looked upon that lord of men and spoke as follows:
"Listen well, O Great King, to that which was spoken by my teacher; I shall declare it to you just as it was told. Having heard it, grant your approval."
Once upon a time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages— the omniscient Sugata, the Teacher, the King of Dharma, the Guide— [dwelt there].
Accompanied by his Saṅgha, bringing joy there as he wandered on his journey through Magadha,
he established auspiciousness everywhere and took recourse upon the bank of the Gaṅgā.
There, the Blessed One, honored by the entire community of monks, sat upon his seat in the midst of the assembly and desired to teach the Dharma.
Then all the worlds came to drink that nectar of the True Dharma:
the gods headed by Brahmā and Śakra, the world-protectors, the Gaṇas, and the rest.
The lord of the Daityas, Garuḍas, Nāgas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kiṃnaras,
as well as Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Rākṣasas of great supernatural power.
Sages and brahmins as well, yogins and ascetics too, kings, kṣatriyas, rulers, princes, and even followers of other sects.
The Vaiśyas, ministers, counselors, guild-leaders, citizens, subjects,
virtuous householders, auspicious people, caravan leaders, and the great multitude likewise [honored him].
Merchants and artisans, as well as those from villages and the countryside,
and others besides, also arrived, desiring to hear the true Dharma.
Having arrived there and joyfully beheld that Śrīghana,
they bowed down, circumambulated him, and worshipped him in due order.
Then all those people, having turned around from every side and being composed in mind, gazed upward and took their seats to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all assembled before him,
began the practice of awakening and taught the sublime Dharma.
Having drunk that nectar of the true Dharma, all the worlds were filled with joy;
having understood the non-distinction of phenomena, they always took refuge in the Triple Gem.
Then that Blessed One, having seen that all the worlds were established in auspiciousness,
approached the bank of the Gaṅgā to perform further meritorious deeds elsewhere.
The Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha, arrived there on the bank of the Gaṅgā;
having summoned the boatmen and looked upon them, he spoke thus: Rm_21.18{18} //
"O ferrymen, I wish to go from here to the further shore of the Gaṅgā;
therefore, ferry me across this river Gaṅgā quickly. (Rm 260) Rm_21.19{19}
Having heard that request, all those boatmen as well—
Disregarding the Lord of Sages together with his Saṅgha, they spoke thus:
"No one has ever been ferried across by us without the payment of a fare."
"If you wish to cross over, give the fare for the crossing.
Having heard what they said, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages, [responded].
Seeing all those boatmen, he spoke to them once more: "Sirs, let it be understood that I too am a boatman here."
For in the past, Nanda, who was swept away by the great river of passion, was delivered by me;
and even the wicked Aṅgulimāla, fallen into the ocean of hatred, was delivered.
The manava, who had fallen into the ocean of pride, was rescued by me;
likewise, uruvilvīkāśyapa, who was submerged in the great ocean of delusion.
In this way, I have also delivered other worlds from the ocean of afflictions;
yet for no sentient being whatsoever was there any fee for crossing over.
"Neither do I ever accept anything nor beg for it anywhere;
likewise, O Nirmāndakī, you all should treat us monks here in the same way."
"Though that Lord of Sages thus entreated them, none at all were willing to cross over the shallow [river] immediately and lead him to the other shore."
They desired to ferry that Lord of Sages across;
however, there was no wise or virtuous boatman here to carry that Sovereign of Munis.
Having fully understood his great supernormal powers, he bowed with palms joined and said:
"O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, [I seek refuge] in you and in the entire Saṅgha."
"May I also deliver them; may he therefore always be gracious to me"—having heard this spoken by him, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages, [replied].
Having gazed upon all those monks belonging to the Saṅgha, he instructed them thus:
"O monks, having boarded the boat, you all must remain composed."
"Having crossed this Gaṅgā, stay there, having taken refuge on the bank"—
when the Lord of Munis had thus commanded, all those members of the community of monks [acted accordingly].
Having quickly boarded the boat, they sat down with composed minds;
then the boatman saw that everyone had taken refuge upon the vessel.
Then the Blessed One, traveling himself through the air by means of his supernatural power, gradually brought that boat to the middle of the Gaṅgā.
Having crossed over in front of him, they took refuge on the shore;
seeing this, all those boatmen, along with the people, stood gazing in astonishment,
consumed by the fire of remorse.
And that boatman, seeing the Lord of Sages suddenly reaching the shore and standing there while he was in the sky, sat down.
Then that boat, having emerged, remained as if paralyzed upon the water;
seeing this, the boatman became overwhelmed with great astonishment.
Then, seeing Śrīghana seated on the bank, that boatman called him to mind and bowed with palms joined in reverence.
Then that moving boat, swiftly impelled by the wind,
suddenly reached the shore and came to a standstill there, remaining perfectly still.
Then all those monks, having crossed over from the vessel,
quickly reached the shore and approached the presence of the Perfectly Awakened One.
There, having seen that they had all approached him, the Blessed One took his seat upon the throne and remained there to teach the True Dharma.
Then that boatman, seeing the Sage Śrīghana seated in the assembly with the community of monks, approached him to pay his respects.
There, having bowed with palms joined to all those members of the Saṅgha in due order, he,
filled with joy, prostrated at the lotus feet of the Lord of Sages.
There, all those boatmen, filled with wonder,
approached him joyfully to hear that teaching of the Dharma.

became faint with the torment of despair, like a man afflicted by disease.
Placing his cheek upon his arm, he remained in the chamber of sorrow;
dejected by the thought of his misfortune, with a face downcast, he reflected thus in his mind:
"Alas, O Fate! What sin did I commit, or what merit and evil deeds did I perform in the past, that such suffering and yet such happiness arise for me here?"
My house is filled with an abundance of many goods;
yet, there is not even a single son who enjoys it there, nor is there a daughter either.
For upon my passing, O lord of men, that king will take all of this wealth as his own, considering me to be childless and thus seizing my entire estate in every way.
All that which I have accomplished and protected with manifold effort will surely perish for me, rendered utterly meaningless.
Therefore, what shall I do here for which no remedy can be conceived?
In every way I am ruined; who now in this world will protect me?
Seeing her husband, the master of the house, thus dejected with worry and downcast in countenance, that lovely wife looked at him and spoke as follows:
"O Master, why do you remain here lost in sorrowful reflection?
What cause for suffering has arisen for you? Tell me that in my presence."
Having heard what was spoken by his wife, that householder sighed deeply;
looking at his beloved wife, he spoke to her thus:
"My dear, what can I say in this matter for which you find no remedy?
I possess great wealth, yet there is no one to enjoy it."
"Surely, upon my death, the king will seize all these riches of mine,
thinking that since I am childless, they are subject to the sovereign."
All that which has been accomplished by me with great effort, even though it has been honored,
will surely perish without purpose due to this calamity.
This sorrow arises within me; what indeed could I say about this?
Who might extract this great dart from my heart?
Thus, dejected by anxiety, my heart burns here;
for that reason I remain thus, like a patient consumed by poison.
Having heard what was thus spoken by her husband, that beloved and charming wife looked at her lord and spoke in order to enlighten him.
For this reason, my dear, do not be despondent in any way;
if you desire progeny, employ the means to attain it.
Even this means may succeed through the grace of the deities;
therefore, having propitiated the deities, joyfully entreat them for progeny.
Then, by the grace of the gods, may our lineage indeed be victorious;
whether it be a son or a daughter who is born, let it be fruitful.
Having heard these words of mine, if you desire to maintain the stability of your lineage, perform worship of the deities and seek to obtain offspring.
Having heard what was thus spoken by his wife, that householder was awakened;
consenting with the words "So be it," he desired to act accordingly.
Then that preeminent householder, together with his wife, rejoiced; having worshipped the Lord of his own lineage, he requested a son from him.
Nevertheless, that merchant’s wife was not pregnant at all;
consequently, he remained there with a weary soul, devoid of hope.
Then that beautiful wife, beholding her husband with a despondent and distressed mind, spoke to him once again as follows:
"O Master, do not yield to despondency; take recourse in fortitude.
Despondency weakens the mind, and one whose strength is diminished possesses no vigor."
(Rm 275) Without diligence, no task whatsoever is accomplished here in this saṃsāra;
therefore, having firmly grasped diligence, worship the gods with a concentrated mind. Rm_23.83{83}
Even if no son were born, or even if no daughter were born,
merit would surely increase through the propitiation of the deities.
Thinking thus, if you desire constant happiness in this saṃsāra,
worship all the gods and devote yourself to them with faith and respect.
Having heard what was spoken by his wife, the merchant husband was awakened;
having replied, "So be it," he desired to worship the gods.
Thus, desiring progeny, that householder, together with his wife,
joyfully propitiated the Creator, the Ordainer, and requested offspring.
Nevertheless, his wife did not become pregnant for a long time;
consequently, with his hopes shattered, he remained there, overwhelmed by grief and despondency.
Then, being further urged by his wife and thus awakened,
he worshipped Viśvaṃbhara and likewise requested offspring.
Nevertheless, she did not at all exhibit the signs of pregnancy;
consequently, that householder became despondent and distressed by his lack of hope.
Thus further urged and enlightened by his wife,
he worshipped Maheśvara and requested progeny.
Likewise, having propitiated Indra, he joyfully requested progeny;
in this same manner, having propitiated and honored all the lords of the world, as well as all the planets and the gods, he likewise requested progeny.
Then, while worshipping his lineage, he likewise offered prayers to Mahākāla, Kumāra, Gaṇādhipa, Bhairava, and the Mothers.
In this way, he likewise saw other gods residing in pleasure pavilions,
established in monasteries, almshouses, hermitages, groves, and crossroads.
He also [subdued] all the lords of the nāgas, residing in gardens, mountains, forests, uncultivated lands, boundaries, and so forth, as well as those dwelling in all bodies of water.
Eagerly propitiating all the gods stationed at crossroads, squares, and main roads, he made this request for progeny.
Nevertheless, even after many months, no sign whatsoever of the arising of a pregnancy-longing appeared in the wife of that merchant.
Then that merchant, the best of householders, seeing the unbroken line of the bamboo,
stood there like a sick man, his soul despondent and devoid of hope.
Seeing his face thus torn by suffering, that beloved woman, looking intently at her husband, spoke to him once more in this way: Rm_23.99{99} //
"O Lord, nothing can be accomplished here through despondency;
considering this, conduct yourself as you wish, enjoying happiness."
"The evil we two committed is now being experienced as its fruit;
what can we do in this matter? For destiny is indeed powerful."
If that which is not destined to be will never come to be, and if what is destined to be never changes,
then all things that are certain to occur will happen in every way.
Thinking thus, having enjoyed happiness as you desire in this saṃsāra,
practice the truth with a concentrated mind by taking refuge in the Three Jewels.
By that very [means], there will always be well-being for them everywhere, both in this world and the next;
having gradually attained the state of awakening, they shall obtain final liberation.
Having heard what was thus declared by his wife, that merchant was awakened;
he paid homage to the Three Jewels and spent some time [in their service].

Then a friend and well-wisher of his, having approached and stood before him, spoke thus to that friend for the sake of producing offspring for him: *The friend and well-wisher of his, having approached and stood before him, spoke thus to that friend for the sake of producing offspring for him.* (Rm 23.106)
"O friend, listen to my words, which I speak for your benefit:
in no way whatsoever does offspring exist for you through this beloved."
Therefore, one must employ a means for the sake of establishing progeny; for one who leaves no lineage behind, every spiritual practice in saṃsāra is rendered meaningless.
Therefore, for the sake of producing a lineage, marry again according to the prescribed rite another young woman who will become a mother to a son.
Perhaps by your good fortune she might even give birth to a son;
then your life would bear fruit, and the continuity of your lineage would be secured.
Having heard what was thus spoken by his friend, that householder was awakened; saying "So be it," he made a vow and escorted that friend to his home.
Then that merchant, the best of householders, having observed another beautiful young woman who was destined to be a mother of sons, married her according to the prescribed rites.
Then that guild-president, delighted by her,
enjoyed pleasures according to his desire and took his delight while she attended upon him.
Then, as that householder was enjoying himself according to his desire, in due time his beloved wife became pregnant before long.
Then, day by day, her fetus grew larger and larger;
having realized that a child was born within her womb, she rejoiced.
Then that lovely Bhadrikā, filled with joy, approached her husband in private and, looking at him, spoke thus: Rm_23.116{16} //
"By good fortune, noble son, you have grown old, yet a child is being born within my womb;
since it is situated on my right side, this must be a male child."
Having heard what was spoken by his wife, that householder was delighted; raising his right arm, he spoke thus out of joy: Rm_23.118{18} //
"Alas! May my desire be fulfilled; may I behold the face of a lineage.
For now I am not born in vain, and the stability of my family shall be preserved."
He should perform my duties, and being supported, he should support [me] in return;
he should receive my inheritance, and the lineage shall endure for a long time.
Whatever gift has been bestowed by me and whatever merit has been accomplished—
may this skill regarding their ripening follow after these two.
Thus, that joyful merchant nourished his beloved and virtuous wife with foods provided with wholesome and beneficial preparations.
Having adorned him with fine fabrics, Chinese silks, and soft, fragrant cloths,
as well as ornaments set with various jewels, he caused him to rejoice.
Thus, having nourished that auspicious and lovely woman with wholesome regimens as her ornaments and having adorned her, he honored her, pleasing her with his favor.
(Rm 277) Having thus seen that pregnant woman, who was delighted by her husband’s great esteem, the first wife reflected once more in this way: Rm_23.125{25} //
If this lovely young woman were to give birth to an excellent lineage,
then all this prosperity would come to depend upon her.
For she alone would be the primary authority for all the world;
who indeed would accept as authoritative an old woman like me, childless?
Therefore, I must now devise a secret plan so that this co-wife of mine shall suffer a miscarriage.
For one scorched by the fire of sensual desire, there is indeed no sin whatsoever;
everything may be done, and one may enjoy everything from every source.
Then that wicked woman, speaking with confidence, gave her a medicinal powder mixed with a drink intended to destroy the fetus.
Seeing that drink offered by her co-wife, she, being auspicious and upright,
suddenly took it with both hands and drank it like one afflicted by thirst.
As soon as she had drunk this, her fetus was shaken; it suddenly began to move violently and was discharged from her through the opening of the womb.
Then that noble woman, having suddenly taken leave of her husband along with his kinsmen, addressed him once more in this way:
"O Lord, this beloved wife of yours respectfully offers me a drink mixed with medicine for the purpose of destroying the fetus. (Rm 23.134)
Having taken with full confidence whatever was given to me, I drink it;
by the mere act of drinking that, my fetus is now being expelled.
Therefore, what shall I do here, since my child is perishing?
All that gift which was prepared for this purpose has become fruitless for you.
Having heard what was thus related by his wife, the merchant became enraged; he summoned her suddenly, rebuked her, and spoke as follows: *Rm_23.137{37}*
"Alas, O you of evil mind, O wicked one, you who accomplish terrible sins!
Even so, this most horrific crime has been committed by you."
For whose sake all the deities were propitiated and entreated, and for whom various kinds of efforts were constantly undertaken by me; ||| Rm_23.139{39} |||
Indeed, all these efforts of yours have been rendered futile by you;
therefore, what is the use of you as a wife here? O most sinful one, depart now!
"I have abandoned you, a sinner; do not remain here in my house. When she heard this spoken by her husband, that woman of sinful intent spoke thus in the presence of her husband and his kinsmen:
"Why do you speak thus, Master? This was certainly not done by me;
surely it is not considered to have been done by me—please investigate this yourself."
"If I have given this substance to destroy her fetus,
then may my own sons, once they have become hungry ghosts, [devour] their children, day and night, as soon as they are born."
"Having thus experienced great suffering, may you always remain long in the miserable destinies"—
having made this oath, he awakened his master.
Having heard what was thus spoken by his wife, that merchant was enlightened;
with his soul finally released from long-standing hope, he died and went to the abode of the hungry ghosts.
This very same woman, the merchant’s wife Durāśayā,
having experienced the fruits of her own deeds, now wanders about in this manner as a hungry ghost.
Because she committed that abortion out of envy,
she has become a female preta of evil appearance and wanders about even now.
And because of that false speech with which she made an oath,
she wanders perpetually in the miserable destinies through the ripening of that karma.
Having given birth to five sons day and night, she, overcome by hunger,
ate all those infant sons of her own yet was not satisfied.
Thus that sinful female preta, having devoured her sons as they were born,
scorched by the fire of hunger, shall wander perpetually in the realm of pretas.
Having understood this, O Nārada, those who desire auspiciousness should always desist from sinful acts and from false speech, and practice the true Dharma.
For when the true Dharma ripens, there is always auspiciousness;
for transgression, there is always suffering; and for one who has entered into both, there is likewise both.
Thinking thus, you who have always gone for refuge to the Three Jewels should constantly worship them with reverence and faith, remaining ever composed in mind.
Those who, having taken refuge in the Buddha, worship him with faith and joy— all of them, having abandoned the miserable realms, proceed to the abode of the Victorious One.
And those who hear the true Dharma and honor it with reverence,
they too, having conquered the afflictions, go to the abode of the Sugata.
Those who, having taken refuge in the Saṅgha, honor and devote themselves to it, all,
being liberated from the miserable states of existence, proceed to Sukhāvatī.
Thinking thus, those who always desire what is auspicious in this saṃsāra should worship the Three Jewels and always practice what is virtuous.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, the wise Nārada,
together with his assembly and all the worlds, consented, saying, "So be it."
Then that mendicant Nārada, standing before him with palms joined in reverence,
bowed to the Blessed One and asked about its purification.
Blessed One, when will that sinful preta be released from that abode of pretas and from those terrible transgressions, and how shall she go to a happy destination?
Therefore, O Teacher of the World, you ought to fully teach the means by which this [world] may be swiftly liberated from miserable states and proceed to a good rebirth.
When Nārada had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the omniscient one, looked toward him and the assembly and spoke as follows:
Listen, Nārada, to that means for the purification of her sin;
I shall now likewise declare the method and the proper time.
When the Lord Lokeśvara, who has compassion for all sentient beings, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, is the sovereign lord of the three realms; Rm_23.164{64} //
Having departed from Sukhāvatī, illuminating all worlds,
he proceeded to the realm of the hungry ghosts (preta) in order to deliver all sentient beings.
Then, touched by that radiance, she was filled with supreme bliss and,
having exclaimed, "What great happiness is mine today?", she reflected deeply.
(Aho! What bliss has arisen! This power has been manifested. Surely a Great Being has come here to deliver sentient beings. (Rm 279) Rm_23.167{67} //
Having gone for refuge to him whose compassionate gaze is thus extended toward sentient beings, I shall always worship him with devotion.
Having thus meditated and reached a firm conclusion, that female ghost was struck with wonder;
remembering him alone, she remained there, longing for the sight of him.
Then the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, composed of compassion and possessing radiant splendor, applied himself there to uplift those in the realm of hungry ghosts.
Seeing him approaching, radiant with light, all the hungry ghosts (pretas) would suddenly come together and entreat him with great reverence: Rm_23.171{71} //
Welcome, O Blessed One, Protector! Be gracious, O Supreme Lord!
Looking upon us with compassion, deliver us from the world of the hungry ghosts.
We always go for refuge to you alone;
having purified us by that act, lead us all to a happy rebirth.
Thus, when he had so requested, the Lord of the World, that treasury of compassion,
having fully taught the True Dharma, further instructed him in this way:
If you all desire constant happiness, remain composed;
recollecting the Three Jewels, venerate them with faith and joy.
Then, liberated from these sins, you shall all be purified;
suddenly attaining the true state, you will become practitioners of the path to enlightenment.
Having been thus instructed by that Lord of the World, the Teacher of the Universe,
all those female spirits (pretikās), upon hearing it, desired to act accordingly.
Then all those hungry ghosts, with purified intentions and joy,
having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, would remember and worship them with humility.
Then, by the merit of that recollection, all those female spirits,
having risen up from the realm of hungry ghosts, shall go to Sukhāvatī.
There, they all went for refuge to the Lord Amitābha;
listening to the Dharma and honoring it, they will practice virtuous conduct.
Then all those beings, the Bodhisattvas Śubhaṃkara,
having attained awakening in due order, shall reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Then that sinful preta, liberated from all her sins,
shall rise up from the world of pretas and attain a happy rebirth.
Thinking thus, those who desire a good rebirth and happiness in this saṃsāra should worship the Three Jewels and always practice what is virtuous.
The merit arising from honoring the Three Jewels can never be exhausted;
having utterly incinerated all afflictions, it shall cause one to attain the state of the Sugata.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, the ascetic Nārada, together with the assembly of his followers, rejoiced, saying, "So be it."
Thus has it been instructed to me by my teacher, and I shall speak of it here;
considering this, O King, you too should always honor the Three Jewels.
And likewise, having caused the subjects to hear the Dharma and awakening them,
establish them on the path to enlightenment and protect them with a concentrated mind.
Then, may there always be auspiciousness for you in every respect and forever;
having gradually attained awakening, may you reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, King Aśoka,
together with his retinue, agreed, saying "So be it," and rejoiced.

And those people who, with joyful minds, hear or cause others to hear this *avadāna* concerning the female preta as told by the Sugata, they all— having constantly performed worship of the Three Jewels, having perfected the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and having brought welfare to the worlds— go to the Buddha-realm, laden with a multitude of virtues. Thus ends the story of the female preta in the *Ratnāvadānatattva*.
(Rm 281) XXIV. The Avadāna of the Female Ghost of Great Supernatural Power.
Then King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence, joyfully [spoke].
Having bowed to the ascetic Upagupta, he made his request with such reverence:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken teaching;
just as it was instructed by my teacher, so please instruct me."
When the king had thus made his request, that wise Arhat ascetic, having heard him,
looked upon King Mahīpāla and instructed him as follows:
"Listen well, O Great King, to that which was spoken by my teacher; I shall explain it to you exactly as it was told for the sake of the increase of your dharma."
Namely: the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Mass of Glory, that Lord of Sages;
the Omniscient One, the Sugata, the Protector, the King of Dharma, the Guide.
Together with the monks who were disciples, and with the novice nuns,
as well as with laymen of virtuous conduct and the assemblies of laywomen.
By Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, and likewise by others desiring enlightenment,
as well as by Brahmā, the lords of the gods and asuras, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras.
By the Siddhas and the Vidyādharas, by the lords of the Nāgas and the Garuḍas, by all the lords of the worlds and likewise by other great ṛṣis.
By Brahmins, kings, and princes seeking auspiciousness, as well as by merchants, groups of ministers, and likewise by hosts of counselors;
By the guild-leaders, the citizens, the householders,
the great men, the merchants, the caravan leaders, and likewise by the groups of artisans;
Together with villagers and country folk, pilgrims and fellow seekers of sacred sites,
as well as other noble and wise people who long for the virtues of the true Dharma.
There, in the delightful Veṇuvana grove,
at the Buddhist hermitage known as Karaṇḍakanivāpa, he was served and honored.
Having fully taught the true Dharma, he dwelt there,
illuminating all beings for their benefit, blazing like a heap of jewels.
At that very time, in that supreme city of Rājagṛha,
there was a householder, a guild-leader, a man of great renown and vast wealth.
Prosperous, resembling the god Śrī himself, and endowed with an abundance of all material wealth,
he took from a family of equal status a wife who practiced the dharma of his own lineage.
Having brought Subhadrā, whose limbs were beautiful, he married her with joy according to the prescribed rites;
thereafter, that sustainer of the household lived with his beloved wife.
Having enjoyed pleasures at will and sporting with his attendants,
that householder then continued to enjoy himself as he desired.
In due time, that beloved wife became pregnant.
Then, at the proper time, she gave birth to a boy of beautiful appearance;
hearing this, his father, the merchant, approached with joy to see him.
There, having quickly approached that boy who possessed auspicious marks,
he stood gazing at him with great joy, never satiated by the sight.
Then, having summoned his kinsmen and performed the birth festival for the infant, he spoke thus: "Let a name be given to him that is well-known."
Having heard that, all those kinsmen reached a consensus and, having summoned the merchant, spoke thus to him in the presence of the assembly: Rm_24.22{22} //
"Since this boy was born under the lunar mansion named Uttarā,
let your son be known by the name Uttara."
Having heard what was thus reported by those kinsmen, that householder likewise caused his son to be known by that very same name.
Then that boy, nurtured by eight nurses,
grew day by day like a lotus situated in a pond.
Then, as he grew up and was gradually instructed by his teachers,
he quickly reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge, beginning with writing.
Then that wise Uttara, accompanied by his peers,
shone as he moved through that city, enchanting the world.
When Uttara had reached the full bloom of youth and was possessed by the intoxication of passion, his father, the merchant, met his end through the power of fate.
Then, in that house, his son Uttara became the master who had attained prosperity, a householder and lord of the world.
Then, established in his family’s traditional way of life and skilled in worldly affairs,
he acquired wealth by engaging in the business of buying and selling.
One day, seeking the Dharma, he went to that bamboo grove, the hermitage of the Jina, in order to behold the Perfectly Awakened One, Śrīghana.
Having approached that place, he beheld the Sage Śrīghana,
adorned with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor characteristics.
Radiating a fathom-wide halo, possessing a form like that of Samantabhadra,
he was like a blazing heap of jewels or a mountain of gems come to life.
Seated in the midst of the assembly, preceded by the community of monks,
raining down the nectar of the Dharma, and honored by all the worlds.
Having seen him there, he was filled with joy; walking before him with palms joined in reverence, he bowed at the feet of that Lord of Sages and took his place to one side.
Having perceived his pure intention there, the Blessed One likewise began to teach the True Dharma, starting from the Noble Truths.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, Uttara was filled with joy;
bowing once more at the feet of the Sage, he returned to his own abode.
Thus that wise Uttara attended daily upon the Teacher of the World, in order to behold him or to drink the nectar of the Dharma.
Then, having drunk that nectar of Dharma from the Lord of Munis,
he desired to go forth into homelessness within the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One.
Then Uttara, standing before that lord of sages,
bowed with palms joined in reverence at his lotus feet and requested ordination.
"O Blessed One, O Protector, O Omniscient One, I go for refuge to you;
it behoves you now to grant me the vow of renunciation."
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages,
looked toward the youth named Uttara and commanded him as follows.
"O Prince, if you desire to go forth into the Buddhist teaching, first obtain your mother's permission; then come here, and I shall grant it to you."
When the Lord of Sages had thus instructed him, Uttara was awakened;
saying "So be it," he bowed at the feet of that sage and went home.
Having reached that house, Uttara was filled with joy;
bowing at his mother’s feet, he spoke thus with palms joined in reverence: *Rm_24.45* {45}
"Mother, today I am going to the monastery, the hermitage of the Sugata;
there I shall drink the nectar of the Noble Dharma issuing from the lotus-face of the Teacher."
Having drunk that nectar of the true Dharma, my thirst increases once again;
I desire to grasp that true Dharma for the sake of complete satisfaction.
Blessed indeed are those virtuous souls, purified in the three spheres,
who, abiding in the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One, always drink the Dharma.
I too, O Mother, always practicing there within the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One,
certainly desire to obtain that nectar of the True Dharma.
"O Mother, having now taken up that vow of renunciation, I wish to practice it in the hermitage of the Sugata; therefore, grant me your permission."
Having heard this from her son and others, she was deeply moved;
gazing long at her son while weeping, she spoke thus: *Rm_24.51*{51}
"Why do you speak thus, my son? Do not speak so before me.
For what reason do you wish to renounce the world, abandoning your own home?"
"What is your suffering, and from where has it arisen? Is there nothing at all that can be seen by me?
Whatever is seen by you must be told before me."
Even now, the grief and mental anguish for your father have not subsided within me;
nevertheless, O daughter, why do you wish to abandon me at this very moment?
Having heard what was thus spoken by his mother, the young prince Uttara looked at her and spoke in order to awaken her understanding.
"O Mother, by your grace, no suffering whatsoever exists for me here;
even at home there is great wealth, and enjoyments according to my desire."
Indeed, cyclic existence is impermanent; the body perishes in an instant.
Life is impermanent and unstable, like a flash of lightning.
Even prosperity is not thus stable; for whom is fortune ever-lasting? For all living beings everywhere, death is certain.
At the time of death, all living beings, having abandoned all possessions—
even their kinsmen, relatives, friends, and companions— depart for the abode of Yama.
(Rm 284) Not even a single person is found to accompany one who has met with death;
at that time, Dharma alone shall be the protector and follower in the abode of Yama.
In that place presided over by the messengers of Yama, one is protected by dharma;
therefore, in every way and at all times, one must indeed practice dharma alone.
One who possesses the Dharma, even while wandering here in this cycle of existence, is always happy;
having experienced true happiness everywhere, he goes to a fortunate rebirth.
Even there, having always enjoyed happiness and performed auspicious deeds,
one should accomplish the true dharmas for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Through the ripening of this merit, he shall take refuge in a true guru;
then, by the grace of the true guru, he shall obtain the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
Then, having attained the conduct of awakening, the wise one becomes a bodhisattva;
thereafter, for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, he should practice the conduct of awakening.
Then, having fulfilled all the perfections in their proper sequence and attained the threefold awakening, one shall reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Thus was it commanded by the Lord of Munis, the omniscient one who seeks the welfare [of beings].
Having heard this and understood it, I desire to practice accordingly.
O Mother, if you also wish to attain this share of merit, then grant me your permission and gladden my heart.
Having heard what was spoken by her son, that mother, her hopes shattered and tormented by the sorrow of separation,
spoke thus while lamenting:
"Alas, my son! Why do you wish to abandon me in solitude?
I have no other son; you alone are my joy."
Even your father, having abandoned me, has by fate gone to the abode of Yama;
where do you likewise wish to go, having likewise forsaken me?
"Alas, my son! How can you be so ignorant? By whom have you been deceived here? Seeing what, and for what reason, do you wish to go forth into the religious life?"
"Alas, my son! Why are you so deluded that, having abandoned these riches, you wish to eat by begging for alms in another's house?"
"Alas, my son! You are but a youth; how could you practice the life of a renunciant?
Having abandoned your home and become a wanderer, how will you always find refuge in foreign lands?"
So how could you abandon him and seek refuge in a foreign land?
Having died here, clad in hempen garments and shaven-headed, he shall become the lord of the earth.
O son, how will you endure suffering when assailed by cold, wind, and heat?
When scorched by the fires of hunger and thirst, who will extinguish your pain?
O son, how would you wander alone, casting away corpses in cremation grounds?
How would you dwell all by yourself in the lonely wilderness or the desolate forest?
Likewise, how could you dwell in the abode of the elements as if in an empty house?
And how could you wander alone, as it were, among enemies and foreign lands?
Who would attend to you when you are tormented by diseases such as fever?
Or who, out of compassion, would provide you with wholesome food and medicine?
"If by chance misfortune should occur, who then would clear [the debt]?
Having considered this, my son, do not exert yourself in the vow of renunciation.
Having heard my words on this matter, dwell in your home and enjoy happiness.
Having heard what was thus spoken by his mother, the son replied in this way:
"The conditions of destiny indeed come to pass everywhere, even throughout all the worlds."
Not even a single friend, companion, or follower exists here;
in death, it is certain that Dharma alone shall be one's companion everywhere.
Thus, for the sake of attaining the true Dharma, the wise who desire the state of nirvana should practice the supreme vow of renunciation.
"Thus it was commanded by that Lord of Sages; O Mother, having heard this, I therefore desire to observe this vow here."
Therefore, if you wish to enjoin me to this Dharma of the Sugata,
you ought out of compassion to grant me your permission.

Having heard this request for her son, the mother, her voice faltering and tormented by the fire of affectionate grief, spoke thus to her son upon seeing him: *iti putrārthitaṃ śrutvā mātā sā gadgadasvarā / snehaduḥkhāgnisaṃtaptā dṛṣṭvaivaṃ sutam abravīt //* Rm_24.86{86} //
"Alas, my son! How can you be so merciless and so exceedingly cruel, that upon seeing your aged mother, no compassion arises in your heart?"
Therefore, my son, if you have compassion for me, your mother,
dwell here with me in this house as long as I live.
"As long as this great prosperity remains stable in your own home,
enjoy whatever pleasures you desire and take your delight."
I shall certainly go to death; for whom indeed would death not come?
Therefore, when I am dead, you may renounce the world as you wish.
Prosperity, too, may come to an end; for whom is prosperity ever stable?
Therefore, when prosperity has utterly perished, subsist on alms-food and observe your vow.
If, even though entreated in this way, you disregard my words and go forth into homelessness by force, with a heart that is merciless and cruel; Rm_24.92{92} //
Then, having gone before you, even within the teaching of the Sugata,
I shall certainly meet my death by abandoning food and consuming poison.
"Knowing these words of mine to be true, O son, enjoy happiness with me here in this house; do not go anywhere else."
Having heard these words of mine, O son, enjoy yourself at home according to your desire; always eating with constant vigor, take your pleasure.
Having heard what was spoken by his mother, Uttara became apprehensive; acknowledging her words with "So be it," he remained at home, devoid of hope.
Then one morning, having risen, Uttara went to the monastery to see that perfectly enlightened Sage.
There, having seen that Śrīghana, Uttara was filled with joy;
having bowed and circumambulated him, he approached him with palms joined in reverence.
Then the Blessed One, the Teacher, having perceived what was in his mind and seeing that he was ready to be awakened, addressed him in this way:
"O Prince, why are you despondent? Tell me before me that which is in your heart; I shall fulfill whatever you desire."
When the Lord of Sages had thus instructed him, Uttara rose up, bowed at the feet of that sage, and with palms joined in reverence spoke as follows: Rm_24.101{1} //
O All-Knowing Blessed One, Teacher, may you understand all that is within my mind, just as I now declare it to you. (Rm 286) Rm_24.102(2)
"O Blessed One, O Protector, O Omniscient One, my mother has not been awakened;
even though she was entreated, she does not wish to grant me permission."
Therefore, you ought to instruct me here in whatever vow is appropriate for accomplishing perfect enlightenment, even if it be otherwise.
When he had thus entreated him, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
seeing his pure intention and having comforted him, commanded him as follows:
"Do not fall into despair, O Prince; take refuge in fortitude.
When the time has arrived, you will certainly become a celibate student."
Therefore, always give gifts in your home to those who seek them according to their desires;
and having recollected the Three Jewels, practice virtue with a concentrated mind.
Through the ripening of this merit, when the time has arrived,
you will attain the vow of renunciation and reach the state of Nirvana.
Thinking thus, O Prince, as long as that mother lives,
remain here always giving gifts in your home and practicing what is auspicious.
Having heard what was thus instructed by the Lord of Sages, the wise Uttara,
having been enlightened, replied "So be it" and became serene.
Then Uttara, having bowed with palms joined to that lord of sages whose lotus-face was most serene, went to his own home with his mind fixed upon him.
Remaining there in his own home, he established a shop there and carried out buying and selling by means of the resources for his family's livelihood.
There, whatever profit exceeding the principal he had gained through his association with the group,
he handed all of that over into the hands of his mother.
Then his eldest son, seeking to appease his mother, gave her all that wealth he had obtained and thus enlightened her: Rm_24.114{14} //
Listen, mother: with this wealth of mine, honor and satisfy your own kin, the needy, the wretched, and the Brahmins.
Having heard what was spoken by her son, that mother Atikuñcikā, greedy and with a heart overcome by envy, spoke thus: Rm_24.116{16} //
"My son, these riches have been acquired by your father with great effort;
you will spend all these riches by giving them to those who seek them."
"As long as the wealth acquired by my father remains, so much shall not be given by me;
only that which has been earned by you yourself shall be at your disposal."
"As long as I live, my dear father, I will not give you anything;
once I am dead, all that shall then be at your disposal."
Having spoken thus, his mother, her mind defiled by envy,
diligently concealed all the wealth and guarded it with extreme care.
That evil-minded woman gave nothing to those who sought it;
having hidden that wealth with great effort, she guarded it closely.
And seeing all the merchants who had returned to their own homes,
he suddenly approached them, reviled, and severely censured them.
(Rm 287) "Are you not illusions in this house? You have come here like hungry ghosts;
like spirits, you wander constantly to eat alms-food in the houses of others."
Thus that woman, evil in intent, reviled and censured all those supplicants in many ways with deceitful speech.
Having heard his mother thus reproaching him and censuring his lamentations, her son Uttara spoke to her.
"O mother, why do you revile those who seek your help?
Shame on you, fallen from righteousness! How will you not fall into hell?"
If you desire happiness always, both in this world and in the next,
gladden all those who are miserable and needy with your gifts.
"If it is done thus, O Mother, there will always be companionship between us;
otherwise, we would have separate meals and dwellings."
If you always have a delight in eating together with me, then,
O auspicious one, practice the noble Dharma by giving to supplicants whatever they desire.
Having heard that her own son had thus rejected her,
the mother, her face split with shame, spoke to that son.
If this is so, and you wish to give even your entire possessions to those who seek joy,
then I shall give all my own goods to them just as they desire.
Having spoken thus, that motherly woman, having awakened her son with a false word,
would have hidden those goods within the house.
Then that wicked woman, with false speech, informed her son:
"Today I shall satisfy the mendicants who have come seeking alms."
Thus, awakening her son with deceitful words and taking possession of it herself, she concealed all that property.
That evil-minded woman gave nothing at all to anyone who asked for it;
she never once ventured to offer even a tribute to any being whatsoever.
Thus that evil-minded woman, greedy and with a heart overcome by envy,
reviled all who sought her aid and, while censuring them, engaged in unwholesome conduct.
Thus, having accumulated only evil deeds, that woman of wicked intent died in due course; despairing and tormented by suffering, she went to the abode of the pretas.
There, one who has reached the realm of hungry ghosts becomes a preta of hideous form,
with limbs covered by their own hair, a needle-like mouth, and emaciated body.
Raised up like a framework of bones, with bellies resembling mountains,
tormented by the fires of hunger and thirst, their limbs are like charred pillars.
Uttering cries of distress and wailing piteously on all sides,
she wandered here and there, searching everywhere for food and drink.
Then Uttara, having performed his mother’s funeral rites with the sacred fire,
dispelled his grief by carrying out the necessary acts such as bathing and purification.
Then that Uttara Vijaya dispelled his mother's grief;
by giving what was desired to those who requested it, he accumulated great merit.
Then, detached from desire and indifferent to the enjoyments of worldly existence, he desired to go forth into homelessness in order to attain the state of final liberation.
Then, having gone joyfully to the Jina’s hermitage in the Bamboo Grove and beholding Śrīghana, he bowed down and approached him with palms joined in reverence.
There, having circumambulated that Lord of Sages together with his Saṅgha,
and having bowed down and stood before him with palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus:
O Blessed One, O Protector, O Omniscient One, may you also take note of this:
that mother of mine, who was my obstacle, has now met her destruction.
Therefore, O Blessed Teacher, let me go for refuge to you;
having bestowed your favor upon me, it behooves you to grant me the going forth.
When he had thus entreated him, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages, touched his head with his right hand and commanded him as follows:
"Come, O youth, practice the holy life here with a concentrated mind";
having said this, the Blessed One, the Teacher, accepted him into the Saṅgha.
When the Lord of Munis said, "Come," Uttara became shaven-headed,
carrying a khikkhirī bowl and clothed in pure saffron robes.
Then, through faith in the Teacher, he became completely purified in the three spheres;
with his self cleansed of all afflictions, he took joy in turning away from cyclic existence.
The wise one, striving in concentration, dhāraṇīs, and vidyās,
abandoned the mass of ignorance and attained the ultimate limit of all the qualities of knowledge.

Having understood that every state of cyclic existence lasts no longer than a flash of lightning, and having realized that the course of all conditioned phenomena is fraught with manifold calamities; Rm_24.153{53}
Having conquered the entire multitude of all afflictions as well as all the hosts of Māra,
he directly attained the state of an Arhat and realized the enlightenment of a Śrāvaka.
Then he, whose self was perfectly purified, free from passion, and having conquered his senses,
possessed a mind as stainless as space and regarded all clods of earth as equal to gold.
He is like an axe and sandalwood—equanimous toward both, free from conceptual construction, and stainless;
he brings about the welfare of all sentient beings and accomplishes the qualities of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
He became a celibate student (brahmacārī), worthy of being saluted, honored, and revered by all living beings, including the worlds of gods and asuras.
Then that Arhat, possessed of great supernormal knowledge, took up residence in a leaf-hut on a beautiful spot on the bank of the Gaṅgā and remained there, absorbed in meditative concentration.
Then one day, his mother, having become a *preta*,
appeared naked, covered in hair, and as pale as a withered pillar.
With mouths like the eye of a needle and bellies resembling mountains,
their limbs scorched by the fires of hunger and thirst, they wander in search of food and drink.
Wailing with a piteous cry and lamenting, she approached; seeing that venerable Arhat, she took refuge in him.
Seeing her thus seated in attendance, the ascetic Uttara asked her:
"Tell me, who are you that have come here in such a state?"
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, that female ghost (pretī) standing before him looked at her son, the ascetic Uttara, and spoke as follows:
"I am your affectionate mother, by whom you were begotten as a son;
now, deprived of food and drink, I have become a ghost and must wander."
Twenty-five years have passed while I have been deceased; indeed,
I do not recall ever having seen water, much less food.
Seeing a tree laden with fruit and in bloom, I pass far away from it;
all those that are fruitless, withered, and flowerless become [my destination].
Seeing lakes filled with water, I go far away from them,
yet they all become dry even at that very moment.
Great happiness is found here at all times for you who have taken refuge at the foot of this tree; what auspicious deed must you have performed in the past?
Therefore, O son, seeing this with compassion and giving rise to pity,
you ought to give cool water to my mother, who is tormented by thirst.
Having heard this request made by her, Uttara, filled with wonder and gazing at that female ghost for a very long time, spoke thus with apprehension: Rm_24.170{70} //
Therefore, Mother, when the moment had arrived, because you were harsh by nature,
you did not give gifts at all, nor did you accumulate any meritorious deeds.
Upon seeing or even hearing of the gifts and meritorious deeds performed by others, the fire of anger then blazed up within his mind.
Not even a single virtuous deed was performed by you as merit;
nor, upon seeing or hearing of one performed by another, did you rejoice in it.
Through the ripening of this karma, you, who were once my mother, have now died;
having become a preta, deprived of food and drink, you wander in this world of existence.
"Now what shall I do, and what will you do here?
At that time, all manner of harm was proclaimed by you, yet you did not hear it then."
Having heard what was said by her son, she was awakened; with eyes parched and shedding tears, she spoke thus to her son: Rm_24.176{76}
Indeed, no gift was given by me, nor was merit accomplished;
nor did I rejoice upon seeing [others' deeds], being overcome by stinginess.
Whatever object, my son, was entrusted by you into my hands,
all of that has been hidden by me in the secret pit.
Therefore, having now extracted it, entrust it to the hands of your kinsmen;
by means of that, my son, feed the Sugata, the Buddha, together with his Saṅgha.
And also have a gift-offering dedicated in my name;
then, liberated from the realm of hungry ghosts, I shall go to the abode of the gods.
Having heard what she had said, Uttara was thus awakened;
having agreed, saying "So be it," he spoke to her again as follows.
"I shall now feed the Sugata together with his Saṅgha;
however, Mother, you too must remain there in the presence of the Sugata."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, that female ghost (preta), overcome with shame,
looked at the Arhat before her and spoke as follows:
"Since I am naked, O son, a female ghost with a disfigured form,
how can I stand in the presence of one so thick with splendor?"
Having heard what was spoken by her, the high-minded Uttara,
looking at that female ghost, spoke again as follows:
When you felt no shame while committing this evil deed,
why do you now feel such shame at the time of experiencing its fruit?
Having heard those words, that female ghost was awakened; saying,
"I shall go accordingly," she quickly departed for her own abode.
Then Uttara went there, summoned his kinsmen,
and having related everything exactly as it had been told by Mātṛ, he reported it all to them.
Having heard that, all those groups of kinsmen were filled with great wonder; they took all that wealth and presented it to him.
Having surveyed all that wealth, Uttara was filled with joy and spoke thus once more to all the clansmen:
"O kinsmen, with all this wealth, I shall now honor and feed that Lord of Munis together with his Saṅgha."
Taking all of this, when those whose intentions were shaken prepared the requisite assembly worthy of a communal meal for the Saṅgha, they presented it to me.
Having heard this prayer, all those kinsmen likewise prepared the necessary provisions for a communal feast with all kinds of materials.
Seeing that, the Arhat Uttara was filled with joy; with a serene mind, he approached the monastery to invite the Teacher.
Having approached that lord of sages together with his retinue, he bowed down with palms joined in reverence; standing there before him, he invited him.
"O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, I desire to honor the Blessed One together with his Saṅgha; may you deign to favor me tomorrow."
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, that lord of sages, looked upon him with favor and, remaining silent, consented to it.
