Then, understanding that the Blessed One had consented, Uttara bowed once more to the Lord of Munis and went before his kinsmen.
There, having invited them along with Uttara,
he spoke to them once again in their presence as follows:
Now that this communal meal for the Saṅgha has begun, you all have assembled here;
you ought to look upon my mother, who has become a hungry ghost (preta).
Having spoken thus and returned to his own hermitage, Uttara was comforted;
seated within his meditation chamber, he remained absorbed in meditative concentration.
Then, having risen at dawn, he went before his kinsmen and quickly prepared the full array of offerings and services.
Then, having approached the monastery in the forenoon, Uttara bowed down to the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, and spoke as follows:
O Blessed One, All-Knowing Teacher, the time has now come;
it is fitting for you, together with the Saṅgha, to be victorious here.
When he had thus entreated him, the Sage struck the gong;
impelled by that sound, the Saṅgha and he [the king] approached that place.
There all those kinsmen, as well as other people, were filled with joy;
they gathered together to see that female spirit who had arrived there.
Then the Blessed One, together with his assembly, arrived there;
having accepted the water for washing the feet that was offered, he took his seat upon a pure throne.
Seeing her, all her kinsmen and other people were also distressed;
crying out, "Alas, what a crime!", they stood there longing for the true Dharma.
Then all those kinsmen, having honored the Blessed One together with his community of monks in due order, satisfied him with food.
Then all those members of the Saṅgha, headed by the Perfectly Awakened One himself,
partook of that food of exquisite flavor and attained full satisfaction.
Then, having removed their bowls and cleansed their hands and other limbs,
they joyfully presented them with a variety of betel leaves and other items for chewing.
There, that elder monk, accompanied by those kinsmen,
bowed down to the Blessed One and his Saṅgha and took refuge with them.
There, the Blessed One, seeing that Uttara had taken refuge,
instructed her in the Dharma after death by means of a name.
Whatever merit indeed arises from this gift, let it go to that female preta;
may this female preta then rise up swiftly from the world of pretas.
Having thus bestowed these auspicious blessings, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
began with the Noble Truths and taught the True Dharma.
Having heard that noble Dharma, all the people were awakened;
having understood the excellence of the Dharma, they became seers of truth.
That preta, having joyfully received that nectar of the True Dharma,
with a perfectly serene disposition, recollected the Three Jewels and went for refuge.
Then she was born in the world of mortals as one possessed of great supernatural power;
even there, she remained wicked, her disposition hardened by envy.
Then that Blessed One, illuminating [the world], went from there with his community of monks; having reached his own hermitage and taken up residence there, he remained teaching the Dharma.
Then that wise, learned, and long-lived ascetic Uttara perceived: "Where is this mother now being born?"
Thus that wise Uttara, having looked all around, saw her who had recently given birth in the abode of a being of great supernatural power.
Seeing his mother and that female spirit, the son Uttara suddenly approached them, and after addressing her, he spoke thus:
"Mother, do you still have the power to give even now?
If you desire constant welfare, perform an act of giving here this very moment."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, she, who possessed great supernatural power,
looked at her son Uttara and spoke again as follows:
"O Nandana, even now I have no desire for giving;
I do not venture to bestow even the slightest bit of wealth."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, the venerable ascetic Uttara,
seeing that his mother possessed such great supernatural power, addressed her.

Even now that body of yours remains, its flesh wasted away while its skin, bones, and hide have grown thick; it was turned back from the world of hungry ghosts because your eyes were shrouded by the darkness of greed.
Shame on you, the utterly corrupt one! What more can I say to you here, since even now you remain possessed of such evil intent?
By whom here shall your mind, submerged in evil, be purified and raised up by meritorious deeds?
And if your dwelling in hell were thus eternal, when would you ever be liberated from it?
Alas! Indeed, the minds of those with evil intellects and wicked intentions are never purified by anything at all.
Having thus rebuked her in many ways,
Uttara then forcibly tore one of the twin sisters from her body and carried her away.
Then he, being worthy, assigned that twin girl to the Saṅgha;
having purchased her there for a price, he should place her under the supervision of a young monk.
There too, having gone at night, she brought that Yamalī;
and when she had been thus abducted, the monk reported it to Uttarā.
Having heard that, Uttara went there, rebuked her by force,
and having carried her away, he restored her once more to that monk.
Again at night she went and brought that female yakṣa;
likewise Uttara also carried her off from her.
Thus, having gone there three times during the night, she carried her off;
and Uttara, having indeed carried her away, gave her to that monk.
That monk also took it and, having sewn it into a foot-cloth belonging to the Saṅgha of the four directions, offered it back.
There, seeing that [garment] sewn and her great supernatural power rendered futile,
she went to her own abode weeping, her hopes shattered.
Scorched by the fire of that thought and remembering her son Uttara,
she passed away and was then reborn elsewhere in the world of the yakṣas.
Realizing thus that stinginess is indeed the root of great evil,
one should abandon that stinginess and practice giving with reverence.
Through generosity the mind is purified; with a purified mind, one becomes wise.
By gradually maintaining the conduct of awakening, one shall attain the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having understood this, if one always desires what is auspicious in all circumstances,
one should abandon stinginess like poison and always practice what is virtuous.
Thus it was told to me by my teacher, and having heard it, I have spoken it likewise;
you too, having understood this, should always conduct yourself accordingly, O auspicious one.
And having diligently awakened the subjects, O Great King, you ought always to protect them once they have been established on the path to enlightenment.
In that way, may you always have auspiciousness everywhere and certainly;
having attained awakening in due course, may you reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard this spoken by that Arhat, King Aśoka replied,
"So be it," and rejoiced together with his retinue.
Those people who are joyful here upon hearing this narrative of the great supernatural power of the Bhūtas,
rejoice with delight and go to dwell in the abode of Śrīghana.
Thus ends the *Pretībhūtamaharddhikāvadāna*, being the twenty-fifth [tale] in the *Ratnāvadāna*.
XXV. The *Dūtāvadāna*.
Then King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence and filled with joy,
bowed to his teacher Upagupta and spoke again as follows:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken word;
it would be fitting for you to instruct me just as it was explained by my teacher."
Having heard this request made by the king, the Arhat Upagupta, possessed of great intelligence,
addressed that lord of men and spoke as follows.
Listen, O illustrious king, to what was spoken by my guru;
I shall relate it to you exactly as it was told, and having heard it, may you rejoice therein.
Namely: the Blessed One, the Buddha, the mass of glory, that Lord of Sages;
the Omniscient One, the Sugata, the Teacher, the King of Dharma, the Guide.
Together with the monks and the disciples, with the nuns and the novices, and also with the assemblies of laymen and the assemblies of laywomen.
At the edge of the city of Rājagṛha, on Gṛddhakūṭa, the best of mountains,
in the great grove of Veṇuvana, at the Karandaṅka feeding ground.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, illuminating the conduct of awakening and teaching the true Dharma, he dwelt there, radiating light.
All the worlds have come together to drink that nectar of the True Dharma—
the gods, the daityas, the nāgas, the yakṣas, the gandharvas, and the kinnaras.
The planets, the Vidyādharas, the Siddhas, the Rākṣasas, and even the Garuḍas;
the hosts of world-protectors, as well as the heretics and the great ṛṣis.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, kings, Vaiśyas, as well as counselors, ministers, merchants, householders, and eminent men; Rm_25.11{11} //
Merchants and caravan leaders, artisans and city-dwellers, as well as villagers, country folk, and even wandering pilgrims.
Likewise, all the other people who had gathered there,
having seen that Śrīghana, bowed down and honored him in due order.
With their palms joined in reverence, they all stood surrounding him. Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all approached him,
taught the True Dharma, which is auspicious in its beginning, middle, and end.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, all the worlds were awakened;
having understood the excellence of the Dharma, they became achievers of enlightenment.
Thus that Blessed One, constantly teaching the True Dharma there,
spent the rainy season retreat having performed benefit for the world together with his Saṅgha.
At that time, in that city of Śrāvastī, there was the most excellent householder and merchant Anāthapiṇḍada, who was a man of great means.
Devoted to the Three Jewels, a donor, and eager for a vision of the Perfectly Awakened One,
[he] bowed down to King Prasenajit and made this request.
Victory to you, O Great King! You too should know that reason why this Lord of Sages has not been seen by us for so very long. (Rm 294) Rm_25.19{19} //
Therefore, we are thirsty for a vision of that Lord of Munis;
O Blessed One, we desire to see that Lord of Munis now.
Therefore, having approached the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World,
you ought to strive for victory here for the sake of the welfare of the world.
Having heard this constant prayer made by that master of the house,
the king, the lord of the earth, spoke to that householder.
"O virtuous one, do you hear where that Blessed One, the Lord of Sages,
is currently staying during the rainy season together with his community of monks?"
Having heard what was spoken by the king, that householder Anāthapiṇḍada looked at the lord of men and spoke again as follows:
"I have heard, O Great King, that the Blessed One, together with his Saṅgha,
is currently staying in Rājagṛha even during this rainy season."
Having heard what was thus related by him, the king then summoned a messenger and reproached him in this manner right there in the city.
"Come, O great hero! Having heard my words, go quickly to that city of Rājagṛha and attend upon the Blessed One."
In our name, offer salutations at the lotus feet of that Teacher;
having bowed down, inquire everywhere after his health and well-being, including his body and all else.
And thus, with reverence, he announced before that Sage:
"O Blessed One, King Kauśalya, the monarch, desires to see you."
Likewise, all the people of the world and the citizens of Śrāvastī now desire to behold the Three Jewels.
O All-Knowing One, they also desire to drink the nectar of Your Dharma;
therefore, it behoves You, together with Your Saṅgha, to come there out of compassion.
Having heard what was spoken by the king, he rejoiced, saying "So be it";
then, bowing with palms joined to that monarch, he departed swiftly for Rājagṛha.
Having gone there to Rājagṛha, that messenger was welcomed;
looking upon him with a very serene mind, he approached Gṛdhrakūṭa.
There, having seen the Blessed One from afar, he was filled with joy;
approaching him with palms joined in reverence and bowing down, he made this request with great devotion.
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, I pay homage to your lotus feet;
may you, the Victor, know that for which purpose I have come here.
Nevertheless, I shall make this request before the Teacher of the World:
"O Blessed One, you who know all things, King Prasenajit is highly skilled."
He pays homage at your feet and inquires after your welfare;
likewise, O Blessed One, do all the inhabitants of Śrāvastī.
The kings and all the people salute your feet and inquire after your welfare; they are all eager for a sight of you.
"We wish to see the Triple Gem," they say;
likewise, they now desire to drink the nectar of your Dharma.
All those headed by the king were like those afflicted by thirst [longing for] nectar;
therefore, it would be well if the Blessed One were now to go there, to the city of Śrāvastī.
Out of compassion, may he, together with his Saṅgha, be victorious.

When this had been said by that messenger, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, looked at that man-messenger and, having addressed him, commanded thus: *ity ukte tena dūtena bhagavān sa munīśvaraḥ / taṃ dūtaṃ puruṣaṃ dṛṣṭvā samāmaṃtryevam ādiśat //* Rm_25.41{40} //
"O man, King Bimbisāra, the sovereign of men, must grant his permission; if he does so, then I shall certainly go."
Therefore, O King, it would be well for me to request his permission from that monarch Bimbisāra; having done so, I shall then depart.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, that messenger respectfully replied,
"So be it," and after bowing to the sage, he approached the presence of the king.
There, having approached King Bimbisāra, he went before him with palms joined in reverence, bowed down, and made this announcement:
Victory to you, O God, Great King! Be gracious and show us favor;
I have come as an envoy from Prasenajit, the lord of the earth.
"O Great King Mahīpāla Prasenajit of Kośala desires to behold the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages."
Likewise, all the people of the world, including the Śrāvastīs and the citizens,
now desire to question the Three Jewels, the lords of the universe.
Therefore, O Lord, you who are the master of the three worlds,
it behoves you out of compassion to grant me permission to follow him there.
Having heard this request made by him, King Bimbisāra looked at the messenger and after a long time spoke thus:
O noble one, if that Blessed One wishes to go there, then what shall I say here? Let him go wherever he desires.
Having heard this command from the king, the messenger was delighted;
he bowed to King Bimbisāra and went into the presence of the Jina.
Having gone there with haste and bowed with palms joined in reverence to that lord of sages, Śrīghana, he made this request with great devotion: Rm_25.53{52} //
"O Blessed One, you have now indeed been granted permission by that king;
therefore, it is fitting for the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha, to proceed there for victory."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages,
looked upon the messenger and remained there in silence.
Then, at the end of the three-month rainy season retreat, that Blessed One, together with his community of monks, set forth,
illuminating all directions after having performed auspicious rites everywhere.
Then that man, acting as a messenger, emerged from that monastery;
suddenly mounting his chariot, he set out upon the road ahead.
There, seeing the Blessed One proceeding on foot along the road, he immediately alighted from his chariot himself.
Thereupon, having approached the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, with haste,
he went before him with palms joined in reverence, bowed down, and spoke thus:
May you, the Lord of the World, be gracious out of compassion for me;
having mounted this chariot, may you be victorious together with your community of followers.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World,
looked upon that messenger-man and instructed him right there as follows:
Mounted upon the chariot of the bases of psychic power, which proceeds with right effort,
I traverse the entire earth unharmed by the thorns of the afflictions.
Having been thus instructed and enlightened by the Lord of Sages, that messenger bowed again with palms joined in reverence and entreated that sovereign of sages:
Although the Blessed One travels by means of supernatural power, nevertheless,
out of compassion, please accept [this vehicle] to bestow favor upon me.
Having heard this request made by him, the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha,
stood upon the chariot by means of his supernatural power and set forth, illuminating all around.
On all those paths, the Blessed One, together with his Saṅgha,
illuminating them and performing auspicious rites, arrived at the city of Śrāvastī.
There, that man acting as a messenger, proceeding swiftly ahead,
went before King Prasenajit and announced this.
Victory to you, O Great King! May you prosper now by good fortune, since that Blessed One, the Teacher, has arrived here together with his Saṅgha.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, King Prasenajit had the entire area along the roads searched and thoroughly investigated.
He adorned [the area] on all sides with parasols, banners, and canopies;
then that king, the monarch, together with his people, went out to meet the Blessed One amidst great festivals accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments and songs.
There, King Samudita, together with his ministers, countryfolk, and citizens,
seeing Śrīghana from afar, approached him on foot.
Having approached there, that king, together with his assembly, bowed down to the lord of sages;
standing before him with palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus upon seeing him.
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, is all well with your body?
Please dwell here in this realm together with your community of monks.
Likewise, all the people of the world, together with the ministers, the country folk, and the citizens,
bowed with palms joined in reverence and made this petition to that Lord of Sages:
Welcome, Blessed One, Teacher, Victorious One, O Treasure of Compassion!
Please remain here always in this hermitage and dwell here out of your compassion.
Having spoken thus, all those people, headed by the king, joyfully caused him to enter the city with auspicious enthusiasm for worship and other rites.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that all those people, headed by the king, were filled with joy, bestowed upon them auspicious blessings and conducted himself accordingly.
There, the Blessed One, having descended near the city gate of Śrāvastī,
proceeded on foot together with his community of monks.
There, that Lord Śrīghana, illuminating all directions and bringing auspiciousness to everyone, entered together with his community of monks.
When the Fully Awakened One, the Sugata, the Victor, had entered that city,
everything became auspicious, pervaded by the sublime radiance of his merit.
The blind beheld forms, the deaf heard sound,
and even those with impaired faculties all became possessed of complete senses.
Their limbs, scorched by the fire of hunger, became fully satisfied;
their limbs, consumed by thirst, likewise became completely satiated.

Those who were poorly clothed and ill-favored became clad in pure garments and possessed of auspicious fortune; those who were afflicted by long-standing diseases became free from illness and strong through him.
Those who were insane became possessed of mindfulness, and the poor became wealthy;
even those who were bound by long-standing enmity came to dwell in a state of loving-kindness.
Even the Caṇḍālas were compassionate, the wrathful became endowed with patience,
those who had gained wealth were free from desire, and the virtuous were devoid of envy.
Those who were miserly have become givers; those who were wretched have had their intentions satisfied;
those who were addicted to unrighteousness and sensual desire have now accomplished the purpose of righteous desire.
Those who were fond of lying became speakers of truth;
those who delighted in slander became worthy of confidential meals.
Those who were wicked speakers of idle chatter became virtuous and upright;
those who spoke harshly and were cruel became speakers of pleasant words.
Even those who were covetous were considered virtuous people proud of their reputation;
and even those intent on killing were seekers of the welfare of sentient beings.
And those who had followed wrong views became seers of the truth of the Dharma;
through their zeal for the conduct of awakening, they all became seekers of merit.
In this way, all other beings as well— those who were suffering and addicted to evil— became happy and came to desire the true Dharma.
Fragrant, pleasant-to-the-touch, and cool breezes blew;
all the quarters became serene, and the clouds rained down flowers.
Divine drums resounded, the great ocean surged,
the earth trembled in six ways, and auspicious fires blazed forth.
All the trees became laden with fruits and flowers,
and the reservoirs of water were filled with water endowed with the eight qualities.
Treasures consisting of many kinds of minerals and gems shone forth;
at that time, the earth became abundant with fully ripened crops.
The cows yielded much milk, the medicinal herbs were endowed with excellent qualities,
the juices possessed superior virtues, and the fruits were delicious.
Thus, at that time, auspicious things occurred everywhere there, and all calamities likewise came to an end in every place.
All the hosts of wicked obstructors also met their destruction there;
and all sentient beings, enriched with happiness, moved about filled with great joy.
Thus, at that time, through the power of the Lord of Sages, there arose everywhere an enthusiasm for the auspiciousness of the True Dharma, free from all affliction.
Thus the Blessed One, having brought welfare there and radiating light,
proceeded toward the king’s palace by way of circumambulation.
There, in a beautiful palace that had been thoroughly cleansed and purified,
adorned with parasols, banners, and canopies, and furnished with spread-out seats;
Having entered and accepted the water for the feet offered by the king, the Blessed One, together with his assembly, took his seat upon a pure throne, illuminating that place.
Likewise, all those belonging to the Saṅgha were also given by the king; having personally accepted them, they took their respective seats.
Thus, seeing the Blessed One, the Mass of Splendor, seated there together with his community of monks, all the people, headed by the king, were filled with joy.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed ritual with all the components of offerings and oblations,
he also fully gratified them with excellent foods as was appropriate for each.
Then, seeing that the Sugata was satisfied along with his assembly, the lord of men removed the alms bowls from their hands and had them washed.
Then, having offered betel-nut, betel-leaf, great medicinal herbs, and elixirs,
and having made a request for forgiveness, he bowed down before him and the community of monks.
There, King Samudita, sitting on a low seat before that Teacher, the Guru of the World, stood with joy to hear the Dharma.
Likewise, the ministers and all the people were filled with joy;
having bowed to that Śrīghana, they took their seats there to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all taken refuge,
addressed the king and taught him the true Dharma.
Listen, O fortunate King; may there be constant health for you.
And may all sentient beings always be devoted to the True Dharma.
Thus, O Great King, having accomplished this with diligence,
protect all beings by establishing them in the auspicious Dharma.
Thus, having performed virtuous deeds in the world and being composed in the conduct of awakening,
and having paid homage to the Three Jewels, gather the Dharma with great care.
Indeed, cyclic existence is impermanent; the body perishes in an instant, life endures but a moment, and only the Dharma follows one along.

Thinking thus, O Great King, having conquered the afflictions that are difficult to defeat with your powers, and having established sentient beings in the auspicious state, protect them and cultivate the true Dharma.
By means of the Dharma, may you go to a good rebirth; having enjoyed happiness always in a good rebirth, and having maintained the conduct of awakening, may you attain awakening while practicing it.
Having understood this, O lord of kings, being yourself established in dharma and acting for the welfare of all beings, conduct yourself always with composure.
Having thus bestowed auspicious blessings upon the king and his subjects,
the Blessed Buddha, together with the Saṅgha, rose to depart for his own hermitage.
Illuminating all the worlds and bringing auspiciousness everywhere,
he departed from that city step by step toward his own hermitage.
Thereupon, all the people, headed by the king, followed that Teacher together with his Saṅgha amidst great festivities.
Thus the Blessed One, having gone together with his Saṅgha, arrived at his own hermitage along with the king and others, and with people full of great enthusiasm.
There, having taken up residence in the monastery within the Jeta Grove park,
that Teacher, seated together with the Saṅgha, taught the Dharma.
Having heard that teaching of the Dharma, all those people, including the king and others, remained there throughout the night, rejoicing with great festivities.
On that very night, that messenger, whose life was short and who was afflicted by fever,
abandoned his body and went to heaven while recollecting the Three Jewels.
(Rm 299) Having been born there in heaven, that messenger, filled with wonder, reflected: "From where have I passed away? Where have I arisen? How so? (Rm_25.125{24})
Then, with his mind, he perceived: "I have fallen from among human beings and have been reborn here in heaven because of my devotion to the Perfectly Awakened One."
Then that son of the gods, who had previously been sent as a messenger, being inspired with faith and recollecting the virtues of the Perfectly Awakened One, reflected once more in this way:
"Aha! By the grace of the Lord of Sages, I have now been born in heaven;
therefore, I shall once again behold that Lord of Sages."
Thus reflecting, that son of the gods, preceded by his messenger, bathed, anointed his limbs with fragrant unguents, and, being wise, clothed himself in pure garments.
Adorned with divine ornaments such as crowns, earrings, and garlands,
and bearing the requisites for divine worship, he moved about together with the god.
On that very night, that son of the gods, together with the deities,
having illuminated it with his radiance, approached that Jeta Grove.
Having beheld the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, in that monastery in the garden,
she bowed with palms joined and approached him before him.
Then, having worshipped that Lord Śrīghana according to the prescribed rite,
and having bowed down and circumambulated him with palms joined in reverence, she took refuge in him.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that his mind was purified,
began by means of the Noble Truths to teach him the True Dharma.
Having heard that noble Dharma, that son of the gods was awakened;
having understood the excellence of the Dharma, he then became one who has seen the truth.
Having shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity— rising with its twenty peaks—
with the vajra of wisdom, he was intent on accomplishing the True Dharma.
With a purified intention, he attained the fruit of stream-entry;
having bowed at the feet of the Teacher, he spoke thus with palms joined in reverence:
O Blessed One, this has indeed not been done for us by our teachers,
nor by our mother, nor by our father, nor by our kinsmen, friends, or relatives.
Indeed, this was not brought about by esteemed brahmins, nor by ancestors who have passed away,
nor by kings, ascetics, or even by other gods.
"O Blessed One, for our sake you have piled up mountains of bones and heads;
you have crossed the ocean of blood, and now it has been dried up."
The path of evil has been closed, and the path to heaven has been opened wide;
the path to liberation has also been shown, and I have crossed over the ocean of suffering.
Through your grace, I have today attained the pure faculties,
the peaceful and lovely state of the Noble Ones, which is the means for accomplishing the qualities of perfect enlightenment.
Today my birth has become fruitful through seeing you here;
through hearing the true Dharma today, I am now truly a son of the Buddha.
Having spoken thus, that son of the gods, filled with joy,
bowed at the feet of the Teacher, the friend of the world, with his hands joined in reverence.
Having circumambulated him three times with a heart full of joy,
and having obtained his permission, he departed for heaven together with the gods.
Having gone there to heaven, he dwelt in a most beautiful celestial abode;
having performed worship to the Three Jewels, he lived happily together with the gods.
Having seen that radiance there, Prasenajit of Kośala was struck with wonder; rising in the morning, he went to the monastery.
There, having seen that Śrīghana, the king was filled with joy;
having bowed and circumambulated him, he stood nearby with palms joined in reverence.
Then that king, rising up and arranging his upper garment over one shoulder,
knelt upon the ground and made this request to the Lord of Sages:
"O Blessed One, who has come to you here in the night?
It would be fitting for you to instruct me regarding that person so as to enlighten me."
When the king had thus made his request, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
looked upon King Mahīpāla and commanded him as follows.
"O Indra among kings, he who arrived here tonight is certainly not another;
rather, it is your own messenger who has come here in the form of a god."
When the Lord of Sages had thus instructed him, the king, filled with wonder,
bowed again to the Blessed One and inquired about that deed.
"Sir, what meritorious deed was performed by him at some time through that messenger,
by which he was born in heaven and even became one who has seen the truth?"
Therefore, O Blessed One, Teacher, please relate all that has been well-done by him,
in order to awaken his mind free from worldly desire.
When the king had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World,
looked upon that great king of Kośala and instructed him as follows.
Listen, O fortunate king, to what was done by that deity;
I shall relate it here for the sake of awakening your mind.
"The messenger sent by you while I was staying in Rājagṛha—
having heard his request, I have indeed come here accordingly."
That noble messenger of yours has come here together with me;
having heard the teaching of the true Dharma, he is endowed with faith and devotion.
Having made offerings to the Three Jewels, he practiced within my teaching;
for that auspicious one, though short-lived, was made to dwell here in this monastery.
When he was joined with the law of time, he abandoned his body and went to heaven.
For that messenger of yours, illuminating this place tonight,
has come here together with the worlds of the gods to grant me his audience.
Having performed worship for me and having also circumambulated me,
he bowed with reverence and, taking refuge in the true Dharma, listened to it with faith.
Having drunk the nectar of my true Dharma, having seen the truth and rejoiced,
he bowed to me and once again dwelt in the heavenly realm together with the gods.
There, remaining in his own delightful abode and sporting with the gods, he dwelt happily, practicing devotion to the Three Jewels.
Through the ripening of this merit, that skillful messenger of yours will enjoy happiness in heaven for a long time and, in due course, attain awakening.
Having understood this, O lord of kings, if you desire great happiness here in this saṃsāra,
you must always practice [virtue] with reverence, O auspicious one.
But prosperity arises quickly from the exertion of devotion to the Three Jewels;
therefore, relying upon those Three Jewels, worship them constantly with a concentrated mind.
Whatever action is performed toward the Triple Gem can never be exhausted;
it shall yield the state of enlightenment and thus bestow a most magnificent merit.
Those who here revere the Three Jewels do not go to an evil destiny;
they always proceed to a good destiny and shall fully attain awakening.
O King, these three are declared to be the foremost designations;
whatever action is performed therein, its maturation is said to be great.
For example, what are the three supreme designations that are traditionally taught?
Those which are applied to the Three Jewels are known as the supreme designations.
Just as, among all sentient beings dwelling within the three realms,
the Buddha alone is the great one, the foremost, the eldest, the most excellent, and the supreme among the best.
Those who, being serene, worship with faith and devotion toward the Buddha—they are all foremost in their clarity; they are the eldest, the best, and the most excellent.
For those who have supreme faith in that [Buddha], the ripening of the fruit is likewise supreme and most excellent;
so it is with all phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned.
And among all of them, the Buddha-dharma is said to be supreme.
Those who have faith in that Dharma are indeed supremely devoted;
for those who are supremely devoted to it, the maturation is also said to be supreme.
And among all assemblies and groups, the Buddha’s assembly is said to be supreme;
those who have faith in that assembly possess the highest degree of serene confidence.
For those who have supreme faith in them, the maturation is also said to be supreme;
for these three designations are declared by the Lords of Sages to be supreme.
Therefore, O King, with a mind fully purified by faith in the Triple Gem,
rely upon them with offerings and always honor them with great respect.
This merit is incalculable, immeasurable, and exceedingly great;
it bestows the attainment of the qualities of supreme happiness upon all sentient beings.
Thinking thus, O King, awaken all sentient beings to their great merit; through your zeal for honoring the Three Jewels, cause them to practice what is auspicious.
In this way, may there always be prosperity for you in every respect and at all times;
having gradually attained awakening, may you reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, the king, being delighted and gratified, joyfully agreed,
saying "So be it," and rejoiced.
Then that king, having risen and bowed to the Lord of the World,
departed for his own city with his people, filled with great bliss and intense enthusiasm.
There, that king, the lord of men, having ascended to the roof of his palace, summoned all his ministers and citizens and commanded them thus: Rm_25.185{94} //
"O ministers and all citizens, listen to my words!
O noble ones, if you have a desire, then worship the Three Jewels with devotion."
As long as this Teacher of the World remains here belonging to the Saṅgha,
so long do you honor this Lord of Sages with all kinds of festivals.
Always going to the monastery and relying upon it with faith,
drink that nectar of the True Dharma and joyfully practice virtuous conduct.
Having honored all the Buddhist monks with every requisite, invite them with faith and always revere them with respect.
Having heard these words of mine, go for refuge to the Triple Gem and,
with the aspiration for perfect enlightenment, practice the conduct of awakening.
In this way, may you always have auspiciousness everywhere and certainly;
having attained awakening in due course, may you reach the state of the Sugatas.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, all those ministers and people, including Vīra and the others, replied, "So be it."
Then all those people, exerting themselves to practice the True Dharma and honoring the Three Jewels, moved about together in great joy.
From that time forth, by the power of the Three Jewels, there was always auspiciousness and freedom from calamity everywhere and at all times.
Thus was it instructed to me by my teacher, and so it is told to you by me;
you too, O King, have always thus gone for refuge to the Triple Gem.
Relying fully upon the True Dharma, always conduct yourself in what is virtuous; and having diligently awakened the people of the world, O Great King,
you must always maintain them by establishing them in refuge in the Three Jewels.
In this way, may auspiciousness be ever certain for you everywhere;
and having attained awakening in due course, may you reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, King Aśoka agreed,
saying "So be it," and rejoiced together with his retinue.
Those who joyfully hear this *Dūtāvadāna*, and those who even listen to it attentively—
all of them go thus to the third heaven, and in the end they also proceed to the world of the Perfectly Awakened One.
Thus ends the *Dūtāvadāna* within the *Śrīratnāvadānatattva*.
XXVI. The *Tairthikāvadāna*.
Then King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence and full of joy,
bowed down to the Arhat Upagupta and spoke thus:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear yet another well-spoken word;
it would be fitting for you to instruct me just as you have been instructed by your teacher."
Having heard this request made by the king, Upagupta, that son of the Sugata,
addressed the lord of men and spoke as follows.
"Excellent! Listen, O Great King, to what was spoken by my teacher; I shall relate it here accordingly, and having heard it, grant your approval."
Namely: the Blessed One, the Teacher, Śrīghana, the Arhat, the Lord of Sages, the Omniscient One, the Sugata, the Protector, the King of Dharma, and the Guide.
In former times, he dwelt right there in the Jetavana monastery together with the monks, the disciples, and all the members of the Saṅgha.
Then, all the world-dwellers who had assembled— to hear the teaching of the Dharma—
[included] gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kinnaras, and rākṣasas.
Also by the Siddhas and Vidyādharas, by the lords of the Nāgas and the Garuḍas,
by the world-protectors together with their armies, and by the Brāhmaṇas and great Ṛṣis.
By yogins and ascetics, by those free from knots and by forest-dwellers, by kings and kṣatriyas, and likewise by princes;
And by Vaiśyas, eminent ministers, householders,
great men, merchants, caravan leaders, artisans, and even the citizens.
There were also people from the villages and the countryside, as well as other pilgrims,
all eager to behold the Three Jewels and desiring the virtues of the True Dharma.
Constantly honored, esteemed, worshipped, and saluted,
he always rained down the nectar of the Dharma for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
At that time, in that city, King Prasenajit, the sovereign of men,
upheld the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One and joyfully venerated the Triple Gem.
Seeing that, all the non-Buddhists, their minds struck by envy and anger,
conspired together, rejected the Buddha's Dharma, and spoke thus:
Sirs, since this Buddha is omniscient, possessed of supernatural powers, and accomplished,
he shall establish all these worlds in his own Dharma.
At that time, not even one here would wish to hear our words;
indeed, all of us disciples would likewise serve the Sugata, the Jina.
Then, being censured on all sides by the people, how shall we conduct ourselves here? Let us go elsewhere.
When all had spoken thus, the twice-born devotee of the heretics, seeing them all as heretics, spoke again in this manner: Rm_26.18{18} //
"Sirs, do not despair; it is entirely appropriate for me to act. I shall employ such means that the Jina may travel elsewhere. (Rm 304) Rm_26.19{19} //
Having thus enlightened all those heretics, that wicked-minded man went into the presence of the king and spoke respectfully as follows:
Listen, O highly fortunate king, to that which is for your benefit;
having resolved accordingly, you should always act with devotion.
Since this shaven-headed monk has brought ruin to the family dharma,
fallen away from the nature of his birth, and reviled the course of worldly existence;
A master of illusion, of contemptible conduct, immoral, and a deceiver of the world,
he has come here himself ruined to ruin others as well.
Therefore, O King, you must never see him;
neither his name should be taken up, nor should his speech even be heard.
One should not offer him honor, nor should anything at all be given;
one should not go to his hermitage, nor should one remain in his presence.
Those who even cast a glance upon that evil-minded monk shall all go to hell; they shall never attain a good rebirth.
And all those who hear that speech shall go to their abode;
tormented by intense suffering, they shall dwell there in remorse.
And all those who offer honor have gone to destruction;
having become poor and fallen into miserable states, they wander about with their hopes shattered.
And those who perform acts of giving there with a mind stained by blood,
they too shall go to hell and experience such sufferings.
Then all those men, marked by their misdeeds and tormented by diseases such as leprosy, went to that hermitage and soon thereafter went to hell.
And those who dwell together with them are all attached to evil;
scorched by the fires of intense suffering, they shall always wander in hell.
And in the houses of those who take my name, may Lakṣmī never ever take refuge; instead, let only Nairṛti (the spirit of misfortune) dwell there.
Those who worship the Buddha here are all likewise unrighteous;
they never attain a good rebirth, for they go only to a distant state.
Thinking thus, O Great King, if you always desire what is auspicious,
you must show him honor and pay him respect, and never anyone else at all.
Whatever Dharma of the Sugata has been falsely conceptualized—
that Dharma of that ill-disciplined one should not be heard by anyone at all.
For he whose dharma is not reckoned anywhere in the Vedas or the Shastras—how can that Buddha be the essence of dharma? Therefore, there is no auspiciousness in him.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, he was awakened;
agitated by the slackening of his zeal for honoring the Three Jewels, he became disturbed.
Then, having heard those words of the lay follower of the heretics, the king, being thus inspired with faith, took a liking for the heretical doctrine.
(Rm 305) There, a certain householder, a wealthy merchant and wise lay follower of the Fully Awakened One, saw that lay follower of the heretics and spoke to him in order to enlighten him. (Rm 26.39)
"O evil-minded one, why do you thus revile even the Buddha, the King of Dharma?
Do not speak thus; otherwise, you yourself shall go to hell for this."
He who was born in the world, having completely conquered all afflictions and defeated all the hosts of Māra, attained the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
How can you, O Buddha, who are praised, honored, worshipped, esteemed, and respected by all the worlds beginning with Brahmā, be reviled by you alone?
How could the Lord, the King of Dharma, the Sovereign of Sages— who has protected the worlds of the three realms like a son— not be worthy of worship?
The Buddha alone is the Lord of the World, compassionate, a mine of excellent qualities,
the benefactor who brings about the welfare of all beings, the teacher of non-duality, and the Guide.
The Omniscient One, the Sugata of auspicious form, who bears the welfare and purpose of all;
the Lord of all vidyās, the Teacher, the one who points out the path to perfect enlightenment.

He who has conquered the afflictions, the knower of the self, the one possessing the six superknowledges, the teacher of the world, the perfectly awakened one, the worthy one, the Victor, the protector, the King of Dharma, and the Lord of Sages.
Therefore, that Blessed One alone is the foremost, the most excellent, the great, and the eldest throughout all the three realms; there is no other whatsoever superior to him.
Therefore, having always performed the refuge-taking with faith, one should listen with reverence to the Dharma of this Lord of Sages.
Those who go for refuge to the Buddha do not go to an evil rebirth;
having always enjoyed happiness in a good rebirth, they go to the abode of the Victors.
And those who hear that Dharma do not go to an evil rebirth;
having always enjoyed happiness in heaven, they shall at the end attain perfect nirvāṇa.
And those who devote themselves to the Saṅghas do not go to an evil rebirth;
always delighting in the Dharma, they enjoy happiness and go to Sukhāvatī.
Thus, those who have always gone for refuge to the Three Jewels,
who constantly honor them with faith, and whose minds are set on awakening— // Rm_26.52{52} //
All of them, being the repositories of the six virtues and seekers of the welfare of all sentient beings,
shall fulfill the practices of awakening in due order and attain the state of perfect buddhahood.
Therefore, this Blessed One alone is the Lord of the World,
the Teacher of the World, the King of Dharma, the Sustainer of the World, the Protector of the World, and the Guide.
Therefore, having gone for refuge with faith in this true teacher, the Excellent Guru,
and having heard the True Dharma at all times, one ought to perform acts of veneration.
And those who reject the teaching of this Lord of Sages never go to a good rebirth; they always go only to a miserable state.
Thinking thus, one should never, under any circumstances, engage in reviling the Buddha;
those who seek what is auspicious should instead practice devotion to the Three Jewels.
All those here who revere the Three Jewels partake in enlightenment;
they become Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, and sons of the Sugatas.
Therefore, even those great beings who are lay followers of the Three Jewels ought always to show reverence toward them with faith.
Having heard what was said by him, that lay follower of the heretics, seeing him to be a lay follower of the Buddha, spoke again as follows:
"Why have you spoken thus? Is the Buddha not an ascetic, a mendicant, Pūraṇa a knower of Brahman, an ascetic, self-restrained, and wise?"
What could the Buddha possibly say in the presence of that Pūraṇa?
For he merely deceives children and yokes them to false dharma.
Pūraṇa alone was the greatest and foremost among all those ascetics and celibate students possessed of supernatural powers; however, Mātaṅga was even superior to him.
Having heard what was said by him, that lay follower of the Buddha then saw the female lay follower of the heretics and spoke to her once again.
Do you know the qualities of that Perfectly Awakened One,
by whose very compassion he has looked upon and protected the world as if it were his own son?
By one who has no compassion for the world, how can the universe be protected? For he who seeks only gain and honor is indeed a hypocrite.
One who possesses ascetic power, knows yoga, is wise, and has attained both supernatural powers and perfection—
if he lacks compassion for sentient beings, how can he be a teacher or a guru of the world?
He who, having seen all sentient beings, awakens them through compassion and unites them with the true Dharma— he alone is the teacher of the worlds.

Therefore, in this world, the Teacher of the world—who bears the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings—is none other than the Buddha himself: the Lord of the world, the Protector of the world, and the Guru of the world.
There is no one equal to the Buddha, who brings benefit to all sentient beings;
therefore, that Lord of Sages is worthy of veneration by Brahmā and the other gods.
Since this Śrīghana is the protector, the possessor of the six superknowledges, the leader, the Lord of Sages, the Arhat, and a portion of Subhadra— who indeed could be superior to him?
Therefore, this Sugata, the Buddha, the King of Dharma, the Tathāgata,
should be honored with devotion and served by all who desire what is auspicious.
Having heard what was said by him, that lay follower of the heterodox sect,
his face scorched by the fire of rage, spoke thus to that Buddhist:
Thus it is said: "Who here is superior to Pūraṇa?
He who is wise, possessed of great supernormal knowledge, and the teacher of the three worlds—he alone [is supreme]."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, that lay follower of the Fully Awakened One also,
with palms joined in reverence, prostrated himself upon the ground and spoke to him in this way:
Who else besides the Buddha is superior even within the worlds of the three realms? What is the use of much talk? The Buddha alone is the Lord of the World.
When he had said "So be it," that hostile follower of the heretics,
his limbs scorched by the fire of anger, then spoke thus to the Buddha:
If the Buddha were superior to the ascetic Pūraṇa, the Arhat,
then my entire possession would be at your disposal, and I myself would become your slave.
If indeed Pūraṇa were superior to the Buddha— being an Arhat of great intelligence—
then all your possessions would surely belong to me, and you yourself would truly become my slave.
When he had spoken thus, that lay follower of the Fully Awakened One also agreed,
saying "So be it," and having deposited the bond, he took possession [of the goods].
King Prasenajit, perceiving this rumor concerning those two,
summoned his ministers and spoke thus in the city: (Rm 307) Rm_26.81{81} //
"Go, all you ministers; having determined the dispute between the Buddha and the heretic, let an investigation be conducted here."
Having heard what was thus commanded by the king, those ministers and people immediately summoned all the citizens and gave them this instruction.
"O sirs, having heard this command from the king, remain composed and quickly cause the bells to be sounded everywhere throughout the entire realm."
Having heard what was thus spoken by those ministers, they, together with their people,
made a proclamation by ringing bells, announcing it everywhere in this manner:
"Let all the citizens listen: on the seventh day from today, a deliberation shall take place here regarding the debate between the Buddhists and the non-Buddhist heretics."
Whoever here desires to see, they have all assembled together to behold the power of both the Buddha and the heretic.
Thus, having caused a proclamation by bell to be made throughout their entire conquered realm and territory, they came before their ministers.
Then all those people, together with their families, approached the presence of the king; having bowed down, they reported this entire occurrence before him.
Then, when the seventh day arrived, all the people gathered together and assembled upon a vast and delightful stretch of ground to witness that event.
Likewise, many gods, eager to behold him,
took their place in the sky and stood there, filled with joy.
Thus, in all the worlds, among kings, ministers, and commoners,
in assemblies numbering many hundreds of thousands from every quarter—
There, the non-Buddhist lay follower, upon that mandala smeared with cow dung,
performed worship with offerings such as perfumes and flowers.
Then, having bowed with palms joined and resting upon his knees on the ground, he adjusted his upper robe and made this request with great reverence: Rm_26.94{94} //
By that truth, the six teachers, Pūraṇa and the others, were Blessed Ones,
possessed of great super-knowledges, Arhats, and practitioners of the holy life.
By this truth, may all these offerings for the worship of these lords of ascetics proceed directly toward them.
Having thus made this earnest prayer, the lay follower of the non-Buddhist sect joyfully took those five offerings and cast them into the sky.
As soon as they were hurled by him, all those [missiles] fell upon the surface of the earth and suddenly vanished from sight.
Seeing that, all those worlds, including the gods and the lords of the earth,
laughed with loud cries and considered him to be merely a heretic.
Having seen that and having heard the cry of "Shame!", that heretic fell down;
then, after a long time, he rose up with his face and heart pierced by shame.
Terrified, looking downward, lusterless and trembling,
with his shoulders slumped and his arrow placed in his hand, he stood there unconscious.
Having seen that, the devotee of the Buddha, his heart filled with joy,
prepared a mandala there on ground smeared with cow dung.
Having worshipped according to the ritual with the fivefold offerings,
he donned his upper robe and knelt upon the ground with both knees.
Standing before the Fully Awakened One, the Lord of Sages, with palms joined in reverence, he remembered him, bowed down, and thus earnestly entreated that Truth: Rm_26.104{4} //
Since this Blessed One, the Buddha, is the guide of all the world,
by that truth may all these flowers become water.
And let this fragrant incense reach through the air the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Glorious Cloud, the Protector.
Having thus made this earnest prayer, that devotee of the Buddha joyfully took all those offerings and cast them into the sky.
All those [flowers] thrown by him flew up into the sky;
all those flowers then proceeded in succession, having become parasols.
The incense was like a cloud, and the water acted like lapis lazuli;
seeing this, the entire multitude experienced great wonder.
Gradually, they all traveled through the air and arrived instantly at the Jetavana monastery, appearing before it face to face.
Having seen that wonderful miracle, the multitude of people also followed along with joy, watching and uttering cries of "Victory!"
There, all the flowers became parasols and rested above the Fully Awakened One, the Teacher of the World and Preceptor of the World.
Having performed a circumambulation, that incense remained before him;
and that lotus also fell from the sky, moving along with the wind.
Having observed that, all those citizens, including the twice-born and others,
being gratified by the lord of sages, attended upon him in the assembly hall.
Having circumambulated him all together with joy and palms joined in reverence, they bowed to the Blessed One, the Sage, and all of them took their places nearby.
And that lay follower of the Buddha, having joyfully bowed to Śrīghana,
stood with palms joined in reverence, ready to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
That lay follower of the non-Buddhist sects, seeing that too, was filled with wonder; considering it to be the great majesty of the Buddha, he approached to behold it.
Then the Blessed One, having seen that they had all assembled before him, taught the Noble Truths and further instructed them in this way: Rm_26.118{18} //
Listen, all you virtuous ones, to what is called the noble Dharma;
that which is proclaimed as the Three Jewels is the most exalted in the three worlds.
Just as for all people dwelling in the three realms of the entire world,
I shall proclaim the true Dharma for the sake of the welfare of everyone.
He is the Perfectly Awakened One, the Teacher of the world, the benefactor of all sentient beings;
the Lord of the world, the Protector of the world—this is the supreme Jewel of the Buddha.
In this regard, for those who have performed good deeds such as giving with faith,
and who are supremely devoted, there is the highest fruit through the ripening of those actions.
Immeasurable and incalculable, it bestows the state of perfect enlightenment;
realizing this, always worship the Perfectly Awakened One here with joy.
And however many conditioned or unconditioned phenomena there may be here in this saṃsāra, among them, dispassion is the great, foremost, and supreme phenomenon.
For those who, being serene, partake here in this jewel of the Dharma,
for them— those most excellently devoted— the fruit of the maturation is supreme.
Having heard this Dharma of the Sugata, which bestows immeasurable and incalculable knowledge of perfect enlightenment, they partake in the vow of restraint.
Whatever assemblies, groups, and communities are known here in the three worlds,
the Buddha-saṅgha is renowned as the foremost among them, the great one, the best in the world.
Those who here partake of this Jewel of the Saṅgha with faith and joy—
for those who possess such supreme confidence, the fruit of maturation is most excellent.
Immeasurable and incalculable, it sets one upon the path to perfect enlightenment;
therefore, devote yourselves with faith and reverence to this Saugata Saṅgha.
This is known as the Triple Gem, which brings auspiciousness to all sentient beings,
grants desired aims, is perfected, and bestows the wisdom of complete enlightenment.
Therefore, those who desire the state of perfect enlightenment should always worship these three jewels with devotion, respect, and diligent care.
Those who, being serene, always and constantly worship the Three Jewels,
do not fall under the power of Māra and become attainers of awakening.
Thinking thus, having seen that Triple Gem, and having expressed your sympathetic joy,
you should pay homage from afar with palms joined in reverence.
Having heard these instructions given by the Lord of Sages, all those people, including the brahmins,
became joyful and went for refuge to the Three Jewels.
There, certain fortunate people went for refuge to the Perfectly Awakened One;
having undertaken the precepts, they practiced the vow of the Sugata.
Some wise ones of noble disposition went for refuge to the Perfectly Awakened One;
having undertaken the vow of renunciation, they practiced the life of celibacy.
Then, having completely conquered the afflictions and become free from desire for the enjoyments of cyclic existence,
they directly attained the state of Arhat and became practitioners of celibacy.
Having observed all this, even that lay follower of the non-Buddhists was struck with wonder; with a deeply serene mind, he went for refuge to the Triple Gem.
Then that heretic, bowing with palms joined before the lotus-feet of that lord of sages, joyfully made this aspiration:
From this day forward, always relying upon the true Dharma of this Lord of Munis, the Teacher of the World, may I become a worshiper of the Three Jewels.
Through the ripening of this merit, in a world that is blind and without a guide,
may I attain the wisdom of perfect enlightenment and become a Sugata, a Jina.
I shall ferry across those who have not crossed; I shall liberate those who are unliberated;
indeed, I shall comfort all who are uncomforted and deeply afflicted by suffering.
I shall bring to nirvāṇa those beings who have not yet attained it from the abode of existence;
I shall always bring about what is auspicious even throughout the worlds of the three realms.
Having perceived that he had thus made a vow for enlightenment with his own mind,
the Blessed One released a smile accompanied by rays of light.
Then those rays, five-colored and extending everywhere in all directions throughout the worlds, having brought about auspiciousness and happiness, streamed forth.
Those rays that had gone downward into all the hells,
having spread forth and illuminated them in this way, brought about auspicious happiness.
Touched by those rays of light, all those inhabitants of hell became free from suffering; having attained happiness, they were filled with wonder.
Then all those sentient beings dwelling in hell, having gathered together in each of the individual hells, spoke thus: Rm_26.148{35} //
"Aha! What a marvel! Why is such great happiness arising this very day?
Have we perhaps fallen from here and been reborn elsewhere?"
Thus, in order to awaken all those who were speaking in such a manner,
the Blessed One dispatched an emanated Buddha toward the hell realms.
Seeing him, all the denizens of hell were struck with wonder and filled with serene faith;
gathering together once more, they spoke thus among themselves:
"Aha! Having passed away from here, we have certainly not gone elsewhere;
rather, it is through the power of this being of unprecedented form that our appearance has become auspicious."
"Surely this Lord of the World, the Buddha, having beheld us afflicted by suffering, has come here out of compassion to deliver us."
Therefore, we all here, having gone for refuge at all times with reverence, faith, and respect, ought now to honor him.
Having thus conversed, they were all thoroughly pacified;
having gone for refuge to him alone and prostrated themselves, they departed.
Then all those hell-beings, liberated from that evil, became completely purified; with their natures made auspicious, they suddenly went to a happy rebirth.
Thus, having rescued all those denizens of hell, those radiances returned there and proceeded before the Perfectly Awakened One.
And thus those rays, having gone upwards, illuminated all the abodes of the gods and all the worlds on every side, and then streamed forth.
Having illuminated everything all around, as far as the very peak of existence (*bhavāgra*),
they extended [their light], and from it these verses issued forth, exhorting them:
Indeed, saṃsāra is impermanent, suffering, empty, and selfless;
merit alone is the essence of the world, so gather that merit with diligence.
Go forth! Strive in the teaching of the Buddha;
shake off the armies of death and practice the vow of the Sugata.
For whoever practices with concentration in this Dharma of the Sugata,
having abandoned birth in cyclic existence, will bring an end to suffering.
Always remembering that Triple Gem and having gone for refuge,
worship it constantly with reverence and faith for the sake of attaining awakening.
Having thus heard that sound, all the gods were awakened;
taking refuge in the Three Jewels, they departed with constant devotion.
(Rm 311) Having thus exhorted the gods from all sides, those rays returned once more and approached the presence of the Buddhas.
There, all those rays, having become one and gathered together,
circumambulated the Sage three times to the right and vanished into his uṣṇīṣa.
Seeing that, all those people in the assembly were filled with wonder;
reflecting on what the Teacher might now teach as the Dharma, they sat down.
Then the venerable Mahānanda, perceiving what was on the minds of the people,
rose with palms joined in reverence, bowed, and questioned that Lord of Sages.
Free from agitation, having abandoned both dejection and pride, the Buddhas are the supreme cause for the world;
these Conquerors, who have vanquished their enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a lotus stalk without a specific reason.

O steadfast one, O Lord of Jinas, having yourself realized this at that time through your wisdom, dispel with your firm, supreme, and auspicious words— the speech of the bull among sages— the doubt that has arisen in the hearts of those listeners who long for it, O Śramaṇa.
The Fully Awakened Lords, whose fortitude is like that of the King of Mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without cause;
and the multitudes of people long to hear the reason for which those Steadfast Ones manifest a smile.
Therefore, you ought to instruct us in whatever task is desired for the purpose of awakening the minds of all sentient beings.
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
looked toward the venerable Ānanda and commanded him as follows.
It is even so, Mahānanda: none of the Jinas, the perfectly awakened Sugatas, ever display a smile without cause or condition.
Listen, Ānanda, to that purpose for which I now manifest a smile;
I shall explain it fully for the sake of awakening all sentient beings.
Do you see how this guild-president, a lay follower of the non-Buddhist sects, having joyfully gone for refuge to me here, indeed makes a formal vow?
Through the ripening of this merit, for the duration of three kalpas, though not yet a knower of the self,
he shall gradually fulfill all the practices of awakening and become a wise one.
Then, having conquered all the hosts of afflictions as well as all the hosts of Māra,
he will attain enlightenment and become the Tathāgata named Acala.
Having heard this and other such instructions from the Lord of Munis, all those monks, their faces beaming with joy, rejoiced with wonder.
Having heard what was thus explained by that Lord of Sages, that heretic rejoiced with wonder and offered his approval.
Thereafter, always and constantly, having honored the worship of the Three Jewels with faith and joy, he practiced the vow of the Sugata.
Thus it was told to me by my teacher, and having heard it, I have spoken accordingly;
you too, O Great King, should likewise become a devotee of the Three Jewels.
O King, having likewise diligently awakened the subjects,
you ought to inspire them toward the enthusiastic practice of honoring the Three Jewels.
In that way, may there always and eternally be auspiciousness for you everywhere;
having attained awakening in due course, may you reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, King Aśoka, that protector of the earth,
acknowledged it as true and rejoiced.

Those men who hear this avadāna of the Tīrthika as told by the best of sages, and those who cause it to be heard with joyful minds, endowed with faith and devotion—they are all Bodhisattvas, bearing the full weight of virtues; practicing the *Bhadracaryā*, they shall enjoy excellent and auspicious happiness and proceed with great joy to the abode of the supreme Jinas.
Thus ends the *Tairthikāvadāna* within the *Śrīratnāvadānatattva*.
XXVII. The *Mālikāvadāna*.
Then King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence and filled with joy, bowed down to the Arhat Upagupta and made this request once more: Rm_27.1{1} //
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken word;
as it has been taught by my teacher, so you ought to teach it."
When the lord of men had thus made his request, that lord of ascetics,
Upagupta, looked upon the king and spoke as follows.
Listen well, O Great King; just as it was spoken by my teacher, so shall I proclaim it to you for the increase of your merit.
Namely: the Blessed One, the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Teacher of the World, the Omniscient One, the Sugata, the Instructor, the King of Dharma, and the Lord of Sages.
At one time, he was staying there in the vicinity of Śrāvastī,
in the great park of Jetavana, in the monastery together with his disciples.
By the monks and novices, by the nuns, by the laymen and laywomen, and also by other hosts of bodhisattvas.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, revealing the conduct of awakening and teaching the true Dharma, he dwelt there, illuminating the world.
All the worlds have gathered together to drink that nectar of the True Dharma,
including Śakra and the other lords of gods, as well as Brahmā and the world-protectors.
The lords of the Daityas, Garuḍas, Nāgas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kiṃnaras,
as well as Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Rākṣasas of great supernatural power.
Sages and brahmins as well, kṣatriyas who were lords of men, vaiśyas, princes, ministers, counselors, and common folk— Rm_27.11{11} //
Householders, caravan leaders, merchants, and artisans as well; citizens, countryfolk, villagers, and even other pilgrims.
Having all come together there, they saw that sage Śrīghana, circumambulated him, bowed down, and attended upon him.
Having worshipped them in due order and bowed with joy, palms joined in reverence, they all circumambulated them, placed them at their head, and took refuge in them.
Seeing them all seated together, that Blessed One, the Sage,
began by means of the Noble Truths and taught the supreme Dharma.
Having heard that Dharma, they were all fully awakened;
having understood the excellence of the Dharma, they became desirous of enlightenment.
At that time, in that city, King Prasenajit of Kośala was a partisan of the non-Buddhist heretics whenever the Sugata was not present there.
But when the Sugata arrived there together with his community of monks,
the king constantly and always paid homage to that Śrīghana.
And at that time, a certain park-keeper there,
having gathered fresh lotuses from the forest, entered the city to give them to the king.
Seeing him there on the road, a lay follower of a non-Buddhist sect joyfully went suddenly before him and requested that lotus.
"O Mālinī, if you wish to sell this lotus,
you ought to give it to me after taking the appropriate price."
At that very moment, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada,
having arrived there seeking flowers, questioned that gardener.
"O Mālin, if you wish to sell this lotus,
you ought to give it to me after taking double the price."
Having heard what was said by him, that lay follower of the heretics also requested that lotus for twice its price.
Having heard what he had requested, Anāthapiṇḍada likewise asked him for that lotus at double its price.
Having heard that, even that heretic, who was full of intoxication, pride, and arrogance,
desired to purchase it for three times its value.
Seeing that, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was inspired with zeal and asked for that lotus at four times its price.
Thus those two householders,
having taken up a price for that lotus amounting to as many as hundreds of thousands, requested Mālin.
Seeing that, the park-keeper also increased his own joy in mutual rivalry;
yet, without giving anything to either of those two, he thought thus in his mind:
This householder, the eminent Anāthapiṇḍada, is indeed wise;
he is unflappable, profoundly steadfast, firm in being, and discerning.
"For whose sake indeed is this lotus being asked for such a price?
Surely there must be some great cause here; of this there is no doubt."
Therefore, let us inquire about this; I shall give it to you, who seek the goal of true virtue.
Having reflected thus with his own mind, that eager park-keeper, beholding the heretic, questioned him with great respect: Rm_27.34{33} //
"O man, for the sake of what purpose do you have this lotus?
Tell me why you wish to sell it for such a price."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, that heretic was filled with joy;
looking toward the monastery attendant, he spoke in order to awaken him.
I shall perform worship to Him who is the Lord of Śrī, the Sustainer of the world, Nārāyaṇa, Janārdana; therefore, give this lotus to me.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, the park-keeper was awakened to understanding;
and seeing Anāthapiṇḍada, he asked about his purpose.
"O good man, for what purpose do you wish to gather this lotus, which is of such great value? Tell that to me."
Having heard those words, the wise Anāthapiṇḍada, looking at that park-keeper, spoke in order to awaken him: Rm_27.40{39} //
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! Since you desire this lotus of yours at a high price, listen as I explain its value."
(Rm 315) Here, the king who is the son of Śuddhodana, a universal monarch and lord of men,
is intent upon accomplishing perfect awakening for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
In this entire world and throughout all realms, agitated by afflictions and lacking meditative composure,
and bereft of the conduct of awakening, the dharma of barbarians prevails.
Having himself undertaken the practice of awakening, he strove to illuminate it,
renouncing his entire kingdom as well as all his possessions.
Relying on the dharma of dispassion and free from longing for the enjoyments of cyclic existence,
he went to Mount Gayāśīrṣa and performed austerities most difficult to practice.
Then, having arisen with the intent to bring benefit to the world, he remained composed;
seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, he stood firm, absorbed in meditative concentration.
There, having conquered all the hosts of Māra as well as the hosts of afflictions,
and having attained the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, he has now become a Buddha.
Thus, this Buddha is the teacher of the world, the lord of the world, the guru of the world,
the sustainer of the world, the protector of the world, the King of Dharma, and the sovereign of sages.
The Sugata is omniscient, glorious, possessed of the six superknowledges, and the leader;
he is truthful, greatly steadfast, and the bearer of the auspicious meaning of the true Dharma.
He was a partial manifestation of Samantabhadra, gentle in appearance and with senses subdued,
adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics.
The Blessed One Śrīghana dwells in the sublime abodes; he is a mine of virtues, the sovereign lord of the entire triple world, and the pacifier of all that is wicked.
He is the conqueror of all Māras, worthy of honor, and the teacher of the path to perfect enlightenment;
he is the bestower of desired objects, surpassing even the qualities of the wish-fulfilling gem.
Pure in moral conduct, of auspicious behavior, a bearer of the vow of patience, and wise;
striving for the welfare of all sentient beings, free from afflictions, a conqueror of all, and accomplished.
Delighting in meditative concentration and dhyāna, he was a sun for the phenomena of enlightenment;
a treasury of wisdom, a man of great knowledge, and proficient in all branches of learning.
He knows all methods and applications; he carries others across by means of his vows; he is the hero who conquers the three worlds; he fulfills the work of perfect enlightenment.
Established in the meditative absorption of the waves of consciousness, he bears the jewel of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment;
he brings about the welfare of all sentient beings and possesses the nature of all forms.
The great Buddha Śākyamuni, the Lord of Conquerors, the Tathāgata,
acted everywhere for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Illuminating all the worlds and bringing auspiciousness everywhere,
I have come here as well to bring auspiciousness to all sentient beings.
At present, he dwells constantly in the Jetavana monastery together with the Saṅgha, illuminating all as he teaches the True Dharma.
"I truly desire to perform a worship for him right now;
for that purpose, I request this lotus at a high price."
Therefore, take the price and give me this lotus;
showing me favor, I shall give you whatever wealth you desire.
If you give this with faith, I shall be greatly delighted;
through the ripening of this merit, you will attain the mind of awakening (bodhicitta).
May you always go to a happy rebirth and never to an evil destiny;
and by gradually fulfilling the practices of awakening, may you attain perfect enlightenment.
Knowing this, O virtuous one, if you desire perfect awakening, take whatever object you have desired and give it to me. (Rm 316) Rm_27.64{63} //

Having heard this request made by him, the florist was filled with joy and spoke thus to that householder, the protector of the helpless: *iti tenārthitaṃ śrutvā sa mālikaḥ pramoditaḥ / taṃ gṛhastham anāthānāṃ bharttāram evam abravīt //* Rm_27.65{64} //
"Aha! The Buddha, possessed of great supernormal knowledge, is never seen;
nor have I ever heard of such great qualities anywhere."
Therefore, I now desire to see that Lord of the World;
indeed, a longing has arisen in me to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
Therefore, having gone there myself, I shall reverently worship that perfectly enlightened one, the Lord of Sages, with this white lotus.
Therefore, O virtuous one, out of compassion, you ought to take me to that hermitage of the Fully Awakened One, the Teacher of the World, and unite me with the True Dharma.
Having heard what he requested, Anāthapiṇḍada, filled with joy,
looked at that gardener and spoke to him once more as follows:
"Excellent, excellent, O illustrious one! Do exactly as you wish.
Come with me and let us worship that lord of sages."
Having spoken thus to the gardener, that householder, seeking to win his favor, took him and proceeded to the monastery in Jeta’s Grove.
There, in the presence of his companions, that householder Anāthapiṇḍada bowed with palms joined toward the Lord of the World and withdrew to one side.
Then that gardener beheld Śrīghana seated upon the throne in the midst of the assembly, surrounded by the lords of sages and preceded by the community of monks.
Adorned with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor characteristics,
he was like a blazing heap of jewels, embellished by the radiance of the sky.
Having seen him, whose form was that of Samantabhadra, gentle in appearance and with auspicious faculties, he rejoiced, bowed down, and performed three circumambulations.
Having cast that lotus down before him, with palms joined in reverence, he joyfully bowed at the feet of that Sage and took his place there in a secluded spot.
And as soon as that lotus was cast, it suddenly ascended into the sky and,
becoming a parasol, shone resplendently above the head of the Sage.
Having seen that, all those people in the assembly were filled with wonder;
exclaiming, "Oh, the majesty of the Buddha! they became serene.
Seeing that, the florist, his heart filled with great wonder and joy,
suddenly rose and prostrated himself at the feet of the Teacher.
Then, having bowed with palms joined before the lotus-feet of the Teacher of the World,
he made a vow from his heart for the attainment of the state of a Perfectly Awakened One.
By the ripening of this merit, may I become a Sugata, a Jina, in this world that is blind, without a guide, agitated by afflictions, and ruined.
He is the one who enables those unable to cross over by themselves to cross the ocean of existence;
likewise, he is the deliverer who rescues those submerged in the sea of afflictions, seeking their liberation.
May I indeed be one who provides true consolation to those who lack confidence in the Dharma,
and may I be one who reveals the path to enlightenment to those who have not seen it.
Knowing that he had thus made this vow, the Blessed One, the All-Knowing, was filled with joy and then manifested a smile.
There, from the lotus-face of the Lord of Sages, as he smiled, divine rays of five colors issued forth and pervaded even the three worlds.
Those rays that went downward illuminated even all the hells; having performed a virtuous act, they brought about the destruction of suffering.
Touched by those radiance, all those inhabitants of hell were freed from suffering, touched by bliss, and, filled with wonder, spoke thus:
"Aha! What great happiness is now arising for us? Having passed away from here, where else have we been reborn? Rm_27.89{86}
While they were thus overwhelmed by anxiety, the Blessed One dispatched an emanated Buddha toward the hell realm in order to awaken their minds.
Seeing that, all those dwelling in hell were filled with great wonder;
looking at one another, they spoke once more as follows:
"Sirs, we have not departed from here to meet anywhere else;
we remain right here in this hell, for we have not moved to any other place at all."
But this man who has arrived here is one whose sight has never been seen before;
surely it is by his power that auspiciousness now arises.
"Surely this Great Being, seeing us tormented by suffering,
has come here to this hell in order to deliver us entirely out of compassion."
Therefore, having always taken refuge in him and having bowed down with constant faith, let us worship him with great reverence.
