Having spoken thus, all those denizens of hell were awakened;
having gone for refuge to that Buddha and bowed down, they worshipped him with joy.
Through the merits arising from their devotion to him, they all rose up from hell;
they suddenly attained a happy rebirth and became vessels for the Dharma.
In this way, all those rays, having rescued all those beings dwelling in the hells, returned once more to the Teacher of the World.
And that radiance which had gone upward, having illuminated the eight directions as far as the very limit of the peak of existence (bhavāgra), spread forth.
And with verses, they thus exhorted all the gods—who were devoted to the pleasures of their divine bodies—from every side with a great and loud voice: Rm_27.100{97} //
Having realized that all of saṃsāra is impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self,
one should always practice the virtuous Dharma with reverence.
Depart from this world; exert yourselves in the teaching of the Buddha.
Having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, honor them always with devotion.
For whoever shall practice this Dharma of the Sugata with a concentrated mind,
having abandoned birth in cyclic existence, will bring an end to suffering.
Having heard this sound, all the gods were awakened;
having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, they departed with concentrated minds.
In this way, those five rays of light, having established all the worlds and even the gods in refuge in the Three Jewels, returned once more to the Sage.
There, all those rays, having become one and formed into a mass,
circumambulated the Jina and entered again into his uṣṇīṣa.
Seeing that, all those people in the assembly were filled with wonder; reflecting, "By what command has this lord of sages come? they sat down.
Then Ānanda, perceiving their thoughts,
rose up with palms joined in reverence, bowed to the Blessed One, and spoke to him.
O Blessed One, for what reason do you manifest a smile? O Sugatas, none of you ever smile without a cause.
Indeed, all these people now desire to hear the purpose for which you are currently releasing a smile by means of a cause.
O Teacher of the World, having explained the purpose for which you manifest a smile,
please awaken all the worlds.
Having heard what was thus spoken by Ānanda, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages,
surveyed all the worlds and spoke to Ānanda.
It is even so, Mahānanda: never at any time do all the Buddhas manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Behold how this virtuous park-keeper,
being inspired with faith, performs such worship for me out of faith and joy.
Through the ripening of this merit, this wise garland-maker,
having attained the thought of awakening, will gradually practice the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Having fulfilled all the perfections and having utterly conquered all the hosts of Māra, he attained perfect enlightenment; now free from afflictions, the Arhat, the Lord of Sages.
The Lord of the World, endowed with the ten powers, who bears the welfare of all sentient beings,
will become the Buddha, the Tathāgata named Padmottama.
Since this person has been inspired with faith in my accomplishment of the True Dharma,
he maintains the vow for perfect enlightenment and performs worship with devotion.
Thus, all those people who, with constant faith, have gone for refuge to the Three Jewels and honor them, shall become sons of the Sugata.
Then those bodhisattvas, great beings, intent upon the welfare of all sentient beings, will become mines of virtuous qualities.
Then, having fulfilled all the perfections in due order,
and thereafter having attained perfect enlightenment, they too shall become Sugatas.
Thinking thus, those who desire the wisdom of perfect enlightenment in this saṃsāra should worship the Three Jewels and always practice what is virtuous.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Munis, Ānanda and all those monks belonging to the Saṅgha were awakened and rejoiced.
And all those people, having heard what was thus spoken by Śrīghana, took refuge in the Three Jewels and, filled with joy, went forth [into the religious life].
Having heard this prophecy concerning himself spoken thus by the Teacher, the Lord of Munis, those present in the assembly also rejoiced, filled with great delight.
From that time forth, always and constantly rejoicing,
that florist practiced the conduct of awakening after having performed worship of the Three Jewels.
Then Anāthapiṇḍada, filled with joy by that encounter,
bowed with palms joined to the Lord of the World and departed for his own abode.
There, that florist, rejoicing with his wife in their home,
took refuge in the Three Jewels and always practiced what was virtuous.
Then, having observed him following the Dharma of the Sugata, that lay follower of the heretics became enraged; approaching him, he spoke abusively.
"O evil-minded sinner, O inauspicious one, why do you act in this way?
You are utterly ruined; you shall experience suffering in hell."
If, having approached one who is unworthy, of evil conduct, and a speaker of false dharma,
you show devotion and honor him, you will surely incur great sin.
Those men who do not revere the Buddha do not go to a good rebirth;
they have gone only to an evil destiny and always wander in what is unwholesome.
Never at any time does prosperity arise in that house,
nor does Lakṣmī ever dwell there, because righteousness is destroyed.
There is nothing at all lacking in the virtuous conduct of that ascetic who subsists on alms;
why then do you always honor him with such faith, as if he were a true spiritual teacher?
The wretched man who, having himself fallen, causes others to fall here in this world,
deceives by proclaiming what is unrighteous as the true Dharma.
How could he—the Teacher, the wise one, the knower, the King of Dharma, the Lord of Sages—not be honored by the virtuous? Indeed, he who reviles him goes to a miserable rebirth.
Thus have I spoken the truth for your benefit, O seeker of welfare;
if you have a desire for the Dharma, act upon it after hearing my words.
Therefore, having abandoned association with the Buddha and bathed at a sacred ford, remain concentrated and worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśāna constantly according to the prescribed rite.
All those here who honor the Brahmin are practitioners of the holy life;
with purified intentions and auspicious, they proceed to the abode of the gods.
Those who always worship Viṣṇu do not go to an evil state;
they always attain a good rebirth, O lords of men.
Those who worship Mahārudra do not go to hell;
having enjoyed all forms of happiness, they go at the end to the abode of Śiva.
Thinking thus, if you desire lasting happiness in this saṃsāra,
then constantly worship and take refuge in these Lords of the Three Worlds.
Having heard these words of mine, resort to those ascetics who are true gurus;
having listened to their sublime Dharma, always practice in auspicious vows.
In this way, may auspiciousness be ever certain for you here at all times;
in the end, liberated from evil, you shall go to the abode of the thirty-three gods.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, that florist became enraged;
addressing that heretic and reviling him, he spoke as follows:
"Why do you speak thus? Do not say so again!
You yourself would go to hell for disparaging the Lord of Sages."
Listen, for I shall here proclaim even a small portion of the virtues of the Perfectly Awakened One; how could they be described in detail by me, one of meager intelligence?
Nevertheless, because it is brief, I shall speak for your understanding;
having heard it, you should reflect upon it and examine what is true and what is false.
The Blessed One alone is the Fully Awakened One, possessed of excellent qualities; neither Viṣṇu nor Hiraṇyagarbha is so praised.
Having heard of the power of their exceedingly noble conduct, reflect for yourselves as to who is truly virtuous and who is not.
Viṣṇu is one who exerts himself with effort; Rudra is a destroyer who is heedless and carries the burden of the unborn [universe] through his powers;
but the Buddha is one whose intention and conduct are characterized by absolute tranquility.
Whom shall we worship—the one who is perfectly peaceful, yet appears in an unpeaceful form?

He who wields the discus brought about the destruction of kings such as Duryodhana; Hari, wielding the Pināka bow, destroyed the three cities; Guha, wielding a firm spear, struck down Krauñca; and the Buddha, seeking the welfare of the worlds, destroyed the power of Māra.
"Only one who is harmful and deceitful is to be protected; one who is to be killed is also [to be protected]—this is the policy of the best of gods.
But for the Buddha, whose singular intention is the welfare and benefit of supreme liberation and the highest prosperity, there is no such distinction between friend and foe."

The words of Viṣṇu, produced by defects such as passion, and those of Śambhu, which result in intoxicated behavior—compare these with the Tathāgata, who brings about the complete pacification of all defects; consider for yourselves who among them truly deserves veneration! Rm_27.153{69} //
One who is intent on slaughter, having cast aside compassion, and one who is engaged in protecting the world out of mercy;
one who is possessed by passion and one who is liberated from passion—of these two, tell me, which is to be honored here? Reflect upon this and speak.

Who among the wise would pay homage to these— Śakra wielding the thunderbolt, Bala wielding the plow, Kṛṣṇa whose weapon is the discus, Skanda wielding the spear, and Rudra who dwells in the cremation ground and wields the trident— all of whom are marked by suffering and fear, devoid of compassion, childish, armed with various weapons, and constantly intent on the slaughter of living beings?

I go for refuge to that Sage, the protector of the worlds, who bears neither a trident nor a beautiful-faced woman upon his lap; who holds neither a discus, a spear, nor a fierce thunderbolt, nor a plough; who is liberated from afflictions, and whose mind is intent on performing the welfare of others.

Rudra carries a woman out of the power of passion; Viṣṇu is devoid of shame and would commit violence; Skanda is more cruel than cruel and acts with ingratitude; Pārvatī has a fierce mouth, is a slayer of Mahiṣa, is a woman under the control of a man, is a meat-eater, and desires drink; Vināyaka is lustful; the Daśabala (the Buddha) is indeed fallen; and a friend is truly without fault.

That Blessed One is our kinsman in the sky, neither enemy nor stranger; he alone is the Teacher, the steadfast Guru of the three worlds. Having heard the power of his speech, which is the excellence of his noble conduct, we have taken refuge in the Buddha out of longing for his preeminent virtues.
The Sugata is not our father, nor are the heretics our enemies;
wealth was never given by that Tathāgata, nor has anything been taken away by Kaṇāda and the others.
Rather, it is because that Blessed One, the Buddha, is solely devoted to the welfare of the world, and because his word is stainless and removes all stains, that we have become monks.
He who is ever and constantly desirous of the world's welfare, acting as its benefactor; he by whom health was restored to the world afflicted by manifold diseases;
and he who perceives all hidden danger as clearly as if it were in the palm of his hand—O virtuous ones, with minds full of devotion, take refuge in that best of sages.
Whether with partial devotion, by chance, out of conformity with others, or even through doubt,
those who pay homage to that Moon among the Lords of Sages also attain the prosperity of the immortals.

This Buddha, honored by the world, is indeed the ancient Hari according to the sacred scriptures; seeing the world subject to birth, old age, and calamity, he has arisen through the exertion of compassion.
Born as the Lord of the Śākya clan, Gautama, the teacher of men with unfailing intellect and savior—what deluded person nowadays does not know him to be solely beneficial?

When, out of passion and hatred, he committed the abduction of the wives of both asuras and suras, and through his delusion and lack of wisdom, he employed the power of illusion to steal the earth—then Hari was worthy of worship and homage; yet people, abounding in delusion, do not bow to the Buddha who is liberated from ignorance, but instead pay honor to him who remains unliberated.

Having abandoned the great earth—which was languid under the burden of its mountain girdle encircled by the four oceans—as if it were a mere trifle cast aside for Hari, King Bali attained [the realm of] Śakra;
whereas King Aśoka, by giving even a handful of dust to a sage, obtained the entire circle of the earth, surpassing even the full orb of the moon.
I have not placed my faith in the Buddha out of hatred for Ṭakṣaka, Kapila, and others;
rather, one should accept the teachings of whoever possesses words that lead to liberation.
Necessarily, one among these must be the All-Knowing One, whose sole essence is vast and intent upon the welfare of the world;
for he alone should be sought by people with extremely refined minds—what is the use of the rest, who are experts in what is useless?
In whom there is not even a trace of a fault, who possesses the virtues of autumn for the sake of the world's welfare—
be he Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Tiriṇa, or Hari— he is indeed a teacher, a friend who performs auspicious deeds.
He in whom no fault exists and in whom all virtues are found—he is the omniscient Teacher of the world; to him I go for refuge.
I go for refuge to him who, through right vision, protects the world in this auspicious [age], and I constantly worship him with joy.
Having seen him, those of pure intention become thoroughly serene;
I, having gone for refuge, worship that very Sugata, the Protector.
Therefore, I take refuge in and worship that very Lord of the Three Worlds, by whom the world of the three realms was protected like a son.
To whomsoever that which was given with pure faith yields the fruit of accomplishing enlightenment—
to that very Śrīghana I go for refuge and worship with devotion.
Since all sentient beings rejoice upon drinking the nectar of the Dharma,
and since they all possess the excellent quality of cutting through suffering by means of that very [Dharma],
I worship with faith and reverence Him alone who bestows glory.
The Buddha alone is the teacher of the world; the Buddha alone is the guru of the world.
The Buddha alone is the lord of the world; the Buddha alone is the sovereign of sages.
Therefore, with my whole being, I have gone for refuge to the Buddha;
having attained the Dharma through faith, I practice it for the sake of attaining awakening.
Those who go for refuge to the Buddha do not go to an evil rebirth;
freed from evil, they enjoy happiness and go to the abode of the Victors.
Those who hear the word of the Sugata do not go to an evil rebirth;
having enjoyed the universal blessings of Samantabhadra, they go to Sukhāvatī.
Those who worship the Lord of the World do not go to an evil rebirth;
freed from evil, they enjoy only happiness and go to the abode of the gods.
This Triple Gem, which has arisen in the world as a mine of excellent qualities—
having gone for refuge to it, I honor it as a lay devotee.
Through the ripening of this merit, for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings,
may one fulfill the stages of the conduct of awakening and attain the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Then, having become a Sugata who bears the welfare and virtue of all sentient beings, and having established those beings in enlightenment, may I attain final nirvāṇa.
Having understood the true Dharma in this way, if you also desire it,
go for refuge to the Three Jewels and honor them constantly with devotion.
Through the ripening of this merit, you shall always thereafter attain a fortunate rebirth;
and having reached enlightenment, may you obtain the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having heard what was thus related by him, he was awakened;
having rejected the dharma of the non-Buddhists, he became a disciple of the Fully Awakened One.
From that time forth, always and constantly eager to hear the true Dharma,
he took refuge in a monastery and paid homage to that Lord of Sages.
Thus it was instructed by my teacher, and having heard it, I have spoken accordingly;
you too, O Great King, should always honor the Three Jewels in this manner.
And having diligently awakened the subjects as well, O Great King, establish them on the path to enlightenment and protect them with a concentrated mind.
By the ripening of this merit, may you always have auspiciousness;
having gradually fulfilled the practices for awakening, may you attain the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, King Aśoka,
together with his retinue, replied, "So be it," and rejoiced.

Those who joyfully hear this avadāna of Mālika as told by the Best of Jinas, and those who, with delighted minds and faith, cause it to be heard, desiring what is auspicious— they all become Lords of the World, Bodhisattvas who have conquered the three stains and the age of strife, great masters who, having enjoyed happiness, always depart at the end with serene hearts for the abode of the Best of Jinas.
Thus ends the Avadāna of Mālika within the *Ratnāvadānatatva*.
(Rm 323) XXVIII. The Avadāna of the King of Pañcāla.
Then King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence, joyfully [addressed him].
Having bowed to his preceptor, the monk Upagupta, he spoke again as follows:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken teaching;
it behoves you to instruct me just as it was explained by my teacher."
When the king had thus made his request, Upagupta, the knower of the self,
addressed King Aśoka and spoke to him as follows.
"Listen well, O Great King, to that which was spoken by my teacher; I shall declare it to you exactly as it was told. Having heard it, grant your approval."
Namely, that Teacher of the World, the Tathāgata Śākyasiṃha,
the Omniscient One, the Sugata, the Protector, the King of Dharma, and the Lord of Sages.
At one time, he was dwelling there outside Śrāvastī, in a hermitage,
in the Jetavana monastery, together with his community of monks.
Then the Blessed One, honored by the community of monks, sat upon his seat in the midst of the assembly and began to teach the Dharma.
All the worlds have assembled to hear that teaching of the Dharma—
the gods, the daityas, the nāgas, the yakṣas, the gandharvas, and the kinnaras.
The Siddhas and Vidyādharas, as well as the Garuḍas and Rākṣasas,
the seers, the learned Brāhmaṇas, and even the kings and Kṣatriyas [were present].
Vaiśyas, princes, ministers, and great men;
merchants, caravan leaders, householders, and even artisans.
Villagers and country folk, as well as pilgrims and others—
even the heretics— all of them arrived at Jetārāma.
Having seen that Lord of the World in the monastery, they joyfully joined their palms in reverence;
having bowed down, circumambulated him, and worshipped him in due order, they remained there.
Then, all of them, filled with joy, turned from every side and,
with composed minds, drew near to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all assembled,
taught the supreme Dharma, which is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end.
Having drunk that nectar of the true Dharma, all the worlds were awakened;
taking refuge in the Perfectly Awakened One, they proceeded to observe the vows of enlightenment.
At that moment, the ruler of Northern Pañcāla set out there to defeat the ruler of Southern Pañcāla.
Between those two kings, Viruddha and Abhimānin, who had five fortresses each,
there was a constant great war characterized by mutual slaughter.
While the war between those two proud kings was thus constantly raging,
there also occurred a famine there that brought destruction to many people.
Then those two cruel kṣatriyas, who were destroyers of one another and possessed hostile minds, though they were both heroes, did not reach a pacification of their enmity.
Having seen that, King Prasenajit of Kośala, the ruler,
reflected for a long time upon the means to pacify that enmity and thought:
Since these two heroic kings are constantly desirous of battle,
they have no wish at all to hear the Dharma that accomplishes perfect awakening.
All the ministers and counselors, as well as all the people and warriors,
did not come here at all even for the sake of seeing the Perfectly Awakened One.
Thus, for those who are always and constantly delighted in acts of violence,
there is no scope whatsoever even for hearing the true Dharma.
Without the Dharma, what essence is there in this human birth within saṃsāra?
Having surely slain one another, they will go to hell.
Fie on that human birth of those for whom it is merely a means to evil,
who— blinded by the intoxication of afflictions, pride, and arrogance— do not behold the Lord of Sages.
And those who here never hear the Dharma of the Sugata—
how could they ever attain the sphere of the *Bhadracaryā*?
Always remaining in the conduct of Māra and conceited because of their afflictions,
they would reject the conduct of awakening and act according to their own whims.
Then, having themselves fallen away, and causing others to fall as well,
wandering about according to their own whims, they would accumulate many sins.
Then, tormented by afflictions and thwarted in their own and others' welfare,
scorched by the fire of intense suffering, they will certainly fall into hell.
Wandering through the hells, they will always be overwhelmed by suffering;
tormented by the fire of remorse, they shall remain so until the end of existence.
Therefore, for the sake of the welfare and benefit of all these worlds,
I ought now to swiftly employ every possible means.
As long as these two heroic kings remain in conflict and do not reach peace,
so long shall there never be any auspiciousness anywhere on this earth.
Therefore, having first diligently awakened these two kings,
I shall cause them to become bound by friendship and affection, free from any state of enmity.
For these two Pāñcāla heroes, Kṣatriyas proud in their honor— once one has informed them of the slaughter of their friend, who could bear to do it?
Only the Buddha, the Teacher of the world and King of Dharma, by awakening them,
would be able to extinguish the fire of their long-standing enmity.
Therefore, having gone there suddenly, I shall entreat the Lord of Sages;
surely, through the power of the Buddha, those two kings will attain friendship.
Having thus resolved, King Prasenajit rose up,
went at once to the monastery, and bowed down before that Lord of Sages.
There, having gone before him and approached with palms joined in reverence,
he reported all that had occurred and spoke thus:
O Blessed One, O Protector, O Omniscient One, may you also take note of how those two kings of Pañcāla have now become your adversaries.
Since all the worlds are opposed when these two are at variance,
therefore war always proceeds here day and night.
When will the sphere of the True Dharma ever belong to all those worlds?
For how could they ever accomplish what is auspicious when they are constantly addicted to battle?
Therefore, may the Blessed One, the Teacher, instruct those two lords of men here,
awakening them by pointing out the path to perfect enlightenment, so that they may practice it for their own welfare.
When the king had thus made his request, that Blessed One, the Sage,
remained silent and consented to dwell there for the sake of that lord of men.
Then that king, the lord of men, perceiving him to be one who was steeped in the sacred scriptures,
bowed with palms joined to that sage and, filled with joy, departed for his own abode.
Then that Blessed One, taking his bowl and covered with his robe,
set forth together with the community of monks, illuminating [the world] and bringing about auspiciousness.
Thus illuminating all the paths, that Lord of Sages,
having brought about welfare in this manner step by step, approached Vārāṇasī.
Having arrived there, the Blessed One, illuminating everything in succession with his radiance,
performed a graceful gait and entered the Deer Park.
There, at dawn, the Blessed One, together with his Saṅgha, sat upon his seat in the midst of the assembly in the Sugata’s hermitage and fully taught the True Dharma.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, all the worlds were filled with joy;
having taken refuge in the Triple Gem, they devoted themselves to it with great reverence.
Then that king of Dakṣiṇapāñcāla, filled with joy,
approached the Deer Park in order to behold the Perfectly Awakened One.
There, having seen that Śrīghana, the king was filled with joy;
approaching him with palms joined in reverence, he bowed and withdrew to stand at one side.
At that moment, the lord of the northern Pañcālas heard it said there in the deer-park: "The Blessed One has arrived."
That king of Uttarapāñcāla, being provoked to anger,
set out to defeat that king of Dakṣiṇapāñcāla.
There, that heroic king, together with his fourfold army and amidst the great enthusiasm of victory-trumpets, suddenly approached.
There, that King of the Southern Pañcālas, having heard that his enemy had arrived, rose up suddenly and bowed down to that lord of sages.
"O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, my enemy has come here;
therefore, what shall I do in this matter? Please grant me your permission."
When that lord of men had thus entreated him, the Lord of Jinas,
having beheld that Yāmyapāñcāla and comforted him, commanded as follows:
"O King, do not fear; remain firm and composed.
I shall employ such a means that he will come under your control. (Rm 28.58)
Having thus instructed him, the Omniscient One then created a heroic general of a great army, endowed with the fourfold forces, and dispatched him from there.
That heroic commander of the army, accompanied by his fourfold forces,
set out while roaming through Northern Pañcāla to wage war.
Beholding that great army approaching and pressing forward,
all the troops of the Northern Pañcālas fled in fear.
Seeing that, the King of Northern Pañcāla was also incensed;
mounting his chariot alone, he advanced toward the Blessed One.
There, having seen from afar that Śrīghana seated in the assembly,
he descended from his chariot and approached him in the Deer Park.
There, that king, the monarch, having approached with palms joined in reverence,
circumambulated him three times and bowed down, having gone for refuge.
Then, after a long time, that king of the Pañcālas rose up and withdrew to a secluded spot there in order to drink that nectar of the true Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that the king had taken refuge,
taught the supreme Dharma, beginning with the Noble Truths.
Having heard that Noble Truth, the king was awakened;
he then desired to hear once more the Dharma that is the means for transcending cyclic existence.
Then that king, the lord of men, having risen with palms joined in reverence and having bowed to the Blessed One, made this request with great respect: Rm_28.68{68} //
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, I go for refuge to you;
having shown me favor in this matter, it behoves you to instruct me correctly.
Blessed One, how is it that sentient beings here, driven by existence, wander through the six realms of rebirth, experiencing pleasure and pain within the ocean of becoming?
By what action do beings become gods, by what action do they become humans, and by what action do they become Daityas? Please explain that correctly.
By what karma do animals exist, and by what karma do hungry ghosts?
By what karma do hell-beings exist? Teach all of that.
There too, they were of many forms; though all had different dispositions, they were inferior, middling, or superior, and were likewise possessed of happiness and suffering.
Having explained all this, may you, the Teacher and Guru of the world,
deign to awaken us to the wandering through the courses of saṃsāra.
When the king had thus made his request, the wise Blessed One, seeing that monarch’s pure intention, instructed him in this way: *Rm_28.75{75}*
"Listen well, O Great King, to the wandering through the realms of cyclic existence; I shall correctly proclaim the Dharma for your complete awakening."
Whatever wholesome or unwholesome action has been performed by way of body, speech, and mind, the world experiences its fruit; there is no other agent for anything whatsoever.
Thus all the Jinas, the teachers of the three worlds, filled with compassion, spoke accordingly: for whatever the fruit of an action may be, such it shall be.

Those men who, out of greed, delusion, fear, and anger, commit acts of killing that cause rebirth in both auspicious and inauspicious states— whether performing such deeds or abandoning the opportunity to do so.
For even after being revived, they certainly go to Saṃjīva;
though slain again and again, they remain there for many thousands of years.
Because they revive there, it is therefore called Saṃjīva.
Those who commit acts of treachery against their mother, father, friends, kinsmen, or companions,
and those who speak slander and falsehoods, go to the Kālasūtra hell.
Because beings there are bound with black cords,
hacked, and split like logs with blazing saws, it is therefore known as Kālasūtra (the Black Cord).
Those who inflict burning upon embodied beings with fires in forests and other places are themselves tormented by fierce flames while crying out in the Tapana hell.
Because it continuously spreads an intense heat of burning,
it is therefore appropriately known by the name Tapanīya in the light.
The nihilist who proclaims the perversion of dharma and adharma,
and who torments others, is himself tormented in the Pratāpana hell.
Because it torments the beings residing there with a fierce fire through an excess of heat,
it is therefore called Pratāpana (the Intense Heat).
Those men who kill goats, sheep, jackals, rabbits, rats, deer, boars, and other living beings, go to the Saṃghāta hell.
There, beings are slaughtered while gathered together, just as bamboos are cut down by a well-directed blow;
therefore, it is renowned by the name Saṃghāta, a designation that corresponds to its actual meaning.
Those men who cause suffering to embodied beings here through body, speech, or mind,
and those who are harsh and cruel, go to the Raurava hell.
Because those being burned there incessantly by a fierce fire emit a terrible cry (*raudra-rava*), for that reason it is called Raurava.
Those who have stolen the property of gods, brahmins, or gurus, and those who seize the wealth of others, go to the Mahāraurava hell while still suffering here in this world.
Because of the ferocity of its fiery burning and the intensity of its roar, it is indeed called Mahāraurava; know that it is even greater than Raurava.
Having committed a grave injury against those superior in virtue,
and having slain one's mother, father, or teacher, one will certainly be cooked in the Avīci hell for an eon.
Even the bones of embodied beings there are shattered in the fierce fire; because there is not even a ripple of happiness, it is called Avīci (the Waveless).
Those who delight in mutual injury and strike embodied beings even when they seek refuge,
are born from that sin with claws like swords, partaking in misery.
Their very nails are swords; they are made of iron, blazing, and sharp.
With these they hack one another down; for that reason they are known as Asinakhās (Sword-nails).
The wardens forcibly made the sinners climb the silk-cotton trees, which were covered with sixteen-finger-long thorns whose sharp tips were glowing with fire.
Those with iron fangs, massive bodies, blazing, and intensely terrifying,
embrace and devour this thief of another's wife.
Even while screaming, they are devoured by dogs, vultures, owls, and crows;
having been torn apart, those men who were betrayers of trust bring about inauspiciousness.
Those who steal the property of others must repeatedly consume glowing iron balls and are made to drink boiling copper.
Those men who took delight in gambling are helplessly and violently mangled by cruel dogs with iron fangs,
even as they cry out for ten million years.
Having killed fish and other aquatic creatures, a man goes to the Vaitaraṇī river, which is ablaze with water mixed with molten copper; there he is constantly burned by fire.
He who, deluded by a mere fragment of self-interest, engages in unrighteous conduct,
is crushed by a wheel while crying out in hell.
Those who have inflicted suffering upon the miserable here in many ways are tormented for a long time in that place by blazing hammers and mountains.
Those men who were destroyers of the bridges of Dharma and who opposed the path— having traveled along a road strewn with razor edges— they must cross it.
Having crushed lice and other insects with their claws, those beings of massive body are crushed again and again by mountains of wool; they cry out for a hundred autumns.
But he who, having undertaken a vow, fails to protect its integrity,
will certainly be cooked in Kukuṇḍa with his flesh and bones falling away.
For whoever lives by even a slight wrong livelihood is devoured by fierce worms, submerged in the mire of excrement.
Even after seeing living beings situated amidst grain,
those who crush them with heated iron beaks are agitated again and again.
Those who are excessively wrathful, cruel, deceitful, and desirous of evil,
and who take pleasure in the misfortunes of others, are born as Yama-rākṣasas.

Whatever evil action— whether of body, speech, or mind— one might perform, even if it be as minute as an atom, it is the seed of all sufferings according to its degree of intensity. [The Section on Hell is completed.]
By that very passion through which even swans, pigeons, and other such creatures— even those with harsh voices—
become deluded and are born in the wombs of insects and the like.
Through anger and enmity one is born as a snake; through arrogance, as Māra; and through pride, as a lord of beasts, such as an elephant or a horse.
Due to faults such as stinginess and envy, monkeys are born with the bodies of *preta*s; and those who are talkative, audacious, and fickle-minded become crows.
Through killing, binding, and envy toward cows, horses, and other such beings,
embodied souls are born as cruel-natured spiders, donkeys, and scorpions.
Men who are prone to anger and envy, having consumed the flesh of a deceased person, are reborn as tigers, cats, jackals, bears, vultures, and wolves.
Those who are generous yet prone to anger and cruelty, men possessing great supernatural power over serpents,
become lords of the Garuḍas through their pride and wrath after passing away from this existence.
Whatever evil karma has been committed by oneself through speech, body, or mind, by that one is born as an animal; therefore, direct your mental disposition accordingly.
Thus ends the section on animals. O Dānavarji, those base beings who steal food that is fit to be eaten or consumed become *kaṭapūtana* pretas who feed upon corpses.
Those fools who cause harm and even deceive others out of craving are born as *kaṭapūtana* spirits, feeding on the impurities of the womb.
Those men who are of base conduct, extremely wretched, envious, and constantly covetous,
are born as preta-s known as galagaṇḍaka-s.
He who does not give anything indeed obstructs the path of generosity;
such a person becomes a hungry ghost (preta) with a vast belly, emaciated by hunger, and a needle-like mouth.
He who guards his wealth for the sake of his lineage, neither enjoying it nor giving it away,
is reborn as a *preta* who receives gifts and becomes a consumer of *śrāddha* offerings.
He who desires to seize the property of others, and who feels remorse even after giving it away,
is born as a *preta* after death, consuming excrement, phlegm, and vomit.
He who, out of anger, speaks unpleasant words that pierce the vital organs,
by that karma becomes a preta with a flaming mouth for a very long time.
But he who, merciless and cruel-minded, incites strife among worms,
insects, moths, and the like, becomes a *jyotika* spirit in the realm of the departed.
He who, even while oppressing the people, gives [only] two village headmen,
is born as a *kumbhāṇḍa* of deformed appearance who feeds upon pus.
Those merciless ones who kill living beings for the sake of food, even if they give [meat] away,
will inevitably become flesh-eating *preta*s and *rākṣasa*s.
Those who are constantly devoted to perfumes and garlands, who have little anger, and who are generous,
are born after death as gandharvas, serving as sources of delight for the gods.
One who is prone to anger and malicious, yet gives something for the sake of some purpose,
that evil-minded person is born as a Piśāca with a deformed face.
Men who are perpetually malicious, fickle, and harmful to others,
yet are constantly devoted to giving, become *bhūtas* after death.
Those who are cruel, wrathful, yet generous, and fond of all gods,
are born after death as yakṣas— beings of cruel nature who are devoted to the gods.
Those who convey their mothers, fathers, and teachers by means of vehicles wherever they desire,
are born as Yakṣas who travel in celestial palaces and are endowed with great happiness.
Due to the fault of craving and stinginess, these beings always become pretas; likewise, yakṣas and others arise from both wholesome and afflicted states. Therefore, one should avoid them.
Thus ends the section on the departed spirits.
Among gods, asuras, and humans, long life arises through non-violence; through violence it is short. Therefore, one should avoid violence.
Skin diseases, fever, insanity, and whatever other ailments afflict human beings,
these arise from the influence of spirits through killing, imprisonment, and beating.
He who does not seize the property of others and does not give through deceit,
even with great effort, does not acquire wealth.
He who, having taken wealth that was not given, bestows gifts as charity,
becomes possessed of property after death, only to become destitute once again.
The man who is neither a taker nor a giver, yet is not excessively miserly,
will certainly obtain stable wealth in its entirety and in abundance.
The man who does not seize the property of others, who is generous and free from envy,
obtains vast, desirable wealth that cannot be taken away.
Endowed with long life, beauty, and strength, illustrious and free from disease,
happy and always successful shall he be who gives food here in this world.
Modest, handsome, an enjoyer of pleasures, well-sheltered, and dear to all living beings—
he who gives garments shall himself obtain fine clothing.
For that embodied being who gives a dwelling here with a well-pleased mind, palaces and all objects of desire arise.
Those men who give sandals, bridges, and the like,
always become happy and obtain vehicles.
Having caused reservoirs such as ponds, wells, and lakes to be constructed,
those people become happy, free from distress, and devoid of thirst.
The glorious one, worthy of refuge by all embodied beings, when worshipped with flowers,
shall become prosperous for him who bestows a grove.
Scholarship is attained through the gift of knowledge and also by the practice of wisdom;
moreover, one becomes free from disease through the gift of medicine and the gift of fearlessness.
By the gift of a lamp, one becomes possessed of sight; by the gift of musical instruments, one possesses a beautiful voice;
and by the gift of beds and seats, a person becomes happy.
The man who gives cows and other such animals here, as well as food endowed with savory flavors,
shall become strong, possessed of a fine complexion, an enjoyer of pleasures, and long-lived.
Through the gift of a maiden, one becomes equal [to the gods], possessed of a retinue,
and through the gift of land, one is born wealthy in both riches and grain.
A leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, the granting of fearlessness, or pleasant speech—
whatever is desired, that very thing should be given to the seeker according to one's ability.
If one gives after having caused affliction here, whether for one's own sake or for some other reason,
or out of a desire for fame and pleasure, one obtains an afflicted result.
He who gives here for the sake of others with a mind filled with compassion, regardless of his own interest, enjoys an unafflicted fruit.
Whatever is given to another at the proper time and according to the prescribed rule— in whatever manner it is given— all that accrues [to the giver].
Having thus repelled others at all times as desired,
one should give what is beneficial and non-contradictory to the Dharma, without causing them distress.
For it is thus that the fruits and other results of a gift being given arise;
indeed, giving is considered the sole cause of all happiness.
Free from passion for the wives of others, he shall obtain his desired wife;
even with his own wife, he should avoid improper places and times, and thus he attains manhood.
The man who does not restrain his mind when it is attached to another's wife,
and who gazes upon improper parts, attains womanhood.
But that woman who loathes her femininity, who is virtuous and free from passion,
and who constantly desires masculinity, shall attain manhood.
But he who practices the celibate life correctly and free from affliction is perceived even by the gods as one possessed of splendor, virtuous qualities, and glory.
Through the practice of the Maghavan fast, a man becomes firm in mindfulness, free from delusion,
truthful in speech, and endowed with fame and happiness.
He who does not create division even among beings who are already divided becomes one with a steadfast mind, surrounded by an inseparable retinue.
But he who always carries out the commands of his teachers with a joyful mind,
and who speaks of what is beneficial and harmful, shall be one whose speech is authoritative and effective.
Those who have risen through the reversal of base conduct and delusion become happy by giving happiness, and miserable by giving misery.
Those who delight in the conceptual proliferations of others, the deceitful, the speakers of falsehood,
and those who are conceited about their physical form, become hunchbacked and dwarfed.
Due to stinginess regarding knowledge, one becomes dull-witted; due to attachment to what is pleasant and aversion to what is unpleasant, one becomes mute.
The deluded soul who hides beneficial words from others falls into deafness.

Suffering is the fruit of evil, happiness is the fruit of merit, and that which is mixed is the fruit of mixed action; one should infer that all such results are outflows corresponding to their causes.
Thus ends the section on humans.
He who always acts with deceit and guile, yet remains free from committed sin,
being fond of strife and a generous giver, shall become a lord of the Asuras.
(Rm 331) Thus ends the section on the Asuras:
He who does not desire happiness for himself, nor would he incur the burden of possessions;
And he, the leader of the planets, shall attain the status of a Mahārājika deity.
One who honors his mother, father, and elders,
who is self-controlled and virtuous, and who does not rejoice in quarrels, is born among the thirty gods.
Those who do not delight in disputation, whose minds are not gladdened by quarreling,
and who are devoted exclusively to what is wholesome— they are indeed those who have crossed over Māyā.
Those men who are learned, upholders of the Dharma, possessed of excellent wisdom, seekers of liberation, and adorned with virtues, go to the Tuṣita heaven.
Those men who themselves engage in the discipline of the gift of morality and possess great enthusiasm will certainly go to the Nirmāṇarati heaven.
Those beings of undaunted spirit are the best among me in terms of generosity, self-control, and restraint;
and those who possess superior virtues certainly attain the state of the Paranirmita gods.
Through ethical conduct one attains heaven, and through meditative concentration especially so;
but through the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, there is for you, in the end, no further rebirth.
This karma, which has been clearly explained as having both auspicious and inauspicious fruits:
through the auspicious, happiness is obtained, while suffering arises from the inauspicious.
Death, disease, and old age—these three must be contemplated;
as well as separation from those who are dear, and the fruit of one's own actions.
Thus one attains dispassion; being secluded, one honors merit and does not incur evil. Listen now to that in brief.
The Lord of Sages has declared that correctly acting for the benefit of others and avoiding harm to others is merit; from the opposite of these, one surely incurs sin.
Thus ends the section on the gods.
Having thus reflected, O Great King, upon the six states of existence within *saṃsāra*, one should always practice what is virtuous, having taken up the Dharma of perfect enlightenment.
Those who, having undertaken the vow of perfect enlightenment, conduct themselves with concentrated mind for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, they become bodhisattvas.
Having understood this, O Indra among kings, if you always desire what is auspicious,
take refuge in the Three Jewels and worship them constantly with devotion.
By the ripening of this merit, having completely conquered all afflictions,
may you gradually attain enlightenment and reach the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having heard this which was thus proclaimed by that Lord of Sages,
the king of Uttarapāñcāla also desired to go forth into the religious life.
Then that king, the lord of men, having risen with palms joined in reverence and bowing to the Blessed One, made this request with great devotion:
O Blessed One, O Protector, O Omniscient One, having gone for refuge to you and having undertaken the vow of perfect enlightenment, I ask how I may always practice it.
Since you are the teacher of the worlds and the instructor of the Dharma of perfect enlightenment,
it behooves you to show me favor by granting me the going forth.
When the king had thus made his request, that wise Blessed One, perceiving the purity of the king's mind, instructed him in this way: *Rm_28.188{9}*
Excellent, O King, highly fortunate one! If you desire an auspicious destiny, come; practice with a concentrated mind the vow within my teaching.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Sages, touching his head with his hand,
formally received that lord of men into the Dharma and the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One.
When the Teacher said, "Come," the king was thus awakened;
clad in robes and carrying a khikkhirī bowl, he became a monk.
Then that king also became dispassionate, free from desire for enjoyments,
devoid of afflictions, pure in soul, and one who had conquered his senses.
Having directly attained arhatship, pure and stainless in his holy life,
he reached the state of perfect enlightenment and became a perfectly enlightened disciple.
Then that knower of Brahman, a yogi, became a venerable teacher worthy of honor and worship even by the inhabitants of the three realms, including the worlds of gods and asuras.
Then the King of Dakṣiṇapāñcāla, greatly delighted,
rose up, bowed with palms joined, and entreated that Lord of Sages.
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, may you be gracious to me out of compassion;
I wish to eat for three months, so please grant me this favor.
When the king had thus made his request, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
looked upon the monarch and remained there in silence.
Then that king, the ruler of men, learning that [the site] had been consecrated by the Blessed One, immediately prepared all the necessary requisites.
Then that king, having daily honored the Blessed One together with his community of monks with foods as they deserved, satisfied them completely.
Having clothed Śrīghana and his community of monks with various colorful robes,
he bowed with palms joined and joyfully made this aspiration:
By the ripening of this merit, may I indeed become a Teacher, a perfectly awakened Buddha and Arhat, who is a sun of the True Dharma in a world that is blind and without a guide.
When that lord of men had thus joyfully made his vow,
the Blessed One, perceiving it, released a smile of auspicious radiance.
The five-colored divine rays produced by that smile spread forth through the three worlds, moving along while illuminating them.
Touched by those rays, all those dwelling in the hells were freed from the exhaustion of their sensations and obtained great happiness.
Then all those inhabitants of hell were struck with wonder and filled with joy;
reflecting, "How can such happiness arise?", they sat down in stillness.
Then the Blessed One, for the sake of awakening the minds of those whose hearts were overcome with wonder, dispatched an emanation there.
Then all those hell-beings, having seen the Sugata with joy,
approached him, prostrated themselves, and took refuge in him.
Then, anointed with that merit, they were all liberated from evil;
purified and virtuous in nature, they attained a happy rebirth.
Then all those rays, having illuminated everything on every side,
extended as far as the Akaniṣṭha abode and shone there equally.
And everywhere, by means of the sounds of verses, they awakened all the gods who were rejoicing,
established them in the auspicious Dharma, and then departed.
Then all those rays, having coalesced into a single mass before the Sage,
circumambulated him three times and entered his great uṣṇīṣa.
Seeing that, all those people in the assembly were uplifted by extreme wonder;
reflecting, "What Dharma might the Teacher teach? they sat down.
Perceiving their mental deliberation, Ānanda arose;
approaching with palms joined in reverence and bowing, he entreated that lord of sages.
"Blessed One, by what cause do you now manifest a smile?
For the Lords of Sages do not manifest a smile without a cause or a condition."
Therefore, since these members of the assembly desire to hear the purpose for which you have released a smile, it behoves you to explain that matter.
Having heard what was thus spoken by Ānanda, the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World,
surveyed all the worlds and addressed Ānanda.
In the very same way, Sadānanda, all the Buddhas, the lords of sages,
never at any time manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Behold, Ānanda, this king, highly gratified,
honors us with faith and devotion for three months with great joy.
Through the ripening of this merit, may this king, a mine of excellent qualities,
gradually fulfill all the perfections and become endowed with the [ten] powers.
Having conquered the entire host of afflictions and having utterly defeated Māra,
the Tathāgata, the Lord of Sages, attained omniscience and enlightenment.
The sovereign of all sciences, the Teacher, the King of Dharma, the Guide—
under another existence, he will become the perfectly awakened Buddha named Vijaya.
Thus, Ānanda, having understood that the purification of a Buddha-field brings about great happiness as its maturation— a blessing that accomplishes perfect awakening— [one should cultivate it].
Having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, those who desire perfect enlightenment should always joyfully practice virtue with offerings and faith.
Having heard what was thus commanded by the Lord of Sages, Ānanda and all those people said, "So be it," and being gratified, they rejoiced.
That king of Dakṣiṇapañcāla, having heard this, was filled with joy;
he paid homage to the Three Jewels and always practiced what is virtuous.
From that time forth, there was always auspiciousness and freedom from calamity there;
with great enthusiasm on all sides, it became like the Kṛta Yuga.
"Thus it was told to me by my teacher, and thus have I now heard it;
you too, O auspicious lady, should always act in this manner as it is here described."
And having diligently awakened the subjects, O Great King, and established them on the path to enlightenment, they must always be protected by you.
Thus, may there always be prosperity for you in every respect and at all times;
and having gradually attained awakening, may you reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, King Aśoka,
together with his retinue, consented, saying "So be it," and rejoiced.
This renowned avadāna, which was told by the Sage to the two kings of Pañcāla—
those who, with joyful minds and clear faith, hear it or cause others to hear it,
are all Bodhisattvas, possessors of every virtue, and enriched with all prosperity and happiness.
Having brought about welfare for the worlds, they proceed with joy to the abode of the best of sages.
(Rm 334) Thus ends the story of the King of Pañcāla in the *Ratnāvadānatatva*.

XXIX. The Avadāna of the Spontaneously Born (Upapādukāvadāna) Then King Aśoka, having approached with palms joined in reverence and having bowed to the ascetic Upagupta, made this request with great devotion: Rm_29.1{1} //
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken teaching;
it behoves you to relate it to me just as it was instructed by your teacher."
Having heard this prayer made by the king, that arhat of great intelligence,
Upagupta, looked upon the lord of men and spoke as follows:
"Listen well, O Great King, to that which was spoken by my teacher; I shall declare it to you just as it was told, and having heard it, you should rejoice."
Namely: the Blessed One, the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Lord of Sages, the Omniscient One, the Sugata, the Teacher, the King of Dharma, the Guide.
At one time, out of affection for his mother, Queen Māyā,
he proceeded to the abode of the Thirty-three gods in order to teach the True Dharma.
There, having gone to the most delightful Nandana grove, the Blessed One took his rest upon a smooth stone slab at the foot of a Pārijāta tree.
There, Śakra and all the other gods, beholding Śākyamuni— the mine of excellent qualities— approached him with great joy.
There, having beheld that Śrīghana, all the gods were filled with joy;
having circumambulated him three times, they bowed down with palms joined in reverence.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, prepared for the Perfectly Awakened One, the Teacher of the World, a throne made of divine jewels, auspicious and radiant.
There, the Blessed One, having seen [the place] blazing with the great splendor of divine jewels,
ascended, took his stand, and remained there, illuminating all.
Then his mother, Queen Māyā,
having arrived and beheld her son, the Lord of the World, approached him.
There, having seen his mother arrived, the Blessed One rose, approached her, bowed down, and spoke thus: *The Root Verses on the Middle Way*, Chapter 29, Verse 13.
Welcome! May it be well with you, mother; may you always enjoy good health.
I have come to behold your face; therefore, please grant me your favor.
Taking your seat upon this throne, sit with a one-pointed mind;
I shall teach you the true Dharma, so listen with a concentrated mind.
Having heard these words thus commanded by the Lord of Sages,
the virtuous mother Māyādevī gazed upon her son and spoke to him.
I come before you to behold your face; may all be well with you always, O son of the Self.
Therefore, for the sake of showing me favor, you ought to instruct me in the Dharma.
Having spoken thus, the virtuous Māyādevī, the mother of the Teacher of the World,
took up her devotional practice and sat down with a concentrated mind.
Then Śakra and all the other gods, filled with great joy,
worshipped that Lord of the World and Māyādevī with the various articles of worship.
Then, having bowed at their feet and performed three circumambulations, they turned back, placing the Dharma before them, and drew near to listen.
Then the Blessed One, seeing those gods standing before him,
began to teach the true Dharma, starting from the Noble Truths.

Then the Blessed One again taught this means for achieving perfect enlightenment to those gods who considered themselves happy: tataś ca bhagavāṃs teṣāṃ devānāṃ sukhamāninām / saṃbodhisādhanaṃ punar evam upādiśat // Rm_29.22{22} //
In saṃsāra, indeed, everything is impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self;
there is not even a trace of happiness here amidst this turbulent mass of afflictions.
Thinking thus, if you desire constant happiness in this saṃsāra,
always practice what is auspicious by maintaining the vow of the conduct of awakening (bodhicaryāvrata).
Go forth and exert yourselves; apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha. Abandoning the conduct of Māra, practice the way of awakening.
Whoever shall practice the conduct of awakening for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings will,
having attained perfect awakening, reach the state of a fully enlightened Buddha.
Thinking thus, all of you here in this saṃsāra, being composed,
practice the vow of awakening after having rendered service to the Three Jewels.
Those who here revere the Three Jewels do not go to an evil rebirth;
always proceeding toward a happy rebirth, they shall gradually attain awakening.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, all those immortals,
realizing that it was indeed the truth, rejoiced, being thus awakened.
Then Śakra, rising up with palms joined in reverence,
bowed to that Blessed One and made this request with great devotion:
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, having taught us the True Dharma in this abode of the gods, you ought to wander through all lands.
We all, O gods, have eternally gone for refuge to you;
having always heard the true Dharma, we shall practice the auspicious conduct.
Then the goddess Mahāmāyā, his mother, also arose;
approaching him with palms joined in reverence and bowing, she spoke to the Blessed One.
"You are blessed, my son, that you fulfill everything exactly as was promised by you in the past;
may there be the accomplishment of all your goals."
Always remaining here for the sake of the welfare of the worlds of the gods, enlightening them and teaching the true Dharma, dwell there radiating light.
Having heard what was requested by his mother, the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World, looked toward his mother and the assembly and commanded thus: Rm_29.36{35} //

O Mother, it is indeed for the sake of the welfare of all beings, not for my own benefit alone, that I undertake the conduct of awakening; may I become a Victor for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Therefore, I shall never remain here with the gods;
I wish to stay for three months during the rainy season, teaching the Dharma.
Having heard this command from the Lord of Sages, her mother, being thus enlightened, joyfully replied,
"So be it," and rejoiced.
In that manner, the Blessed One, illuminating the conduct of awakening and fully teaching the true Dharma, remained there in the celestial realm for three months.
All the gods, headed by Śakra, went for refuge to the Three Jewels;
having constantly heard the Dharma with reverence and faith, they attained liberation.
Then, there in heaven, auspiciousness free from all affliction prevailed at all times,
and enthusiasm for the practice of the true Dharma spread everywhere.
And at that time, in that hermitage outside Śrāvastī,
in the Jetavana monastery, Maudgalyāyana took up residence.
Then all those members of the Saṅgha, seeing the ascetic Maudgalyāyana stationed in the monastery, desired to hear the Dharma.
Then all those members of the Saṅgha, as well as other people and virtuous folk,
approached with joy to hear that teaching of the True Dharma.
There, all those people, having honored and bowed down to their teacher Maudgalyāyana, took their seats to listen to the Dharma.
Seeing them seated together, that son of the Conqueror, Maudgalya,
taught the supreme Dharma, which is virtuous in its beginning, middle, and end.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, all those belonging to the Saṅgha were awakened and became intent upon the practice of the True Dharma.
Then all those monks, with palms joined in reverence and filled with joy,
bowed to Maudgalyāyana and questioned him thus with great respect.
"Venerable Blessed One, Teacher, upon what now do you rely? Having fully taught the True Dharma, where do you dwell without conceit?"
Therefore, since the Blessed One, our Teacher, is present here,
he ought to instruct us in that truth and awaken our minds.
Having heard this request made by them, the wise Maudgalyāyana looked upon all those monks belonging to the Saṅgha and spoke thus:
"O sirs, I have heard that the Blessed One, our Teacher, is now in heaven;
therefore he remains there, teaching the Dharma to his mother and the gods."
Then, at the end of the three months of the rainy season, the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World,
would indeed descend there himself to perform what is beneficial for the world.
Having heard this which was proclaimed by that Arhat, all those people belonging to the Saṅgha rejoiced and returned each to their own abode.

Then the Blessed One, having summoned his mother there in heaven along with the gods led by Indra, instructed him as follows: *The Root Text of Cause and Effect* (Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa) by the Venerable Vasubandhu. Homage to the Buddha. In this world, there are three types of karma: those that have already ripened, those that have not yet ripened, and those that will ripen in the future. Among these, what is the nature of karma that has already ripened? It is that which has produced its fruit and whose efficacy has been exhausted. What is the nature of karma that has not yet ripened? It is that which has not yet produced its fruit. What is the nature of karma that will ripen in the future? It is that which, having been performed and accumulated, will produce its fruit at a later time. Furthermore, there are four types of karma: black karma with black ripening, white karma with white ripening, black-and-white karma with black-and-white ripening, and neither-black-nor-white karma with neither-black-nor-white ripening. What is black karma with black ripening? It is unwholesome karma. What is white karma with white ripening? It is wholesome karma pertaining to the desire realm. What is black-and-white karma with black-and-white ripening? It is mixed karma consisting of both wholesome and unwholesome actions. What is neither-black-nor-white karma with neither-black-nor-white ripening? It is the karma of the form and formless realms, as well as the supramundane karma. Moreover, there are five types of karma: karma to be experienced in the present life, karma to be experienced after rebirth, karma to be experienced in subsequent lives, karma that is indeterminate, and karma that is determinate. What is karma to be experienced in the present life? It is karma that produces its fruit in this very lifetime. What is karma to be experienced after rebirth? It is karma that produces its fruit in the very next lifetime. What is karma to be experienced in subsequent lives? It is karma that produces its fruit from the third lifetime onwards. What is indeterminate karma? It is karma for which the specific timing of ripening is not fixed. What is determinate karma? It is karma for which the timing of ripening is fixed. Regarding the relationship between karma and its results, it is taught that there are three fruits: the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), the fruit of dominance (*adhipatiphala*), and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*). Furthermore, there are four fruits when considering the cause of disconnection (*visamyogaphala*). It should be understood that all conditioned phenomena are the result of causes and conditions. Just as a seed produces a sprout, so too does karma produce its various effects. Through the power of ignorance, beings perform various actions; through the power of craving, they grasp at those actions; and through the power of clinging, they give rise to existence. Thus, the cycle of birth and death continues. Therefore, one should cultivate wisdom to see things as they truly are, abandon unwholesome actions, and practice wholesome deeds. By doing so, one may gradually transcend the suffering of saṃsāra and attain the state of liberation. This is the essential teaching on the law of cause and effect. [End of the *Root Text of Cause and Effect*] (Note: The provided source text contains a mix of Sanskrit terms and Tibetan commentary. Thus let everyone reflect: whatever karma has been performed in saṃsāra, its fruit is surely experienced, certainly in accordance with one's intentions.
By whomsoever an action was performed, by that very person is its fruit experienced;

Karma is not burned by fires, nor is it washed away by waters;
it is not dried up by winds, nor does it perish within the earth.

rather, it is experienced everywhere by all beings wandering through existence.

As many beings as there are, O monks, born from the four modes of birth— all elemental creatures, whether moving or stationary— Rm_30.9{9} //
All these living beings as well, moving within the existence of conditioned formations and experiencing the fruits of their own performed actions, wander through the six realms of rebirth.
However many living beings there are, even in all the hells,
they wander about, afflicted by suffering, experiencing the results of their own past actions.
All of them, too, meet their death at the time ordained by their own destiny;
yet, according to the karma they have performed, they wander through further existence.
For whom is there no birth and death? For life indeed ends in death;
so it is for as many beings as there are among the hungry ghosts, even in all the abodes of the pretas.
Experiencing the fruits of their own actions, they wander about, tormented by suffering;
and at the end of their karma, in the course of time, they all likewise meet death.
In accordance with the deeds they have performed, all living beings who move through the realms of conditioned existence receive rebirth.
For whom is there no birth and death? For life indeed ends in death; so it is for all those animals and living beings within the animal realms.
All those who experience the fruits of their actions wander about, following after what they themselves have done;
and all of them, at the end of their karma, must likewise go to death in the course of time.
And they too receive rebirth according to their karma,
among all living beings who move through the realms of conditioned existence.
For whom is there no birth and death? For life indeed ends in death.
As many as are the human beings and sentient creatures in the mortal worlds and upon the earth, they wander, experiencing happiness and suffering, reaping the fruits of their own actions.
And all of them, at the time when their work is finished, go to death;
and they also obtain rebirth again in accordance with their karma.
And those wise brahmins as well, all of them experts in the scriptures,
devoted to the six duties, possessed of discernment, and dwelling in the four divine abodes;
All of them too, experiencing their own karma while wandering through existence, meet death in due course; for who indeed is not subject to death in this world?
However many wise sages there may be, oceans of the virtues of the five super-knowledges,
they all, while wandering in existence, eventually meet death at the appointed time.
And even those wise non-Buddhist ascetics who undergo great and arduous penances—
they too, at the appointed time, meet death and pass into further existence.
Even those who are wise and yogins, absorbed in the meditation of yoga—
all of them likewise certainly go toward death at the appointed time.
And those wise lay followers as well, who possess pure morality and uphold their vows—
all of them too inevitably pass away at the time of death.
And even those heroic kṣatriyas, kings who are guardians of the world—
they too all surely go toward death when their time has come.
And even those ministers who are wise and teachers of counsel for the sake of one's welfare—they too all certainly go at the appointed time; death is inevitable.
And even those great ministers who are thus intent on protecting the kingdom—
all of them certainly go toward death when their time comes.
And those venerable great heroes who are intent on crushing the wicked—
even they all certainly go toward death when their time has come.
And even those who are wealthy, eminent, virtuous, and doers of good—
all of them likewise certainly go toward death when their time has come.
And even those wise merchants, caravan leaders, and masters of wealth—
all of them likewise inevitably proceed toward death at the appointed time.
And even those artisans who are wise, who accomplish virtuous ends for the benefit of others—even they all go forth toward death at the appointed time; it is certain.
And even those who are farmers, who accomplish their aims for the sake of their livelihood—
all of them likewise certainly go to death when their time comes.
And those Vaiśyas who are lords of their subjects and benefactors of all goods—
even they all certainly go toward death when the time arrives.
And even those astrologers who possess excellent qualities and are most skilled in knowing the ordinances—
even they all inevitably go to death when their time arrives.
And those physicians who possess great wisdom and bring about the pacification of all diseases—
even they all certainly go to death when their time arrives.
Even those wise ones who are composed of the elements and have brought all beings to peace—
even they all certainly go to death due to their dissociation [from the body].
And even those heroic ministers, all of whom accomplish their tasks and purposes—
all of them too, through the dissolution of their bonds, will certainly go to death.
In this way, all other worlds as well—whether inferior, middling, or superior—all inevitably go to death; indeed, who is not under the power of death?
And the Gandharvas, those great heroes, who surpass the gods and possess great supernatural power—even they all surely depart; death is certain for those devoid of essence.
And the kumbhāṇḍas—those great heroes, most terrifying and possessed of great strength—even they must at the appointed time depart; everywhere death is certain.
Even the Nāgas of great pride and the Garuḍas of great supernatural power—all of them likewise inevitably go toward death when their time comes; this is certain.
Even the great heroic yakṣas, and the gods and asuras of great supernatural power—
all of them likewise pass away in time, succumbing to death when their efforts cease.
And the Kinnaras, those great heroes who travel through the air and possess great supernatural powers—
even they all, devoid of enthusiasm, go at the time of death to the abode of Yama.
Even the perfected ones, the great heroes who accomplish all their aims and purposes— even they all must at last succumb to death, rendered powerless in the face of time.
Furthermore, even those of great wisdom who accomplish the welfare of all beings—
all of them likewise invariably go toward death at all times.
And the Rākṣasas, who are most terrifying and possess great heroism and prowess—
even they all surely go toward death, rendered powerless.
In the same way, other beings as well— creatures such as lions and tigers,
as well as beasts, birds, and even worms and insects— [attain liberation].
Whether born from eggs or born from sweat, all living beings alike,
as the time comes, inevitably meet death, experiencing the destiny ordained by fate.
And even the Daityas, who are great heroes, possessed of great prowess and great supernatural power—
all of them likewise inevitably meet death when their time has come.
Even Śakra and the other lords of the gods, along with all the deities who partake of nectar—
even they, having fallen from heaven in the course of time, wander through the six realms of existence.
Even the celestial nymphs, with their divine limbs who move at will according to their pleasure—
all of them, when their time comes, fall away and go to the abode of Yama.
Even the Vidyādharas, possessed of great supernormal powers and wandering at ease according to their will—
all of them, lacking any power to resist, go in due time to the presence of Yama.
In this way, other worlds as well— those inhabited by living beings wandering through existence—
all experience their karma and likewise meet death in due time.
Even for all those who dwell in the subterranean realm (rasātala) and experience the fruits of their own actions, life indeed ends in death.
And for all those who move within the realm of desire and act according to their own deeds, life indeed ends in death.
And for all those who have gone to the realm of form (rūpadhātu) and are absorbed in the enjoyment of meditative concentrations (dhyāna), life indeed ends in death.
And even for those formless gods who are beyond sight and untainted,
the life of all of them indeed ends in death.
And those monks who are arhats, free from afflictions, with senses conquered,
liberated from the conduct of Māra, non-conceptual, and stainless;
Moreover, for all of them, life indeed ends in death;
for whom would death not exist? For every being born, death is certain.
And those Pratyekabuddhas who are Sugatas, free from afflictions, with senses conquered, non-conceptual, unattached, and practitioners of solitary meditation; Rm_30.62{61} //
Moreover, for all of them, life indeed ends in death;
for whom is there no death in existence? For one who is born, death is certain.
The Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, who bring benefit to all sentient beings,
possess great supernormal powers and great fortitude, and dwell in the four sublime abodes.
The lords who are masters of the ten stages, who delight in the ten perfections,
who have attained mastery over the welfare of sentient beings, and who are endowed with the power of dhāraṇīs.
Moreover, for all of them, life indeed ends in death;
for whom is there no death in existence? For one who is born, death is certain.
The Tathāgatas, the perfectly awakened ones, the omniscient, the Sugatas, the Victors;
the conquerors of Māra, the lords of the world, the masters of sages possessing the six superknowledges.
The Kings of Dharma are excellent teachers, the guides endowed with the ten powers;
they are the creators of universal auspiciousness and dwellers in the four sublime abodes.
All those Blessed Ones, even within the realms of the three worlds, having practiced the conduct of awakening and having taught the true Dharma everywhere, [passed away].
Having performed auspicious rites everywhere and having made the world consist of Dharma,
he established all sentient beings upon the path to enlightenment, endowed with virtue.
Having completed all the activities of a perfectly awakened Buddha, they enter final nirvana;
at the proper time, they also proceed toward the most perfectly pure nirvana.
Realizing thus that death is certain for everyone in this saṃsāra,
he began an effort to abandon all sufferings born of conditioned formations.
Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena, arising from the conceptualizations of ignorance;
they are the basis of afflictions, the root of great suffering, destructive, and impure.
Therefore, those men who wish to abandon the sufferings of saṃsāra should renounce attachment to illusion and practice according to the Buddha’s teaching.

Those who, out of devotion to the Buddha's teaching, have gone for refuge to the Triple Gem and, having undertaken the vow of complete enlightenment, conduct themselves with concentrated minds; // Rm_30.75{77} //
May they all, being virtuous in nature, free from afflictions, and pure in intention,
attain the conduct of awakening and always act for the benefit of sentient beings.
Then, having fulfilled all the perfections in due order,
and having attained perfect enlightenment, they shall become Sugatas and Jinas.
Then, having established auspiciousness throughout all the worlds,
he diligently settled the world of living beings upon the path to enlightenment.
Then, having attained nirvāṇa, they shall enjoy themselves in the abode of the Jinas;
at that time, those pure-souled ones will be absorbed in their own dwelling.
Thinking thus, in order to attain one's own bliss through the practice for awakening,
exert vigor in the three bodies and conduct yourselves within the Buddha’s teaching.
What is the Dharma without the body? What is speech without virtue? What is the mind without vigor? And what is vigor without restraint? (Rm 350) Rm_30.81{83} //
As is a flower, so is the body; as is a ripe fruit, so is the frame.
Having fallen to the ground in an instant, how can that body still be beautiful?
Just as a clay vessel made by a potter is destined for destruction, so too should one regard this body as perishing in an instant; having realized this, one should practice self-restraint.
Realizing that the body is as pithless as the trunk of a plantain tree— fragile and subject to dissolution— arise and practice the way of the Sugata.
Having realized that the body is like a mass of foam, devoid of inherent qualities, and momentary in its destruction,
one should maintain great enthusiasm for vigor and practice the vows of restraint.
Life and the body are not stable at all, like a drop of water upon a leaf;
realizing this, one should practice the vow of the Sugata in order to attain perfect enlightenment.
Those who, having undertaken the vow of the Sugata, conduct themselves for the sake of attaining awakening,
do not go to an evil rebirth, but always go to a good rebirth.
Therefore, those who desire the auspicious means for awakening within saṃsāra should always worship the Three Jewels with devotion, having gone to them for refuge.
The merit produced from honoring the Three Jewels is never exhausted anywhere;
by the power of this merit alone, every sin is overcome.
Merit alone is the friend of the world; evil alone is the enemy of the world.
Therefore, by propitiating that friend of merit, may you conquer the enemy of evil.
The meritorious person is always the best in all parts of the world;
having enjoyed happiness according to their desire, they go to the blissful realm of Sukhāvatī.
Having heard this, all those members of the Saṅgha said, "So it is," and having realized its truth, they proceeded to observe the vow of the Sugata.
This was told to me by my teacher, and thus it has been spoken by me here;
you too, O Great King, should conduct yourself in this way upon the auspicious bull [of Dharma].
And having diligently awakened the subjects, O Great King,
and established them in the auspicious Dharma, they should always be protected with great care.
In that way, may you always have auspiciousness everywhere at all times;
and having gradually attained awakening, may you reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, King Aśoka said,
"So be it," and after bowing down, he roared his approval along with his retinue.
Those people who, with serene minds, listen to this well-spoken *Anityatā-sūtra*,
having enjoyed happiness and being devoted to virtuous qualities, go at the end to the abode of the Sugata.
Thus ends the Sūtra on Impermanence within the *Śrīratnāvadānatattva*.
XXXI. The Legend of the One Become a Preta.
Then King Aśoka, standing before him with palms joined in reverence, bowed down to Upagupta and spoke again thus out of joy: Rm_31.1{1} //
