"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken word;
it behoves you to instruct me just as it was explained by my teacher."
When the king had thus made his request, that lord of ascetics, with a gracious mind,
looked upon the great king Aśoka and instructed him as follows.
Listen well, O Great King, to that which was spoken by my teacher; I shall declare it to you, and having heard it, grant your approval.
Namely: the Blessed One, the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Lord of Sages, the Omniscient One, the Arhat, the Teacher of the World, the King of Dharma, the Tathāgata.
Once upon a time, there, outside Śrāvastī, in the hermitage within the great grove of Jeta’s Wood, in a monastery adorned with jewels.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, illuminating the conduct of awakening and teaching the true Dharma, he dwelt together with his community of monks.
There, those monks were arhats and also members of the Saṅgha;
they were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seeking the welfare of all sentient beings.
The bhikṣuṇīs of pure morality, those observing vows with virtuous intentions, the faithful laymen and laywomen who serve the Three Jewels; Rm_31.9{9} //
All those belonging to the Saṅgha also came there to hear the True Dharma;
they bowed down to Śrīghana in due order and performed three circumambulations.
Having placed him at their head in due order throughout that assembly,
they stood before him with palms joined in reverence, gazing upon him with great respect.
Then, the lords of the gods, including Śakra and Maheśvara,
as well as all the guardians of the world, arrived there with their armies, forces, and mounts.
The lords of the asuras along with their armies, the yakṣas, gandharvas,
and kiṃnaras, the rākṣasas, garuḍas, nāgas, siddhas, vidyādharas, and others;
In this same way, other people as well as brahmins, great seers,
ascetics, yogins, heretics, and those who practice austerities [should follow].
Kings and Kṣatriyas as well, monarchs and princes, Vaiśyas, eminent ministers, counselors, and great men.
The generals along with their armies, householders, the people of the city,
merchants, caravan leaders, the wealthy, and even the artisans as well.
Others were from the countryside, as well as villagers and pilgrims;
likewise, there were other people who desired the virtues of the True Dharma.
Having all arrived there, they beheld that sage Śrīghana;
having bowed, circumambulated, and honored him in due order with joy.
Then all of them, having bowed and placed him at their head on every side,
stood with concentrated minds to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all assembled,
taught the supreme Dharma, beginning with the practice of awakening.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, all the worlds were awakened;
having gained enthusiasm for the means of attaining perfect enlightenment, they rejoiced exceedingly.
And at that time, in Śrāvastī, there was a householder who was wealthy, possessed of great riches, faithful, illustrious, like Kubera himself, and accomplished.
Then, he went to the delightful Jetavana monastery to behold there the Fully Awakened One, Śrīghana, the Lord of Sages.
There, having seen that lord of sages, Śrīghana, seated in the assembly hall, the merchant was filled with joy; he prostrated himself and approached him.
There, having circumambulated him and bowed with joy and palms joined,
he drew near before him to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
Seeing him seated nearby, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
perceiving his pure intention, taught the Noble Truths.
Having heard that Noble Truth, the merchant was awakened; weary of cyclic existence, he then desired to go forth into homelessness.
There, that merchant, his soul perfectly serene, rose up with joy;
bowing with palms joined to the Sage, he requested ordination.
"O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, I go for refuge to you;
out of compassion, it would be fitting for you to grant me the vow of renunciation."
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the Sage, seeing him and perceiving the purity of his intention, gave this instruction:
If you have faith, my child, in the vow of the Sugata’s teaching, come and practice with focused mind the holy life, the supreme vow.
Having spoken thus, the Teacher of the World touched that head with his left hand and formally received the merchant into the Buddha's teaching.
There, he was ordained by that Lord of Sages; shaven-headed and holding a mendicant’s bowl, the monk, clothed in his robes, shone with splendor.
Then that monk, self-knowing, a recipient [of offerings], and honored by the world,
gathered the requisites he had received and accumulated the goods obtained.
Whatever wealth he had acquired or accumulated, he never at any time made even a small portion of it a shared offering for his teacher, along with his fellow students.
Likewise, with a heart overcome by envy and a mind intent on evil,
he consumed everything for himself and gave nothing at all to anyone.
Then, at that time, having been afflicted by illness and joined with the law of time, he died;
remembering that accumulation of wealth, he was led away to the abode of the departed spirits.
Even though he had become a hungry ghost, upon remembering that accumulation of wealth, he returned to his own storehouse and remained there, occupying his own seat.
Then all those monks, seeing that deceased ascetic in that storeroom, struck the gaṇḍī and performed the ritual for his cremation.
Then, having taken him outside and performed the cremation rites with fire,
they all returned and arrived at the door of that storehouse.
Then, having opened the door of that cave and taken up his bowl and robe to inspect them, he beheld that hungry ghost.
Seeing that deformed ghost, holding an alms-bowl and clad in a monastic robe, all those monks wandered about, deeply agitated.
Then all those monks, standing before the Blessed One, bowed down and reported this entire account of what had occurred.
Having heard that, the Blessed One, for the sake of favoring that preta and to cause terror among the world, approached that place.
There, that preta approached from afar the Blessed One,
who was adorned with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor characteristics.
He beheld the Sage Śrīghana, whose radiance surpassed a hundred suns, who shone for a fathom’s width, who was adorned like a jewel-limbed being of auspicious splendor.
There, that hungry ghost, his heart pierced by shame upon seeing [the king],
stood with palms joined in reverence, bowing down and weeping, his mind now filled with devotion.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that the preta had been inspired with faith,
addressed him in words with a voice as deep and resonant as Brahmā’s.
"O gentle-faced one, it was by you alone, with your own evil mind, that this was done for your own destruction;
having taken up the bowl and robes, you have practiced the vow in vain."
Since you have been born in a state of woe, having become a preta of hideous form, what is the use of weeping here now? You must enjoy the fruit of your own past deeds.
It is well; now, in this very moment, clarify your mind toward me, and turn your mind away from these material requisites.
Lest you die here and go again to hell, take refuge in the Saṅgha; by that, you shall go to a good rebirth.
Having heard these instructions given by the Lord of Sages, that preta rose up and distributed the bowl,
the robes, and the goods to the Saṅghas.
Then, having bowed to the Saṅghas in the city and fallen at the feet of the Blessed One,
he joyfully and with palms joined confessed the evil he had committed.
O Blessed One, O Protector, O Omniscient One, whatever evil has been committed by me—
with a mind overcome by stinginess, being utterly deluded and of wicked intellect— [may it be purified].
O Teacher, I now reveal all of that before you;
therefore, forgive my transgression and may you, my Guru, be gracious.
When he had thus made his earnest request, the Blessed One, filled with compassion,
gazed upon that hungry ghost with a steady look and beheld him for a long time with joy.

Thereupon, for the sake of liberating him from that [wrong] means and for the purpose of directing him toward a good rebirth, the Blessed One gave this instruction regarding the sacrificial fee: Rm_31.58{58} //
"Indeed, whatever merit arises from this gift, may you obtain that merit;
arise quickly from this most dreadful world of the departed spirits."
Having heard what was thus commanded by the Lord of Sages, that preta was delighted;
having responded "So be it" and bowed, he became filled with joy.
Then that Blessed One, having fully taught the True Dharma— the means for attaining auspiciousness— to that preta, returned to his own abode together with the Saṅgha.
Thus, having heard that true Dharma spoken by the Jina, that preta took refuge in the Three Jewels and, being awakened, constantly practiced it.
Then, at that time, the deceased man, afflicted by a burning fever, smelled [the fragrance],
and having performed the recollection of the Three Jewels, he died and went to the abode of Yama.
Then, impelled by Yama, that preta, through his true merits arising from the recollection of the Three Jewels, departed from that place for the realm of the pretas of great supernatural power.
There too, filled with wonder when that had arisen, he constantly remembered that Lord of Sages and, having gone for refuge, worshipped him with faith.
Then he should reflect thus: "From where, and by what path, have I come?
By the power of what merit do I now obtain such great happiness?"
Thus, when his [suffering] was removed by the power of his mental merit—
through the merit of recollecting the Three Jewels— that possessor of merit reflected upon it.
Then, having recognized this and becoming eager to honor the Three Jewels,
he thought thus in his mind regarding how to behold the Perfectly Awakened One:
"Aha! I have obtained happiness through the grace of the Perfectly Awakened One;
therefore, I must now by all means behold that Lord of Sages."
Having reflected thus in his mind, that preta of great supernatural power bathed,
put on clean garments, and adorned himself with divine jewels and ornaments.
With his limbs anointed with the five fragrances, pure and with a purified intention,
he took up the five offerings for worship and proceeded to the hermitage of Jetā.
There, having illuminated the Jeta Grove on all sides with his radiance,
he proceeded joyfully to behold Śrīghana in the monastery.
There, having seen that Śrīghana, he was filled with joy; with palms joined in reverence, he bowed, circumambulated him, and drew near before him.
Then, having joyfully honored that Sugata, the Protector,
and having bowed with palms joined, he withdrew to a secluded spot to listen to the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that his mind was purified,
began the conduct of awakening and instructed him in the true Dharma as follows:
Listen, O virtuous one, to the cause of pleasure and pain in this saṃsāra; I shall explain it to you, so that having fully understood it and composed yourself, you may practice what is auspicious.
That person who desires true happiness in this cycle of existence must,
at the outset, go for refuge to the Three Jewels with faith and devotion.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, one should give gifts according to their desires;
one should dedicate the ripening of this merit toward my own perfect enlightenment.
A gift given in this manner yields a great fruit in its ripening;
it shall increase further by degrees and never diminish at any time.
One whose self is encompassed by this merit shall become a wheel-turning monarch, a lord of men;
a teacher, a sovereign of Dharma, a king, a Bodhisattva, and one of great steadfastness.
Even then, that great donor, out of a desire for the welfare of all sentient beings,
having made offerings to the Three Jewels, should give gifts according to their wishes.
Through the ripening of this merit, that wise man of pure intention,
having maintained the vows of excellent conduct, shall always venerate the Three Jewels.
By the ripening of this merit, he shall become the lord of the thirty-three gods;
even there, he will always and at all times worship the Triple Gem with faith.
While practicing the perfection of ethical discipline for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings,
one should mentally dedicate that merit toward the attainment of awakening.
By the ripening of this merit, he shall become the lord of the Suyāma heaven;
there too, he will always be diligent in honoring the Three Jewels with faith.
Practicing the perfection of patience for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings,
one should dedicate that merit toward the attainment of the state of perfect enlightenment.
By the ripening of this merit, he shall become the lord of the Tuṣita heaven;
there too, he will always go for refuge to the Three Jewels with faith.
Exerting oneself in the perfection of vigor for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings,
one should dedicate that merit toward the attainment of the state of perfect enlightenment.
Through the ripening of this merit, he shall become a Nirmāṇarati deity;
there too, he will always be intent upon honoring the Three Jewels with faith.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, delighting in the perfection of meditative concentration,
one should dedicate that merit for the attainment of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
Through the ripening of this merit, he shall become a sovereign lord who exercises mastery;
even there, he will constantly delight in serving the Triple Gem with faith.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, one who delights in the perfection of wisdom should mentally dedicate that merit toward the attainment of enlightenment.
By the ripening of this merit, he shall become a sovereign Brahmā;
even there, he will always be diligent in honoring the Three Jewels with faith.
One who maintains the application of skillful means for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings should mentally dedicate that merit toward the attainment of enlightenment.
By the ripening of this merit, one shall become a sovereign Great Brahmā;
there too, always through faith, one shall be diligent in honoring the Three Jewels.
Concentrated in his vow for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings,
he should dedicate that merit in every way toward the attainment of enlightenment.
By the ripening of this merit, he shall become a sovereign lord of Maheśa;
there too, he will always be diligent in honoring the Three Jewels with faith.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, one who is exerted in the perfection of power should dedicate that merit toward the attainment of awakening through profound meditation.
Through the ripening of this merit, one shall become a sovereign of Bodhisattvas;
there too, always through faith, one will be fully inspired by the Three Jewels.
Delighting in the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, may he,
through that merit, attain enlightenment and become a Victorious One, a King of Dharma.
Then that Sugata, the Teacher, the Lord of the World,
the Guide, the Omniscient One, the Arhat, the possessor of great supernormal knowledges, the Tathāgata, the Sovereign of Sages—
Then, having conquered the hosts of Māra and illuminated the conduct of awakening,
and having established all sentient beings in virtue, he will pass into nirvāṇa and proceed to a happy rebirth.
Thinking thus, whoever in this saṃsāra desires an auspicious state should always be diligent in honoring the Three Jewels with such faith.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, let him practice giving with reverence;
then, through those merits, he shall gradually attain all the perfections as well.
"Having fulfilled [the perfections] and attained the great superknowledges, one shall reach awakening.
Thinking thus, those who desire what is auspicious should always practice virtue.
Through virtue one shall go to a good rebirth; through evil one shall go to a miserable state.
But evil arises from greed, born from a mind defiled by envy.
Even though he desires happiness, such a person, being always evil-minded and wicked, finds no happiness at all; he is one who takes his refuge in miserable rebirths and the hells.
The fool who reviles the true Dharma will become devoted to evil deeds;
therefore, casting aside stinginess, one should uphold the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having made the vow for perfect enlightenment, one should always practice in well-restrained conduct.
Through the ripening of this merit, may he always enjoy the happiness of cyclic existence,
be enthusiastic in honoring the Three Jewels, and delight in the conduct of awakening.
Then, having fulfilled all the perfections in their proper sequence and attained auspicious awakening, one shall reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Thus, having fully understood this, you have gone for refuge to the Triple Gem;
having resolved upon the mind of awakening, always practice within the excellent restraint.
In that way, may there always be well-being for you at all times and in every respect;
having attained awakening in due course, may you reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, he was awakened;
and having promised "So be it," he rejoiced, being filled with serene faith.
Then, having joyfully prostrated before that Lord of the World with palms joined,
and having circumambulated him three times, he bowed again and returned to his own abode.
Having arrived there with a serene mind, that preta of great supernatural power also took refuge in the Three Jewels and always conducted himself with joy.
Having seen that radiance during the night, all those monks were filled with wonder;
rising in the morning, they bowed and questioned the Lord of Sages.
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, who has come here tonight?
Having related this event, please awaken us all.
When he had been questioned thus by those monks, the Blessed One, that Lord of Sages,
seeing all those members of the Saṅgha, instructed them in order to awaken them.
Listen, all you monks: I shall relate in great detail this entire account of how he who came here tonight arrived.
That merchant, who was a great devotee of the Sugata’s teaching,
having joyfully gone forth with faith, practiced the holy life here with delight.
Though he had gone forth as a renunciant, he was overcome by stinginess and possessed evil intentions;
having acquired wealth, he never gave even the slightest thing to anyone at any time.
Having merely made a collection and placed it in the storehouse,
they guarded it with great effort and did not distribute even a small portion of it.
Then, when that time had arrived, having reflected upon his accumulation of wealth,
he died and was reborn in the realm of the pretas, appearing as terrifying as the very nature of a preta.
Remembering that accumulation of wealth, his mind agitated by stinginess,
he returned once more to his own abode and sat down in despondency.
Having seen that preta stationed there, I approached him;
having taught him the noble Dharma, I awakened him and inspired faith in him.
Then, with a mind full of serene faith, he offered all those goods— his bowl and robes— to me and my community.
By the power of this merit, he took refuge in the Three Jewels;
then, passing away from that state in due course, he became a preta of great supernatural power.
There, with a heart full of serene faith, he joyfully recalled the Three Jewels and came here during this night to drink the nectar of my true Dharma.
Having drunk the nectar of the True Dharma in my presence, he was filled with serene faith;
eager to achieve perfect enlightenment, he dwelt joyfully in his own abode.
This man was the guild-president and no other who arrived here at night;
because he relied on the evil of stinginess, he became a deceased spirit (preta) after dying.
Therefore, those who desire what is auspicious should cast aside stinginess and renounce it;
for stinginess is declared to be the root of evil throughout the three worlds.
Thinking thus, conquer in every way this most wicked enemy, avarice, which in this saṃsāra is a mine of suffering and the ender of happiness.
Those who have indeed uprooted stinginess from their own minds are alone the truly proud,
the heroes, the brave, the wise, and the discerning.
And those who are unable to conquer envy in any way whatsoever— how can they be heroes, victors, or men of distinction, when they are merely consumers of the afflictions?
Those in whose minds envy— the source of evil deeds— does not arise, they alone are happy, radiant, victorious, and destroyers of the afflictions.
As long as stinginess, that evil disposition, is not conquered in the mind, what is the use of your being brave heroes, O you who in an instant follow after the afflictions?
Those heroes who are under the power of the afflictions are neither steadfast nor wise;
for a mere moment, their intentions become distorted as they act upon some slight sign.
Then those deluded ones, tormented by the afflictions, burned by the fire of passion,
and scorched by the fire of malice and anger, would perceive nothing at all.
Consequently, like the blind in the light, they would not walk upon the true path; instead, being intoxicated by passion and heedless, they would wander only along wrong paths.
Then, those who follow the conduct of Māra, being attached to wicked people and possessing false views, will act according to the instructions of evil friends.
Then, having disparaged the true Dharma, they will constantly and with focused intent exert themselves to create obstacles to the practice of giving and other virtues.
Then those wicked evildoers, acting like madmen though claiming to be protectors,
being themselves ruined, would likewise bring ruin upon others as deceivers.
Then, tormented by afflictions and devoted to great expedients,
they commit most terrible sins with their intentions filled with fear.
Then, even after eating food they desired, they would become attached even to forbidden women; behaving perversely, they would roam about in mutual hostility.
Then, bitten by the serpents of their sins, struck down by great suffering,
and overwhelmed by intense agony, they died and went to the abode of Yama.
There, King Yama, having seen that person of evil intent,
immediately handed him over to the executors of his deeds and urged them on.
There, the messengers of Yama will seize them suddenly by force and,
according to their karma, punish them in accordance with the prescribed rule.
There, having enjoyed those pleasures intended for the gods, they will be driven by the messengers of Yama to wander even through the hells in order to experience [further suffering] on all sides.
There, having experienced those enjoyments intended for the gods, they become exceedingly distressed; overcome by unbearable agony, they sit down, wretched and emaciated.
Thus, having enjoyed those pleasures fit for the gods for a long time, they eventually fell from there and,
having gone to the hells, experienced only sufferings in hell.
When, at the end of their destiny, they are struck by intense and extreme suffering,
they shall, with equanimity, recollect the Three Jewels and pay homage.
Then, having seen those Sugatas and being thoroughly impelled by compassion,
they shall lift them up with the radiance of their eyes and send them to the abode of the gods.
There, endowed with happiness, they shall joyfully remember the Three Jewels;
having always taken refuge in them, they shall proceed with concentrated minds.
Likewise, through the ripening of that merit, having entered the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One,
they shall perform acts of veneration with faith and listen to the Dharma with respect.
Having obtained that taste of the nectar of the True Dharma, they will be completely gladdened;
having attained the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), they will practice giving with reverence.
Then, through the ripening of that merit, being well-disciplined and striving for restraint,
they shall accomplish the auspicious conduct by bringing about the welfare of all sentient beings.
Then, having conquered the hosts of enemies that are the afflictions through the very power of vigor,
those pure-souled ones, absorbed in yoga, meditated.
Having reached the further shore of the ocean of wisdom, they shall obtain the jewel of knowledge;
then, having conquered the hosts of Māra, they will be completely purified in the three spheres.
Having attained perfect enlightenment, may they reach the state of a fully awakened Buddha.
Thinking thus, one should sever the root of all evils— namely, stinginess— in this saṃsāra, and always practice what is virtuous while seated upon the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
Then may there be constant auspiciousness for you in every way throughout existence;
having gradually attained awakening, you shall reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard these instructions given by the Lord of Sages, all those members of the Saṅgha were delighted; having awakened to the truth, they rejoiced with serene minds.
"Thus was it instructed by my teacher, and thus have I heard it;
so you too, O King, having abandoned envy, always conduct yourself in what is auspicious."
And you, O King, having diligently awakened the people,
should always establish them in virtue by directing their intention toward the conduct of awakening.
In this way, may you always have prosperity in every respect throughout all states of existence;
and having gradually attained awakening, may you reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, King Aśoka,
together with his retinue, replied, "So be it," and rejoiced.
Those greedy merchants who, with minds overcome by misfortune, hear this *Pretībhūta-avadāna* or cause others to hear it with joyful hearts and faith—

having abandoned stinginess, taken refuge in the Three Jewels, and being devoted to all sentient beings— they give gifts with serene minds, constantly practice virtue, and go to the abode of the Buddhas.
Thus ends the *Pretībhūtāvadāna* within the *Śrīratnāvadānatattva*.
XXXII. The *Virūpāvadāna*.
Then King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence and filled with joy, bowed to the ascetic Upagupta and made this request with great devotion: Rm_32.1{1} //
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear yet another well-spoken word; it behoves you to instruct me just as you have been instructed by your own teacher."
When the king had thus made his request, that wise Arhat ascetic, having heard him and looking upon the great king Aśoka, instructed him as follows:
"Listen well, O Great King, to that which was spoken by my teacher; I shall declare it to you just as it was told, for the sake of the increase of your dharma."
Just as in this way, at one time in the past, that Lord of Sages, the Blessed One,
the Teacher of the three worlds, the King of Dharma, the Tathāgata—
The omniscient Śākyasiṃha, the Arhat, dwelt together with his Saṅgha in this monastery within the Jeta Grove at the Śrāvastī hermitage.
Then, in the midst of that assembly, he took his seat upon a well-adorned lion throne in order to teach the Dharma for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
There, all those monks had assembled, as well as the nuns,
the ascetics, the wanderers, and likewise the laymen and laywomen.
Bodhisattvas observing their vows and longing for the qualities of perfect enlightenment,
as well as Nirgranthas, other heretics, ascetics, and great seers—
The gods, such as Brahmā and Śakra, the world-protectors of great supernatural power,
as well as the Daityas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Rākṣasas.
The Siddhas and Vidyādharas, as well as the Nāgas and Garuḍas,
the Sādhyas, the Grahas along with the stars, the Vasus, and the hosts of Apsarases;
Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, kings and princes, Vaiśyas, ministers, counselors, guild-masters, and eminent men.
Householders, merchants, caravan leaders, and even the wealthy;
artisans, city-dwellers, and those from the countryside as well as those from abroad.
Villagers and pilgrims as well, seeking to hear the true Dharma,
all approached and sat down together in the monastery.
There, having seen that Śrīghana, they were all thoroughly gladdened;
having bowed and circumambulated him, they proceeded before him.
There, all those people, having honored that Lord of Sages in due order and having bowed down to him, took their places to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all taken refuge,
began the practice of the way of awakening and fully taught the true Dharma.
Having drunk that nectar of the True Dharma, all those worlds, beginning with the Tridaśas, realized it was truth and rejoiced, being awakened.
At that time, there lived in Śrāvastī a householder who was a citizen of the city,
immensely wealthy, glorious, and like a great mountain in his abundance.
Having brought his beloved wife— who delighted in her own family and practiced the dharma of her own lineage— he [placed her] in the Samyavyūha according to the prescribed rite.
Then, inflamed by passion, he, being constantly incited by that beautiful woman, took his pleasure with her, enjoying happiness according to his desire.
Then, while that householder was enjoying himself according to his desire,
in due time his virtuous wife, her limbs grown thin, became pregnant.
Then, in due time, she gave birth to a boy who was ill-favored in appearance,
ill-colored, of an evil form, deformed, and with a distorted body.
Seeing that boy, his mother’s hopes shattered and her heart despondent, she thought: "Alas for me! What is the use even of such a son?"
Then Janaka, having heard that he had been born with such a deformed body,
ugly and of an unfortunate appearance, reflected thus:
"Alas! What evil deed was committed by me in a previous birth, by which this son is born with such an unfortunate form and disfigured?"
Therefore, what means should I employ here? I do not even know;
fie on me, by whom—upon the birth of a son—happiness has been stolen away through shame!
Nevertheless, what shall I do? For by fate this child has been born to me;
therefore, even though he is deformed, this son must be protected by me as my own offspring.
Having heard what was said by her husband, that wife also spoke thus:
"Indeed, the fruit of whatever evil deed was committed by these two is being experienced."
That which is not destined to be does not become an object of enjoyment; and that which is destined to be cannot be otherwise.
All living beings experience only that which is destined to be enjoyed in every circumstance.
"Therefore, I shall protect this child here with great effort," having said this, that woman, her face distorted, stood there deeply ashamed.
And seeing that deformed son born, his father too became one whose heart was rent with shame, despondent and devoid of energy.
Alas! What sin must I have committed in a previous existence, that this boy has been born so deformed and of such ill-favored appearance?
Nevertheless, what can I do? For this indeed arises from destiny;
for all living beings must experience that which is to be enjoyed by destiny.
"Inevitably, these things happen to all embodied beings;
therefore, this young son of mine must be protected by me."
Having reflected thus, the father then beheld the face of that infant;
with his countenance overwhelmed by shame, he stood there contemplating the power of destiny.
Then, having summoned his kinsmen and performed the birth festival,
his father said to them, "Give him a name that is renowned."
Then all those kinsmen, having reached a consensus and having addressed that householder, instructed him thus in the city: Rm_32.38{38} //
"Householder, since this son born to you is deformed,
let him be known on earth by the name Bālaka."
(Rm 361) Then, out of affection, that Virūpa was nurtured with great effort by his mother;
gradually he grew and flourished like a lotus situated in a pond.
Then, when he had reached the state of youth,
Virūpa became ashamed upon seeing his deformed appearance reflected in a mirror.
Then, feeling ashamed, deformed, and utterly bewildered,
his soul tormented by sinful thoughts, he reflected thus in his mind:
"Alas! What sin have I committed that I am now of such wretched form?
What use have I for this body? Death here would surely be better for me."
"What shall I do? I am deformed; where shall I go with such a hideous appearance?
Of what use is this life of mine, which is nothing but a vessel for suffering?"
Therefore, having abandoned my home here and taken refuge in a forest grove,
I shall meditate upon the Perfectly Awakened One, the Sugata, and pass away for the sake of liberation.
Death will inevitably come to all living beings;
therefore, I have no desire for such a deformed life in this body.
If, living long in this world, I should meet with suffering while being reviled,
then, having meditated upon the Buddha, the Sugata, I shall remain [in that state] until the release of my life.
If I were to die now, having meditated upon that perfectly awakened Victor, then,
through that merit, my soul would surely go to a happy rebirth in every way.
Those who, mindful of the Buddha, the Sugata, meet death by their own hand, do not go to an evil rebirth; they indeed proceed to Sukhāvatī.
Therefore, being wise and virtuous, they should abandon their lineage and home;
having meditated on the recollection of the Fully Awakened One, they dwell in the solitary forest.
Having thus beheld that, I have gone for refuge to the Fully Awakened One;
and with mind composed and always mindful, may I dwell in the solitary forest.
Having thus reflected in his mind, Virūpa, with a serene intellect,
abandoned his prosperous home and took refuge in a dilapidated garden.
There in that secluded grove, taking refuge in a leaf-hut and recollecting the Blessed One, he remained absorbed in meditative concentration.
Then the Blessed One, the Teacher, perceiving him standing there with such a purified intention, prepared to deliver him.
Then the Blessed Lord, accompanied by the community of monks,
beholding Virūpa in that garden, approached him like the radiant sun.
Touched by its radiance, that deformed man was filled with true happiness;
filled with wonder, he beheld him approaching together with his assembly of monks.
Beholding that lord of sages, Virūpa was utterly bewildered;
feeling ashamed, he rose up and moved away from there to flee.
There, the Blessed One, seeing that Virūpa had fled,
suddenly obstructed his path with his supernatural power and stood before him.
Thus being restrained by that ruler, he, though deformed,
was in no way able to escape despite his great effort.
Exhausted in spirit, disfigured, and with a heart full of shame,
he stood there in fear like one blind by day, seated within his leaf-hut.
There, seeing him sitting dejected with shame, the Blessed One then entered the meditative absorption of the attainment of cessation.
Then, O Blessed One, that Teacher arose from that samādhi,
himself manifesting a deformed self with a distorted physical form.
Then, taking a clay bowl filled with food,
he slowly approached the leaf-hut of that Virūpa.
There, seeing that Virūpa of deformed appearance approaching him, Virūpa was filled with joy and spoke thus:
"Welcome, O friend! From where have you come here?
Stay; let us both dwell here in this permanent abode, endowed with happiness."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, the Blessed One, assuming that deformed appearance, said,
"I have come here to see you," and drew near.
Remaining there and engaging in conversation, the Blessed One, assuming that hideous form,
gave to that Virūpa food consisting of divine nectar.
Having eaten that food which had been given by the lord, Virūpa was delighted;
at that very moment, his limbs became fully nourished and his senses were gratified.
Then the Blessed One, the Teacher, seeing him filled with joy,
remained there in his own form, shining brilliantly as he radiated light.
Beholding him, whose limbs possessed a gentle and auspicious form, who was a mass of splendor and whose senses were purified,
that deformed man was struck with wonder and spoke thus:
"Aha! How is it that you are so exceedingly handsome?
Whose ripening of merit is this? You ought to tell me before my very eyes."
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
gazing upon Virūpa in order to awaken him, commanded him as follows:
"O virtuous one, I possess a great vidyā, the supreme means for achieving perfect awakening;
it is known as the Mother born from the clarity of mind, and it possesses great power."
By the power of that very [merit], O auspicious one, I have come to possess pure faculties,
with limbs and form like those of Samantabhadra, captivating the hearts of all sentient beings.
Having thus instructed them, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, sat upon that auspicious seat there and began to teach the True Dharma, illuminating all.
Then all those members of the Saṅgha, possessing gentle forms and auspicious faculties,
turned toward the Lord of Munis and stood before him, holding him in honor.
Seeing them all sitting together, gentle in appearance and pure in their faculties,
and perceiving that they were the Sugata, he was filled with wonder.
"Oh, what great fortune has been attained by me here now,
that this Lord of Sages has come for my sake together with his assembly!"
"Surely this Lord of Sages, impelled by my own past actions,
has come here out of compassion together with his Saṅgha to teach the sublime Dharma."
Therefore, having gone for refuge with faith to this Lord of Sages,
I am worthy to listen to the Dharma of the Sugata with reverence and a concentrated mind.
Having thus reflected in his mind, Virūpa was filled with joy;
approaching with palms joined in reverence and bowing down, he took refuge in that Lord of Sages.
Then, by the power of the Buddha's merit, prosperity appeared there for that Virūpa, bestowing divine enjoyments.
At that time, although he was deformed, he became divine, handsome, and beautiful;
though his three bodies were completely purified, he possessed the essence of virtuous qualities and a portion of auspiciousness.
Then, his heart overflowing with supreme faith upon seeing this great marvel,
he joyfully prostrated at the feet of that sage with palms joined in reverence.
Then, having risen and beheld that Lord, the Blessed One, together with his assembly, he, with a serene soul, made this request with great reverence:
O Blessed One, by the grace of the Teacher’s compassionate gaze,
this splendor has appeared here within me, and I have become exceedingly beautiful.
Having seen this great marvel, my mind finds delight in always practicing the vow of restraint while remaining under your protection.
Therefore, O Blessed One, O Protector, out of compassion for the Buddha's teaching,
it behoves you to take me under your care and establish me in the auspicious Dharma.
O Lord of the World, with faith I have gone for refuge to you;
having gone forth and taken up the vows, I shall practice here with concentrated mind.
Having heard that request thus made, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages,
perceiving his pure intention, addressed him and commanded as follows:
"If you have the desire, my child, to practice the vow of the Sugata, then first obtain your father's permission; once you have done so, he will grant it."
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, he was filled with joy;
having bowed with delight at the feet of that sage, he then proceeded on his way.
Having gone there to his own home, he bowed at his father’s feet with palms joined in reverence; standing before him, he spoke thus with great respect: Rm_32.93{93} //
Therefore, in that garden, overcome by shame and despondency at the thought "I am deformed," I dwell as one who knows yoga, sitting within a leaf-hut and meditating.
There, that Blessed Buddha himself, accompanied by his Saṅgha, having come in person,
being a knower of skillful means, awakens [beings] and bestows the enjoyment of the nectar of immortality.
Having consumed that nectar which was given, I have become beautiful in form;
Lakṣmī has also appeared, and thus such auspiciousness arises for me.
"Knowing that all this is solely through the grace of the Lord of Sages' compassionate gaze, and certainly not otherwise, O Sugata, be forever gracious."
Having seen this great marvel, my mind has become serene;
today, it pleases me to practice the vow within the teaching of the Buddha.
It is with joy that I have come here previously to make this prayer;
therefore, O Father, please grant me your permission for this out of compassion.
By the distribution of this merit, may you also go to a happy rebirth;
and having enjoyed happiness there at all times, may you proceed to the abode of the Victors.
Thinking thus, be gracious in this matter; do not set your mind otherwise. Granting favor through faith, bestow upon me your permission.

Having heard this prayer, that householder was filled with wonder; seeing his own son after a very long time, he spoke to him thus: Thus, having heard this request, that householder was struck with amazement; seeing his own son after a very long time, he spoke to him as follows.
Oh, how fortunate and meritorious you are, my son,
since that one has now approached out of compassion and protects you as a Buddha.
If you have that desire to practice the vow of the Sugata,
go for refuge to the Buddha and observe the vow with a concentrated mind.
Having heard what his parents had said, Virūpa was appeased;
bowing at his parents' feet, he immediately departed from the house.
Then, having gone to the hermitage of Jetā, that Virūpa was filled with joy; bowing at the feet of the sage, he made this request with great reverence: Rm_32.106{6} //
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, you who have received permission and have come together with the assembly;
therefore, out of compassion, it behooves you to grant me the vow of restraint.
When he had thus prayed, the Blessed One touched his head with his right hand and formally received him into the teaching.
There he went forth, weeping; though deformed and shaven-headed, he shone, clad in his robes and carrying an alms-bowl.
Then that monk, self-knowing, self-restrained, and having conquered his senses,
realized that the conditioned states of cyclic existence are subject to momentary destruction.
Having shattered the multitudes of ignorance, he was resolutely intent upon the factors conducive to awakening.
Then that ascetic, devoted to the dhāraṇīs, vidyās, and samādhis,
having conquered the entire host of afflictions, directly attained the state of an Arhat.
Free from desire for the gains and honors of cyclic existence, possessing a stainless intention,
with the three bodies completely purified, he is non-conceptual and untainted.
He, a practitioner of celibacy and a knower of yoga, became worthy of honor, worship, and salutation even by the worlds of gods and asuras who wander within the three realms.
Then all those monks, having seen that supreme ascetic, were filled with wonder; bowing to that sage, they asked him about his past deeds.
"Blessed One, what karma was performed by this Arhat in the past,
by which he is now born with such a wicked form and disfigured?"
And because he has been inspired with serene faith by you, the Blessed One, the Teacher,
he becomes fortunate, handsome, and devoted to virtuous qualities.
And because he has taken refuge with faith in this teaching of the Buddha,
he has suddenly conquered the hosts of afflictions and attained arhatship.
Therefore, having related in full detail all his life stories and everything he did in the past, awaken us all.
When all those monks had thus entreated him, that Lord of Sages,
having looked upon all those monks belonging to the Saṅgha, gave this instruction:
Listen, all you monks, to what was performed by him in the past;
I shall relate that entire karma for the awakening of the whole world.
Just as in the past there was the Buddha, the Tathāgata named Puṣya—
the omniscient one, the Arhat, the Teacher of the world, the King of Dharma, and the Lord of Sages.
Having brought about universal welfare on all sides, that Blessed One, the Lord of the World,
proceeded to teach the Dharma of the Sugata everywhere.
Thus, throughout all the worlds, that conqueror of Māra, together with his Saṅgha,
took up residence in a royal capital in the northeastern direction.
There, the Blessed One, the Teacher, who bears the welfare of all sentient beings as his purpose, taught the Noble Dharma, which is virtuous in its beginning, middle, and end.
Having drunk that nectar of the true Dharma, all the world was awakened;
having paid homage to the Triple Gem, they always proceeded toward what is auspicious.
There, the Blessed One Puṣya, surveying the world all around with his Buddha-vision, saw two sons of the Conqueror in order to bring about their welfare. (Rm 365) Rm_32.127{26} //
At that time, there were two Bodhisattvas, sons of the Conqueror: one named Śākyamuni and the other, the wise Maitreya.
The mental continuum of the wise Maitreya has been brought to maturity,
yet the beings who are to be trained by that Teacher have not yet been matured.
"But the lineage of those to be converted by Śākyamuni has not yet reached maturity.
Having seen this, the Sugata Puṣya reflected thus.
"Alas! Śākyamuni has not ripened his own continuum;
for the sake of ripening my own continuum, I shall practice in his presence."
Having reflected thus, that Tathāgata Puṣya, together with his Saṅgha,
went to the Himavat mountain and proceeded along, illuminating it.
Having entered that jewel cave, the Lord of Sages sat upon an auspicious seat, having meditated and attained the meditative absorption of the fire-element (*tejodhātu*).
And at that time, Śākyamuni, possessing noble intelligence,
approached his presence in order to gather fruits and roots.
There, in that jewel cave, he beheld the Sage, the Tathāgata Puṣya,
seated in the full lotus posture, absorbed in meditation and radiant with light.
Adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics,
blazing like a string of jewels, his radiance surpassed that of a hundred suns.
He gazed upon the King of Dharma, who was gentle, possessing a splendor exceeding that of the divine, whose form was auspicious in every way, and whose lotus-face was most serene.
There, having seen that Sugata, Śākyamuni was filled with joy;
suddenly bowing with palms joined, he honored him with offerings out of delight.
Then, standing on one foot for seven nights with joy, he made a prostration with palms joined and praised him with this verse: Rm_32.139{38} //
Neither in heaven nor on earth, neither in this world nor in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa,
neither in the divine residence of the gods nor in the cardinal or intermediate directions.
Let him wander over the entire, flourishing earth with its mountains and forests;
for where is there another great śramaṇa equal to this bull among men?
Having praised that Sugata, the Sage Puṣya, with these two verses,
Śākyamuni joyfully devoted himself to him for seven nights with great enthusiasm.
Then, at the end of seven days, having arrived with joy under the Puṣya constellation,
he gazed upon Śākyamuni, who was being praised all around, and spoke to him.
Excellent, excellent, O Great Being! It is well that you have thus exerted yourself;
by this power and vigor, O best of the twice-born, you are truly endowed.
Having praised the Tathāgata today, nine eons will pass;
then, having gradually fulfilled the perfections, you shall attain perfect enlightenment.
Having thus instructed him, that Lord of Sages, the Jina Puṣya, the sovereign of Dharma,
surrounded by those of great renown, remained there devoted to meditation and shone forth.
That Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, the best of the twice-born and possessed of great wisdom,
always took refuge in and honored that Puṣya with true devotion.
While the Buddha remained there, the goddess who dwelt in the cave was unable, by any means whatsoever, to enter that cave.
Then she, having become exceedingly misshapen, with distorted limbs and a hideous form,
assailed that Sugata Puṣya as he was absorbed in meditation.
Likewise, even after drinking for a very long time, that evil-minded Bhīṣma was not able to disturb in the slightest the mind of that sage.
Then, apprehensive, distressed, and her mind struck with wonder,
she approached him, bowing down, to behold him in his true form.
There, he beheld that Sugata, the Tathāgata Puṣya, the Lord of Sages,
adorned with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor characteristics.

He beheld him whose gentle radiance surpassed all else, whose splendor exceeded that of a hundred suns, whose form was peaceful, whose limbs were most auspicious, and who was absorbed in meditative concentration.
Upon seeing him, she thought, "This is a virtuous soul who has attained great perfection," and approaching him with a beautiful form, she showed her favor.
There, having bowed with palms joined before the feet of that sage and standing in his presence, she, being deeply humbled, requested him thus to grant her forgiveness.
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, forgive what I have done toward you; O Lord of the World, for you are indeed the sovereign of the dharma of patience.
Therefore, O Protector of the World, I have come to you for refuge;
having always taken full shelter in you, may I worship you with faith and joy.
O Lord of the World, since I desire to honor you here together with your Saṅgha according to the prescribed rites, it would be fitting for you to dwell there.
When he had thus requested it, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages,
seeing that she was pure in intention, remained silent and consented to it.
Considering that the Teacher had thus accepted [the invitation],
she rejoiced and quickly and suddenly prepared the full array of food offerings.
Then, having approached with joy, she honored that lord of sages with the components of worship and fully satisfied him and his assembly with divine foods.
Then, even after the meal was finished, she bowed with palms joined in joy; having asked for forgiveness, she made this request while standing humbly before him: Rm_32.162{61} //
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, abiding in your refuge, I shall serve you with constant attendance, remaining composed in mind.
Therefore, O Lord of the World, forgive whatever I have done in vain;
may you, the Teacher, the Perfectly Awakened One who is the source of forgiveness, be gracious.
Having heard this request made by her, the venerable sage Puṣya looked upon that goddess and taught her the True Dharma.
Listen, O Goddess, to the Dharma for the sake of attaining auspiciousness in this world and the next;
protected by Dharma in the world, one shall be happy everywhere.
Therefore, at the outset, one should listen with faith to the excellent Dharma of the Sugata;
thereafter, having honored the Triple Gem, one should give gifts to those who seek them.
Then one becomes possessed of the three pure bodies, possessing pure morality and virtuous intention;
thereafter, one attains the meditative concentration of truth and becomes a source of patience for all sentient beings.
Through exertion in the practice for the sake of perfect awakening, one shall utterly conquer all afflictions;
thereafter, established in meditative absorption and concentration, one shall obtain the jewel of wisdom.
By the power of that sublime jewel, conquering all Māras for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, may he attain the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Thinking thus, those who always desire what is auspicious in this saṃsāra should,
after hearing the Dharma, always practice giving according to their wishes.
And if you too always desire such happiness endowed with virtue, then,
having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, practice giving as you wish.
Dedicate this merit toward the attainment of perfect enlightenment;
by the ripening of this merit, you shall surely attain awakening.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, that goddess, being thus enlightened, joyfully promised "So be it" and rejoiced.
Then that Sugata, the Tathāgata Puṣya, together with his Saṅgha,
rising up while illuminating [the world], took refuge in his own hermitage.
For this one here is Virūpa, and that deity who dwells in the cave;
you must consider this to be the truth indeed, and certainly not otherwise.
Thinking thus, those who always desire happiness in this saṃsāra should worship the Three Jewels and always practice what is virtuous.
In the ripening of wholesome karma, there is always only wholesomeness;
likewise, for black [karma] there is only suffering, and for mixed [karma], there is a mixture.
Karma is never exhausted anywhere at any time without being experienced;
by whomsoever an action was performed, by that very person its fruit is experienced.
Karma is not burned by fires, nor is it moistened by waters;
it is not dried up by winds, nor does it perish within the earths.
Action never occurs otherwise than as it was performed, nor anywhere else in any way whatsoever;
in whatever manner an action was originally committed, it will certainly bear fruit in that very same manner within one's family.
That deity, dwelling there in the cave with evil intent,
having assumed deformed limbs and hideous eyes, assailed Puṣya.
As the ripening of this evil deed, for even five hundred births he was always in this world of existence one with deformed limbs and distorted eyes.
Freed from this sin, even now in this very place, he who was deformed, misshapen, and possessed of an unfortunate appearance has become beautiful.
And that deity, her heart tormented by remorse,
became devoted to Puṣya the Buddha and went for refuge.
Having honored him with divine foods and served him with joy through faith,
they obtained infinite happiness in existence as the ripening of this merit.
Having approached this very teaching of the Buddha with faith,
he attained the vows of renunciation and directly realized arhatship.
Thus, having fully understood this, always practice what is auspicious;
then, having attained awakening, you shall reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, all those members of the Saṅgha rejoiced, saying, "It is true," and they reflected upon it.
Thus has it been instructed to me by my teacher, and here it is told by me; you too, O Great King, must always conduct yourself in this way for the sake of what is auspicious.
And likewise, O King, having diligently awakened the subjects and established them on the path to enlightenment, one should always protect them with great care.
By that, may there always, eternally, and everywhere be auspiciousness for you;
having gradually attained awakening, may you reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, King Aśoka, being awakened, agreed,
saying "So be it," and rejoiced.

O humans, those who with joyful minds hear or cause others to hear this *Avadāna* of Virūpa as taught by the Teacher and others, and those who, delighting in merit, [listen] with glad hearts— all of them,
endowed with glory and possessing every virtue, having experienced true happiness and being devoted to the Buddha, go to the supreme abode of the Sugata and attain great joy.
Thus ends the Virūpāvadāna within the Ratnāvadānatatva.
XXXI. The Kṣemāvadāna.
Then King Aśoka, standing before him with palms joined in reverence,
bowed down to the ascetic Upagupta and spoke once more as follows:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken word;
it would be fitting for you to teach it just as it was explained by my teacher."
When the king had thus made his request, that wise Arhat ascetic, having heard him and gazing upon King Aśoka, spoke as follows:
Listen, O illustrious King, to that which was spoken by my preceptor;
I shall relate it to you exactly so, for the sake of the increase of your dharma.
Long ago, in the city of Śrāvastī,
there was a great king, a lord of the earth, known as Prasenajit, the ruler of Kośala.
At that time, in Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta;
he was a great monarch, a protector of the earth, and a sovereign of kings.
Then, due to the commencement of a great battle between those two rival kings, the ocean became agitated in its depths.
There, that Kṣatriya king Prasenajit, the lord of men,
having performed the rites for auspiciousness, was accompanied by all the women of his harem.
Accompanied by his fourfold army, making a great roar with high spirits,
he raised the Vaijayantī banner at the border of the Kośala kingdom.
Having gone quickly to the outskirts, endowed with vigor and enthusiasm,
he tied up a wooden plank there and stood upon it as if in a city.
Having heard that, King Brahmadatta, the Kṣatriya sovereign,
performed the rites for auspiciousness and set out accompanied by his inner apartments.
Accompanied by his fourfold army, proclaiming his enthusiasm for victory and raising the Vaijayantī banner, he approached the bank of the river.
Taking refuge right there, endowed with vigor and enthusiasm,
he remained in that city as if having fashioned a wooden frame.
There, that king, the lord of men Brahmadatta,
being deeply enamored, took his pleasure with his chief queen, providing her with all manner of service.
Then that queen, delighting in sport with the king,
being pale-complexioned and taking pleasure in eating little, manifested the signs of pregnancy.
Likewise, at that very moment, King Prasenajit,
deeply enamored, took his pleasure with his queen, sporting with her.
Then that great queen, who followed her husband’s play,
though having little appetite for food, being fair-complexioned, bore the signs of pregnancy-longing.
In due course, when the great queen had lost her advanced pregnancy,
the two women with slender limbs became thin, their breasts full yet turned the color of turmeric.
Then, in due time, the chief queen of King Brahmadatta,
the lord of the earth, gave birth to a son of divine portion who was exceedingly beautiful.
Having heard that, King Brahmadatta was filled with joy;
approaching him suddenly and seeing his son, he could not reach satiety.
On that very same day, at the proper time, the wife of that king Prasenajit also gave birth to a daughter who was divinely and exceedingly beautiful.
Endowed with the characteristics of a jewel among women, her limbs were beautiful and captivating; she was like Rati, auspicious in form, pleasing, and resembling the goddess of delight.
Having heard that, King Prasenajit was filled with grace;
approaching her suddenly, he beheld his daughter with exceeding joy.
Upon seeing her, that lord of men also became as if possessed by me;
gazing at her alone for a very long time, he remained perfectly motionless.
For both of those kings, shoulder-bearers were appointed,
who constantly carried news of their activities as offerings to their respective lords.
When the spies of Prasenajit heard that a son had been born to King Brahmadatta, they recognized him and were filled with joy.
Having approached King Prasenajit suddenly,
they bowed with palms joined in reverence and made this announcement right before him:
Victory to you, O Great King! Listen to what has occurred there:
a son has now indeed been born to King Brahmadatta.
At present, O King of Kings, auspicious enthusiasm is prevailing there;
therefore, having established a relationship with you, he shall return to his own city.
Therefore, be gracious, O Great King; do not fear, for it shall turn out well.
Having made peace with him, may you dwell in happiness as you please.
Having heard what was said by them, King Prasenajit,
realizing that this was indeed the truth, became serene and free from doubt.
Likewise, those secret agents who had been dispatched by Brahmadatta then heard that a daughter had been born to Prasenajit.
Then, having suddenly approached there in the presence of King Brahmadatta and bowed down, they reported this as follows:
Victory to you, O Great King! Listen to what has occurred there:
a daughter has now indeed been born to King Prasenajit.
That maiden was of beautiful limbs, like a celestial nymph, resembling the goddess Rati;
she was endowed with all auspicious marks, lovely, and like the very embodiment of delight.
Therefore, O Lord, auspicious enthusiasm now proceeds therein;
for that reason, he ought by all means to establish a connection with this place.
Having heard what was thus spoken by them, King Brahmadatta,
acknowledging it as "well said," reflected in this manner right there.
Oh, how wonderful is this great fortune on a single day,
since a noble son has been born to me here, and to that noble son, in turn, a daughter is born!
Therefore, having respectfully requested that auspicious lady, who is the very embodiment of beauty, from Prasenajit,
let us establish an alliance with him here for the sake of our son and proceed accordingly.
Having thus resolved, King Brahmadatta was appeased;
he summoned his noble messenger and spoke to him thus in the presence of the city: (Rm 371) (Rm_33.40{40})
"Go, messenger, with respect to that protector of the earth, Prasenajit;
having approached him, entreat him on my behalf with these words of mine, awakening his mind."
King Brahmadatta speaks thus with great respect:
"I now desire to establish a relationship with you."
Since our two sons were born on the same day,
your daughter is known as Bhadrikā, and my son is also named Bhadrika.
Therefore, we ought certainly to establish a relationship between these two;
thus, you should grant your own daughter to my son.
Even though such an alliance has been established, as long as we both live,
there will surely be a permanent cessation of enmity, and the bond of friendship shall not be broken.
Then, for both of us, there will always be well-being in all directions regarding the sense objects;
it will be free from calamity and filled with auspicious energy—of this there is no doubt.
"O virtuous one, by my word, King Prasenajit of Kośala is to be petitioned by you; may you have auspicious success on your journey."
Having heard these instructions from the lord of men, that messenger was enlightened;
saying "So be it," he bowed to the king, rose up, and then departed.
Having gone there in haste, he approached King Prasenajit,
bowed with palms joined in reverence, and standing before him, spoke as follows.
Victory to you, O Great King, Lord! For the purpose for which I have come here, I shall now fully declare; you ought to listen.
The great king Brahmadatta joyfully inquires after your welfare at all times, constantly and in every respect, even throughout all his realms.
Furthermore, that king Brahmadatta spoke thus once more:
"I now desire to establish a relationship with you."
Since the two children were born to us here on the same day,
your daughter is known as Bhadrikā, and my son is also named Bhadrika.
Therefore, we ought certainly to establish a bond between these two;
thus, you should grant your own daughter to my son.
Even though such an alliance has been made, as long as we both live,
there shall surely be a permanent cessation of enmity, and our bond of friendship shall not be broken.
Then, for both of us, there will always be well-being in every respect;
it will be free from calamity and filled with auspicious energy—of this there is no doubt.
"O virtuous one, at my word, King Prasenajit of Kosala should be entreated by you; go therefore with a concentrated mind."
Having thus instructed me, O Great King, I have indeed been sent by King Brahmadatta, the ruler of the earth, into your presence.
O King, just as it was commanded by that lord of kings, so too must you act; this is the way and not otherwise.
Thus, may there always be well-being for you as long as you live;
may there surely be auspiciousness and vigor in every respect—of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too ought to bestow your daughter Bhadrā here upon the son of King Brahmadatta.
Having heard what was thus related by him, that lord of Kośala remained silent for a moment and reflected within his mind as follows:
"Aha! Peace arises for me, since that lord of kṣatriyas, having abandoned enmity, now desires to form an alliance."
Therefore, having now given this daughter Bhadrā to that king exactly as he commanded, I shall establish peace for the attainment of auspiciousness.
When this is done, there will surely be constant security everywhere, even among all objects of the senses, for both me and that king; it cannot be otherwise.
Having thus reflected and reached a firm conclusion, Prasenajit of Kośala addressed that messenger, looked upon him, and spoke as follows:
"O virtuous one, I shall always carry out with reverence and firm resolve that command given by the lord of men, just as it was instructed."
"O virtuous one, having thus related all this in great detail according to my word,
you ought to please that lord of men."
Having heard what was thus declared by that lord of men,
the messenger, being gratified, replied "So be it" and rejoiced.
Then that messenger, having joyfully bowed to, beheld, and taken leave of that king, the lord of Kośala, departed from there filled with delight.
Then, having gone quickly and approached King Brahmadatta,
he bowed at his feet with palms joined in reverence and spoke as follows:
Victory to you, O Great King! May you prosper now by good fortune;
consider that everything you have desired has been accomplished.
"Just as you have commanded, so have I informed him.
Having heard this, the king was delighted and gave his assent.
Thus, having firmly resolved upon the truth, protect it as it has been taught;
then, O auspicious one, may there always be well-being for you in every respect, even amidst all sensory objects.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, King Brahmadatta,
being enlightened, rejoiced and was filled with serene confidence.
Then King Brahmadatta, the lord of the earth, accompanied by his fourfold army and sounding instruments of victory, celebrated with great festivities.
Then, being praised by the world and even by the gods, he set forth and,
traveling swiftly, arrived at his own city.
Then that protector of the earth, Prasenajit, being delighted,
set forth with his fourfold army, proclaiming his enthusiasm for victory.
Then, returning while being praised by the people and even by the immortals,
that king proceeded there and arrived at Śrāvastī.
Having arrived there in his own city, Prasenajit of Kośala sat upon the terrace of his palace, accompanied by all the women of his harem.
Seeing his daughter Bhadrikā, he, with a mind full of serene joy, repeatedly exclaimed: "Oh, what a blessing has been born for me!"
Then, having joyfully performed the birth ceremony for that daughter and summoned all his kinsmen, he instructed them in the city as follows:
"Venerable sirs, please listen: establish for this daughter of mine, Bhadrā, a suitable name that is well-known. (Rm 373) Rm_33.83{83} //

Since on the very day this girl was born we have attained security, let her therefore be named Kṣemā.
Thus all those kinsmen, having reached this consensus,
took leave of the Lord of Kośala, bowed down to him, and spoke as follows.
Listen, O King, to what our intention is as we declare it:
let him give her a name that shall be renowned upon the earth.
On the day that this daughter was born, there was safety in every direction; therefore, let her name be made famous on earth as Kṣemā.
Having heard what they had thus spoken, King Janaka joyfully bestowed upon his daughter the name "Kṣemā," as it had been requested.
Then that girl, nurtured by eight nurses,
grew and flourished like a lotus in a lake.
Likewise, King Brahmadatta, having gone into his inner apartments,
looked repeatedly upon that son and rejoiced, filled with delight.
Thereupon, having performed the birth festival for that infant, the king, his father,
summoned all his kinsmen and spoke thus in the city:
"Sirs, let a name be given to this son of mine, a child of auspicious appearance, one that is endowed with letters of good omen."
Having heard these instructions from the lord of men, all those kinsmen, filled with joy, gathered together in one place and spoke thus among themselves: Rm_33.94{94}
Since even as soon as he was born he brought security from all sides,
let his name certainly be Kṣemankara (Bringer of Security).
Thus all those kinsmen, having approached the presence of King Brahmadatta and bowed down, addressed him in this manner.
Listen, O King, to the name we shall give to this child; may that name, endowed with auspiciousness, spread your glory throughout the world.
Since even as soon as he was born, he brings security in every respect,
let him therefore be named Kṣemaṅkara (Bringer of Security), the Delighter of the World.
Having heard what was told by them, King Brahmadatta gave that very name to his son, which had already been widely known.
Then that boy, nurtured by eight nurses,
grew and flourished like a lotus in a pond.
Then, in due course, that prince attained the state of youth;
having relied upon his teachers, he gradually learned the scripts.
Having studied in this manner according to the proper sequence, that wise Kṣemaṃkara quickly attained mastery in all the sciences and arts, reaching the highest level of knowledge.
Then that lovely young prince, cherished by pleasure,
roamed about the city and took his delight together with his peers and ministers.
Then that girl Kṣemā, as well as the daughter of Prasenajit,
gradually reached the state of maidenhood, becoming lovely and most beautiful.
Then that auspicious girl, Sumati, who was devoted to virtue,
learned the art of writing in due course by attending upon her elders.
Having studied in this manner according to the proper sequence, that wise and discerning Subuddhimatī reached the further shore of all the sciences, arts, and branches of knowledge.
Then that noble lady Kṣemā, accompanied by her female friends,
rejoiced with joy upon hearing the Dharma spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One.
Then that prince Brahmadatta,
being exceedingly wise and longing for pleasure, desired to see Kṣemā Sundarī.
Then, having summoned a messenger and instructed him while propitiating him,
he himself should send him forth with a garland of excellent jewels for the sake of Kṣemā’s welfare.
Then that messenger, taking the garland and traveling swiftly,
arrived at the city of Śrāvastī and went to the residence of Kṣemā.
There, that messenger, seeing a certain female friend who had approached her, went up to her, greeted her, and spoke thus in secret: *Rm_33.111* {11}
"O Bhadrā, taking this jewel garland sent by Prince Kṣemaṃkara to Kṣemā, deliver it to her."
Having spoken thus, that messenger gave the jewel necklace into the hand of Kṣemā’s friend in private, took his leave, and departed suddenly for his own city.
There, that friend of hers went before Kṣemā,
presented that gift, and spoke thus in private:
O blessed lady, behold this auspicious [garland] sent to you by your husband;
embracing it, consider it as your husband himself.
Having heard what was spoken by her, Kṣemā, her heart filled with shame and terrified by the poisonous fire of passion, remained for the day with her face cast downwards.
Then that maiden Kṣemā, after a long time, addressed her friend who stood before her, and while causing her heart to tremble, spoke thus: Rm_33.117{17} //
"Are you speaking thus because my master is here? You shameless woman, tell me: by whom was this gift sent to you?"
Having heard this spoken by the wicked Kṣemā, that female friend related in detail the entire account of her life from birth to the present before the Lord.
Having heard what was thus related by her friend, that daughter of the king,
Kṣemā, became despondent in her heart, distressed by the wanderings of saṃsāra.
Then, rising suddenly from there, the maiden Kṣemā approached her father,
bowed at his feet, and with palms joined in reverence spoke thus:
"Father, I do not seek sensual pleasures, but rather the pursuit of virtuous qualities;
I shall cultivate those virtuous qualities, so please grant me your permission."
"Since I have gone forth into the Buddhist teaching and attained meditative concentration, having established myself in the holy life, O Lord, I ask to go forth and practice."
Therefore, O Father, out of compassion, grant me permission to accomplish the vow for awakening; in every way, please bestow your favor upon me.
Having heard this request made by his daughter, the lord of Kośala looked at the young girl and stood with a mind full of doubt.
Then King Janaka, having summoned and gazed upon his own dear daughter Kṣemā in order to awaken her [to the truth], spoke thus:
"O daughter, it is not possible for me to do this; therefore, forgive me, since by your birth such security has been produced in my kingdom."
Even then, my daughter, you were promised by me to Kṣemaṃkara, the son of King Brahmadatta, according to his vow.
Therefore, my son, fulfill the word as it was promised by me; do not, under any circumstances, obstruct my attainment of the peace of renunciation.
"I shall do exactly as I have vowed; it shall not be otherwise.
Having reflected thus, O daughter of a noble family, act according to the dharma of your lineage upon hearing these words of mine.
Having heard what her parents had said, Kṣemā was deeply grieved;
rising up and returning to her own quarters, she sat down in silence.
Then King Janaka, having summoned the messenger with respect and related this entire account, spoke as follows:
"Go, O virtuous one, to the city of King Brahmadatta, the lord of men; having reported this news there, awaken him in this manner."
Since this daughter of mine, Kṣemā, desires to go forth into the religious life,
you ought to come here at once and take her [as your wife].

having abandoned birth in cyclic existence, bring an end to suffering.
Having thus exhorted all the gods on every side with these proclamations,
all those rays returned there before the Sage.
There, all those rays, having become one and condensed into a single mass,
circumambulated the Sage and entered into the circle of hair between his eyebrows.
Seeing that, all the people seated in the assembly were filled with wonder and reflected thus: "What kind of Dharma might the Teacher teach here?"
Then Ānanda, having risen with palms joined in reverence and filled with wonder,
bowed to the Blessed One and made this request with great devotion:
"O Teacher, the Sugatas never laugh without cause or condition;
for what reason, O Lord of the World, do you laugh now?"
O All-Knowing One, upon seeing your smile, all these members of the assembly remain with their minds overcome by wonder.
Therefore, O Teacher of the World, having explained for what purpose you manifest a smile,
you ought to sever the doubt of all beings.
Having heard what was thus spoken by Ānanda, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages,
looked toward Ānanda and the assembly and commanded as follows:
"It is exactly so, Ānanda, just as you have said.
Indeed, Buddhas never manifest a smile without a cause or a condition."
O Ānanda, that for which I now manifest a smile here, I shall declare that truth; listen to it with reverence.
Since this wise park-keeper, Ānanda, out of faith offers me a tooth-stick and performs acts of hospitality, [I shall accept it].
By the ripening of this merit, for thirteen eons he shall never at any time go to any state of woe whatsoever.
This Great Being, always striving to accomplish the true Dharma,
possessing excellent virtues and enjoying happiness, will become a Bodhisattva.
Then, at the end, this one of great supernormal knowledge, with the three spheres completely purified,
having attained individual enlightenment, became a Pratyekabuddha, a Sugata, a Jina.
Named Vimala, he will be a benefactor and a bringer of welfare to sentient beings;
a practitioner of celibacy, pure in soul, he will become a protector of the world.
Thus, Ānanda, having understood this somewhere within the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One, even a small gift should be given; its fruit shall be even greater.
Having heard this instruction given by the Lord of Sages, all those members of the Saṅgha and the people seated in the assembly were enlightened and rejoiced.
And that monastery attendant, having heard that prophecy made by the Sugata,
always desired with joy to perform acts of veneration toward the Three Jewels.
Having heard that, the great donor, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada,
bowed with palms joined to the Jina and, filled with joy, went to his own home.
Then the Blessed One, the Teacher, having arisen together with the Saṅgha,
sat upon his own seat and remained absorbed in meditative concentration.
Then that laborer also, filled with joy from head to foot,
remained present and proceeded to practice the worship of the Three Jewels.
Thus was it instructed by my teacher, and thus have I heard it; so I speak.
You too, O Great King, should always honor the Three Jewels in this very way.
O King, having likewise diligently awakened the people,
you should always engage them in the enthusiastic practice of honoring the Three Jewels.
By that, may you always have auspiciousness everywhere at all times;
having attained enlightenment in due course, may you reach the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, King Aśoka,
together with his retinue, replied, "So be it," and rejoiced.
Whoever here hears this avadāna of the monastery attendant, and whoever listens to it attentively,
they shall all enjoy every kind of auspicious and excellent happiness and, having done so, go to the abode of the Victors.
Thus ends the Ārāmika-avadāna in the Ratnāvadānatatva.
XXXV. The Śobhita-avadāna.
Then the great king Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence and full of joy,
bowed to the ascetic Upagupta and made this request with devotion:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken word;
it behoves you to relate it to me just as it was instructed by your teacher."
Having heard this request made by him,
the wise Arhat Upagupta looked at that lord of men and spoke as follows:
Listen, O illustrious King, to that which was spoken by my guru;
I shall indeed relate it here for the sake of awakening your mind.
Namely: the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Lord of Sages, the Omniscient One, the Arhat, the Protector of the World, the King of Dharma, the Tathāgata.
That perfectly awakened one remained there in that city of Kapilavastu,
in the beautiful Nyagrodha grove, together with his community of monks.
And at that time, in that city of Kapilavastu,
there was a Śākya named Mahāsādhu, glorious and resembling the lord of yakṣas.
Known as the foremost in all the world and possessing an abundance of every kind of wealth,
he had a wife named Surūpā, who was beautiful and like Rati herself.
She was virtuous, lovely, beloved, and a follower of her own family's dharma;
with her, that illustrious one, being deeply enamored, took his pleasure.
Having enjoyed pleasures at his will, he sported, thoroughly delighted.
Then she, being beautiful, became pregnant;
