her belly gradually grew, she turned pale in complexion, ate very little, and became emaciated.
Then, O Sūta, at the proper time, she gave birth to a son who was divine and beautiful,
handsome with excellent limbs, gracious and captivating.
At his birth, many great wonders appeared as well,
by which the entire city was made resplendent.
Hearing that he had been born so beautifully adorned, his father approached him in haste with joy; beholding him, he stood there with a heart filled with wonder.
Then, filled with joy, he summoned his kinsmen along with his relatives; having performed the birth festival for him, he spoke in order to proclaim his name.
"O kinsmen, all of you, having observed his physical characteristics as they are,
ought to establish him according to a name that is well-known."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, and having observed the omens for his sake, all those kinsmen spoke thus to that Śākya: Rm_35.16{16} //
"O virtuous one, since he who is born from our selves shall adorn the city,
let his renowned name on earth be 'Śobhita' (The Adorned)."
Having heard all that was thus related by those kinsmen, he caused his son to be known by that very name.
Then, cherished and protected by eight nurses,
Śobhita grew and flourished like a lotus born from a lake.
When that boy had grown up and attained the state of youth,
his father then entrusted him to a teacher for the purpose of acquiring knowledge.
Then, by means of the scriptures, he was taught writing in due order by his teacher;
being thus instructed, he reached the end of all branches of knowledge.
Then that wise Śobhita, proficient in all branches of knowledge,
who had been devoted to the doctrines of the heretics, became disenchanted with the life of a householder.
Always going to the groves of the heretics, he took delight with the heretics in the enthusiasm of challenging them to treatises, vanquishing those who propounded opposing doctrines.
And at that time, the Blessed One, seated there in the Nyagrodharucira hermitage, began to teach the Dharma to the assembly.
Then all those monks, as well as the nuns who had assembled, the vow-observers, the mendicants, and other laymen and laywomen [were present].
Bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, and likewise other śrāvakas—
all of them approached together to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
There, having bowed to that Śrīghana and having circumambulated him on all sides,
they all stood before him, placing him at their head and gazing upon him.
Then other gods as well arrived, such as Brahmā and Śakra,
as well as the four world-protectors and all the lords of the worlds.
The Siddhas and Vidyādharas, as well as the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras;
the Rākṣasas, Garuḍas, and Nāgas, and others of great supernatural power.
Ascetics and yogins, as well as the Nirgranthas and other heretics;
sages and brahmins, as well as forest-dwellers and those practicing celibacy.
Kings, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, ministers, counselors, and common people;
guild-masters, wealthy men, citizens, caravan leaders, and great folk.
Merchants and artisans, as well as those dwelling in other lands, villagers and country folk, and even wandering pilgrims; Rm_35.32{32} //
Having all approached together and beheld that Śrīghana with joy,
they honored him in due order, bowed down, and performed circumambulations.
Having bowed again with palms joined and having circumambulated him on all sides,
they stood there with concentrated minds to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
Then Śobhita, having heard that and filled with curiosity,
suddenly approached that place to behold the assembly.
There, having approached suddenly, he beheld that lord of sages,
radiant and seated in the midst of the assembly of all the worlds.
Adorned with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor characteristics,
radiant with a fathom-wide halo, possessing a splendor exceeding a hundred suns,
gentle, with tranquil faculties, lovely, and possessing a form as auspicious as Samantabhadra.
Having seen him, his mind became exceedingly serene; he bowed down and performed a circumambulation.
In order to hear his teaching of the Dharma, he took up residence there in a secluded spot;
then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all assembled there, [proceeded].
Beginning with the Noble Truths, he fully taught the True Dharma;
then, having heard that Noble Dharma, all of them, including the gods and others, [were transformed].
(389) Having understood the excellence of the Dharma and being awakened, the people resolved upon the thought of enlightenment and became intent on honoring the Three Jewels.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, they became practitioners of the path to enlightenment;
at that time, Śobhita also heard the supreme Noble Truths.
Awakened and serene in soul, you have become detached from cyclic existence;
you have shattered the mountain of the view of a self-existent body, which rises with twenty peaks.
Having abandoned [the defilements] with the sword of knowledge, he attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truths, his soul purified, and longing for the virtues of the True Dharma,
he desired to go forth into homelessness in order to attain the state of a Perfectly Awakened One.
Then, having approached that lord of sages and master of the world with palms joined in reverence, he joyfully made this request of him:
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, I have come to you for refuge;
I desire to go forth into the religious life—therefore, out of compassion, may you be gracious.
Having heard this request made by him, the Blessed One, that lord of sages, looked upon Śobhita, addressed him, and commanded as follows: *Rm_35.47{47}*
If you desire to go forth into homelessness in the Buddha's teaching, then having obtained your father’s permission, come; I shall grant you the vows.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, Śobhita, filled with joy,
bowed at the feet of that sage and quickly departed from there.
Having gone there to his own home, he bowed at the feet of his parents and, standing before them, related this matter and requested thus with great reverence: Rm_35.50{50} //
"Father, today I am going to the Nyagrodharucira forest;
there I shall see that Buddha Śrīghana seated amidst his assembly."
Blessed are all those disciples, the Bhikṣus of the Bhadrika school,
whose faculties are tranquil, whose conduct is perfect, who are Arhats, and who lead the holy life.
For only those who have gone for refuge and devote themselves to the teaching of the Lord of Sages find their human birth fruitful within this cycle of existence.
And for those who, having heard the true Dharma of the Lord of Sages, practice self-restraint, their journey through existence in this cycle of rebirth shall be truly substantial.
And for them too, the essence of existence consists in the acquisition of birth, material goods, and virtues,
as they practice their vows by performing service to the Saṅgha with offerings.
What is the use of their human birth, which is a fruitless means for all accomplishments,
for those who, even after meditating upon and recollecting the Jina, never at any time worship him?
And for those who never anywhere hear the true Dharma spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One, what could their birth in this world be but a mere instrument of evil?
And their birth in the human state is fruitless and a means to suffering,
for they never at any time perform acts of reverence toward the property belonging to the Saṅgha.
Thus, for those who indeed dwell in their homes enjoying pleasures like cattle, what is the purpose of their birth in this cycle of existence? It is surely only for the sake of sin and suffering.
Thus all those living beings wander in the ocean of existence,
because they have never at any time seen the Three Jewels anywhere.
Likewise, for us as well in this saṃsāra, birth is fruitless;
for even prosperities are indeed meaningless without devotion to the Three Jewels.
(Rm 390) If dharma is not attained within this cycle of existence where birth serves the purpose of dharma,
what is the use of such a life that accomplishes nothing but the unwholesome?
Therefore, death this very day is better than such a life devoid of the means for achieving dharma and artha;
for what is the use of that life which is merely a means for false suffering?

Those by whom the great festival of worshiping the Blessed One has never been experienced, who have not heard any of the Dharma, and who have not performed acts of merit for the Saṅgha— [for them, there is no joy].
No safety was granted to those who were afraid, nor were the hopes of the poor fulfilled;
they merely became thorns in their mother's womb, leading only to her sorrow.
Blessed are they, happy in the world, most auspicious and pure in disposition;
those noble beings, great-souled and glorious, who are the refuge of virtuous qualities.
Those who, having gone for refuge to the Buddha, meditate and remain composed through mindfulness, drink the nectar of the true Dharma and practice the vow of the Sugata; Rm_35.67{67} //
Having given gifts as desired for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings,
they were compassionate, possessed of very gentle natures, and intent upon the welfare of all beings.
They are zealous in the practice for attaining perfect enlightenment, dedicated to the welfare of all sentient beings,
free from afflictions, pure in nature, and possessed of a mind immovable in meditative concentration.
Possessing wisdom, great in fortitude, and having attained the jewel of perfect enlightenment,
they were Arhats who had taken the vow of renunciation— free from conceptual construction and untainted.
Subsisting on alms, free from affliction and fear, with their senses subdued, they had completely conquered ignorance; having attained true knowledge, they were confident and self-assured.
Moving according to their own will, being the very self of all sentient beings,
they were free from longing, devoid of worldly exertion, without misery, and possessed of unshakable resolve.
Free from intoxication, free from egoism, noble, and devoid of pride;
free from deceit, free from the sense of "mine," unscarred, unattached, and without possessions.
With shaven heads, carrying begging bowls made of *khikkhira* wood, and clad in robes,
these ascetics possess the appearance of the Sugatas and teach the liberation of the three vehicles.

Those who abide in the four divine abodes, who teach the path to perfect enlightenment for the sake of the welfare of themselves and others, are to be venerated, worshipped, and accepted as authoritative.
They go to a happy rebirth, and in the end they go to the abode of the Victors;
having attained perfect awakening, they shall even become Sugatas themselves.
Having heard this truth thus commanded by the Lord of Sages, my mind no longer desires to wander here in this cycle of existence.
Having taken refuge in the Three Jewels within the auspicious teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One,
and having maintained the vows of renunciation, he now desires to practice the holy life.
Moreover, at the time of my birth, this [world] was illuminated by splendor;
my riches increased, and I became as beautiful as a celestial being.
"All that has now surely come to pass for me through the ripening of my former auspicious deeds and dharma; know this, O Father, and do not think otherwise."
Thinking, "This is surely so," my mind once again desires to perform the means for accomplishing the True Dharma, the vow of the Sugata.
For this reason, father, I entreat you with such earnestness;
therefore, grant me your permission, if there is any desire for what is auspicious.
By means of the distribution of this merit, you too, having gone to the abode of the gods and enjoyed celestial pleasures, shall dwell there for a long time.
Then, at that time, having fallen from heaven and come here to the world of mortals,
you shall always practice virtue after having paid homage to the Three Jewels.
Through the ripening of that auspicious merit, with pure intentions and possessing virtuous conduct,
you shall go to the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One and listen to the True Dharma with reverence.
Then, through the ripening of that merit, having gone for refuge to the Saṅghas and served them with honors, you shall attend upon them with great respect.
Then, through the ripening of that merit, you shall attain the mind of awakening;
thereafter, for the sake of the welfare of the world, you shall practice the conduct of awakening.
Then, having fulfilled all the perfections in due order,
and having subsequently attained awakening, you shall reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having understood this, for the sake of attaining the state of a perfectly awakened one,
he granted me permission, as I was desirous of that state of perfect awakening.
Indeed, saṃsāra is impermanent, life is fragile and perishing in an instant,
and the body of all who wander through existence likewise perishes in an instant.
Even prosperities are never stable, and a virtuous moment is extremely difficult to find;
birth in the human state is not always obtained, being exceedingly rare.

Even there, the inclination toward the Dharma is difficult to find; and even when it arises, it is not stable—especially that supreme Dharma of the Sugatas which is the means for accomplishing the state of perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining the state of perfect enlightenment, I desire the Dharma of the Sugata;
by granting me permission for that, please gladden my mind quickly.
Without Dharma, what essence is there here in objects of enjoyment, wealth, or even virtues?
What is the point of experiencing sensual pleasure or remaining in the home like a beast?
Therefore, since you will not grant me permission, I shall not remain even in my home;
having renounced all possessions, I will go to the forest of asceticism.
In that case, what is the point of staying in a secluded place and practicing difficult austerities?
I shall die by abstaining from food; death is certain everywhere.
For whom does death not exist? Where is there no fear of death? Death alone, possessing great power, devours all worlds.
Therefore, what is the use of despondency here, since there is no means to restrain this?
For events that are destined to happen occur even for the great.
At the time of death, there is no companion whatsoever who follows along;
indeed, at that time, the Dharma alone shall be the companion who follows along.
Thinking thus, virtuous people do not wish to remain in this saṃsāra;
seeking what is auspicious, they renounce all possessions and go forth into homelessness.
Likewise, having seen that fear of death and being filled with apprehension, I have gone for refuge to the Perfectly Awakened One and am resolved to practice his vow.
Thus, you should set aside all such matters and ought not to say anything at all;
rather, with a perfectly serene mind, you should simply grant me your permission.
Having heard this request thus made by their son,
his parents stood there, their minds overcome with astonishment and fainting.
Then, summoning their fortitude, the two of them, having finally beheld that very son of theirs after so long,
stood as if painted in a picture, afflicted by the pain of separation.
(Rm 392) Then that Śākya king Janaka, awakened by what he had said,
his face streaming with tears upon seeing his son, spoke thus: Rm_35.105{5} //
"Alas, my son! What indeed could I say now?
For you yourself are steadfast, wise, learned, and discerning."
Since you desire to go forth into the Buddhist teaching,
take refuge in the Teacher and practice the vow with a concentrated mind.
Having heard what was thus spoken by his parents, Sobhita was filled with joy;
having prostrated at the feet of his parents, he immediately departed from the house.
Then, having gone quickly, he entered the monastery adorned with banyan trees and approached the Sugata, the Arhat.
There, having gone before him with palms joined in reverence, he joyfully bowed down to that Lord of the World and made this request with great devotion: Rm_35.110{10} //
"O Blessed One, O Protector, O Omniscient One, having obtained your permission, I shall go forth;
therefore, it behoves you now to grant me the going-forth."
Abiding in your refuge, having gone forth and maintained the vow of the Sugata, and always taking up its precepts, I shall practice the conduct of awakening.
When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
touched his head with his right hand and commanded him as follows.
"Come, dear child, and having taken up the vow, practice the way of the Sugata.
Having said this, the Lord of Munis received him into his own community.
When the Lord of Sages said, "Come," he became adorned as a shaven-headed ascetic,
carrying a khikkhirī bowl and clad in a kāṣāya robe.
Then that monk Sumati, having become indifferent to the course of cyclic existence,
shattered all the masses of ignorance and attained confidence through his realization.
Having conquered the entire host of afflictions, he directly attained the state of an Arhat.
Then that Arhat, possessed of great supernormal knowledges, with the three spheres completely purified,
free from defilements, of perfectly pure self, with pure faculties, was a bearer of the portion of the Victor.
Free from conceptual construction, possessing equanimity, a celibate student, and stainless, he is devoid of longing for the gains and honors of worldly existence; his disposition is like space.
That son of the Conqueror became honored, worshiped, and saluted by all the worlds of gods and asuras who wander within existence.
Seeing that, all the monks, their minds agitated with wonder,
bowed to you and asked about those deeds performed in the past.
"Blessed One, what meritorious deed was performed by him in the past, and where,
such that he is born into a noble family and is as exceedingly beautiful as a celestial being?"
At his birth, there occurred even most wonderful deeds by which this entire city was made to shine as if with moons.
Moreover, in your teaching as well, one who has gone for refuge to the Three Jewels,
having maintained the vows of renunciation, may even become a mendicant and an Arhat.
Having related all of this, may you, the Teacher and Preceptor of the World,
deign to awaken us all and those present in this assembly.
When all those monks had thus entreated him, that Lord of Sages,
looking upon all the ascetics and the assembly as well, commanded them in this way:
"Listen, all you monks, to everything that was done by him in the past;
I shall relate it all for your complete awakening."
Just as in the past there was the Teacher Krakucchanda, the Tathāgata,
the omniscient one, the Arhat, the Lord of the World, the King of Dharma, and the Sovereign of Sages.
Then that Blessed One, illuminating the practice of enlightenment in the world and fully teaching the true Dharma, wandered everywhere.
Thus that Blessed One, the Teacher, having brought auspiciousness everywhere,
stayed in the hermitage near the great city and capital of Śobhāvatī.
Residing in a monastery, a dwelling of the Sugata, illuminating [the world] and teaching the true Dharma, he lived there together with his community of monks.
Having heard that the Lord of Sages had arrived there together with his assembly, the great king Śobha approached in order to see him.
There, King Śobha saw that Sugata,
the Sage Krakucchanda, seated and surrounded by the community of monks.
Approaching with joy, standing before him with palms joined in reverence, and bowing down with a most serene countenance, he made this request with great devotion: Rm_35.134{34} //
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, you are the Teacher and the Guru of the world;
therefore, for our benefit, it behooves you to teach us the Dharma.

When he had thus made his request, the Blessed One, looking upon Śobha, the lord of kings, gave him this instruction: *iti saṃprārthite tena rājñā sa bhagavān api / taṃ śobhaṃ kṣitipāleṃdraṃ samālokyaivam ādiśat //* Rm_35.136{36} //
Listen with focused attention, O King, for the sake of the welfare of all beings;
for the purpose of your own well-being, I shall speak to you of the Dharma that accomplishes perfect enlightenment.
Indeed, everything in saṃsāra is impermanent, empty, and without self;
the world of living beings has arisen from illusion and afflictions and is not eternal.

Therefore, O Indra among kings, having understood that what essence can there be in this [world], which is purposeless and a means to suffering, conquer the afflictions and conduct yourself in what is auspicious.
Through virtue one shall go to a good rebirth; in a good rebirth there is always happiness.
O auspicious lady, one should always conduct oneself with happiness; may you become such as that.
From merit, auspiciousness always and certainly arises everywhere;
indeed, merit first arises even from the sight of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
By the power of this merit, may one obtain the hearing of the true Dharma;
and being thoroughly attached to the savoring of the taste of that true Dharma, may one exert oneself with enthusiasm.
From that enthusiasm, a desire to hear further will arise;
and once that desire has arisen, one should honor [the teaching] with respect and joy.
Having approached a true guru, one should always listen to the true Dharma;
having attained the quality of tasting the nectar of that true Dharma, one becomes filled with joy.
A practitioner of the true Dharma should joyfully honor and respect the monks;
then, having heard that Dharma and desiring the qualities of perfect enlightenment,
he should venerate the Three Jewels and act for the welfare and benefit of both himself and others.
Through the ripening of this merit, he was born into a family that is a repository of glory;
for the sake of the welfare of the world, he should give gifts as desired.
Through the ripening of that merit from giving, that donor shall go to a happy rebirth;
established in a happy rebirth, he who possesses good conduct shall thus practice restraint with ease.

(Rm 394) By means of the merits arising from his excellent conduct and vows, that one of purified intellect should act with compassion and friendly speech for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings. Rm_35.148{48}
Then, through the ripening of that merit, that wise and discerning person shall accomplish all tasks for the sake of the welfare of both himself and others.
One whose self is purified by this merit, free from afflictions, and pure in intention, shall become wise, possessing the concentration of meditative absorption, dhāraṇīs, and vidyās.
Then, carrying the caravan of the qualities of awakening and the accumulation of merit,
and having reached the further shore of the ocean of wisdom, one shall obtain the jewel of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
By the power of that jewel, one who knows all methods and means,
for the benefit of all sentient beings, should practice the vow of the conduct of awakening, which is the treasury of all virtues.
By those merits, that Great Being, who brings auspiciousness to all sentient beings,
shall become one who delights in the True Dharma through his vow for perfect enlightenment.
Then, with a soul purified by Dharma, having utterly conquered the wicked afflictions,
he shall become one who gathers all that is beneficial for the sake of others, possessing the great superknowledges and power.
Then, having conquered the hosts of Māra and being completely purified in the three spheres,
he becomes an Arhat who has attained full awakening and reaches the state of a Perfect Buddha.
Then that Sugata, the Teacher, having made the world consist of Dharma and having established it upon the path to enlightenment, entered nirvāṇa and returned to his own abode.
Then that Jina, the Lord of the Dharmadhātu, remained absorbed in his own abode;
he is the stainless one, whose form is light, pure and universal in appearance.
Having understood this, O Lord of Kings, those who desire the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha should always practice virtue after having paid homage to the Three Jewels.
In that way, may there always be well-being for you in every respect;
and having attained awakening in due course, you shall reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard this instruction from the teacher, King Śobha,
being thus enlightened, replied, "So be it," and rejoiced.
From that time forth, that lord of the earth took refuge in the Three Jewels;
having acted for the benefit of all sentient beings, he always practiced what was virtuous.
At that time, in that place and regarding that subject, there was always an auspicious festival;
and all the people moved about with enthusiasm for their delight in the true Dharma.
In this manner, King Śobha served that lord of sages together with his community for three months, providing them with food according to their needs.
Then, at the end of three months, that king of the earth, having bowed to the Lord of Sages Krakucchanda together with his assembly, joyfully made this request:
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, you who are always accompanied by the Saṅgha, please deign to remain here out of compassion to teach the True Dharma to us.
When the king had thus made his request, the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World,
looked upon King Śobha and commanded him as follows.
"O King, I would not become a Sugata for the sake of your benefit alone; rather, as a Jina, I would come into existence for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings."
Thus, illuminating the conduct of awakening in all worlds,
may I wander together with the Saṅgha to proclaim the true Dharma.
(395) "O King, if you always possess devotion, faith, and a mind directed toward me, then, having erected a stūpa dedicated to my name, venerate it perpetually."
Whatever action is performed toward him is indeed performed toward me;
for those possessed of devotion, the fruit is equal, whether he remains in this world or has attained final liberation.
Just as you have gone for refuge to me with faith, O King of kings, so too,
having paid homage to the Triple Gem, proceed thus in virtue with joy.
Likewise, having always gone for refuge with faith to this stūpa,
and having performed worship to the Triple Gem, practice virtue with a concentrated mind.
Thus, may you always have security in every respect,
and having attained awakening in due course, may you reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having thus instructed Śobhā, the king, the Fully Awakened One (Saṃbuddha) cut off his own nails and hair and gave them to him with reverence for the purpose of a stūpa.
Having prostrated before that which was bestowed by the Lord of Sages, the king, filled with great joy and delight, accepted it and departed for his own palace.
There, that king, the lord of men, out of reverence placed those nails and hair within a relic chamber and had a magnificent stūpa constructed with precious gems.
Then that king, having installed him according to the prescribed rites,
constantly worshipped him with great festivals and served him with joy.
Then, on a certain day when an auspicious festival had arrived,
all the members of the assembly gathered together and came to behold that stūpa.
Seeing him, all those members of the assembly were filled with great faith and joy;
having honored him with various flowers, they worshipped him amidst great festivities.
There, one member of the assembly, seeing this and saying "I am poor," went to his own home out of shame during that great festival of worship.
Then, having seen him in his own house, all those members of the assembly reproached him repeatedly and expelled him from the midst of the assembly.
Then, distressed by shame and tormented by the fire of remorse, he thought: "Alas, how wretched I am! How shall I remain all alone?"
Then, recollecting the Sugata, even though he was poor, he gathered flowers from all sides and worshipped that stūpa with them.
Then, having circumambulated him with palms joined in reverence, he, filled with joy, bowed at his feet and made this aspiration with delight: Rm_35.184{84} //
"By the ripening of this merit from having worshipped the stūpa of the Lord of Sages here with flowers, may I become possessed of glorious prosperity."
Having made this vow, that poor man went for refuge to the stūpa; having worshipped it, he offered his devotion, thoroughly gladdened.
"Monks, let it be understood that he who was that poor man is indeed this Śobhita;
because the stūpa was honored with flowers, he has become thus possessed of abundant glory."
I shall also fully relate whatever other good deeds he performed in the past; listen to them all with respect.
Thus it was in former times, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a householder,
a merchant of great means, virtuous and skilled in business affairs.
Then one day, as he was walking slowly near his house,
a Pratyekabuddha who was ill approached him for alms.
Seeing him arrived near his house, he, struck with compassion, would suddenly approach, bow down to him, address him, and lead him to his own home.
There, that merchant, having seated that sick Pratyekabuddha upon a throne and honored him, joyfully covered him with a cloth.
Having offered him a vessel filled with milk-rice together with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
and having bowed with palms joined, he reflected thus in his mind:
Since this Sugata, while ill, was honored by me with devotion,
through the ripening of this merit, may I become one who possesses well-being and is wise.
Thus, gladdened by this aspiration, the merchant,
having honored him with great respect, led him to his own hermitage.
"Monks, you should know that he who was that illustrious guild-leader and great multitude was none other than this Mahābhijña Śobhita, the Arhat of great intelligence."
At that time, he respectfully covered a sick pratyekabuddha with a cloth, provided him with alms-food, and honored him.
Through the ripening of this merit, he became thus adorned and prosperous;
for five hundred births he was a mine of excellent qualities.
Furthermore, I shall fully relate how all that was previously accomplished as a meritorious deed by him; listen to it with respect.
Just as formerly the Teacher Kāśyapa was an Arhat, a Tathāgata, omniscient, a Sugata, a Protector, a King of Dharma, and a Lord of Sages; ||| Rm_35.200{100} |||
In Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park, that Perfectly Awakened One, together with his Saṅgha,
dwelt and taught the Dharma for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
And at that time, in Vārāṇasī,
there was a householder who was devoted to the Perfectly Awakened One, virtuous, yet poor and a wood-gatherer.
One day, while going to the mountain to fetch wood,
he saw there at one spot a great stūpa covered with grass.
Having seen it, he approached and, having uprooted all those grasses on every side, he swept them away and thoroughly purified the ground.
Then, seeing him adorned, the merchant was filled with joy;
having bowed and circumambulated him, he reflected thus in his mind:
"Since this stūpa of the Sugata has been swept and cleaned by me,
through the ripening of this merit, may I become a divine beauty."
May I be adorned with splendors surpassing even those of the gods and be possessed of great prosperity;
and may I, with devotion, please the future Buddhas as well.
Then, having gone to his teaching and taken refuge in the Triple Gem,
may I attain the state of an Arhat through ordination and proceed to perfect nirvāṇa.
Having thus made this vow and having bowed to that abode of the Jina,
he then took a piece of wood and returned to his own home.
Then that illustrious Sumati, having become a doer of meritorious deeds, enjoyed happiness for a very long time; when his time came, he died and went to heaven.
Having enjoyed divine pleasures in heaven together with the gods, he rejoiced;
thus, after experiencing happiness for five hundred births, he wandered through existence.
In this regard as well: "If this glorious one has entered my teaching, and having taken up the vows of renunciation, practices [them], he may even become an Arhat. (Rm 397) (Rm 35.212)
Know all that to arise from the merit of having cleansed that stūpa;
for whatever was intended there, it is now accomplished accordingly.
He who was the poor wood-gatherer is indeed this Śobhita;
you should not think he is someone else—of this there is no doubt.
Thus, throughout the entire cycle of existence, for all living beings alike,
whatever action has been performed, its fruit is certain to follow in exactly that same way.
Karma is never exhausted anywhere at any time without being experienced;
otherwise, the fruit of karma could never come to pass in any way whatsoever.
Thinking thus, those who always desire happiness in this saṃsāra should worship the Three Jewels and always practice what is virtuous.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, all those members of the Saṅgha and all the people became seekers of the Dharma, desiring to attain perfect enlightenment.
Thus was it told to me by my teacher, and thus have I heard and spoken it;
you too, O Great King, should likewise be devoted to the True Dharma.
And having diligently awakened the subjects, O Great King,
and established them firmly on the path to enlightenment, he ought always to protect them.
When this has been done, O Great King, all will be auspicious for you;
having attained awakening in due course, you shall reach the state of a Perfect Buddha.
Having heard this which was proclaimed by that Arhat, King Aśoka,
together with his retinue, acknowledged it, saying "So be it," and rejoiced.
Those humans who, with faith and great clarity, hear this noble account of Śobhita,
or cause it to be heard with a joyful mind, and those who desire perfect enlightenment—
all of them are bodhisattvas, endowed with all virtues, practicing the conduct of awakening.
Having enjoyed pleasure to their heart's content, they depart for the abode of the One Possessing the Ten Powers, having abandoned [all worldly things].
Thus ends the Śobhita-avadāna within the Ratnāvadānatatva.
XXXVI. The Muktā-avadāna.
Then King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence,
approached and bowed down to the ascetic Upagupta, and spoke once more as follows:
"Venerable sir, I wish to hear another well-spoken teaching;
it behoves you to instruct me just as it was explained by my teacher."
Having heard this request made by the king, that wise Arhat ascetic looked toward the great king Aśoka and spoke as follows:
Listen well, O Great King, to that which was spoken by my teacher;
I shall relate it here for the purification of your mind.
Thus it happened: in the great city of Śrāvastī, there was a wealthy and virtuous guild-leader named Puṣya, who resembled Śrī himself and was highly esteemed by the people.
His wife was named Rāmā, possessed of beautiful limbs and equal to Śrī in splendor;
she practiced the family dharma and followed the conduct of her husband.
Together with his virtuous wife Puṣyā, that wise Sanmati enjoyed pleasures according to his desire and took delight in attending to her.
Then, in due time, that beloved wife, pregnant and with her belly swelling,
gradually became pale in complexion, thin, and devoted to eating very little.
Then, in due time, she gave birth to a daughter who was divinely beautiful, radiant, and adorned with a garland of pearls bound upon her head.
Seeing that girl born, adorned with a pearl necklace fastened upon her head, her mother became filled with wondrous joy.
Having heard that, her father Puṣya, his mind uplifted with wonder, approached;
and seeing his daughter, he stood gazing at her in amazement.
Then all those kinsmen, relatives, friends, and well-wishers,
having heard that she had given birth, quickly came out of respect to see her.
There they gazed for a long time with joy upon that lovely maiden, adorned with a garland of pearls upon her head, beautiful to behold and possessed of most auspicious limbs.
Or perhaps she is a daughter of the gods; surely she is venerable and not a mere mortal woman, since even as soon as she was born, she has illuminated the city with her splendors.
Having spoken thus, all those kinsmen, relatives, and friends,
gazing at her for a very long time in wonder, departed from that place.
Then Janaka, having joyfully performed the birth festival for her and having invited all his kinsmen, spoke thus to the city: Rm_36.16{16} //
"Sirs, having seen this auspicious sign of my daughter,
let her name be proclaimed in such a way that it becomes well-known throughout the world."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, all those kinsmen and relatives, perceiving the cause for that, spoke thus to Puṣya: Rm_36.18{18} //
"O virtuous one, since she was born with a garland of pearls upon her hair,
let her name certainly become established as 'Muktā'."
Having heard what was thus related by all those kinsmen,
Puṣya gave that well-known name to his daughter.
Then that girl, released by her nurses and nurtured by them,
grew with all her limbs fully nourished like a lotus in a lake.
Then that lovely girl grew up as a young maiden;
having attended upon her elders, she gradually learned the sciences.
There, that wise Sumati, having been released and having gradually mastered the scripts,
reached the further shore of all treatises, arts, and sciences, becoming truly discerning.
Then, devoted to giving and gladdened by her aspiration for the true Dharma, she constantly bestowed upon all supplicants whatever they desired.
All the beggars, having seen her house, gathered there;
taking the wealth she gave them, they departed filled with joy.
Then a certain Brahmin, his soul agitated by greed upon seeing her pearl necklace among her hair, went home and took possession of it.
There, having seen that maiden who was to be given in marriage, the brahmin approached her, offered words of blessing, and requested her with great respect as follows.
May victory be yours always, O auspicious lady; may you live long, endowed with happiness.
May everything be accomplished for you exactly as your heart desires.
"O blessed lady, having heard of your virtues from afar, I have come here for that very purpose; listen as I speak to you, and having heard it, may you be gracious toward me."
Since this pearl necklace, so beautifully adorned, is bound upon your head,
give it to me here and delight my heart.
When he had thus made his request, she was released as the recipient;
desiring to bestow her upon him, she spoke thus to that brahmin:
"Excellent, O Brahmin! Stay for a moment; do not go anywhere else.
Having obtained the permission of my parents, I shall give this woman to you as well."
Having spoken thus and comforted that enticed brahmin,
he suddenly went before his parents and addressed them in this way.
"Father, Mother, a Brahmin seeking alms has come to our house;
he begs for this pearl necklace that is worn upon my head."
Therefore, I wish to give this to that virtuous brahmin;
if you have any compassion for me, please grant me your permission.
Having heard what was thus spoken by his daughter, the father, struck with amazement,
gazed at his daughter for a very long time and, after addressing her, spoke as follows:
"O child, having perceived what, would one thus cut off from one's own head a son— who is like an eye— and give him to a petitioner?"
If you desire to give your daughter to the Brahmin who seeks her,
then bestow upon him whatever other wealth he requests, according to his wish.
Having heard what was thus spoken by her father, that wise daughter Muktā looked at her father, bowed down, and spoke as follows:
"Listen, dear father, as to why I wish to give away even this pearl necklace produced from my own head; I shall explain it to you."
In this saṃsāra, human birth is indeed impermanent and difficult to obtain;
both the body and life are momentary in their destruction, like water upon a blade of grass.
Even there, many diseases abound and prosperity is exceedingly fickle;
the attainment of a favorable moment is difficult to find, and a mind intent on the Dharma is likewise hard to obtain.
"What is permanent here in this saṃsāra? For who indeed could remain forever?
Thinking thus, O Father, I wish to give you this impermanent garland of pearls.
"Who else besides a human being would be able to give a gift?"—
even considering this, I desire to give here at least a single *kajā* [of gold].
"Thinking, 'Who indeed can have confidence in death when it has seized one?'— even with this thought in mind, O Father, I wish to give you this garland of liberation."
In this world, whose life within the body remains established by its own will?
Having understood this, O Father, I wish to offer you this garland like a flower.
"Who here is not afflicted by diseases and the defilements arising from the gods?
Having reflected thus upon this world, I desire to give this pearl.
"For whom is prosperity stable in the home? Even those who have fallen do not remain [in that state].
Knowing this, I therefore wish to give away this one who has the form of a flower."
And who here would have a pure vision that remains constant at all times,
even after having thus fully understood this desire to give?
"Even though I have seen that such an attitude toward the Dharma never arises in any way whatsoever, my mind still desires to give these flowers."
"O father, I wish to give you this [hair] of mine, which was produced by destiny, situated upon my head, and resembling fine locks of hair, for the sake of obtaining the jewel of the True Dharma."
And for how long shall I live? For all beings death is certain;
as long as this [world] is not liberated from life, even this [person] will perish though liberated.
Since this hair upon my head shall perish along with my life-breath,
it will perish in every way— whether it be given away or not given.
"O Father, having observed this divine matter, I wish to lift up even Kaja and give her to you, just as one might offer a garland of flowers that has been cast away."
Therefore, do not create an obstacle here for my accomplishment of the true Dharma;
by granting me your permission, make my request fruitful.
If you do not grant permission, you will reap the fruit of obstructing a gift;
from that, evil karma will arise for you, and through it, you shall go to an evil rebirth.
If you fulfill my wish by granting me permission,
then may merit arise for you, and through that, may you indeed go to a happy rebirth.
Having always enjoyed happiness in a good rebirth, you shall also proceed toward auspicious states;
then, having attained complete awakening in due course, may you reach Buddhahood.
Knowing this, father, it does not behove you to prevent me here;
rather, having granted me permission, you ought to fulfill my truthful resolve.
Having heard what was thus related by his daughter, her father Sumati was awakened;
and beholding his daughter released, he spoke as follows.
"Everything that you have thus related is indeed the truth.
If you have the faith to give, then bestow it; why should I prevent you?"
When her father had thus given his permission, she was released and greatly rejoiced;
she then desired to take off that pearl necklace which had been produced from her head.
Then that mother, seeing her beloved daughter released,
and seeing even her hair loosened as she desired to tear off the garland, [was filled with joy].
Suddenly embracing her tightly, she prepared to restrain him;
with eyes smeared by falling tears, she spoke thus while lamenting:
"Alas, beloved! O daughter of your own self, how could you have known this now?
For even though she was born from your own body, you wish to give her away as if she were a stranger!"
Having cut off your own head-born hair and a necklace of pearls born from your own deity,
what else do you see here that you wish to give to the Brahmin?
If you have such an intense desire for giving, then give whatever is desired;
however, do not give these very locks of hair to any petitioner.
"This is my own body, born from me, as dear as life itself;
therefore, consider how this can be cut away and given."
If you were to tear this [flesh] from your own head by force and give it to me,
then she would surely and certainly perish along with her life.
When life and the body have perished, who could practice the Dharma again?
Without the Dharma in this saṃsāra, every accomplishment is meaningless.
For it is said that in saṃsāra, the life of the self-identity is indeed the root of the Dharma;
therefore, that body which is the support for life must be protected with great effort.
Whatever practice of the Dharma is performed in saṃsāra for the sake of protecting body and life—
what purpose is there in practicing the Dharma in saṃsāra without body and life?
The means for achieving dharma, wealth, pleasure, liberation, and so forth, are the causes of happiness;
yet when life and the body are absent, for whose sake would there be any means of happiness?
Since you do not wish to give even your own life in this way, for what purpose do you desire to give?
It is for the sake of protecting the life of one's own body that one practices the means of merit, such as giving.
Having sacrificed one's own body and life, for what purpose is merit accomplished?
One's own body and life are for the sake of excellence; one should acquire the rain of the substance of virtues.
Thus have I spoken the truth for your benefit, O dear daughter;
having heard this, protect it like your own eyes and do not give it to anyone who asks for it.
If you have a desire for this bull, then having given it away, perform another vow at home according to your wish; thus, practice virtue with ease.
By the ripening of this merit, may all be auspicious for you everywhere;
may you never go to an evil rebirth at any time, but always attain a fortunate state.
Reflecting thus upon your son, and having heard the true Dharma proclaimed by the Sugata,
perform service to the Three Jewels and observe the vows happily at home.
Purified by this merit, you who always produce auspiciousness shall,
in due course, attain perfect enlightenment and reach the state of a fully awakened Buddha.
Having heard this which was thus related by her mother, that daughter of Muktā also rose up,
and with eyes parched by tears, she went slowly to the chamber of grief.
There, seated upon the surface of her bed, with thoughts fixed on the gift of pearls,
she remained absorbed in meditation after recollecting the Perfectly Awakened One.
There, though her senses were overcome by sleep and stupified by that meditation,
she remained with her desires ceased, having called to mind that very Śrīghana.
Seeing her standing there in that manner, the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages,
addressed her as if in a dream and awakened Muktā in this way:
"O child, do not despair; this lotus shall be given to you.
Let it be given after being uprooted, and it will appear once more."
Having heard this conversation, she arose as if from a dream;
freed [from her previous state], her mind overcome with wonder, she stood perfectly still.
Then, remembering that Lord of the World and agitated by thoughts of him,
she desired to know whether this could indeed be true.
Then, having herself joyfully taken from her own head with her hand that pearl necklace which she beheld, she fashioned it into a sacred thread (*śāstra*).
Immediately thereafter, that [image], adorned with garlands of pearls and equal in appearance to her,
arose upon her head and shone brilliantly.
Beholding her, that maiden was filled with extreme amazement;
she went suddenly before her mother and reported this to her.
O Mother, by the grace of the compassionate glance of the Lord of Sages today,
may that which was vowed by me certainly be fulfilled.
Having spoken thus, she was released with joy; and having shown both her upraised locks of hair before her mother, she addressed her in this way:
O Mother, with my hopes frustrated, I lie upon the surface of the bed;
having meditated upon the Fully Awakened One in my mind, I remain intent on the thought of giving.
When sleep crept upon my heart as I was slumbering in meditation,
I heard this very command issued by the Lord of All.
"This pearl necklace, grown from my hair, should be given by you with joy;
it will certainly appear once again, even more beautiful than this."
Having heard this, I was awakened and thought, "Could this be true?
and so, lifting her up, I looked at her with great joy.
Immediately after that, O Mother, behold this necklace of pearls, equal in size to my head, which has appeared upon my head.
Having spoken thus, the daughter joyfully released herself before her mother,
and placing a pearl necklace before her while showing it to her, she spoke as follows:
With joy, I compose this *Mātṛkā* for the instruction of the world;
therefore, I shall indeed go to bestow it upon the teacher of the three worlds.
Having heard what was thus related by her daughter, the mother,
seeing that pearl necklace and her daughter’s hair, was filled with joy and delight.
Gazing at her daughter again and again, she spoke to her thus:
"O blessed and auspicious daughter, you are fortunate, for you have obtained exactly what you desired."
Thus it shall surely be accomplished for you through the power of the Perfectly Awakened One;
therefore, take up this [vow] exactly as you have intended.
Therefore, O daughter, you ought to honor that lord of sages and give [the gift] to him; for that which has been promised by you will certainly be fulfilled as truth.
"By the power of this merit, may you always attain a good rebirth.
Thinking thus, offer [this] to the Teacher of the World and worship him with devotion. (Rm 403) (Rm 36.104)
And so, having taken it in this manner, he ought to give it to this twice-born man;
for when you have thus consented and the matter is accomplished, there shall be auspiciousness everywhere.
Human birth is fruitful, and one always abides in a happy state.
Having heard what was spoken by her mother, her heart filled with joy,
she promised "So be it" and desired to act accordingly.
Thus she reported this entire occurrence before her husband;
and having heard it, her husband Puṣya also rejoiced with great delight.
At that time, in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove monastery,
the Blessed One, the Arhat, dwelt there together with his community of monks.
There, that Teacher of the Three Worlds, elucidating the conduct of awakening,
began to teach the Dharma for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings together.
Then all those monks, the śrāvakas such as Cailaka and others,
the bhikṣuṇīs, the practitioners of vows, and even the hosts of bodhisattvas—
The assemblies of laymen and likewise the laywomen—
all of them, having taken refuge [in him], stood together with concentrated minds.
Likewise, the gods headed by Śakra, the celibate practitioners headed by Brahmā,
the Dānavas, the world-protectors, and the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras [were present].
Rākṣasas, Garuḍas, Nāgas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others;
ascetics, yogins, Nirgranthas, and even Tīrthikas.
Sages and brahmins as well, ascetics of great supernatural power, kings and kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and even princes; Rm_36.115.
The guild-leaders, ministers, counselors, householders, and great men;
the merchants, caravan leaders, citizens, and even the artisans.
Both those from the villages and the countryside, as well as inhabitants of other lands—
all of them approached and, having beheld that Śrīghana, were filled with joy.
Having bowed, circumambulated, and worshipped them in due order,
they joined their palms in reverence, bowed again, and moved around them on all sides.
They approached with composed minds to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all assembled,
taught the True Dharma, which is auspicious in the beginning, middle, and end.
Having heard that true Dharma, all those awakened beings were enlightened;
for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, they became practitioners of the path to awakening.
Then that maiden, released and rejoicing with her friends,
took the pearl necklace and approached to hear the Dharma.
There, having seen that Śrīghana, she joyfully bowed with palms joined,
circumambulated him three times, and stood before that Teacher.
There, having first placed that pearl necklace before her with palms joined in reverence,
she bowed at her feet and, with a serene countenance, drew near to listen to the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having perceived her intention and purified state of mind,
began to teach the true Dharma, starting from the Noble Truths.
Having heard that true Dharma, she was liberated and awakened;
having understood the excellence of the Dharma, she became one who yearned for enlightenment.
There, that maiden, having shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity with the sword of wisdom, attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Then Bhadrikā, having been liberated and having seen the Truths, was filled with joy;
with palms joined in reverence, she bowed at the feet of the Teacher and returned to her own home.
Then, with a very serene disposition, she took her own hair together with its pearl necklace and joyfully gave it to that brahmin.
Taking that garland of pearls, the Brahmin was filled with joy;
having bestowed auspicious blessings upon her, he quickly departed for his own home.
Thus, having gone there, Muditā honored the Three Jewels and practiced the virtuous Dharma according to the desires of all who sought her aid.
Then, having heard of her virtues, many who were lustful for desire desired to solicit her, offering gifts of jewels as tribute.
The princes Bhū and Bhuja, having joyfully given their own jewels along with messengers to her father Puṣya, earnestly entreated him with devotion.
Likewise, there were sons of brahmins, sons of ministers who were full of desire,
sons of vaiśyas, and others such as the sons of wealthy merchants.
The sons of caravan leaders, as well as the sons of artisans,
and likewise the sons of great merchants, and others too, were all infatuated by desire.
Seeing that Subhadrāṅgī, adorned with pearls and wearing pearl ornaments, they were all scorched by the fire of passion and longed for the nectar of her face.
Having given garments, ornaments, and jewels to her father through messengers individually,
he thus earnestly requested Puṣya for her hand.
Thus entreated by them individually through their messengers, Puṣya,
upon seeing those gifts presented, remained there with a deeply agitated heart.
Then Puṣya, rising from there with a dejected mind in the chamber of sorrow,
went and sat upon the surface of his bed, reflecting thus in his mind:
"Alas, great sorrow has arisen within me; what shall I do now?
I have but one daughter, yet my supplicants are many."
"If I give it to one, all the others will become my enemies;
what shall I do in this situation, since I cannot conceive of any other means?"
Thus, with his face dejected by anxiety and afflicted by the poison of delusion, he remained standing.
Seeing her father situated there in such a state, utterly bewildered, she approached him together with her son; having bowed down, she questioned him as follows:
"Father, what is the sorrow in your mind that you remain thus dejected today?
Tell me the truth; awaken this daughter of yours."
When his daughter had thus entreated him, the wise Janaka,
having gazed for a long time upon his son Muktā, spoke as follows:
"O daughter Subhadrāṅgī, what indeed can I say in this matter?
For you are my only daughter, yet there are many who beg from you."
"If I were to give you, the one divine beauty, to just one person,
all those others would become my enemies and doers of harm."
Thus, my soul consumed by anxiety, I remain in this state and not otherwise;
for I see no means by which my fear may arise.
Having heard what was thus spoken by her parents, that liberated daughter looked at her father and, seeking to enlighten him, spoke as follows: (Rm 405) Rm_36.148{46} //
"O father, I do not seek sensual pleasures; having gone forth into the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One and maintained the vows of renunciation, I shall practice the virtuous life."
"Thus my mind is resolved; indeed, I shall not act otherwise.
Therefore, do not despair in this matter, but grant me your permission."
When his daughter had spoken thus, the wise Janaka Puṣya,
having gazed upon his own daughter, spoke again as follows:
"O daughter, how indeed can you endure the practice of renunciation?
For you are but a young girl, with limbs so beautiful, a maiden accustomed to living in comfort."
Therefore, as long as you remain a maiden dwelling in your home,
practice devotion to the Three Jewels and observe the vows of a lay follower.
Having heard what was thus spoken by her father, that wise daughter,
having promised "So be it," was enlightened and gave her joyful consent.
Thus, that Bhadrikā, liberated, pure in virtue, and well-cultivated,
having paid homage to the Three Jewels, lived according to the vows of a laywoman.
When that lovely young woman, adorned with pearls and exceedingly beautiful,
was seen by the youngest son while she was spread out upon the food, she was without a protector.
Then that son of Anāthapiṇḍada, named Supriya,
being greatly delighted yet tormented by the fire of sensual passion, became dejected in mind like a sick man.
Seeing that son afflicted by sensual desire, Anāthapiṇḍada observed the cause of his distress, comforted him, and spoke as follows:
"O son, why do you now remain like one afflicted by disease?
Therefore, tell me what your heart desires."
Having heard what his father had said, Supriya, sighing deeply and looking at his father, spoke thus slowly.
"Father, that girl of beautiful limbs, adorned with pearls and exceedingly radiant—
having seen her as being suitable for me, she captivates my heart."
My mind has been scorched by the fire of passion and longing for that;
it now behoves me to employ the means to extinguish that fire of passion.
Having heard what was spoken by his son, the father Anāthapiṇḍada desired to make a request for the sake of saving his son's life.
Then, having summoned a messenger, he spoke thus in the city: "O good man, go and say this to the householder Puṣya himself."
"O virtuous one, that daughter Bhadrā should be given by you to my son;
for if this alliance is made, it will bring us happiness for as long as we live."
Having said this, he requested that Puṣya give his virtuous daughter, named Muktā, to his son; "He ought to grant her to him in every way."
Having heard what was said by him, and having replied "So be it," that messenger took the gift and approached Puṣya.
There, placing the gift before him and seeking to gladden him,
he reported everything exactly as he had been instructed by Yathānāthabhṛt.
Having heard all that was said and being thus enlightened, Puṣya addressed his own daughter Muktā and spoke as follows.
"O dear daughter, my child, you who have been supported by me as one who is helpless—
since you have been requested for my own beloved son, please grant your favor."
Having heard what was spoken by her father, that virtuous daughter was released;
looking at her father and bowing down, she spoke thus:
"I do not seek sensual pleasures, dear father; having gone for refuge to the Perfectly Awakened One, I shall maintain the vows of renunciation and practice the auspicious conduct."
Having heard what was thus spoken by his daughter, Puṣya, his heart deeply moved,
gazed at his daughter for a long time and spoke to her once again as follows.
O son, how can you speak thus? Do you not consider that when the master of the house is present, by whom is his word not heard?
Therefore, as long as she has reached maturity, you, along with your followers,
should practice devotion to the Three Jewels and observe the vows while living happily at home.
When the elders have settled [this matter], then you, having taken the vows of renunciation in a Buddhist hermitage, should practice the auspicious conduct.
Having heard what was thus commanded by her father, that wise daughter,
considering how the word of her parent could not be transgressed, spoke as follows.
"I do not seek sensual pleasures, my dear father; I seek the accomplishment of the True Dharma.
Nevertheless, since your word must not be transgressed, I shall obey your speech."
"If, having taken my oath, he grants me his word of truth, I shall surely choose him as my husband; this is my firm resolve."
Having heard what was thus spoken by his daughter, Puṣya was awakened to understanding and reported this entire account before the messenger.
The messengers, having heard that news, quickly replied, "So be it," and reported it in detail before Anāthapiṇḍada.
Having heard this, Anāthapiṇḍada was also filled with joy,
and he reported this entire account to his son.
Having heard this related by his father, the wise Supriya promised "So be it" and announced it in the presence of the messenger.
And the messenger, having heard those words, went before Puṣya and reported this entire account in detail.
Having heard that which was thus related, Puṣya spoke in the presence of his wife;
she too, having heard it from her mother, reported it before her daughter.
Having heard what was thus instructed by her mother, that virtuous daughter,
having replied "So be it," remained silent and attended to that task.
Then Janaka, perceiving that the constellation Puṣya was presided over by his daughter,
quickly prepared all the requisites for her marriage.
Then that Puṣya Janaka, having summoned Supriya, the son of Anāthapiṇḍada, honored him and treated him with equal respect.
Then, having resolved that his daughter was now free, King Janaka, under the asterism Puṣya, bestowed her upon Supriya according to the prescribed rites.
Then that husband Supriya, having brought his beloved wife— the beautiful woman who had been released— back to his own home, enjoyed himself with her, eating and drinking as he pleased.
Thus that noble lady, having been released, lived happily in her home for some time;
rejoicing and delighted, she enjoyed herself with her husband according to her desire.
Then, as old age approached their bodies, that couple bowed at the feet of their parents and made this request with great reverence:
"O parents, we both desire to fulfill that truth which was performed for our complete success;
therefore, you ought to grant us permission."
Having heard this prayer made by the two of them, and seeing that the husband and wife were indeed intent upon the *śrāddha* rite, the father and mother spoke thus:
If you both have the desire to practice the vow of the Sugata,
then, for the fulfillment of that truth, proceed with concentrated minds.
Thus permitted by the two of them, the joyful couple bowed at the feet of their parents and immediately set out from the house.
Then the two of them arrived at the Jetakodyāna monastery and,
having bowed down to the Blessed One, requested ordination.
"O Blessed One, O Protector, O Omniscient One, you know that which is true for us both;
we shall fulfill that truth, so please grant us both the going forth."
When they had thus prayed, the Blessed One touched their heads with his right hand, looked upon them, and after addressing them, commanded as follows:
Thus practicing, having undertaken the supreme vow of renunciation,
they remained composed in the holy life for the sake of the welfare of themselves and others.
When the Lord of Sages had thus instructed them, both of them shaved their heads,
took up begging bowls, and were clothed in the saffron robes of their Master.
Then, having shattered the mass of ignorance and attained proficiency in true knowledge,
they conquered the entire host of afflictions and directly realized the state of Arhatship.
Then those two, pure in soul, with the three spheres completely purified,
having conquered their senses, of perfect conduct, free from conceptual construction, and stainless—
They were practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin) beyond compare, worthy of worship, honor, and veneration by all the worlds dwelling within the three realms.
Having seen that, all those monks, their minds uplifted with wonder,
bowed down to the Blessed One and asked him about his former deeds.
"Blessed One, what meritorious deed was performed by these two in the past, and where?
Having explained all of that, please awaken us all."
When all the monks had thus made their request, that Lord of Sages,
looking upon all those disciples and monks, gave this instruction:
Listen, monks, to the karma performed by these two in the past;
I shall declare it all to you, and having heard it, may you approve it.
Just as in the past there was a Teacher, the Lord of Sages named Kāśyapa,
the omniscient Arhat, the Protector of the World, the King of Dharma, the Tathāgata.
The Blessed One, the Conqueror, dwelt for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī together with his Saṅgha.
At that time, there was a great and wise man there, illustrious and like the god of wealth,
who was a constant devotee and listener to the true Dharma of that lord of sages.
Then that wise donor, for the sake of the welfare of all the world,
requested there the alms-offering of five-year-old grain.
(Rm 408) He desired to constantly and uninterruptedly serve the Lord of Sages, Kāśyapa, together with his Saṅgha, providing them with perpetual offerings and meals. Rm_36.213{11} //
Then, having received the king’s command, he was filled with joy;
mounting the back of an elephant, he caused the ringing of bells to sound.
There, throughout the entire region surrounding Vārāṇasī,
he began to wander with his attendants, begging for alms from the people.
Seeing him, the caravan leader's wife, Bhadrā, who was virtuous and of noble character,
joyfully removed a pearl necklace from her head and gave it to her.
Then, seeing her head uncovered by that pearl necklace, he was struck with wonder and questioned her further.
"O blessed lady, where is that pearl necklace which was on your head? It is not to be seen.
To whom did you give it, or by whom was it taken? Tell me that."
Thus questioned by her husband, she, delighted and with palms joined in reverence,
bowed to him and spoke as follows to console him:
"Noble son, be gracious here; do not give way to anger.
For this was given by me with faith even for the sake of begging alms from Chandaka."
Having heard what his wife had said, the caravan leader, while traveling thereupon,
ransomed it with a great price and gave it back to her.
Upon seeing that pearl necklace, even his beloved wife did not accept it, thinking, "This was given by me to the Teacher."
Then that caravan leader, her husband, looking at his lovely and dear wife with eyes moist with affection, spoke to her once more in this way:
"O blessed lady, this which was purchased by me at a high price is being given to you;
why do you not wish to accept it from me? Indeed, how can this be so?"
Having heard what was said by her husband, she took that pearl necklace given again by her lord and gladdened her husband’s heart.
Then she, though attached to sensual pleasures, desiring the virtues of the true Dharma,
took that limb used for worship and went joyfully to the Teacher’s hermitage.
There, having applied fragrant ointments to that Perfumed Chamber,
having strewn it with beautiful flowers, and having bowed down and performed circumambulations, she remained there.
Then, filled with joy, she cast a pearl necklace before that Kāśyapa, the teacher of the world, and bowed down with palms joined in reverence.
Then, by the power of the Buddha,
that pearl necklace instantly came to rest upon the head of that Teacher, shining brilliantly as it illuminated him.
Seeing that, her face beaming with joy and longing for the qualities of enlightenment, she bowed at the feet of the Teacher and with delight made this aspiration: Rm_36.230{28} //
By the ripening of this merit, may I please such a Teacher, a Jina,
and may I become a recipient of such qualities in every way throughout existence.
Thus that beautiful lady, having always made her vow before that Teacher, the Guru of the World, devoted herself to him with a deeply serene mind.
"O monks, you should consider that this Subhāvinī, who was the wife of that caravan leader, is indeed she who has been liberated; it is not otherwise."
At that time, having honored Kāśyapa, the Teacher of the World, with articles of worship out of faith, she offered him a pearl necklace.
Through the ripening of this merit, she has now been born into a noble family;
moreover, a pearl necklace grew upon her head simultaneously with her birth.
Just as she made that aspiration there, so now,
having come to me as her teacher, she has attained Arhatship in person.
For in this way, whatever action is performed by someone, its fruit is experienced by that very person;
karma is never exhausted without being experienced, nor can it ever be otherwise.
Thinking thus, those who always desire what is auspicious in this saṃsāra should rely upon the true Dharma and always practice what is virtuous.
Those who always practice what is auspicious do not go to an evil destiny;
they proceed only to a happy rebirth and shall fully attain awakening.
Having heard this instruction from the Lord of Sages, all those members of the Saṅgha likewise replied, "So be it," and being thus awakened, they rejoiced.
"Thus has it been commanded by my Teacher; I have heard it, and so do I speak.
Having heard this, O King, you must always act accordingly toward what is auspicious."
And having diligently awakened the subjects as well, O Great King, establish them on the path to enlightenment and protect them with a concentrated mind.
For in this way, may there always be constant well-being for you everywhere;
and having attained enlightenment in due course, may you reach the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, King Aśoka,
having pledged "So be it," rejoiced together with his retinue.
Those humans who hear this *Muktāvadāna* and those who even listen to it—
all of them, having performed auspicious deeds, shall become thus happy and go to the abode of the Sugata.
Thus ends the Story of the Pearl (*Muktāvadāna*) within the *Ratnāvadānatatva*.
XXXVII. The Story of Dhīmatī.
Then King Aśoka, filled with joy and with palms joined in reverence,
bowed to the Arhat Upagupta and spoke to him once more:
Venerable sir, those great beings, the Bodhisattvas, always practice giving in this way, bestowing everything exactly as desired upon all who seek it.
Even though it is given away in this manner, that wealth is indeed not exhausted;
rather, it increases even further. How is this so? Please instruct me on this.
"By the power of what vow does prosperity increase?
It behoves you, my Teacher, to correctly instruct me in that vow."
When the king had thus made his request, the wise Arhat Upagupta, having heard him and looked upon that lord of men, spoke as follows:
Listen, O fortunate King, to that which was spoken to me by my preceptor;
I shall relate it to you for the sake of the increase of Dharma in the world.
Those who are established in truth and meditative concentration, pure in conduct, and seekers of the auspicious,
practice the supreme vow of the Great Goddess Vasudhārā.
The wealth in their homes never diminishes even as they constantly give it away;
rather, it increases all the more through the power of the *vasudhārā*.
Just as in the past there was the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Lord of Sages,
the Omniscient One, the Arhat, the Teacher of the World, the King of Dharma, the Tathāgata.
Once, the Blessed One dwelt there in the vicinity of the city of Vārāṇasī,
in the Deer Park, the abode of the Jina, together with his Saṅgha.
Then Śakra and the other immortals, as well as Brahmā and the other brahmins, and all the lords of the worlds, came to drink that nectar of the Dharma.
The Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Daityas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas,
Kinnaras, Rākṣasas, Garuḍas, Nāgas, and others as well, had assembled there.
Ascetics and yogins, as well as heretics practicing austerities,
the Nirgranthas, those free from passion, sages, and celibate students.
In this way, other worlds as well, desiring the Dharma of the Perfectly Awakened One,
joyfully assembled there to drink that nectar of the True Dharma.
The great king named Viśvabhadra was the sovereign of that city;
his beloved queen was the virtuous lady named Ratnamālā.
Then there was his virtuous son named Sūryaprabha,
and his daughter, a maiden in the form of Ramā, named Vimalā.
Other members of the household as well, his kinsmen, friends, and relatives,
and even the family priests and other twice-born men learned in the Vedas [were there].
And the Vaiśyas, ministers, counselors, householders, and eminent men;
the merchants, caravan leaders, artisans, and citizens as well.
Villagers and country folk, as well as pilgrims,
and all other people likewise, arrived there together.
Having arrived there and beheld the Perfectly Awakened One, Śrīghana, seated in the assembly and honored by the entire Saṅgha, they approached him with joy.
There, all those people, having honored him in due order and having circumambulated that Lord of Sages three times, prostrated themselves before him.
Turning all around to drink that nectar of the true Dharma, they stood before him with reverence, having composed their minds and paid him honor.
Then the Blessed One, seeing that they had all assembled,
taught the supreme Dharma, beginning with the conduct of awakening.
Having heard that true Dharma, all the worlds were awakened;
having attained the mind of enlightenment, they became practitioners of the path to enlightenment.
At that time, in Vārāṇasī, there was a householder,
a merchant named Dharmadhvaja, who was a generous, virtuous, and eminent man.
His wife was dear and beloved, renowned as Śāntamati;
he also had many sons and daughters.
Grandsons, laborers, servants, female slaves, male slaves,
as well as numerous dependents, kinsmen, friends, and well-wishers;
All those who depend upon him have been nourished by him, sustained, and protected;
for indeed, all those who have sought refuge are to be supported by the householder.
Even those seeking wealth always gathered in his house in great numbers,
and with their auspicious blessings, they constantly increased his great enthusiasm.
That donor Dharmadhvaja, having satisfied all those supplicants with whatever goods they desired, gladdened them.
As he continued giving in this manner, his wealth gradually came to an end;
seeing that, the householder became tormented by the fear of obstacles to his generosity.
Then, remaining in that abode of grief, reflecting on the depletion of his prosperity,
he stood sighing, dejected in spirit, and devoid of any desire for enjoyments.
Then his beloved wife, the wise Śāntamati, seeing her husband with such a dejected countenance, questioned him thus: Rm_37.33{33} //
"O Lord, seeing what do you remain thus in sorrowful reflection?
Tell me what is in your mind, so that the suffering which arises for you here may be addressed."
Having heard what was spoken by his wife, that husband, sighing deeply,
looked upon his beloved and dear wife and spoke thus.
"O beloved, great sorrow now arises in my heart,
because my wealth is exhausted and no means for its acquisition exists here."
I have many sons, grandsons, and others; numerous members of my family; laborers and other servants; and people such as female and male slaves.
There are many other servants who must be maintained day and night,
and many seekers and beggars who constantly arrive;
how shall I satisfy them all, for my wealth is gradually being exhausted?
Surely all my supplicants will depart from this house empty-handed,
their faces weary and broken, having gone away without hope.
(412) Thus, as my heart is despondent with anxiety, suffering arises within me;
scorched by the fire of that suffering, I remain thus utterly bewildered.
For what happiness could there be in the home without the great enthusiasm for giving?
What essence is there in merely eating like a beast, devoid of true happiness?
Having heard what was thus spoken by her husband, the virtuous Śāntamatī then comforted him and, seeking to enlighten him, spoke as follows:
"Noble son, why has this sorrow arisen in your heart even here?
What can be accomplished by despair? It only burns the mind."
Events that are destined to occur will happen even for the great;
therefore, casting aside despondency, proceed with a concentrated mind toward what is auspicious.
Having heard what was thus spoken by his wife, the husband, sighing deeply,
looked upon that beloved and dear wife and spoke to her as follows.
"O beloved of virtuous mind, I do not know what auspicious deed ought to be done;
therefore, you should enlighten me by explaining the means."
Having heard what was spoken by her husband, the virtuous Śāntamatī comforted him and spoke in order to awaken his understanding.
"Noble son, great hero, I shall tell you the means:
in Kauśāmbī, at the Ghoṣira Monastery, resides the Lion of the Śākyas, the Lord of Sages."
The Sugata, the Buddha, is omniscient and compassionate toward the lowly and the distressed;
he is master of all sciences and arts, possesses the six superknowledges, and is profoundly wise.
The Lord of the World, the Conqueror of Māra, the Tathāgata Vināyaka,
is adorned with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor characteristics.
He was radiant with a fathom-wide halo, possessing a splendor exceeding that of a hundred suns;
he was like a walking jewel, gentle, and auspicious in every way.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, he dwelt there together with his Saṅgha;
having gone there and bowed down, listen with reverence to that Buddha.
Then that Blessed One, the Buddha, would prescribe that means.
Having heard what was thus commanded by his wife, Dharmadhvaja replied,
"So be it," and that husband was filled with joy.
Then that Dharmadhvaja, taking his wife Velā with him, proceeded;
having gone to the monastery, he paid homage from afar to the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha, and took his seat in one place.
Then the Blessed One, seeing Dharmadhvaja in distress,
although he already knew that Kāma had arrived, spoke thus to Dharmadhvaja.
"O virtuous one, tell me why you have come here and remain; please instruct us.
Having heard this command from the Teacher, Dharmadhvaja likewise [replied].
With palms joined in reverence, he bowed to the Blessed One and spoke thus:
"O Blessed One, whatever you may know, I go to no one else, O Lord; my sole purpose is in you. Thus he reflected, "I shall ask you this one thing."
Just as my great prosperity has waned and I am falling into poverty,
please instruct me on how that wealth may once again reach increase.
"By the power of what vow does prosperity increase?
It behoves you, my Teacher, to correctly instruct me in that vow."

Having heard this prayer thus offered by him, the Blessed One, with joy, addressed Dharmadhvaja and, looking upon him, spoke as follows: (Rm 413) *iti saṃprārthitaṃ tena śrutvā sa bhagavān mudā / dharmadhvajaṃ tam āmaṃtrya saṃpaśyann evam abravīt //* Rm_37.61{61} //
"Listen well and with a concentrated mind; I shall explain that ritual procedure to you.
Having heard it and being awakened by it, perform it according to the injunctions."
