The Vasudhārā vow, exactly as I heard it in the past,
was taught by the one with a voice as deep as the ocean of Vajradhara.
In this manner, first of all, having performed the consecration on the pure ground,
one should smear it with clay, cow dung, and water, and then beautify the area.
Then, having propitiated the true guru and bowed with joy and palms joined in reverence,
one should honor him and thus pray for the excellent Vasudhārā vow.
Then, having bathed in the sacred ford together with his preceptor, he— pure in intellect,
clothed in clean garments, pure in heart, and abiding in the divine states of Brahma— [proceeded].
In the month of Bhādrapada during the dark fortnight, or again in Māgha,
on the third lunar day, one should perform the vow after invoking the Goddess.
On the preceding day, one should nail down the obstacles situated in all directions;
having laid out the thread there on a level ground according to the ritual rule.
One should draw the mandala of the Goddess, adorned with her retinue and images.
Having thus prepared that mandala, well-wrapped with seven grains,
it was then surrounded by auspicious jars bearing the emblems of the eight yakṣiṇīs.
Having adorned that maṇḍala with banners, flags, parasols, and canopies, the Vajra-holder established it according to the ritual procedure.
One should honor and beautify [the site] with various flower garlands, lamps blazing brightly, and fragrant incenses.
Then, recollecting the goddess together with her retinue within that mandala,
and having meditated and kept vigil, he should pass that night.
Then, having risen at dawn and bathed in the sacred ford, one of purified intellect,
clothed in clean garments, should cleanse his own body with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then, having bowed to the true guru and carrying his command upon his head, he,
being pure, should take his seat facing north.
Then, having bowed to the Guru and gone for refuge to the Three Jewels,
one should meditate upon the Goddess together with her retinue within the maṇḍala, invoke her, and worship her.
Then, having respectfully offered [the gift] before him and bowed with palms joined in joy,
and having performed recitations, hymns of praise, and so forth, one should perform the confession of misdeeds.
Having rejoiced in the merit, one should pray for the vow of awakening.
Then, having performed a circumambulation and bowed with the eight limbs prostrate and palms joined,
the Guru should purify the pure, yellow thread— which has been spun from sixteen strands— with the mantra.
Then, reciting the *dhāraṇī*, that preceptor, together with his teacher,
should give that vow-text to the disciple for the sake of protection and bestow the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Having taken that vow-thread and fastened it upon his own hand,
the practitioner of the vow shall not remove that thread until the completion of the vow.
Then, the observer of the vow, having given a gift of dakṣiṇā to the guru according to his ability,
should satisfy him completely by bowing with the eight-limbed prostration.
Then, one should cause the offering (bali) to be presented to the yakṣas, yakṣiṇīs, and world-protectors (lokapālas), consisting of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and an abundance of milk-rice.
Then, having performed a request for forgiveness together with his preceptor,
he should perform the protection rite at the beginning of the third watch of the day using *yavapūraka* offerings.
At the conclusion of the recitation, having bathed again and while remembering that Goddess together with her retinue,
one should worship her according to the prescribed rite at night while reciting the Śrīdhāraṇī.
In this manner, one should constantly worship Śrī Vasundharā at the four junctions of the day for as long as one lives, or according to one's capacity, for one year.
One should observe the vow for six months, one month, or according to one's ability for nine,
seven, five, or even three days.
One should observe the vow for a day and night, or likewise for a single watch; then,
on the following morning, having bathed with a pure disposition,
the observer of the vow should worship that Goddess together with her retinue according to the prescribed rite.
Then, having honored the guru with garments, ornaments, and a subterranean chamber,
and having bestowed them along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he should likewise offer himself.
Then that guru, having taken [the mandala] and having given it to that disciple along with a blessing,
and having made a request for forgiveness, should dissolve that mandala.
Then the king, having taken that [image], stored it in the treasury;
having kept it there, he should always and constantly worship it with due respect and devotion.

Having worshipped the serpents in the river according to the prescribed rite and offered that remains of the floral offering (nirmālya) consisting of the residue of dust, one should cause it all to flow away into the water.
Then, having taken that water and gone home, one should sprinkle it everywhere within the chamber of the maṇḍala with great festivities.
Then, for the sake of completing that vow, one should duly invoke the goddess Kumārikā at night, worship her, and satisfy her with offerings.
Having worshipped all the yogins and yoginīs, headed by the true guru, he should fully satisfy them with food according to their desire.
Then, having bowed to that wheel together with its retinue, the practitioner, with palms joined in reverence,
should ask for forgiveness, show humility, and pray for the attainment of glorious prosperity.
Then, that wheel together with its retinue, being thoroughly pleased by his devotion,
shall grant to that observer of vows abundant prosperity and wise speech.
Then the goddess Vasudhārā took up residence in his house;
having filled it completely with all kinds of wealth, she remained there forever steadfast.
Then, having taken that wealth and bestowed it upon all supplicants according to their desires, and having enjoyed existence as he pleased, he should live in happiness.
Thus, O householder, having understood this great Vasudhārā vow,
undertake it according to the prescribed ritual and practice it with devotion in your home.
Then, in their home, there shall always be auspiciousness free from affliction;
that Great Goddess too, together with her retinue, shall dwell there firmly.
Then all their prosperity, endowed with auspiciousness, increased;
it arose within their abode and never underwent depletion.
Then, having enjoyed all happiness and having given as desired,
and having performed service to the Three Jewels, practice virtue with a concentrated mind.
Through the ripening of this merit, you shall always thereafter attain a good rebirth;
practicing the conduct of awakening, you will reach awakening and obtain the state of a Buddha.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, the householder Dharmadhvaja,
with a joyful and serene soul, desired to observe the vow.
Then, filled with joy, he bowed with palms joined to that Teacher of the World,
the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, and entreated him thus with great reverence:
O Blessed One, All-Knowing Teacher, I have gone for refuge to you;
bearing your command upon my head, I shall practice this vow.
Therefore, O Teacher, may you out of compassion grant me permission for that;
I shall indeed practice exactly as it has been instructed by you here.
When he had thus made his supplication, the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World,
recited and bestowed upon him the *dhāraṇī* of the Great Vidyā of the Goddess.
Dharmadhvaja, too, having bowed with palms joined to that Lord of Sages and having received that dhāraṇī, recited it with great joy.
Then, with a deeply serene mind, Dharmadhvaja, with palms joined in reverence,
bowed down to that lord of sages and master of the world, and departed for his own home.
Then, having reached his own home with the lotus of his face beaming with joy,
he addressed his wife Śāntimatī and spoke thus:
"O beloved, you are blessed and auspicious, since I have been awakened by you;
I have now attained the jewel of the perfectly enlightened one's teaching."
Just as it was fully instructed by the Lord of Sages, the Teacher,
so shall we two observe that vow of the Goddess with great devotion.
When her husband had thus spoken, Śāntamatī, filled with joy,
gazed upon him with a steady look and addressed him in this way:
"O Master, tell me how it is ordained in the scriptures;
we shall certainly act exactly as it has been instructed by the Lord of Sages."
Having heard what was thus spoken by his wife, the husband Dharmadhvaja then looked upon his wife Śāntamati with joy and spoke to her as follows.
Listen, O blessed lady, for exactly as it was instructed by the Lord of Sages,
so shall I explain to you the ritual procedure for that vow of Vasudhārā.
When her husband had spoken thus, his beloved Śāntamati,
beholding him, spoke joyfully as follows:
"O Master, having related in great detail everything exactly as it was instructed by that lord of sages, please gladden my mind."
When his wife had spoken thus, Dharmadhvaja then related everything in great detail,
exactly as it had been instructed by the Lord of Sages.
Having heard that, Śāntamati, being awakened and filled with approval,
likewise desired to practice the vow of that great goddess.
Then, having bowed to her husband, the virtuous Śāntamatī spoke thus in order to prepare the necessary materials for the commencement of that vow: Rm_37.123{23} //
"O Lord, we two shall observe the vow according to the ritual procedure for the sake of Vasulakṣmī;
please grant me your permission so that I may prepare the necessary materials for it."
Having heard what his wife had said, Dharmadhvaja was delighted and urged her on, saying,
"Let all the necessary preparations be made."
(Rm 416) Then, all of them being delighted, even as they were preparing the necessary materials, she addressed her husband and, showing him [the preparations], spoke thus: Rm_37.126{26} //
"O Lord, everything has been accomplished and perfected by me; may you be gracious in this matter.
Therefore, having formally requested the true Guru, he ought to undertake the vow."
Having heard what was thus spoken by his wife, Dharmadhvaja respectfully propitiated a true guru and, having bowed down, joyfully made this request: Rm_37.128{28} //
"Venerable sir, let us observe the vow of the goddess Śrī Vasudhārā;
therefore, having propitiated the goddess, please instruct us in the teaching of that vow."
When he had thus entreated him, that true guru, having promised "So be it," acted exactly as instructed by the Lord of Sages.
Likewise, in the month of Bhādrapada, during the dark fortnight,
on the second lunar day, that wise and true guru, having bathed at a sacred ford and dressed in clean garments, [proceeded].
Having commenced according to the prescribed ritual, he drew the mandala;
having installed the Goddess there together with her retinue, he worshipped her.

Then, on the following day, the third, he purified Dharmadhvaja— along with his wife— who had bathed well and was dressed in auspicious garments, by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then that couple, having heard what was instructed by the teacher, composed themselves accordingly and joyfully undertook the vow.
Having joyfully performed the vow exactly as instructed by the teacher,
and having completed all the rites such as the *gaṇacakra*, the two of them rejoiced.
Then, having taken up residence in his house, the goddess Vasudhārā remained there forever, well-pleased, filling it with every kind of wealth.
Then, in his house, prosperity increased day by day; there were various kinds of goods, including precious gems, minerals, fine garments, and grain.
Seeing them thus grown up, that master of the house, together with his wife, was filled with wonder; with a face like a lotus blooming with joy, he offered his praise.
Then, having given gifts to all who desired them according to their wishes,
and having paid homage to the Three Jewels, he enjoyed happiness and practiced virtue.
Seeing that, an eminent brahmin named Viṣṇudāsa, who was wise and lived near that house, had his mind uplifted with wonder.
Sighing, he addressed his wise, charming, and virtuous wife, who was pure in intention, and spoke to her once again as follows:
Behold the abundance and prosperity in the house of Bhadra’s friend;
what dharma was performed by him, by which such glory has thus increased?
"What sin have we committed that such calamity should always befall us?
What shall we do in this matter so that prosperity may increase?"
I do not know the means by which one might instruct me in what is beneficial;
blessed are those wealthy men who enjoy happiness according to their desires.
What is the use of those who, though possessing excellent virtues, are wretched and impoverished? Better to give up one's life than to live in such a state.
Of what use are even their excellent virtues to those in whose home there is no prosperity?
A man who possesses wealth is considered wise and of noble birth, even if he is devoid of virtue.
For all learned men, even those possessed of excellent virtues, are subject to the wealthy.
Even one who possesses wealth but lacks virtue is honored by people like a guru;
those devoid of wealth are not honored even by Brahmins, however learned they may be.
"Fie on my life, for even that of a brahmin is thus full of suffering;
it would be better to die this very day than to live on for long."
"What is the use of this life, which is nothing but the experience of suffering?
Therefore, I wish to die here; I would rather not live on, bearing such misery."
Death is inevitable for all living beings;
how then could I, being present here, truly conduct myself in this world?
Thus lamenting, the brahmin Viṣṇudāsa, deluded and with tears trickling from his parched eyes, stood there sighing repeatedly.
Seeing her beloved husband lamenting in this manner, that wise and dear wife consoled him and spoke these words in order to awaken his resolve.
"O Master, do not despair; remain firm and take courage.
For what can we do here? By fate, those two have not arrived at home."
Nevertheless, maintaining fortitude, exert yourself with a concentrated mind;
through effort, every means—such as virtues, material goods, and so forth—is accomplished.
Therefore, on this matter I shall speak for your benefit; listen, O Lord.
For a wife is one who directs herself toward the welfare of her husband and master.
Since this householder, your husband Dharmadhvaja, is dear to you and is a friend, a companion, and a great saint, let him be questioned with respect.
"O Lord, let it be done exactly as he has commanded;
then our prosperity may also become equal to his."
Having heard what was said by his wife, that pilgrim Viṣṇudāsa, because it was contrary to the Buddhist doctrine, spoke thus, though unwillingly: Rm_37.158{58} //
"For we are brahmins, O auspicious Queen of the Earth;
that ritual has never been mentioned anywhere in the Vedic scriptures."
Therefore, how is it that you have abandoned the customs of your own family and taken refuge elsewhere?
Having received the instruction of the Buddha, let us observe the vow with prosperity.
Those who, having abandoned their own family traditions, have gone elsewhere for refuge and practice vows with minds agitated by the desire to obtain wealth and success; // Rm_37.161{61} //
Having fallen away from their own duty, they will experience afflicted enjoyments even in this world;
being diseased and miserable in nature, they will go to an evil rebirth when they die.
"Thus it is, O auspicious lady; I have no desire for this inauspicious vow of the Buddhist goddess.
Better to give up my life than to perform any other such vow."
We too, having undertaken the vow of that goddess Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign of our lineage, shall observe it always with great devotion.
Then that illustrious Mahādevī, having taken refuge in our home,
being propitiated, shall grant all desired wealth.
"Thus we two shall observe the vow of that Mahālakṣmī;
therefore, prepare all the necessary materials for that vow with great care."
Having heard what was said by her husband, that wise woman was filled with joy; consenting with the words "So be it," she prepared all the necessary materials.
There, that wise woman went before Śāntamati,
related that entire account to her, and requested the necessary materials.
Śāntamatī, being greatly delighted, joyfully gave to that wise woman every single thing that she requested.
Taking that wealth, she came before her husband;
having presented it all and comforted him, she spoke thus:
"O Master, everything has been accomplished by me exactly as you commanded;
now, therefore, begin the vow of that Great Lakṣmī."
Having heard what his wife had said, Viṣṇudāsa was delighted and began to perform the Mahālakṣmī vow according to the prescribed rules.
In the month of Bhādrapada, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
having duly established the mandala and other requirements, one who is pure in conduct and composed in mind [should proceed].
Together with his wife, having invoked that Mahālakṣmī and worshipped her according to the prescribed rite, he performed that vow with joy, praying for prosperity.
Then that brahmin, having perfectly completed that vow,
with his wife and a very serene mind, proceeded while recollecting that prosperity.
In that way, prosperity arose and flourished in his house;
seeing this, the couple there attained great joy.
Then that greedy brahmin, having seen those riches with joy,
hid them all in a secret place and did not spend even the slightest bit of it.
Furthermore, tormented by craving and with his heart struck down by stinginess,
he gave no gift whatsoever of any property to anyone anywhere.
Having thus carefully guarded that wealth and deposited it with great effort,
he concealed it himself and did not even desire to enjoy it.
Nevertheless, that greedy-souled man, ever miserly yet desiring wealth,
resorted to the rich and accumulated riches by begging.
In that manner, Arjuna acted; no wealth increased in his house, but day by day it fell into decline and gradually went to ruin.
Then that greedy brahmin, seeing all those wealthy men who were seeking his favor at home, became exceedingly enraged; he reviled them and censured them.
As the ripening of that evil deed, all the wealth that was hidden in the house was stolen by thieves and consumed by fire.
Then that brahmin, tormented by the fire of intense suffering,
remained at home with his wife, impoverished yet undismayed in his hope.
At that moment, the father of that wise woman,
a twice-born man named Hariśarman, began to perform a sacrifice in his house together with his wife.
Then he [dismissed] all his kinsmen, relatives, friends, and well-wishers,
as well as his sisters, nephews, sons-in-law, and even their sons.
And he respectfully invited all his daughters as well.
There, all those kinsmen of yours— your relatives, friends, and well-wishers, as well as your sisters, nephews, sons-in-law, and even their sons— [were present].
Likewise, his daughters, grandsons, granddaughters, and others as well—
all of them approached and stood before him with great reverence.
There, having become wretched and unfortunate, she was not even invited by her father to that great festival of the sacrifice.
Then that wise woman, having heard of her father’s great sacrificial festival, thought:
"How is it that my father, my mother, and even my kinsmen have forgotten me?"
Thus, her heart smitten by the poison of anxiety, she fainted;
lacking even the will to eat, she remained in her home overcome with shame.
Likewise, at that time, Viṣṇudāsa, having heard of the great enthusiasm for the sacrifice in the house of the king of the gods, spoke thus to his wife: Rm_37.193{43} //
"How is it, O blessed lady, that we two have been forgotten by our father? For what reason were we not invited, while everyone else was invited?"
Having heard what was said by her husband, that wise woman, deeply ashamed, spoke thus to her husband Viṣṇudāsa, seeking to enlighten him: Rm_37.195{45} //
"What shall I say here? Since we possess no wealth in our home, even my mother does not wish to invite us out of shame."
Thus that wise woman, her face and heart contracted with shame,
lamented together with her husband and remained in the house, devoid of hope.
Then, remembering that wise woman who had not yet arrived,
she summoned a certain maidservant from the city and spoke to her thus:
"O friend, if that daughter of mine is seen by the wise one,
you must quickly meet him with my words and speak thus to him."
A great festival of sacrifice is being held in your father’s palace;
why then do you not come? You ought to go there together with your husband.
"Having been thus instructed by my mother, I have been sent to your presence;
therefore, first speak those words of my mother: 'Hear this and come.'"
Having heard what was commanded by her and having replied, "So be it," that maidservant then departed from there and went to the residence of the wise woman.
Having seen that wise woman there, the maidservant approached her and reported everything exactly as she had been instructed by her mother.
Having heard what was said by her, that wise woman, shedding tears and sighing deeply while remembering her mother, spoke thus in lamentation: Rm_37.204{54} //
"Alas, mother! How is it that I am remembered by you only now?
Would a sinful daughter, a partaker of suffering, ever come to you?"
At that very moment, her husband Viṣṇudāsa approached;
seeing that maidservant, he asked, "For what purpose [have you come]?"
When he had thus questioned her, that maidservant, with palms joined in reverence,
bowed to the brahmin and related this entire account.
Having heard that which was thus related, the brahmin Viṣṇudāsa,
his eyes parched with falling tears, spoke thus to his wife:
"What shall we say, O wife, when this calamity has befallen us by fate?
Nevertheless, summoning your courage, go to see your father's mind."
Having heard what was said by her husband, that wise woman Kuvāsinī took her sons and daughters— now devoid of ornaments— and departed slowly.
Then, having arrived at her mother’s house and seeing her parents before her,
that wise woman went forward, bowed, and stood with her heart struck by shame.
Seeing their daughter with her hair disheveled and her heart filled with shame, her parents asked, "What have you seen that you have come here? and thus restrained her.
Then that wise woman paid homage, in due order, to all her kinsmen, brothers, relatives, sisters, elders, and friends.
Seeing her, all her kinsmen, as well as her brothers,
relatives, sister, and friends, laughed at her upon seeing her and spoke thus:
Seeing them all laughing in that manner, she was overcome with extreme shame;
summoning the memory of her own destiny and sighing deeply, she withdrew to a secluded spot.
Then that Hariśarman, together with his family priest, having commenced the sacrificial rites according to the rules, completed them as he desired.
Then, having honored those kinsmen, relatives, and friends as well, he respectfully dismissed them, for they were exceedingly gratified.
Then all those kinsmen, relatives, friends, and well-wishers,
being delighted, praised him and went joyfully to their respective abodes.
Then all those kinsmen, relatives, and friends, being well-settled, sat down together, engaging in conversation with various stories.
Then that wise woman, having eaten later on, remained alone in a secluded place;
taking her son and daughter with her, she wandered about in the abode of Śiva.
There, having spread out some grass, she sat down together with her sons and daughters,
sighing deeply from the constant anxiety and suffering of poverty.
There, Viṣṇudāsa, having eaten later and being free from anxiety,
heard that [the goddess] was staying in the temple of Śiva and approached to stay with her.
Then, seeing her husband approaching, that wise woman,
her eyes red and with tears trickling down, spoke thus while lamenting:
"Fie on my life as a poor woman! For what is the use of such a life?
Indeed, even my parents no longer look upon me with compassion or affection."
Although all my sisters and even my own daughters were equal to my parents,
I was not honored by them with the same respect as I was by them.
Fie on the life of a poor woman, and fie even on birth as a human!
What is the use of beauty, or virtues, or even of learning, without wealth?
"Alas, O Fate! What terrible sin did I commit in the past, that I possess no prosperity, and even my parents show me no compassion?"
Therefore, what shall I do here? Where shall I go for refuge?
Who will protect me, tormented by the suffering of poverty arising from my own fate?
What is the use of such a life? Death is indeed better at this moment;
for all who are born must inevitably die.
Thus lamenting with various outcries, she looked again and again at her son, her daughter,
and her husband, and, pained by compassion, she wept.
Seeing her thus lamenting and weeping,
Viṣṇudāsa sighed, comforted her, and spoke as follows:
"O beloved, do not weep here; what can we do now?
Whatever sin was committed by us two, its fruit must indeed be experienced."
Therefore, maintain your composure here and remain steadfast; what need is there for much speaking?
Inevitably, such events come to pass even for the great.
That Śiva too was three-eyed, blue-throated, and clad in the directions as his garment;
he was intoxicated, his limbs smeared with ashes, and though he held a skull, he also bore bones.
Even Viṣṇu, that heroic Janārdana, was made to wander in saṃsāra;
he too became a servant to Bali, and as a thief, he was struck by the arrow of a hunter.
Even Brahmā, the lord of the world, was afflicted by desire and committed an act with one who should not be approached;
he was bound, struck down, served as a slave to his enemy, and had his head severed.
In former times, Rudra, out of anger, severed the fifth head of Brahmā;
grasping that head which was difficult to cast off, he wandered about the universe.
Rudra went to Śaṅkhatīrtha and released that head;
thus the Kapālamocana Tīrtha was established at the second whirlpool.
Thus it is stated in the *Utkalakhaṇḍa-kṣetramāhātmya*;
likewise, other people, sages, and ascetics as well [have spoken thus].
Those whose souls are consumed by the fire of anger go even to the hells;
in this same way, all people experience their own respective destinies.
Beings, experiencing both happiness and suffering, wander in the ocean of existence;
in an instant they obtain prosperity, and then they become impoverished.
All worlds, beginning with the gods, are enjoyers of their own performed karma;
thus, one should understand that in this saṃsāra, pleasure and pain arise from one's own destiny.

Do not despair; maintaining fortitude, act accordingly. Remembering the Lord of your own lineage and worshipping him according to the prescribed rites, take refuge in him with faith and worship him constantly with a concentrated mind.
Then, through the ripening of that merit, may our evil go to destruction;
thereafter, there shall be prosperity and abundance, and then we two shall obtain happiness.
"Having heard these words of mine, now summoning your fortitude, take both your son and daughter and depart; let us go home."
Having heard what was spoken by her husband, that wise woman, thus enlightened,
proceeded slowly with her husband, placing her son and daughter before them.
There, having gone to her own home and stayed for a moment, she became despondent;
then, rising up to see Śāntamati, she departed slowly.
There, that wise woman, standing before Śāntamati with her face smeared by flowing tears and sighing deeply, spoke thus: Rm_37.248{98} //
Śāntamati, filled with great shame, went there to witness that [sacrifice] which had been set in motion by her father’s great enthusiasm for the ritual. Rm_37.249{99} //
Even my sisters, kinsmen, relatives, and friends, upon seeing me,
all laughed at one another as they conversed.
(Rm 422) And all my nephews, their hearts filled with rage upon seeing me,
and seeing my son and daughter, blew upon them and struck them. Rm_37.251{1} //
All those sisters were honored by their parents with due respect, yet I was not even honored; they would not even deign to look at me.
Even at night, I was not granted shelter in their house out of disrespect;
instead, sitting in a temple of Śiva, I passed that night with great difficulty.
Thus, scorched by the fire of the suffering of great shame, I even desire to die; what then is the use of such a life?
O auspicious lady, if you possess compassion for me, who am suffering,
then you ought to instruct me in the means of acquiring wealth.
Having heard what she had said, Śāntamati, overcome with compassion,
looked upon the wise Dhīmatī, comforted her, and spoke thus:
"O wise one, I possess the means for the practice of the Great Auspicious Wealth (Śrīmahāsampat).
If you also have a desire for this, I shall explain it; listen to that."
If you have faith in the goddess Vasulakṣmī, observe her vow;
then the great goddess Śrīvasundharā shall dwell in your home.
Then, by the grace of the compassionate gaze of that Great Goddess,
prosperity shall arise for you and increase within your home.
Then, having given gifts to those who seek them with faith according to their desires,
and having performed worship of the Three Jewels, practice virtue and enjoy happiness.
By the ripening of this merit, may you always attain a happy rebirth,
and having gradually reached enlightenment, may you obtain the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Thinking thus, if you have the desire to achieve the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha,
go for refuge to the illustrious Goddess and, having composed yourself, observe her vow.
Having heard what was thus commanded by her, that wise woman, with joy, bowed to Śāntamati and spoke these words with palms joined in reverence: Rm_37.263{13} //
"Excellent, noble lady! Having maintained the vow and gone for refuge to the Glorious Goddess, and having performed devotion to the Triple Gem, I shall always practice virtue, O auspicious one."
Therefore, O Lady, out of your compassionate gaze, grant me that instruction;
for as long as I live, I shall devotedly observe the vow of the Illustrious Goddess.
Having heard what she had said, Śāntamati, looking intently at that wise woman with great respect, spoke to her once again in this way.
"If it is true, O blessed lady, then having bathed and clothed yourself in clean garments, go to that Lord Śrīghana; remembering him, let us both make our request."
Having heard this instruction given by her, that wise woman, with joy,
went immediately to her own home, bathed, and dressed herself in clean garments.
Taking hold of parched grain, unbroken rice, and flowers, he suddenly and joyfully spoke thus in the presence of Śāntamati as she was departing: Rm_37.269{19} //
"O blessed lady, I have arrived exactly as you instructed;
having called that Lord of Sages to mind, I pray here for a meeting with him."
Having heard what was thus spoken by her, Śāntamati respectfully took leave of that wise woman and went joyfully to the edge of the palace.
There, Śāntamati, standing together with Dhīmatī at the marketplace,
knelt upon the ground facing the direction where the Blessed One was stationed.
Having received the upper robe together with parched grain, unbroken rice, and other offerings,
and holding a handful of flowers along with water, he bowed and made this request to the Sage:
O Blessed One, Protector, Omniscient One, you too surely know that this wise and virtuous woman has come for refuge to the Blessed One.
For she now desires, according to the instructions of the Teacher and in accordance with the prescribed rule, to observe the vow of the illustrious Great Queen Vasudhā.
Therefore, having arrived here, O ocean of compassion, it behoves you out of mercy to instruct him in the glorious *sādhana* and the supreme vow.
Having thus made this earnest supplication to the Teacher of the Three Worlds, Śāntamati recollected him three times, bathed him, and then cast that water and other offerings into the [receptacle].
All those lotuses, parched grain, unbroken rice, dūrvā grass, and kuṇḍa flowers that she had cast were suspended in the sky like autumn clouds.
Then, traveling through the air like birds,
they proceeded and arrived at the monastery in the Ghoṣira Garden in Kauśāmbī.
As the Lord of Sages stood there, his head shone brilliantly in the sky; those [celestial bodies] remained stationed above him, gleaming like parasols.
Seeing that, all those monks belonging to the Saṅgha stood there filled with wonder, reflecting, "From where has this invitation come? Rm_37.281{31}

Thereupon Ānanda rose, went before him with palms joined in reverence, and having bowed down to that Lord of Sages, questioned him while filled with wonder: * *tatrānandaḥ samutthāya sāṃjaliḥ purato gataḥ / taṃ munīndraṃ praṇatvaivaṃ papracha vismayānvitaḥ //* Rm_37.282{32} //
"Blessed One, from where do these lotuses, parched rice, unbroken grains, and flowers come? It behooves you to explain that."
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, the Blessed One, that lord of sages,
addressed Ānanda and, looking at him, spoke as follows:
In the city of Kāśī, there was a brahmin named Viṣṇudāsa who was impoverished;
yet he was Dharmadhvaja, wealthy and glorious, a householder who resembled the Lord of Wealth himself.
They both had two virtuous wives: Śāntamatī, who was like Rāmā, and the wise Brāhmaṇī Bhadrā, who was poor and deeply afflicted by suffering.
They both desire to observe the vow of the illustrious Vasudhārā;
therefore, this offering has been brought by me for the purpose of inviting her.
Therefore, you ought to go yourself to Kāśī and, in the house of those two, instruct them in the ritual procedure for the vow of Śrī Vasudhārā.
Having heard these instructions from the Lord of Sages, he said, "So be it," and placing the Teacher’s command upon his head, he departed through the air for Kāśī.
There, from the sky, that Ānanda descended before the house of Śāntamati and stood illuminating it like the moon, the essence of nectar.
Beholding him seated there, the wise Śāntamati was suddenly filled with joy and approached to pay him homage.
Then, having approached him, the wise Śāntamati,
beholding that Ānanda, bowed down and joyfully made this request:
"Venerable sir, I pay homage at your feet; we have come to you for refuge.
Therefore, out of compassion, may you look upon us with favor and be gracious."
Since you, our teacher, have taken refuge in this house,
please instruct us in the ritual procedure for the vow of the Great Goddess Vasudhārā.
Since this wise and auspicious lady wishes to observe a vow through your instruction, for the sake of the great queen Vasulakṣmī.
Therefore, out of compassion, you ought to instruct her fully and in due order on the ritual procedure for the vow of the Great Goddess Śrī Mahādevī.
Having heard this prayer thus offered by Śāntamati,
and seeing that both of them were filled with joy, he replied, "So be it."
Then that wise woman, having bowed with palms joined to that son of the Jina, her face beaming with joy upon seeing Ānanda, made this request with delight: Rm_37.298{48} //
"Venerable sir, I am a sinful woman, a partaker of suffering by my own fate;
therefore, having gone for refuge to you, I desire the vow of the Earth."
Therefore, O Teacher, you have come to my home out of compassion;
it behoves you to instruct me according to the rules and grant me the vow.
Having heard this request made by her, Ānanda, the son of the Jina,
rose there and proceeded to the house of that wise woman.
Thereupon that wise and virtuous woman, endowed with peaceful intelligence,
went quickly to her own home and spread out that seat.
Then that wise woman, having joyfully washed the feet of the Teacher with pure water and having prostrated herself, made this request:
"Venerable Arhat of great supernormal knowledge, for the sake of showing me favor,
you ought to take your seat upon this throne and teach the Dharma."
Having heard that request, Ānanda, with a serene mind,
accepted the seat offered to him and remained there, radiating light as he entered into meditative absorption.
Upon seeing him, that brahmin Viṣṇudāsa was also moved to grace;
bowing with palms joined, he suddenly approached and took refuge there in solitude.
Then that wise and virtuous woman, accompanied by Sāntamati,
honored Ānanda and gratified him with food.
Then, having offered her salutation and seated herself on a low seat,
she spoke thus with palms joined to Ānanda, who possessed the great supernormal knowledges:
"O Venerable One, having joyfully accepted your command upon my head,
I shall certainly observe the vow of the illustrious goddess Vasudhārā."
Therefore, O Venerable One, you who are the Teacher, out of compassion and favor, ought to instruct me in that method according to its proper sequence.
When Viṣṇudāsa had thus prayed with a virtuous mind, Ānanda,
having heard him and looking at that brahmin, spoke as follows.
Listen, O Brahmin, to that which was instructed by the lord of sages as it was heard by me;
thus I shall explain to you the procedure for the Śrīvratam in its proper sequence.
Likewise, on the third lunar day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, or in the dark fortnight of Māgha, or always during the bright fortnight; Rm_37.313{63} //
At a sacred ford, in a temple, on a pure plot of ground, or in one's own homes,
one should properly perform the purification of the site with cow dung, earth, and water.
Having risen at dawn and bathed in sacred waters,
one who practices purity should perform the threefold sipping of water (ācamana) and purify the body with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), which is like nectar.
Possessing pure ethical discipline and meditative concentration, clothed in perfectly pure garments,
he should maintain the mind of awakening and uphold the instructions of the true guru.
Having properly drawn the mandala on level ground according to the ritual rules,
one should adorn it with banners, parasols, flags, and canopies.
Outside of that maṇḍala, and again outside the circle of flames,
he [should place it] with five rows of garlands together with parched grain and unbroken rice.
Then, having encircled [the area], one should place jars in order on the outside,
filled with water from sacred fords (tīrtha), covered with yellow cloth, and marked with signs.
There, having duly invoked the goddess Śrīvasudhā together with her retinue in the prescribed sequence,
and having worshipped and established her, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
Likewise, on the third day, having bathed at dawn and being clothed in clean garments,
he sits upon his seat at midday, facing the northern direction.
First, having worshipped the Guru, one should worship the Three Jewels;
then, one should meditate upon the Great Goddess Vasudhārā, the bringer of auspiciousness.
Having invoked her together with her attendants and respectfully offered water for the feet and the guest-offering (argha),
he worshipped her according to the ritual rules with an offering consisting of yellow lotuses.
Having first arranged all the necessary requisites, he presented them;
then he should correctly recite that dhāraṇī and the mantras in their proper sequence.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, one should offer praise, perform the confession of sins,
express rejoicing in merit, and pay homage while recollecting [the Buddha].
One should likewise perform circumambulations and prostrate with the eight limbs;
then, having stabilized the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one should pray for one's desired goal.
Then, having offered the bali-oblation, he should satisfy the spirits;
thereafter, having made a request for forgiveness, he should pray for the success of his vow-thread.
Having taken up the vow-thread (vratasūtra), which is divided sixteenfold and provided with sixteen knots, one should bind it upon the hand for the sake of protection.

One who seeks jewels obtains jewels; one who seeks wealth obtains wealth;
one who seeks enjoyments obtains enjoyments; and one who seeks fame obtains fame.
One who seeks wealth obtains wealth; one who seeks virtues obtains virtues;
one who seeks knowledge obtains knowledge; and one who seeks what is auspicious obtains what is auspicious.
One who seeks honor obtains honor; one who seeks victory obtains victory;
one who seeks dharma obtains dharmas; and one who seeks happiness obtains happiness.
One who desires a kingdom obtains a kingdom; one who desires a home obtains a home;
one who desires fields obtains fields; and one who desires flavors obtains flavors.
One seeking a wife obtains a wife; one seeking daughters obtains daughters;
one seeking sons obtains sons; and one seeking grandsons shall obtain grandsons.
One who seeks knowledge obtains knowledge; one who seeks liberation shall attain liberation;
likewise for all other things and even all implements.

Strong in the power of right understanding and steadfast, he shall attain the knowledge of awakening;

and having reached the state of a Perfectly Awakened One, he shall attain the state of final liberation.
Thus, O Brahmin, having understood this, if you desire the True Dharma,

Thus, may there always be auspiciousness and freedom from calamity in your home;

Likewise, having given gifts and yourself observing that vow,

he will certainly become a Bodhisattva, devoted to the discipline of the Bodhisattva conduct.
All the Sugatas and the Bodhisattvas, the sons of the Victors,
having observed the Vasudhārā vow, sustain the three worlds.
Having heard this which was thus instructed by that Arhat, the brahmin joyfully desired to practice the vow of the illustrious Vasudhārā.
Then Viṣṇudāsa, his lotus-like face beaming with great joy upon beholding his wise wife, spoke to her thus:
"O beloved, you are blessed and auspicious, since through your efforts I am now indeed attaining this jewel of a vow belonging to the Goddess Śrī."
Just as it has been instructed here by this teacher, so indeed,
having gone for refuge to the illustrious Goddess, I desire to practice the vow.
Therefore, you too, having composed yourself and with such reverence, ought to take refuge in the illustrious Goddess along with me and observe the vow.
Having heard what was spoken by her husband, that wise woman, expressing her approval,
looked at him and spoke to her husband once again as follows:
Thus, having established ourselves in truth and having gone for refuge with faith,
we both observe the vow of the Illustrious Goddess here with great reverence.
Having spoken thus, the virtuous and wise Bhadrā, with sudden devotion and joy, prepared the complete collection of materials for the observance of her vow.
Then, having bowed with joy and palms joined in reverence to her guru Ānanda,

"Venerable sir, on the day of the vow for the illustrious Mahādevī, you have arrived;
having instructed them according to the prescribed rule, let them observe the vow."
Having heard that request made by her, Ānanda, the son of the Jina,

There, having purified the ground according to the ritual rules, Ānanda drew the maṇḍala, established it, and consecrated it with mantras.
Likewise, having bathed at the sacred ford, the couple, clothed in clean garments,

Then, by the command of that Teacher, the couple sat down in due order upon pure seats, positioned facing the north.
Having purified all the materials, such as the products of the cow and so forth,

Then, having completed that vow and having given a gift along with a priestly fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, they bowed and dismissed that maṇḍala.
Then, having taken that powder and placed it in the treasury as prescribed,

"Aho! Truly, it is exactly as the Teacher of the World has taught.

Blessed is that wise Śāntamatī, who is also of noble character,
since she shall observe the vow of you, O Śrī Vasudhārā.

Having attained awakening in due course, he will reach the state of a Buddha.

Then, O Brahmins, her father heard from the talk of the people that great prosperity had arisen in the house of his wise daughter.
Then that brahmin, having joyfully and suddenly addressed his wife’s mother, spoke thus in her presence:
"O wise wife, have you heard what is now being said in the house: that a great fortune has indeed arisen for me?"
Having heard what was thus related by her husband, she, filled with wonder, said to that husband: "How could this be true?"
Having heard what was spoken by his wife, that twice-born Hariśarman,
filled with wonder at what she had related, spoke thus:
"My dear, wise lady, I have truly heard that a great abundance has now arisen in our home through the grace of Vasundharā."
Even if this is not known by the people, let that wise daughter be summoned here to your own home and questioned by you in this manner.
"How has such great prosperity now arisen in your house?
My daughter, tell me this truthfully," he said.
Having heard what was thus related by her husband, that wise mother,
acknowledging it with "So be it," spoke thus to her own friend:
Listen, friend, to what has now occurred in the house of my wise daughter:
a great abundance of wealth has arisen through the grace of Vasundharā.
"Thus have I heard this truth; indeed, I wish to see it.
Therefore, summon that daughter and bring her here with due respect."
Having heard what was thus related by her, that friend Supriyā,
having replied "So be it," went to the residence of Dhīmatī.
Having approached that wise Subhadrā and beheld her, she was filled with wonder and joy, and after bowing, spoke thus:
"O blessed lady, I have been sent here by my mother to summon you;
therefore, you ought to come at once, accompanied by your own daughter."
Having heard what was thus related by her, that wise woman, smiling with joy as she looked at her friend, spoke to her mother in this way:
"O, does my mother remember me? For what reason and how is it that she does not remember me now, when I am suffering from the pain of poverty?"
Nevertheless, I wish now to see my mother’s face;
I shall return in such a way as to fulfill my mother’s desire.
Having spoken thus, that wise woman then adorned her son with ornaments,
clothed him in fine garments, and decorated him completely.
And she herself, having adorned herself, was clothed in fine silk garments and graced by her limbs beautified with magnificent ornaments of jewels.
Then, accompanied by that female friend and together with her sons and daughters,
she set out and, along with the people, went to her mother’s house.
There, having seen that wise woman arrive, the mother approached her as she beheld both her excellent son and her excellent daughter.
There, seeing her mother accompanied by her son, the wise woman approached her suddenly, bowed, and inquired after her well-being.
Her mother also, together with her son and grandson,
suddenly embraced that wise daughter and joyfully inquired after her well-being.
Then that wise daughter, accompanied by her son and granddaughter,
approached her father's house while traveling together with her mother.
There, seeing his daughter Sādhumatī accompanied by her son and daughter,
the father, observing this, went out to meet them with joy.
Beholding Janaka, that wise woman, accompanied by her son, approached him with a smile; having bowed, she inquired after his well-being.
The father, too, having beheld that wise Śubhāṃśikā and having conversed with his son and daughter, joyfully inquired after their well-being.
The father and that mother as well, having taken up their wise and virtuous daughter,
along with their grandson and granddaughter, went to their own home with joy.
There, her mother respectfully washed the feet of both her granddaughter and grandson, and quickly brought them to her own home.
Having spread that seat himself with great care, he respectfully gathered his daughter,
his grandson, and his granddaughter, and seated them all there.
Taking her seat there, that wise woman stood with a smile, having positioned her daughter on her left side and her son on her right.
Hearing that she had arrived, all the tribesmen came out of joy to see her and approached Sādara with haste.
Likewise, all those kinsmen, as well as friends and ministers,
came to inquire after her welfare when she had thus arrived at her own home.
Likewise, those sisters and all their sons,
having heard that Dhīmatī had arrived there, went forth to see her.
In this way, other people as well, having heard that the wise and well-adorned Subhūṣaṇā had come to her mother’s house, approached in order to see her.
There, seeing that wise and beloved woman adorned with fine garments and ornaments,
all those people, including her kinsmen, were filled with wonder.
Then her younger sisters, kinswomen, and other relatives, friends, and well-wishers—
all of them bowed respectfully to her and joyfully inquired after her welfare.
Likewise, that wise woman also bowed to those venerable kinsmen, relatives, and friends,
and inquired after their well-being.
Then her mother, with joy and respect, presented that wise woman with food endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor.
Having respectfully presented Sītā with food accompanied by delicious flavors, he spoke to her as follows.
"O wise and beloved one, take this delicious enjoyment and eat it;
O Sauti, O daughter of a charioteer, whatever you desire has been spoken by the descendant of Saudāsa. (Rm 431)
King Janaka, having dispelled all delusion, along with his sisters,
brothers, and brothers-in-law, showed great honor to her and provided her with every comfort.
Having heard that they had all acted with such respect, the wise woman then recalled her former circumstances and reflected thus in her mind:
"I was not honored by these people, nor was this son honored;
O daughter, it is not that they honor me, but rather they value only wealth here."
"When there was no prosperity in my house and I was poor and miserable,
then all these people did not even look at my face."
"Now that wealth has arisen in my house, even though I am thus filled with happiness, everyone honors me with great respect. (Rm 37.447)
Since I am not honored at all, but rather wealth alone is esteemed,
let him by whom that [wealth] is honored enjoy this respect.
Having thus reflected in her mind, she looked upon all her own ornaments for her son and daughter and took them up.
Then that wise woman, having spread out all those ornaments upon a bronze vessel, addressed him with respect as follows:
"O sirs, all these ornaments are dear to me;
eat this food prepared with meat at your pleasure and with ease."
In this saṃsāra, wealth alone is always respected with great care;
for according to one's wealth, a person is either honored or reviled in the world.
In this world, a man who possesses wealth is honored even if he is low-born and devoid of virtue;
whereas one who is destitute is not honored, even if he is virtuous and well-born.
Everywhere, one receives consideration and food according to one's wealth;
through the pursuit of riches, even a fool or a base person becomes fortunate.
As long as a man possesses wealth in his home, he is honored in the world;
but when he is deprived of wealth, then he behaves like a mere beast.
Thus, even as she was speaking, she took up all her ornaments once again and fastened them back in their proper places.
Then, having eaten a little of that food, she, accompanied by her own daughter,
bowed to her parents and, being appeased, went to her husband's house.
There, that wise woman, having bowed at the feet of her husband Viṣṇudāsa,
stood before him and reported the entire account of what had occurred.
Having heard this account concerning his wife, that brahmin husband was delighted; seeing his virtuous wife, he spoke to her thus:
"You are fortunate and truly auspicious, since by following your instruction and undertaking the Śrīdevī vow, I have attained great prosperity."
"My dear, I consider you here— born of that lineage originating from the Jewel—
to be equal in my own mind to the illustrious Vasudhā, the Great Queen."
Having spoken thus, the brahmin husband Viṣṇudāsa, with palms joined in reverence,
bowed to that wise and most auspicious woman and spoke again as follows.
"O beloved, by your grace my birth has now attained fulfillment,
since I have become a devotee and observer of vows of the goddess Śrī Vasundharā."
By that [act], all the evil I have committed is now exhausted;
yet prosperity has arisen, and it shall never diminish for us.
In the same way, we too have always gone for refuge to this illustrious goddess;
having undertaken the vow according to the prescribed rite, let us now practice it, O auspicious one.
Having made offerings to the Three Jewels and having given to those in need whatever they desired,
and having performed virtuous deeds throughout our lives and enjoyed happiness, may we proceed [to higher realms].
Through the ripening of this merit, may we always go to happy rebirths,
and having attained perfect awakening in due course, may we reach the state of a Buddha.
Having heard what was spoken by her husband, that wise woman rejoiced;
thus, having always undertaken the Vasundharā vow, she practiced it auspiciously.
Then that wise woman, having come before Śāntamati and reported all these events, spoke as follows:
"O dear friend, O highly fortunate one, by the grace of your compassion, may all my sin be destroyed; may that birth of mine become fruitful."
Prosperity has been fully attained by me; may it never come to an end.
Therefore, for as long as life lasts, I shall indeed remain under the protection of the Goddess and worship her.
You alone are the Teacher, for there is no other who instructs in the True Dharma;
therefore, by the power of my merit, may you attain the state of a Perfectly Awakened One.
When this had been said, Śāntamati, having heard it with joy and looking at that wise woman, spoke to her once again as follows:
O auspicious and wise lady, established in refuge in the Perfectly Awakened One with constant devotion, undertake the Śrīdevī vow and practice it with focused concentration, O virtuous one.
By the ripening of this merit, may you always go to a happy rebirth,
and having attained awakening in due course, may you reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.

Thinking thus, one should practice here in this saṃsāra that which is auspicious and a means for achieving dharma and worldly purpose; since dharma exists for the sake of the world's welfare, you should practice dharma for the sake of the world.
Having heard what was spoken by her, that wise woman was awakened;
having joyfully assented, saying "So be it," she went to her own home.
From that time forward, that wise and virtuous woman always performed the worship of the Goddess Śrī at home and, having given gifts, she practiced auspicious conduct.
Likewise, in her house, prosperity increased day by day;
it became a means for all beings to enjoy and a source for accomplishing the Dharma.

"Thus was it instructed by my guru; thus have I heard it, and so I speak.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should observe the Vasudhārā vow."
O Great King, having diligently awakened the subjects as well,
establish them in the refuge of the Goddess Śrī and always cause them to observe her vow.
In that way, may you always have security everywhere and certainly;
having attained awakening in due course, may you reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard what was thus instructed by that Arhat, King Aśoka,
together with his retinue, approved, saying "So be it," and rejoiced.
Those wise ones who, with great clarity, listen to this avadāna that yields auspicious fruit,
and cause it to be heard with a joyful mind out of their love for the conduct of awakening—
they are all bodhisattvas, possessors of every virtue, and enriched with every excellence.
The glorious ones, the best in the world, having gone to the abode of the Jinas, dwell there enriched with happiness.
Thus ends the Dhīmatī-avadāna in the Śrī-ratnāvadānatatva.
XXXVIII. The Vasundharā-avadāna.
Then King Aśoka, with palms joined in reverence and full of joy,

The ministers and soldiers, householders and eminent men,
merchants and caravan leaders, as well as artisans and the citizens.
Villagers and country folk, as well as inhabitants of other lands—

O Blessed One, Omniscient Teacher, all these members of the assembly,

Listen, Ānanda, I shall proclaim that which was spoken by the Lord of Munis,
as it was heard by me from the deep resonance of the ocean-like Vajradhara.
For example, in the past there was a king named Sūryodaya,
a sovereign emperor and lord of men, in the delightful city of Śrīpura.
At that time, being passionately attached to the ten unwholesome deeds and falling under the sway of women, all the men there, through the instruction of evil friends,
proceeded to engage in actions rooted in the ten unwholesome roots.
Then, due to the fault of that sin, great calamities were set in motion;
assailed by those calamities, the earth became utterly agitated.
Thereupon, famine arose everywhere on earth in all lands;
then, all those men gradually became impoverished.

Then all those people, like the blind treading upon a wrong path,

Alas, what suffering for human beings! For those men who are devoted to evil become poor, merciless, and cruel, facing the very gates of hell.
Therefore, even here in the world of mortals, let us diligently observe the vow of the illustrious Vasudhārā for the sake of pacifying the suffering of poverty.
Then all those people, having heard this, seen it, and rejoiced in it,

Then, O auspicious lady, all those men, purified by that merit, shall always move about in prosperity, happiness, and with great devotion.

shall become Bodhisattvas, Great Beings, practicing for enlightenment.
Then, having been established in the six virtues and being devoted to the worship of the Three Jewels,

"For this reason, we have all come before the illustrious goddess;

Alas, what suffering for humanity, wherein there is no Teacher nor true guru!
Therefore, all those men engage in unwholesome conduct and remain in poverty.

For this reason, for the sake of pacifying the suffering of those mortals,
we shall establish them in the vows of restraint and enjoin them toward awakening.
Having thus resolved, that goddess Vasulakṣmī, overcome with compassion,

Just as there is one Vasundharī and a second Mahālakṣmī, she assumed a third form as Kumārī; thus she became the triple-formed goddess (Trimūrti).
Then that illustrious Mahādevī, intending to go to the abode of mortals herself,
addressed both Nandimukha and Aśvaghoṣa and commanded them thus:
"Nandīmukha and Aśvaghoṣa, you ought by all means to accomplish this great task of mine exactly as I have requested."

Having heard what was thus commanded by the queen, Nandika and Aśvaghoṣa, with palms joined in reverence, bowed to the queen and spoke as follows: *ity ādiṣṭaṃ tayā devyā niśamya tau kṛtāñjalī / nandimukhāśvaghoṣau tāṃ devīṃ natvaivam ūcatuḥ //* Rm_38.54{54} //
"O Goddess, what great task do you have? Please inform us of it certainly;
we shall surely carry out whatever you command immediately."
Having heard what was thus related by the two of them, the great queen Śrīvasundharā, her face radiant with joy, spoke to them as soon as she saw them:
"Listen, gentle-faced ones, to that which is my task for you, which I shall now declare; having focused your minds accordingly, you ought to perform it immediately."
All those men on the surface of the earth who are impoverished and exceedingly miserable,
being wicked and devoted to evil deeds, become those whose mouths are the gates to hell.
Therefore, I now desire to deliver them all by every means;
assuming three forms, I shall go to that earth.
O King Mahīpāla, we shall first discipline and establish that very Lord, the sovereign of all the world, in the Dharma.
Where the king himself, established in righteousness, conducts himself with composure,
there all his followers shall practice righteousness with devotion.
Wherever the king applies himself, whether to what is unwholesome or wholesome,
all the people of that world will indeed follow suit with great respect.
Thus, at the outset, he should be diligently applied to the duties of a king;
thereafter, that king should establish all people in righteousness.
Then all those people, O auspicious lady, turning away from the ten unwholesome actions and delighting in the true Dharma, shall proceed with their minds composed.
Then all those people, intent on mutual benefit,
having paid homage to the Three Jewels, would always practice within the vows.
Then, having performed what is always beneficial, they shall go to Sukhāvatī;
there too, maintaining their vows, they shall move about endowed with happiness.
Then, having gradually mastered all the perfections as well,
they should always act with devotion for the welfare of all sentient beings while practicing them.
Then those bodhisattvas shall possess the jewels of the qualities of the true Dharma;
they will become pure-souled mahāsattvas, sons of the Conquerors.
Then all those wise ones, having purified the three spheres and attained the awakening of the three vehicles, shall reach the state of perfect buddhahood.
For this reason, in order to discipline those beings,
I now go to the surface of the earth having assumed a form with three manifestations.
Therefore, having heeded my words, you two ought to go to the earth;
having gone there, bring that king back by every means possible through diligent effort.
Then, having brought him under my control and awakened him through diligent effort,
and having made him a practitioner of the true Dharma, I shall cause him to observe my vow.
Having heard what was thus commanded by the Great Queen,
Nandika and Aśvaghoṣa bowed to the queen and spoke as follows.
"O noble Queen, bearing your command upon our heads,
we shall go, bring the King here, and restore him to life before you."
Having spoken thus, with joyful faces and palms joined in reverence,
they bowed at the feet of the Goddess and then departed from that spot upon the earth.
Having assumed the form of the Triple Manifestation (Trimūrti), Vasulakṣmī herself,
accompanied by her companions such as Śrīdevī, arrived at the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having gone there to the surface of the earth, they beheld on all sides a beautiful great garden, adorned with lotus ponds.
Having seen both of them there, they stood for a moment at rest;
then, seeing them seated together, they spoke thus to one another.
"Aho! How delightful is this world of men, adorned with ponds and gardens!
So how can we go about here to carry off the king?"
There, Nandīmukha said: "Assuming divine bodies as beautiful as celestial women, let us proceed while singing the songs of the gods."
Surely that king, the lord of men, having seen our divinely beautiful forms and being tormented by the fire of desire, will strive to seize us.
Then, having quickly and with great effort brought that king here,
we shall delude and subjugate him and deliver him to the queen.
Having thus conversed and reached a mutual agreement,
Nandimukha and Aśvaghoṣa both assumed the forms of women.
Then, with voices as delightful as those of celestial nymphs, the two of them sat down in the abode of Durgā, singing divine songs.
Having heard that celestial music of theirs, the people living in that city approached to see it, their minds overcome with curiosity.
Seeing them with their divine forms, they were all filled with wonder; saying, "These must surely be celestial maidens," they gazed upon them.
Beholding those divine portions, they were all uplifted with wonder;
exclaiming, "Oh, how marvelous! they returned to the city after a long time.
There, those two celestial maidens did not remain in one place; every day they wandered about, singing in the four directions.
Thus, having witnessed his conduct, all those citizens as well,
their minds overcome by extreme wonder, moved about full of admiration.
Then those citizens, their hearts filled with wonder and apprehension,
went before the king, bowed down, and addressed him thus:
Victory to you, O God, Great King! You too should understand this;
nevertheless, we have come here to report a great marvel.
Therefore, here in this portion of the celestial grove, two women of auspicious marks,
singing divine music, have taken refuge in the place of Durgā.
And every day, O two celestial maidens, you wander joyfully about, moving through the four directions while singing divine music.
"O King, we have all come here for no other purpose than to ask: what will that omen be—whether auspicious or inauspicious? (Rm 38.94)
Having heard this report submitted by all those citizens,
the lord of the earth reflected for a moment and then, having seen [the matter], spoke thus:
"Conversing with women or singing songs will never lead to anything auspicious.
Having said this, he became despondent and reflected thus in his mind:
Surely there would have been no safety for you here, O Mānava,
had those two women not been sent by someone through their illusory power (*māyā*), having fashioned them in the form of women.
"What could this possibly be? Surely it is not a favorable omen.
What remedy shall I employ? I do not think anyone will point out what is beneficial."
Thus, with a dejected soul and sighing deeply,
the king sat within his chamber of grief and did not go anywhere outside.
Perceiving that the lord of men remained thus, having not gone outside,
Nandīmukha, upon seeing Aśvaghoṣa, spoke as follows:
"Aśvaghoṣa is that lord of men; nevertheless, he would not go outside.
Therefore, what shall we do here, since the king will not go outside?"
Having heard what was said by him, Aśvaghoṣa reflected; looking toward Nandimukha and seeking to awaken him, he spoke thus: Rm_38.102{2} //
Listen to the means for Nandimukha by which that king may be led away;
I shall explain that method for the abduction of the king.
When that house of the king is consumed by the illusory fire,
then the king, terrified and enraged, shall flee outside.
Then, having diligently summoned that king from afar,
we shall quickly bring him suddenly before the queen.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, Nandīmukha was enlightened;
responding with "So be it," he desired to act accordingly.
Then, having reached an agreement, the two of them quickly vanished from there as well and went to the king's palace, which was set ablaze by them with illusory fire.
Seeing that, the king was terrified and suddenly rushed out;
he quickly extinguished that blazing fire by means of various expedients.
Then that king, the lord of the earth, beset by the moat of anxiety and dejected in spirit within a chamber of grief, remained there and reflected:
"Aha! This fruit is indeed immediate, born as it is from the cause of women's song.
Therefore, what shall I do here so that this inauspiciousness may be stilled?"
Furthermore, another great portent and inauspicious omen might occur here;
how shall I provide a remedy for this? I do not know.
Thus, his soul dejected by anxiety and utterly bewildered,
the king sat within the chamber of grief and did not emerge at all.
Nevertheless, seeing him seated in his own quarters and not coming outside,
Nandīmukha and Aśvaghoṣa spoke to him once again in this way:
Nevertheless, that king, the monarch, will not come out at all;
so what shall we do here by which the king might quickly go forth?
Then, having observed this and reflecting upon it, Aśvaghoṣa addressed his companion Nandīmukha and spoke as follows:
"O friend, even though that great king is thus, he will not come forth here.
Therefore, what is the use of delay? Let us carry him away with effort!"
Having assumed the form of a boar, who now swiftly causes destruction everywhere in his delightful garden while he is on his rounds?
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, Nandīmukhī said, "So be it," and having given her promise, she looked at her friend and spoke as follows.
"We shall act in this manner for the successful accomplishment of the queen's purpose.
Having thus reached an agreement, the two of them went to that garden.
There, having beheld that beautiful lotus pond strewn with various flowers, they both stood for a long time gazing upon it.
Then Nandīmukha, seeing that delightful garden and the lotus pond rich with fragrance, spoke thus with great joy: Rm_38.121{21} //
"Ah! This garden is delightful and this excellent lake is most beautiful;
it must not be destroyed—how could we possibly destroy it?"
Having heard what was said by him, Aśvaghoṣa reflected;
and seeing that garden and the lake, he spoke thus after a short while:
"Let us quickly accomplish for the Queen exactly what she has desired;
therefore, let us now destroy this [palace] in order to carry off the king."
Having spoken thus and having made a pact with Saumata, those two, relying upon that great being,
assumed the form of boars and went to the shore of the lake.
With blood-red eyes and bristling hair, filling the quarters of the sky with their roar,
they resembled lions and tigers, their faces terrifying with their fangs.
There, spreading out, they both proceeded to destroy that garden and that lake as well, moving everywhere in every direction.
Seeing those two boars, the terrified garden-keeper suddenly fled from there and went to the royal palace. (Rm 38.128)

Having approached there and bowed at the feet of the king with palms joined in reverence, he, his face distorted by terror, made this announcement right before him: *The King of the Nāgas, having heard that the son of the Sage had been seized, came here with his entire retinue, desiring to take him away.* (Rm 38.129) *But seeing me standing here, he was filled with fear; and having abandoned the son of the Sage, he departed quickly, O King, together with his followers.* (Rm 38.130) *Therefore, O Lord of the Earth, you should grant me safety; for I am terrified, and my life is now dependent upon you.* (Rm 38.131) *For it is said that even the gods, including Indra, cannot harm one who has sought refuge with you, O King, provided they do not act with hostility.* (Rm 38.132) *But if you do not grant me protection, O Lord of Men, I shall surely go to Yama’s abode today, deprived of my life-breaths.* (Rm 38.133) *If you do not protect me from the Nāga, I shall enter the fire, or swallow poison, or cast myself down from a mountain peak.* (Rm 38.134) *Or else, I shall go to the hermitage of the Sage and serve as a slave to the son of the Sage, for I have no other recourse.* (Rm 38.135) *Therefore, O King, grant me freedom from fear; for I am terrified and have come to you for refuge, seeking your protection.* (Rm 38.136) *If you do not grant me safety, I shall surely die today; and when I am dead, what will you gain, O King?
