"Victory to you, O Lord! You should know that there is a lake in the garden where two boars have now approached and are wandering about, intent on destroying it."
Therefore, O Lord, quickly summon all the people of your entire army here and dispatch them at once to the forest to slay those two.
Having heard what was thus spoken by him, the king became greatly incensed;
he suddenly summoned his army and set out himself to slay those two.
Then that king, the lord of men, together with his ministers, army, and citizens,
suddenly approached that garden while sounding musical instruments.
There, having seen his ministers, army, and citizens, that king addressed them all together and instructed them once more as follows:
"O all you people, having prepared yourselves and become composed,
stand here surrounding [him] on all sides and gaze upon him."
"I shall stand in the eastern direction; in the southern, my ministers along with their counselors;
in the western direction, the generals; and let the citizens stand in the north."
In this manner, let all the ministers and others, concentrated in every direction, remain alert and stand surrounding him on all sides.
In whatever place you two boars are unable to find one another,
and from whichever direction they have fled, you should indeed punish those situated in that direction.
Having heard these words of mine, all of you, being composed,
prepare yourselves, look about, and, turning back, carry out [my command].
Having heard what was thus commanded by the king, all those people replied, "So be it," and proceeded to remain as instructed.
Likewise, the king stood in the east, the assembly of ministers in the south, the generals in the west, and the citizens stood in the north.
Thus, those people, together with the king, the ministers, the army, and the citizens,
having made themselves ready and looked on, all stood there with concentrated minds.
Thus, having stationed themselves, blocking all directions,
they silenced the sound of every musical instrument with their great roars.
Having heard that sweet and great roar and seeing them standing all around, the two of them let out a mighty cry.
Then, as violent winds suddenly arose and created darkness throughout the world, those two rushed toward the king.
There, being touched by those two, the king fainted;
overcome by terror, he trembled and fell to the ground.
Then, rising after a long time and looking around, "Where are these two?
he suddenly mounted his horse and went forth, following after them.
Likewise, those ministers, counselors, soldiers,
and citizens— all of them, following the king, fled in pursuit.
Mounted upon the king’s horse and followed by that boar, he fixed an arrow to his bowstring and entered the forest with great speed.
(Rm 441) There, having quickly cast off their illusory boar-bodies and mounted a horse, they gathered [their forces] and urged them forward into the midst of the forest.
There, that horse, possessing great speed like the wind itself,
leaped over rivers and mountains and galloped through the great forest.
Then those ministers, counselors, generals, soldiers, and subjects,
seeing the king entered into the deep forest, returned from their exhaustion.
Then that great hero Sena, traveling along the path of the Lord,
quickly moved forward without attachment, with a water-pot in his hand.
Like a shadow that accompanies it, he followed him with speed through the interior of the forest.
There, due to excessive speed, the king, though composed in meditation, was struck by the wind;
as he ran from his horse, he fell to the ground beneath a tree.
There, the king stood for a moment unconscious and fainted;
then Sena, sighing deeply, rose up with great effort.
Then, having comforted the king himself and taken hold of him,
he should place him upon that seat and cause him, who is overcome with fatigue, to rest.
Then that king, seeing the horse standing before him, sighing and afflicted by thirst, looked at Sena and spoke thus: Rm_38.158{57} //
"Alas, O Sena! A great hardship now arises for us here, in that we are sinking in this vast, impenetrable forest far away."
Therefore, what shall we do here, since all people have passed away?
In this remote and desolate wilderness, who indeed can point out the path?
Since I was here afflicted by extreme thirst, distressed by the heat and the wind,
and scorched by the fire of exhaustion and suffering, I have now been liberated even through my fortitude.
Therefore, O Sena, my protection of life depends on you;
for that reason, search even further and bring back the cool nectar.
Having heard what was spoken by the king, Saineya rose up suddenly;
consoling his master and looking at him, he spoke thus: Rm_38.163{62} //
"Do not despair, O Indra among kings, for you are a resolute Kṣatriya;
therefore, summoning your fortitude, you ought to remain steady for a moment."
Therefore, O lord of men, having searched even further for that water which is like nectar, I shall quickly bring it and give it to you.
Therefore, O Lord, until I have returned here having fetched water,
you must remain with the horse, maintaining your composure by all means.
Having thus informed his lord, that king of men,
and having comforted him with excellent water, the general departed quickly to search for it.
There, having looked all around and gazing everywhere,
he did not find any good water, and seeing [only] a vehicle at a great distance, he went toward it.
There, having heard the sound of the celestial river, Sena quickly followed that sound and proceeded toward it.
Having reached the bank of the celestial river there, he composed himself and,
suddenly resorting to the water, drank the delicious liquid.
There, his heart filled with great satisfaction, he looked all around and beheld on the opposite shore of that pure island hosts of celestial nymphs.
Seeing those hosts of Apsarases, Sena was filled with wonder;
gazing at them with joy, he stood as if fixed in a painting.
Seeing him standing there, all those celestial nymphs cried out together, "How have you come here? Who are you? Go away!"
Having heard that he was being summoned by them in this manner, Sena himself,
by their power, quickly crossed the celestial river and approached.
There, having approached all those hosts of apsarases, he,
with palms joined and a very serene face, bowed down and addressed them thus:
"O Great Queen, you should know that I am a servant and a follower of the great king Sūryodaya, who is renowned throughout the three worlds."
When the king's garden had been destroyed by the two boars,
the king then ran swiftly after them in order to slay those two boars.
The king was carried away by a horse; I alone abandoned him, and now he has fallen from that horse here in the forest as he was galloping too fast.
Taking refuge at the foot of an aśoka tree, afflicted by the heat and wind,
weary and tormented by thirst, he stood there desiring to drink water.
Having searched for that water everywhere, it could not be found anywhere;
yet, hearing the sound of a river here, I suddenly approached it.
"By the turn of my fortune, I have been sent here and have arrived; oh, now I obtain the sight of you goddesses, the Bhavāntīs! Rm_38.181{80}
Having spoken thus, Sena looked [at them] and, with palms joined in reverence, stepped forward;
he bowed to all those goddesses and apsaras and questioned him.
"O goddesses, for what purpose do you also remain here? If it may be told, you ought to instruct me regarding that matter."

Having heard what he had thus prayed for, the lord of the apsarases addressed Sena and instructed him as follows: "O Sena, go to the city of the Daityas; there you will find a maiden named Śaśilekhā, the daughter of the Daitya king. She is endowed with supreme beauty and possesses a splendor like that of the moon. Take her by force and bring her here. Thus commanded by the lord of the apsarases, Sena departed for the city of the Daityas. There he beheld the maiden Śaśilekhā, who was like a second goddess Śrī herself. Having seized her by force, he brought her back to the abode of the lord of the apsarases. There, she lived happily with him, enjoying all manner of pleasures. Meanwhile, the Daitya king, having learned of this through his spies, became enraged and dispatched a great army against him. However, Sena, relying on the power of the apsarases, defeated that host in battle and returned victorious to his own home. Thus, through the grace of the lord of the apsarases, Sena attained both sovereignty and the fulfillment of his desires. [The King said: "O sage, tell me how the lord of the apsarases came to possess such power. [Sauti replied: "In ancient times, O King, there was a king named Uśanas, the son of Śukra. He performed a great sacrifice for the sake of obtaining an apsarā. Pleased by his penance and devotion, the Lord of the Gods granted him a boon. The king chose an apsarā of incomparable beauty and splendor. The Lord of the Gods then bestowed upon him the apsarā named Menakā, who was adorned with celestial ornaments and possessed a radiance like that of lightning. Having obtained her, the king rejoiced, and through her, he begot a son named Sena, who was endowed with great prowess and destined for sovereignty. It was because of this that the lord of the apsarases acquired such power. [The King said: "O best of sages, tell me how the maiden Śaśilekhā came to be born and how she attained such beauty. [Sauti replied: "In the lineage of the Daityas, O King, there was a king named Virocana. He had a daughter named Śaśilekhā, who was born from a portion of the moon-goddess Rohiṇī. From her very birth, she was endowed with such exquisite beauty that she surpassed even the celestial nymphs. Because of her peerless loveliness, she became known throughout the three worlds as Śaśilekhā. [The King said: "Tell me, O sage, how the maiden Śaśilekhā met with Sena and how they lived together in happiness. [Sauti replied: "When Sena brought the maiden Śaśilekhā from the city of the Daityas, she was filled with joy at being united with him. They lived together in that celestial abode, enjoying every pleasure, like the god Indra and Śacī. Through their union, a son was born who was named Bali, who later became a mighty sovereign of the Daityas. Thus, O King, did the maiden Śaśilekhā attain her husband and live in bliss."
O Mānava, you do not know that we all observe this supreme vow of the great goddess Śrīvasudhā.
Having heard this explanation given by the goddess, Sena was delighted;
desiring to undertake that vow, he bowed to the goddess and spoke thus: Rm_38.186{85} //
Be gracious to me, O Great Goddess; since this vow belongs to Śrīdevī, I too desire to observe it—teach it to me.
Having heard what he had thus requested, that goddess was deeply gratified;
considering him to be Sena, the wise and steadfast one, she spoke to him again as follows.
"O Mānava, if you also have a desire for the Śrīvasudhā-vow, then behold it here; let the vow now be completed."
Afterwards, having fully explained to you the ritual practice for the vow of the Illustrious Goddess,
I shall instruct you in the procedure exactly as it was proclaimed by the Perfectly Awakened One.
Having spoken thus, that goddess Apsaras summoned all those hosts of Apsarases and likewise undertook the commencement of her vow on the bank of that river.
There, having taken refuge in them all, the goddesses, proceeding according to the sequence and according to the rule, undertook and completed the vow.
Having observed that vow, Sena was filled with joy;

prostrating himself in the eight-limbed salutation and joining his palms, he spoke thus: (Rm 443) Having observed that vow, Sena was filled with joy; prostrating himself in the eight-limbed salutation and joining his palms, he spoke thus: (Rm_38.193{92})
"Ah! By my good fortune, the vision of the Śrīdevī-vrata has been attained;
by that, my intellect is purified of sin and my inner enemy is now cleansed."
Be gracious, O Great Goddesses; with eyes of compassion, look upon me all of you, and having bestowed your favor, deign to grant [permission] for my vow.
"Having gone for refuge to the illustrious Goddess, I shall always practice [her path].
Therefore, you ought to fully instruct me in the ritual procedure for that vow."
Having heard this prayer made by him, the chief goddess,
upon seeing that army of pure nature, instructed him thus:
Listen attentively, O virtuous one; the procedure for the vow is now being declared, just as it was spoken by the deep resonance of the ocean-like voice of Vajradhara.
In the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, or likewise in the bright fortnight, and similarly in the month of Māgha, or indeed in all months; Rm_38.199{98} //
On the second day, having bathed at the sacred bathing place (upātīrtha) and being clothed in clean garments,
he should thoroughly cleanse the surrounding areas on the pure ground.
Having smeared [the ground] with clay, cow dung, and pure water, and thus purifying it,
he [decorated it] there with colors made of jewels and the five kinds of powdered minerals.
Having commenced according to the prescribed rule with flower-powders, or rice-flour, or likewise with stone-powders, one should mark out the lines in the proper sequence.
The preceptor, together with his disciples, should construct the mandala in due order;
there, he should draw the symbols of the goddesses and other deities according to the ritual procedure and in the proper sequence.

One should encircle it on all sides with seven rows of rice; then, there should be sixteen jars filled with water from sacred fords (*tīrtha*), covered with yellow cloth, marked with the emblems of the sixteen deities, and thoroughly purified.
They were provided with the five jewels, nectar, medicinal herbs, and young sprouts,
and were equipped with golden tilakas, parasols, banners, and small flags.
Having placed [the image] outside within a row of yellow lotuses,
one should surround it in due order and decorate it with banners, chowries, and canopies.
One should adorn [the area] on all sides with various fragrant flower garlands,
with incense possessing sweet scents, and with rows of lamps.
Then, having meditated upon the goddess Śrī Vasundharā together with her retinue within that mandala,
and having invoked, worshipped, and installed her, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
Then, having worshipped at the three junctions of the night according to the prescribed ritual,
and having offered an oblation consisting of the five nectars, one should proceed while keeping the Goddess in mind.
Then, on the third day at dawn, having bathed in the sacred ford with fragrant substances and pure water, he was clothed in two clean yellow garments.
Having sprinkled oneself with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should purify oneself;
then, having meditated upon the Goddess together with her retinue within the maṇḍala and having invoked her, one should worship her.
Likewise, those observing vows, having bathed and being clothed in pure yellow garments,
should purify all things by sprinkling them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then all those observers of the vow, headed by their preceptor, took their respective seats at midday, facing the directions of the king of the yakṣas in due order.

Having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels and bowed first to Vajradhara, they remained composed, holding fast to that which was instructed by the Master exactly as it was taught. (Rm 444) Rm_38.214{13} //
Having meditated upon the Goddess together with her retinue within the mantra, one should worship her in the proper sequence.
For example, the Guru, the Teacher, [visualizes] in the void the great yellow lotus arising from the syllable *drīṃ*, and upon that, a moon disc;
arising from that, the mountain of jewels, the glorious Bhava, and above that—
One should meditate on Śrī Vasundharā as being seated upon a golden jar (bhadraghaṭa).

Yellow in color, with one face, beautiful, six-armed, and seated in the graceful posture; her right hands display the gesture of granting boons and the gesture of salutation with joined palms holding jewels.
In her left [hands], she holds a jar of fortune (*bhadraghaṭa*), the Prajñāpāramitā manuscript, and a handful of grain;
she is most beautiful, wearing a crown of Ratnasaṃbhava Buddha.
In the second enclosure, at the back, is the Victorious One Vajrāsana, yellow in color, draped in yellow silk and adorned with divine jewel ornaments.
The resonance of the ocean of Vajradhara, bearing the granting of the supreme [boon] and fearlessness.
To the south is Lokeśvara, red in color and two-armed, holding the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) and a vajra in his hands;
he stands in the royal playful pose (*rājallīlā*) upon a vajra-paryaṅka seat.
Likewise, Vajrapāṇi is on the left, his hand holding a boon-granting gesture and a vajra;
he is green, possesses a royal grace, and is seated in the vajraparyaṅka posture.
Then Queen Līlā, seated upon a couch of living beings,
was honored in the presence [of the king] with the authority over all articles of enjoyment by means of her two arms.
To his left is white Varuṇa, seated upon a sattva-paryaṅka,
holding a citron (bījapūraka) resting on his lap with both hands.
On the southern side of Nīlabha is Bhadra, seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture;
with one hand he holds a citron, and the other is likewise placed upon his lap.
Civikuṇḍalin is situated in the southeast;
he is slightly red in complexion and stands with a citron fruit resting in his lap, held evenly by both arms.
In the southwest stands Kelimālin, dark-complexioned,
holding a citron fruit resting in his lap with both hands.
And in the northwest stands the one named Mukhendra, yellow in color,
holding a citron in his two hands which rest upon his lap.
In the northeast is Carendra, white in color, seated upon a being in the sattvaparyaṅka posture,
with two arms holding a citron fruit resting in his lap.
In that third enclosure, in the east, stands the goddess Guptā;
she is green in color and holds a chowrie in her two arms.
In the southwest resides the goddess named Vasuguptā, who is red in color;
with her two arms she holds a parasol resplendent with all kinds of jewels.
And Sarasvatī, the goddess, is likewise stationed in the northwest;
she is yellow in color, holds a banner in her hand, possesses beautiful limbs, and bestows all branches of knowledge and their objects.
In the northeast, the goddess named Candrakāntā is likewise stationed;
she is white, bearing a banner, and adorned with ornaments of all kinds of jewels.
At the eastern gate stands the great yakṣa Māṇibhadra,
possessing the luster of saffron and holding a mongoose and a citron in his two arms.
On the right, the one named Pūrṇabhadra likewise stands there, blue in color,
holding in his two hands a cluster of jewels and a citron fruit.
In the west is Dhanada, red in color, seated in the sattva-paryaṅka posture,
holding a fine vessel and a bījapūraka fruit with his two arms.
In the north likewise stands Vaiśravaṇa, yellow in color,
holding in his two arms a jewel and a citron tree bearing blossoms and fruit.

Having thus meditated upon all these deities, headed by Śrīdevī, in their proper order, and having invoked them, one should then offer water for the feet, water for sipping, and the sprinkling of water.
Then, having established them all within the mandala in their proper order,
one should worship them according to the ritual with the sixteen-fold components of worship.
Fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings—
these five modes of worship bestow the fruit of absolute liberation.
Thus are the five services: water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), as well as the bath, the honey-mixture (madhuparka) worship,
and likewise fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the food offering (naivedya).
And Pūtanācamanīya—these ten are proclaimed.
Thus are the ten services:
the seat, welcome, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping,
the honey-mixture, further sipping, bathing, garments, and ornaments.
One should employ fragrant flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and sandalwood in the worship; these are the sixteen modes of service.
Then one should likewise recite the mantra of the Goddess’s own heart as well as her *upahṛdaya*,
and all her other mantras as many as a hundred thousand times.
Then, having praised [the deity] with hymns and other offerings, with palms joined in reverence and full of joy,
and having performed circumambulations, one should again prostrate with the eight limbs.
Then, standing with palms joined in reverence, one should perform the confession of sins,
as well as the rejoicing in merit and the request for the [Buddha] to remain.
Then, for the satisfaction of all beings, one should offer a bali-oblation consisting of milk-rice, pure juices, and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), while reciting the verses.
Likewise, all those observers of vows, having maintained everything with concentrated minds,
should perform the vow in due order exactly as prescribed by the scriptures.
Then all those observers of the vow should give a gift accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to their preceptor, and they should also bow with reverence to the deities.
Then, having performed a request for forgiveness, the Guru should bestow upon those observing the vow a yellow thread divided into sixteen parts and knotted sixteen times.
Having joyfully received that scripture, all those observers of vows tied it to their own hands for the sake of protection and kept it until the completion of their vow.
Then all those observers of the vow, having maintained their aspiration for prosperity and having bowed and offered a request for forgiveness, should rise and go about their way.
Then, three days and nights hence, they should observe the vow by consuming flour made from barley and wheat together with all five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
Then all those observers of the vow, having bathed and being composed in mind,
should remain awake at night after lighting rows of lamps.
Having recollected that goddess together with her retinue, reciting the dhāraṇī as well,
and having performed the recitation, hymns of praise, and so forth, they should remain present and please her.
Thus they all passed that night, and then, in the same manner,
having bathed at the sacred ford with fragrant waters in the morning and being clothed in clean garments, they set out once more.
Having meditated upon that goddess together with her retinue and having invoked her in due order,
they should worship her with all the offerings of worship with due reverence.
Having performed recitations, hymns of praise, and so forth, and having rejoiced with palms joined in reverence,
they should also perform circumambulations and prostrate themselves with the eight limbs of the body.
Then, standing before him, they should perform the confession of sins,
as well as the rejoicing in merit, and they should pray for his firm establishment.
Then, for the sake of the practice of awakening and for the benefit of all sentient beings,
they should pray for the perfect attainment of all material goods according to their wishes.
Then, having honored the guru and given gifts along with a priestly fee (dakṣiṇā),
they should satisfy him with devotion and respect by performing prostrations.
Then, having offered the bali-oblation to the spirits and requested whatever is desired,
and having also made a request for forgiveness, one should dismiss them according to the ritual rules.
Then that teacher, the preceptor, having also requested forgiveness and having completed that vow, should recite the Vratasūtra.
Then, having taken up the consecration water, even one observing the vows should perform the consecration;
and having bestowed auspicious blessings, one should dismiss that mandala.
Then, having taken that powder and placed it in a well-secured storehouse,
one should always pay homage to it with constant reverence.

Furthermore, one should offer all flowers and other such items that have become *nirmālya* into water containing the presence of the Nāgas; having worshipped the Nāgas and offered all of that, one should cause it to flow away.
Having taken that river water, one should then perform [the rites] at home;
there, in all the houses, one should sprinkle them with those waters.
Then, having invoked her into that place within the mandala according to the ritual procedure,
one should worship the Great Goddess Śrī Kumārī and indeed satisfy her.
Having obtained his favor, one should perform the *gaṇacakra* according to the rules,
honoring him with appropriate worship and satisfying him with food as well.
Having thus completed that vow, all of them, being filled with joy,
should practice until the end of existence while recollecting the Great Goddess Śrīvasudhā.
Having thus taken refuge in the Śrīdevī according to this procedure,
one should, having composed oneself according to the rules, observe the vow with great care.
From that time forth, the goddess Śrī Vasundharā herself would come to his house, and having established security everywhere, she would dwell there forever.
From that time forth, may there always be auspiciousness everywhere in his house;
may there surely be constant joy, free from all affliction.
Then, in his house, prosperity increased day by day;
it became filled with all kinds of wealth, arising just like that of Śrīda.
Moreover, even if he is thus capable, the faithful and wise man,
having bathed and put on clean garments, should cleanse his entire house inside and out.
Having thus displayed an image of the Śrīdevī, or even a painted cloth [mandala],
and having worshipped it according to one's ability, one should always recite the dhāraṇī.
And the goddess Śrī, accompanied by her retinue, shall dwell in his house as well;
thus there shall be auspiciousness and freedom from calamity in that place.
Then, in his house, prosperity increases day by day;
filled with all kinds of wealth, it shall never diminish anywhere.
Alternatively, having likewise prepared a mandala with yellow powder from the previous day,
one should spend that night there according to the prescribed rule.
Having bathed in the morning with fragrant water, clad in pure yellow garments,
practicing celibacy, and being purified in soul, he has gone for refuge to the Triple Gem.
Having meditated upon that goddess Śrī Vasundharā with a concentrated mind,
and having worshipped her according to one's ability, one should recite the dhāraṇī with faith.
And having brought prosperity to his house as well, the Goddess shall dwell there forever;
then, in that manner, his wealth will certainly increase progressively.
Then, having bathed in that manner at dawn, the wise man, clothed in clean garments, observing celibacy, and having composed his mind, took refuge in the Triple Gem.
Having spread out the cloth painting (paṭa) and the image of the Goddess in a clean place,
and having worshipped it according to one's ability, one should recite the dhāraṇī three times.
And having brought prosperity to his house as well, the Goddess shall dwell there forever;
likewise, great abundance will certainly increase there.
Alternatively, having bathed in that manner, the wise one, clothed in clean garments,
observing celibacy, pure in soul, and having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels;
Having prepared a mandala with sandalwood paste in a pure place or house for the Goddess,
one should likewise meditate upon the Goddess, invoke her, and worship her.
One should recite the dhāraṇī in this manner and perform recitations, praises, and so forth;
having performed circumambulations and bowed down, one should thus pray for the treasure.
And having brought about auspiciousness and freedom from calamity in his house as well, the Goddess herself shall certainly dwell there, taking up residence for all time.
Then, in that house, prosperity endowed with all kinds of wealth will surely increase, and a treasure-trove shall also emerge.
Alternatively, it may be in one's own pure house, or even in a treasury or storehouse,
or likewise in another's house that is pleasing and well-cleansed.
Then, in the presence of the Tathāgata and also of Lokeśvara,
as well as in the presence of other bodhisattvas and likewise of the deities—
Having likewise prepared the maṇḍala of the Goddess Śrī with sandalwood paste,
one should meditate upon it according to the rules in the mind, invoke her, and worship her.
In this manner, one should worship the Tathāgatas, the Lord of the three worlds, and likewise other bodhisattvas, according to one's ability.
Then, having meditated upon that goddess together with her retinue, one should recite [her name] with a concentrated mind;
and with faith and a devoted heart, one should also chant the dhāraṇī.
And likewise, one should recite with joy along the path for one uninterrupted day and night, or similarly for three, five, or seven days and nights.
And the teacher, having likewise performed [the ritual] three times at night and three times during the day,
should offer the bali-oblation to the world-protectors and the spirits according to the prescribed rule.

Then the patron, with due respect, should provide all necessary implements and other requisites along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the recitation of the scripture, and likewise to others as well.
Then,
having bowed with palms joined and requested forgiveness as well,
he should joyfully pray for the perfection of material resources that serve as the means for attaining perfect enlightenment.
Then, having completed everything with these [rites] and having performed their dismissal,
one should satisfy all the teachers and others with appropriate food offerings.
Having collected all the colored powders from that mandala along with the flowers,
one should place them in a small box or a storehouse and keep them there forever.
Wherever that dust is cast, there prosperity increases;
it becomes filled with all kinds of wealth and shall never be exhausted anywhere.
Having worshipped the nāgas in the river, one should cast away all other remains of offerings, including the food offerings, banners, and so forth, and let them flow away.
Then that *dhāraṇī-vidyā* shall become perfected through recitation;
wherever it is recited, there prosperity shall increase.
Thus has the truth been declared by all the lords of sages;
considering the practice of the Śrīdevī to be auspicious, perform that vow accordingly.
Whoever has thus gone for refuge with faith to the illustrious Mahādevī, and having composed himself according to the rule, practices her vow with devotion;
All the hosts of Māra who cause affliction to sentient beings shall never be able to inflict any harm upon him anywhere.
All the gods, beginning with Śakra, as well as all the lords of the Daityas, the planets, the stars, the Siddhas, the Sādhyas, and the Vidyādharas; Rm_38.308{7} //
And all the world-protectors, as well as the gandharvas and kinnaras,
all the yakṣas and rākṣasas, and even the nāgas and garuḍas.
All the Mātṛkās and Bhairavas, along with Kumāras and Vināyakas, as well as Mahākālas, Ḍākinīs, Śākinīs, and others likewise;
Likewise, all the yoginīs and the heroes, such as Yamāntaka and the others,
always and eternally protect those who have taken refuge in the Śrīdevī.
Furthermore, all the hosts of spirits and the ill-intentioned piśācas [will not harm] that practitioner who observes his vows and recites the dhāraṇī.
All diseases such as fevers, and even those such as epilepsy, [are cured].
Insanities, pustules, all forms of leprosy,
and scabies never touch the body of one who observes the vow of Śrīdevī.
And likewise, all calamities that cause great affliction shall never enter his country, his home, or his body.
Wherever the vow of Vasundharā and the Dhāraṇī are practiced,
there the wicked hosts of Māra and their calamities do not enter.
Kings, fire, water, thieves, and other such evils, as well as the wicked, the deceitful, and the fraudulent,
shall not be able to cause even the slightest harm to those who observe the vow of Śrīdevī.
And whoever, possessing devotion for Śrī Vasudhārā, has gone to her for refuge,
constantly practices her recollection and observes the wandering vow.
And whoever, with joy, recites this dhāraṇī of that Great Goddess while remembering it, and likewise always instructs others in it as well; Rm_38.319{18} //
Whoever correctly writes this dhāraṇī, or causes it to be written, and having taken up what has been written, installs it and honors it in his home; Rm_38.320{19} //
And whoever, having written the heart-mantra of the Goddess upon a birch-bark leaf,
constantly wears it with devotion on the head, the neck, or the arm;
And for all of them as well, even all the obstructive and calamitous Maras would never, at any time or place, be able to cause them harm.
All those bodhisattvas dwelling within the three realms rely upon the perfection of generosity through the power of this vidyā.
Even if they satisfy all sentient beings with every kind of requisite,
those who always practice giving in this way proceed upon the path to enlightenment.
Having thus fulfilled all ten perfections in due order,
and having conquered all the hosts of Māra, they shall attain the perfection of enlightenment.
And all kings, such as universal monarchs (cakravartin) and other rulers,
protect their subjects and the worlds through dharmas arising from the vow of Lakṣmī.
In this way, other worlds as well— whatever possess the fullness of prosperity,
great wealth, and vast enjoyments, and are endowed with all material goods— [are likewise seen].
Having given gifts and always enjoyed happiness throughout their lives,
all those who act thus should be known as such by virtue of the grace of Lakṣmī.
Those great beings who, having undertaken the vow of the Goddess Śrī, bestow upon all supplicants whatever they desire, are illustrious and endowed with excellent virtues.
Endowed with the perfection of fame, the abodes of all branches of knowledge and arts,
they were righteous-souled, renowned as great lords, wise, and speakers of truth.
They were virtuous, fortunate, and auspicious, dwelling in patience and gentleness;
their faculties were mild, their limbs were pure, and their intentions were beautiful, moistened with compassion.
Possessing great strength, vigor, and enthusiasm, free from afflictions and well-composed, they have conquered their senses; they are profoundly steadfast, endowed with wisdom, and discerning.
They were experts in the methods of skillful means, seeking the welfare of all sentient beings;
they possessed well-formed aspirations and meditative concentration, and were powerful practitioners of the holy life.
Those who possess knowledge and discernment, who bring auspiciousness to all sentient beings,
become Bodhisattvas, lords of the world, and sons of the Buddha.
Those ascetics who have passed away, those who are present, and those yet to come—
all of them, too, [attain their goal] through the power of the merit of the Great Goddess’s vow.
Having gradually fulfilled all the perfections with equanimity, they indeed attain awakening; thus shall they obtain it, and not otherwise.
Knowing this, having mastered the supreme Dhāraṇī of the Great Knowledge, the Illustrious Goddess,
recite it constantly and observe the vow with devotion.
This is the Great Sovereign Goddess, the Fortune of Awakening, the glory of the Lord of Jinas;
she is the mother of all Buddhas, their nurse, their progenitor, and their protector.
Invincible to all the wicked, the destroyer of all obstacles,
the auspicious Mistress of Great Knowledge, she is the slayer of all misfortunes.
By merely taking refuge in her, those human beings who observe her vow never again fall into the fire of poverty, suffering, and grief.
They shall obtain inconceivable jewels and other riches, as well as the qualities of wealth and property, and attain happiness consisting of fame, dharma, purpose, and desire.
This merit is incalculable, immeasurable, and exceedingly great;
indeed, it cannot be calculated even by all the Lords of Sages.
It is possible to count all the merits of vows and recitations;
but who is able to count this merit of the vow?
Since this likeness to his vows is found nowhere else, how could anything superior to it exist in the world? It is not seen anywhere at all.
Such a great jewel of merit, difficult to find even throughout the three worlds,
is obtained by human beings on earth solely through devotion to the Three Jewels.
Therefore, having understood this, you have gone for refuge to the Triple Gem;
having invoked the goddess Śrī according to the ritual rules, practice the vow with a concentrated mind.
By the power of this merit, may he always attain a happy rebirth;
endowed with glory and prosperity, may he be a donor who bestows happiness.
Having attained the threefold enlightenment, may they reach the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
For this reason, you have yourself come for refuge to the Great Goddess;
therefore, while observing the vow, propagate it everywhere throughout the world.
Having heard what was thus commanded by the Great Queen, Sena bowed with palms joined in reverence and spoke thus to that goddess: Rm_38.350{49} //
"O Goddess, I shall do exactly as you command, bearing your order upon my head;
therefore, be gracious, O Great Goddess, and bestow upon me the dhāraṇī."
Having heard this request made by him, the goddess was greatly pleased; looking at Sena and addressing him, she commanded as follows: *Rm_38.352{51}*
"Excellent, Sena! You should take up this supreme dhāraṇī of the Goddess;
recite it yourself and teach it to others according to the prescribed ritual."
Having thus instructed him, that goddess Śrī, the Earth, in the form of an apsarā,
bestowed upon him that *dhāraṇī* of the goddess while reciting it amidst the armies.
Having bowed down to that Great Goddess with palms joined in reverence, Sena joyfully and with faith took up the *dhāraṇī* and *vidyā* of the Illustrious Goddess.
Then that celestial nymph respectfully gave Senā a cake made of wheat and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) for his protection.
Having seen that flour which had been given to him, Sena was delighted;
yet, having bowed to the king and remembered him, he did not eat it himself.
Then, having cast off her form as a divine apsarā, she appeared in person bearing the threefold form (Trimūrti),
seated upon a auspicious jar situated in the center of the lunar disc.
She displayed her own form, encircled by a halo of radiance;
the other goddesses likewise assumed their own forms before Queen Vasundharā.
Turning back and placing them in front, they stood in all directions fanning them with banners, flags, and yak-tail whisks,
appearing exactly as described.
Then Sena rose up and, with joy, repeatedly prostrated himself before that goddess and her retinue with his eight limbs, his throat choked with emotion.
Then Sena, having prepared that paste of the five nectars and having brought that water, went suddenly into the presence of the king.
There, Sena, seeing the king approaching from afar,
set forth all that [food] beginning with the ambrosia and presented it to him.
Then Sena, beholding that king, with palms joined in reverence and a joyful countenance,
bowed down and stood before him with great delight.
Having seen all that, including the ambrosia and other things, the king was struck with wonder and asked him: "Why has this delay been made?"

When the king had thus questioned him, Sena, having approached that monarch and beholding him, spoke as follows with due humility: (Rm 451) Thus questioned by the lord of men, Sena, having drawn near, looked upon that king and spoke these words with propriety.
"Forgive me, O Great King, for the reason why I delayed;
having related all of that, I shall also awaken you."
First, O Great King, drink this nectar from the celestial river;
eat this fivefold nectar as well, and this well-ground flour.
Having spoken thus, he took up his water-pot and offered it,
as well as the five nectars for enjoyment and flour-cakes, before the Lord.
Having seen all that, beginning with the nectar, the king was delighted;
taking up the water-pot, he drank that delicious nectar.
Then that king, satisfied and his heart gladdened by freedom from craving,
partook of those five nectars as well as the edible flour-cakes.
Then that king, satisfied and gladdened by great joy,
looked upon the wise and steadfast Sena and spoke thus:
O noble-minded one, you too drink this nectar that is like ambrosia;
eat this excellent cake, which is a source of enjoyment and a food of immortality.
When the king had thus commanded, Sena, fully adorned,
took all that nectar and the rest and consumed it himself.
Then, taking that remainder, the gratified Sena presented it all to the horse and gave it away as a gift of diversion.
And that horse, having beheld all those things such as the nectar and so forth,
tasted them and, while enjoying them, attained great bliss.
Then that king, the monarch of purified intent, joyfully addressed Sena and questioned him once again as follows.
"O Sena, this ambrosia and other things which you have brought—where and how did you obtain them? You ought to tell me the truth."
When the king had thus made his request, Sena, with palms joined in reverence and full of joy, bowed to his lord the monarch, looked upon him, and spoke as follows: Rm_38.379{80} //
Listen with focused attention, O King, as I report to you this nectar and other things which I have obtained and brought here.
Because you were afflicted by thirst here,
I have been wandering anxiously through that forest, searching for water while looking about.
"Water is not to be seen anywhere here in this desolate forest;
therefore, go much further away and wander about to search for water."
Even there, no water was to be seen anywhere at all;
then, hearing the sound of a river from a great distance, he followed it.
Following that sound, I went and beheld the celestial river;
there I also saw hosts of goddesses engaged in the practice of vows.
There, having observed their cries, they called out with great devotion;
then, by their power, I crossed that river and proceeded.
There, all those hosts of apsaras summoned me and spoke, saying, "From where and how have you come here? Tell us."
Then, having approached all those hosts of apsarases, bowing respectfully with palms joined, I addressed them thus in their presence:
The great king Sūryodaya, the protector of the earth and lord of men,
had two boars causing havoc in his pleasure garden.
Having heard that, the king, together with his ministers, army, and citizens,
mounted his state elephant and set out to slay the boars.
There in the garden, those kings and others stood on all four sides, surrounding it completely and crying out "Alas! Alas! in lamentation.
Then those two most formidable boars, together with Sāgara,
emerged from the garden and rushed with great speed toward the presence of the king.
There, out of anger, that king pursued those two boars;
mounting his horse, he entered the forest with speed and roamed about.
There, the king fell from his horse as it was galloping with speed;
afflicted by fatigue, heat, and thirst, he sat down at the foot of a tree.
Wandering about in search of water for that king who was afflicted by thirst,
I did not see any water anywhere in a certain desolate forest.
Then, having gone even further and searching for water everywhere,
I wandered about until, hearing the sound of a river from afar, I approached it.
"For this purpose, O goddesses, I have come here suddenly from afar;
therefore, may you be gracious, for you are beheld by me through my good fortune."
When I asked, "For what purpose do you ladies dwell here, having taken refuge in this place? all those goddesses were propitiated by me.
Having respectfully addressed me, they spoke thus before me:
"O Mānava, you do not know that we have taken refuge here with you;
therefore, listen with a concentrated mind as we explain the reason for this."
"We have all gathered here to observe the vow of that illustrious goddess, the divine Māheśvarī Vasuṃdharā."
Therefore, observing our vow in this matter, remain for a moment with a concentrated mind;

There, seeing her husband, she approached him suddenly with palms joined in reverence; having prostrated, she sat down upon the seat together with that husband of hers.
There, that king, joyfully beholding his beloved queen, asked after her welfare and questioned her once more as follows:
For what reason have you gone there, and from where have you now come?
Having explained all of this, awaken my mind.
Having heard this command from her lord, Cūḍadevī related the account of her own adventures and informed him of the course of events on the road.
Then I went quickly to see the goddess Vasundharā;
having heard the sound of a river from afar, I approached that place.
There on the bank, I saw women carrying water-jars for the Goddess; when I asked them, "From where have you come? they replied:
"Let it be understood by you that these jars, filled with nectar, are being carried by us for the purpose of bathing the Great Goddess Vasudhārā."
This river flows with the nectar of the bath of the Great Goddess;
therefore, having washed your face in this nectar, look upon it.
Having heard what was thus instructed by them, she replied, "So be it," and being awakened,
she likewise washed her mouth with the nectar of that river.
Then, having quickly crossed that river Śrīsundarā, where the assembly with their retinues was seated, I approached it.
There, having approached the goddess Śrī Vasundharā together with her retinue and having bowed with palms joined in reverence, I took refuge in a secluded spot.
Then, as soon as she saw me, the illustrious Mahādevī asked this:
"From where and for what purpose do you come? Let that be told here."
Having heard that, with palms joined in reverence, having bowed and performed a circumambulation, I approached that Great Goddess together with her retinue and spoke thus: Rm_38.853{90}
"I am the beloved queen, the consort of King Sūryodaya;
I have come here with joy to pay my respects to you."
"Whatever vow was not properly observed by me, a woman of feeble fortune,
you ought to forgive that great transgression of mine."
"O Great Goddess, I have always remained in your refuge;
now, indeed, I wish to once again undertake the vows correctly."
Therefore, O Great Queen, having again shown me your favor,
you ought out of compassion to cause me to undertake that vow.
Having heard this request of mine, the illustrious goddess Vasundharā looked upon me with a compassionate gaze and instructed me thus:
"Excellent, my child! If you have the desire for me to observe this vow, then go to your own home and, together with your husband, perform the vow with devotion."
Then I myself will come and behold your temple;
having taken refuge there, I shall grant you the boon you have requested.
Having heard this instruction given by the Great Goddess, I was awakened;
I then questioned that goddess Śrī Vasundharā once more with great reverence.
"O Queen, what has been pointed out by the people standing on the road is being told by me;
therefore, it behoves you to explain it and enlighten me."
Having heard that, the Great Queen related to them all exactly how those various deeds had been performed by them, just as they had occurred.
Then, with faith and mere devotion, I respectfully worshipped that Vasundharā, the goddess Śrī, along with her retinue.
Then, having performed a circumambulation with joy and palms joined in reverence,
he prostrated himself with his eight limbs before the lotus feet of the illustrious Mahādevī.
Then that goddess, together with her retinue, vanished in an instant;
rising up thereafter, he did not see that goddess anywhere at all.
Then, my heart overcome with wonder, I joined my palms in reverence there;
having called to mind the Goddess together with her retinue and bowed down, I proceeded slowly from that place.
There, having encountered all those sinners along the way in succession,
I informed them of what had been commanded by the Great Goddess and thus brought them relief.
Then all those sinners, tormented by my words,
took refuge in the Blessed Goddess, cast off their bodies, and proceeded to heaven.
Having rescued these beings through the grace of the illustrious goddess,
I have returned here in safety and have obtained the sight of you.
Having heard this entire account reported by Queen Cūḍā,
the sovereign king was astonished and spoke as follows.
"Aha! By good fortune and through the grace of the Goddess Śrī, you have been obtained as my wife and queen; you are the very vow that brings me the wealth of prosperity."
Likewise, O Queen, I shall always observe the vow here together with you, my consort, with great devotion, exactly as you have commanded.
What is the use of this enjoyment of a kingdom without you, my queen?
For this alone is true worldly existence: that one should observe the vow together with one's wife.
Therefore, let us both always seek refuge here in the Illustrious Goddess;
having honored her vow with faith, let us worship her with great devotion.
Having thus instructed them, the king, filled with great joy,
returned to the glorious city accompanied by those two who were full of high resolve.
He took delight and enjoyed himself with that auspicious goddess;
then, in the course of time, Queen Cūḍā conceived a child in one day.
In the seventh month, during the hour of Brahmā, she gave birth to a son adorned with the marks of royalty, who was pleasing to behold and possessed well-developed limbs.
Then the father, having summoned all his ministers and counselors,
questioned the preceptor Śrī Senagupta regarding the cause of [his son's] birth.
Having reflected thus, Senagupta spoke to the king, awakening him to the truth.
Do not despair here, O Indra among kings, for you are endowed with the marks of royalty;
this yoga is universal, so hear now its fruit for seven months.
In the first month one should know there is the *kalala*; in the second, the *ghana*;
in the third, the mouth and the hard parts; and in the fourth, the collection of bones.
In the fifth month it is covered with skin; in the sixth, the limbs emerge;
and in the seventh, consciousness is attained—such are the characteristics of the state of the womb.
The child who is born in the seventh month is indeed fortunate;
having become a sovereign emperor, he rules the earth with excellent policy.
"Therefore, O lord of men, that child must be protected with great effort.
Having heard these words of the teacher, the king was overjoyed and had the birth rites and other ceremonies performed with great festivities.
Then the preceptor Senagupta, considering that he had performed the auspicious rite of the vow,
gave him the name Maṅgalodaya as well.
Then the boy, endowed with splendor and strength, grew rapidly day by day like the moon in its bright fortnight.
Then, in the royal palace, the king, together with his wife and sons,
arrived joyfully, eager for the Vasundharā vow.
Then, when the day of the vow had arrived, that king, the lord of the earth, having reached an agreement with his wife, desired to observe the vow.
Then, having prepared the full requirements for that vow according to the prescribed rule,
he performed everything exactly as instructed by the preceptor.
Having undertaken the vow of the Goddess Śrī, that king, together with his queen,
performed it with great devotion according to the prescribed rites until it was fully completed.
At that moment, the goddess Śrī Vasundharā herself, accompanied by her retinue, arrived there and took up residence, illuminating the surroundings.
Having beheld in person that goddess Śrī Vasundharā, who was attended by her retinue, the king, together with his wife, stood before her.
Having quickly offered water for the feet and honored him with the various articles of worship,
she circumambulated him, bowed down, and fell prostrate before him with palms joined in reverence.
Then the illustrious Mahādevī Vasulakṣmī, having beheld the king together with his wife, rose and, looking at them, commanded as follows:
Listen, O illustrious king, to that which you desire;
I shall tell you all of it, for these words of mine are true.
When Mahālakṣmī had thus instructed him, the king, together with his wife,
joyfully bowed with joined palms to the goddess and entreated her with great reverence as follows.
Homage to you, O Śrī Mahādevī; be gracious, O Supreme Goddess!
Grant me that very boon which is the purpose of your endeavor.
Having heard this request made by the king, the illustrious Maheśvarī looked upon that protector of the earth together with his wife and commanded him thus:
"Excellent, O King! Having yourself undertaken this vow, cause it to be observed everywhere.
After you have accomplished this great task for me, then depart for my abode."
Having spoken thus, the illustrious Mahādevī Vasundharā,
together with her retinue, vanished at that very moment and went to her own abode.
Then the king, together with his beloved, seeing that queen and her entire retinue vanished, stood for a moment filled with wonder.
Then, having thus taken refuge in the Goddess Śrī along with his wife, that lord of the earth always maintained and observed her vow.
Likewise, she instructed the vow of the Goddess Śrī throughout all the worlds; having awakened them through diligent effort, she caused it to be practiced everywhere.
Thus that king, having caused the queen’s vow to be observed everywhere,
always brought about the welfare of all sentient beings.
Through the ripening of this merit, that king, endowed with glory,
having obtained divine and even more excellent pleasures, always practiced what was auspicious.
Then that king, the ruler of men, having given to all supplicants whatever they desired,
always practiced his vow with the aspiration for perfect enlightenment.
Thus that king, the lord of the earth, rejoiced together with his wife and,
out of devotion, undertook one hundred and eight vows dedicated to the Goddess Śrī.
Then, having consecrated his own son as his successor upon his own throne for the sake of worldly dharma and purpose, he went to the Tuṣita heaven together with his wife at the end.
Then, together with his beloved, he approached the presence of the illustrious Goddess;
having performed worship at all times, the glorious one remained there, moving about in auspiciousness.
There, having always acted for the benefit of sentient beings and being endowed with happiness,
he will fulfill all the perfections and attain the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
From that time forth, in all worlds, a constant and perpetual enthusiasm for honoring the Three Jewels proceeded, as if it were an established duty.
At that time, the Goddess herself promulgated this vow upon the earth;
thus it has been heard by me, as it is proclaimed by all the sages.
This was told to me by my teacher, and having heard it, I have likewise spoken it;
you too, O Great King, should thus practice that vow of the Goddess Śrī.
In that way, may you always have security everywhere and certainly forever;
indeed, may inexhaustible great prosperity arise for you, like that of Śrīda.
Then, having become a vessel for prosperity and having given to supplicants whatever they desired,
and having performed worship of the Three Jewels, may you attain the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Thinking thus, O Great King, and awakening the people as well,
establish them in the refuge of the Illustrious Goddess and always promote the observance of her vows.
Likewise, in order to bring about the welfare of sentient beings and to attain the jewel of perfect enlightenment,
the *dhāraṇī-vidyā* of the Illustrious Goddess should always be maintained with devotion.
By the power of this merit, may you both always and everywhere in existence possess auspicious energy and remain forever free from affliction.
By all the perfectly awakened ones of the past as well, the welfare of the world was accomplished through the Lord of Sages and the jewel-like dhāraṇīs and vidyās of the Śrī-devī.
Likewise, even now, all those currently living have performed meritorious deeds for sentient beings by means of the three goddesses and the jewels of the *dhāraṇī* mantras toward the Lord of Sages.
And likewise, all the future Lords of Sages shall everywhere bring about auspiciousness through the jewel-like dhāraṇīs and vidyās of the Śrīdevī.
May all the Sugatas, the Protectors, and the compassionate Bodhisattvas,
through the grace of the Glorious Goddess, practice the conduct of auspiciousness.
Having taught the noble True Dharma, they bring about the welfare of the world;
thus, by those desiring the jewel of perfect enlightenment in order to accomplish the welfare of the world,
one should practice for the benefit of the world while upholding the dhāraṇī of the Illustrious Goddess.
And those who, with faith, respect, and devotion, always recite, listen to, or cause others to recite this *dhāraṇī* of the illustrious Mahādevī;
Having written it down in a book or having placed it in their home with constant reverence,
those who honor it with faith and worship, holding their hands in *añjali*, pay homage to it.
Likewise, those who always wear this jewel of the *dhāraṇī-vidyā* of the Illustrious Goddess, having written it upon birch bark and bound it to their arm, neck, or head;
In the homes of all these people, and even in their domains,
may there always be auspiciousness everywhere, forever free from obstacles.
Famines, calamities, great portents, and afflictions shall never at any time prevail anywhere within their domain.
And various fevers and diseases that cause total destruction—
may they never at any time touch their bodies anywhere.
Even indolence would be wholesome, and even poison would become nectar;
for in their bodies, even that which is harmful acts as a benefit in every respect.
The gods beginning with Brahmā and Śakra, as well as the wicked fires,
the servants of Yama, the rākṣasas, and even the garuḍas—
And the nāgas and the winds, as well as the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras;
the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and kaṭapūtanas.
Likewise, even other wicked beings who cause fear to all sentient beings will all be unable to create obstacles within their domain.
All these gods and others, dwelling in the worlds of the three realms,
shall also protect them when propitiated by the power of the goddess.
All their undertakings shall be fully accomplished without obstacle;
indeed, no hindrance whatsoever shall arise anywhere within their bodies.
For those who go everywhere, may there always be gain, success, and auspiciousness; may there never be any obstacle whatsoever.
By the power of the compassionate glance of the Śrīdevī, may there be success in accomplishing all aims in every respect, and never any obstacle.
All the world-protectors as well as the gods and others of great supernatural power, ascetics, yogins, perfected ones, seers, and those practicing celibacy— [all these were present].
The planets, the hosts of stars, all the yoginīs and the bhairavas, the ḍākinīs, the eight mātṛkās, and even the hosts of mahākālas;
In this way, there are also other lords of heroes, crushers of all that is evil,
who assume terrifying forms and are the agents of creation, maintenance, and destruction.
Having beheld all those servants of the Goddess Śrī with joy, may they,
moved by compassion and acting as her followers, protect them at all times.
All the monks, who are Buddhas, Arhats, and practitioners of the holy life,
as well as the goddess Śrī, having seen [the future], will protect her with serene minds.
And all the Pratyekabuddhas, having beheld those attendants of the goddess Śrī from afar with their keen vision, would protect them with gracious minds.
And all those Bodhisattvas, filled with compassion, having granted whatever boons were desired to those lay disciples of the Goddess Śrī, shall protect them.
All the Sugatas and Buddhas, having always beheld with their clear vision those who abide in the refuge of the Goddess Śrī, shall be filled with compassion for them.
In this way, all the lords of the world— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others— along with the goddess Śrī, the Dhāraṇīs, and the Vidyādharas, shall protect [her] with devotion.
"Thus it has indeed been declared by all the lords of sages endowed with the great superknowledges;
this was instructed to me by my teacher, and having heard it, I speak it thus."
O King, having heard this, you too should likewise observe that vow of the goddess Śrī;
then, by the power of the merit of the vow of the great goddess Śrī, [your desires shall be fulfilled].
Great prosperity shall increase, remaining inexhaustible and ever-stable at all times.
Then, having taken that wealth and given it to all supplicants according to their desires, wander about performing virtuous deeds; enjoy happiness while protecting your subjects.
By the ripening of this merit, you shall never go to an evil rebirth;
always proceeding toward a happy rebirth, may you dwell in happiness while practicing the Dharma.
Thinking thus, O Great King, you have gone for refuge to the glorious Goddess;
having heard the True Dharma yourself, O Lord, cause the people to hear it as well.
For all beings in saṃsāra, Dharma alone is a true friend and companion;
therefore, one should diligently acquire Dharma itself in this world.
And among all dharmas, the supreme and most excellent is the Dharma of the Sugata.
Since goodness is ever-present throughout all worlds in saṃsāra,
therefore those who always desire what is auspicious everywhere in saṃsāra should listen to the Dharma of the Sugata with faith and reverence, treating it with due honor.
Those who here listen to the Dharma of the Sugata with faith and reverence do not go to an evil rebirth; they always proceed to a happy state.
And those who cause others to hear the Dharma of the Sugata do not go to an evil destiny; indeed, they go only to a happy destiny.
And whoever explains and analyzes the Dharma of the Sugata, they too do not go to an evil rebirth; they shall proceed to Sukhāvatī.

Even for one who might exist in the Kali age, crowded with the afflictions of the five corruptions, the Dharma of the Sugata is difficult to find; both the speaker and the listener are difficult to find.
Then, seeing those people afflicted by suffering, struck by compassion and pity,
he would renounce attachment to his own body and life and teach the Dharma.
For he alone, the son of the Victor, being possessed of great supernormal knowledge, steadfast, wise, and discerning,
shall be the conqueror of all afflictions and the vanquisher of Māra.
And furthermore, at that time, even amidst a mass of afflictions so thickly crowded together,
he who would joyfully listen to the True Dharma, having sacrificed his own body and life— Rm_38.962{99}—
He too is wise, a great hero, the crusher of all afflictions;
having attained the path to perfect enlightenment, he should indeed be known as one dear to the Victors.

Furthermore, he who, even in the Kali age when the true Dharma has thus disappeared, being free from attachment and possessing a body that finds no pleasure, shall proclaim the true Dharma to others; Rm_38.964{1} //
He too shall be a son of the Sugata, a great sage, confident,
desiring the welfare of all and every being, a wise and accomplished Bodhisattva.
And whoever, having heard from another the true Dharma proclaimed by the Sugata,
rejoices with a serene mind, he too shall become a son of the Sugata.
They would surely obtain all that merit which comes from bathing at all sacred fords;
good people should certainly act in this way everywhere—of this there is no doubt.
Whatever great merit belongs to one who protects all living beings and creatures, may they all obtain that entire merit.
Whatever monks there may be who are arhats, whoever should honor them all—
the fruit of that merit, they would indeed obtain it all.
If one were to joyfully honor all those up to and including the Pratyekabuddhas,
may they obtain from that act whatever fruit of merit they desire.
Whoever should always honor as many Sugatas as there may be,
they would obtain even more merit than that which those [Sugatas] themselves possess.
If one were to give with faith as many cows as there are on the surface of the earth,
the merit he would obtain would be even greater than that which they [the recipients] might acquire.
And for one who should give a heap of gold and jewels as large as Mount Meru, their merit would be incalculable; those [merits from the previous gifts] do not even approach a fraction of it.
He who, with faith, should offer the entire earth together with its oceans and mountains—his merit is exceedingly great; and you, O Samyāyu, are even greater than he.
If one should also give medicinal herbs, materials, objects of enjoyment, and so forth with faith,
their merit shall be incalculable, and those [who receive them] shall obtain even more than that.
Whatever great merit those might obtain who, for thousands of eons, subsisted only on grass and water— more than that would he receive.
Whoever should perform thousands of millions of sacrifices with faith and joy, they would obtain great merit; those [who hear this] would obtain even more than that.
Likewise, may they all obtain even more merit than whatever merits there are arising from the practice of giving and vows.
Thus has this truth been declared by all the lords of sages;
it was taught to me by my teacher, heard by me, and shall now be spoken.
Having fully understood this truth, if you desire perfect enlightenment,
always listen to the sublime Dharma and pay homage to the Three Jewels.
And having diligently awakened the subjects as well, O Great King, establish them on the path to enlightenment and protect them with a concentrated mind.
Then, may auspiciousness be certain for you always and everywhere;
having attained awakening in due course, may you reach the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Having heard this which was taught by that Arhat, King Aśoka,
together with his retinue, approved, saying "So be it," and rejoiced.
Then that Arhat Upagupta took up residence in the monastery;
and the great king Aśoka likewise always practiced the Dharma accordingly.
Having thus explained this, Jayaśrī, the son of the Jina,
addressed all the assemblies of disciples and commanded them as follows:
Whoever hears this great jewel-garland of well-spoken words as it is being proclaimed,
or whoever joyfully causes others to hear it;
Those who, having heard it, rejoice; those who, having seen it, bow with joy;
and those who, always honoring it with faith, worship and devote themselves to it.
May there always be auspiciousness for all of these therein;
and may the glory of victory increase everywhere and at all times.
May all calamities, portents, and hosts of obstacles,
as well as the wicked throngs of Māra, always go to their destruction.
May prosperity always remain firmly established in their homes; and may their enjoyments of virtue, wealth, and pleasure be fully accomplished and ever-increasing.
May they be free from disease, long-lived, and endowed with happiness; may they cease from evil deeds and always engage in what is wholesome;
and having honored the Three Jewels, may they live as celibate practitioners.
Having acted for the benefit of all sentient beings and always enjoyed auspicious happiness,
may they gradually fulfill the perfections and proceed to the state of the Sugata.
By the power of this merit, may there always be constant auspiciousness, abundance, and freedom from calamity everywhere and at all times.
May all sentient beings, exerting themselves, accomplish the true Dharma;
through their zeal in honoring the Three Jewels, may they all go to a happy rebirth.
May the clouds rain in due season, may the earth be rich with crops,
and may the cows yield abundant milk and be filled with affection for their calves.
May trees always be endowed with flowers and excellent fruits;
may kings be most righteous, and may ministers abide in statesmanship.
May all the armies and warriors conquer the wicked;
may all calamities be pacified, and may the subjects be endowed with happiness.
Free from disease, endowed with happiness, and possessed of glory and prosperity—
may Brahmā and the other world-protectors, who possess great supernatural power and guard the ten directions,
always protect all living beings after having conquered obstacles and performed auspicious deeds.
May all beings in the worlds of the three realms practice mutual loving-kindness toward one another,
and having rendered service to the Three Jewels, may they practice the conduct of awakening.
May all behold auspicious things; may no one commit evil.
Upholding the Buddhist teaching everywhere, may they go to the abode of the Victors.
Thus, for the purpose of fully elucidating the conduct of awakening, that one who resembled a king of sages, Jayaśrī,
instructed all his disciples with this garland of glorious avadānas.
Having heard it, they all— along with the world— became noble-minded and rejoiced.
Relying upon the true Dharma, they always honored the Triple Gem with devotion and lived free from negligence.
Wherever this king of kings among sūtras may be set forth even in the Kali age— whether one speaks it, hears it, causes others to hear it, or practices it—

may all the Perfectly Awakened Ones always look upon all these people with eyes of compassion and grant them well-being until the end of existence. May all the goddesses who are the Perfections, constantly bestowing auspiciousness there, fulfill the equipment for awakening for the benefit of the world.
By means of this nectar-essence of the True Dharma, born from the radiant mouth of the Omniscient One,
may there be constant pacification of suffering for all beings who are afflicted by the fire of the mental defilements.

Thus ends the narrative of the Vasudhārā vow within the *Subhāṣitaratnāvadānatattva*. May there be prosperity! In the year 1028, on the second lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, under the constellation Pūrvaphalgunī, in the Suddha yoga, on Wednesday; when the sun was in the sign of Aquarius and the moon was in the sign of Leo—on this very day.

This book is complete. Written by the Vajrācārya Śrī Dharmarāja, who resides at the Cakramahāvihāra consecrated by Mānadeva; by this merit, may there be the attainment of Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa.
May this [act] not cause greed for other books or for fine baths.
